The four talks take up composition, mass, water-colors, and charcoal in turn, with examples from London and the Thames among other places. Smith says a white umbrella and a stool with three legs were the sum of his studio appointments. Aspiring sketchers get practical advice from a working painter, plainly told.
2760-celebrated-crimes-complete:
Alexandre Dumas, pere, gathers his whole Celebrated Crimes in this complete edition in eight volumes, dated 1910. The contents run from the Borgias and the Cenci through the massacres of the south to the marquise de Brinvilliers and beyond.

Murderers, queens, poisoners, and impostors parade through Renaissance Italy, Reformation France, and revolutionary Europe. Dumas turns trial records and chronicles into vivid narrative, with romantic fire throughout. The set serves as a library of true crime, told by one of fiction's great storytellers. Eight volumes of murder, treason, and poison fill the set.
27614-notes-and-queries-number-219-janua:
Notes and Queries, a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, published volume nine, number 219, on Saturday, 7 January 1854, at fourpence, or fivepence stamped. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

The number opens its ninth volume with notes on a Strawberry-Hill gem, the Ancren Riwle, and an order for the suppression of vagrancy of 1650 and 1651. Letters of eminent literary men and the burial-place of Archbishop Leighton follow. Queries ask after the domestic letters of Edmund Burke, with minor queries on Farrant's anthem, tailless cats, saltcellars, and General Braddock.
277-trinity-site:
The United States Department of Energy's National Atomic Museum tells the Trinity story in brief. Trinity Site covers the first atomic test, Jumbo, the Schmidt-McDonald ranch house, notes, and bibliography. The test took place on July 16, 1945, in the final month of World War II.

Conducted by the secret Manhattan Engineer District on the Alamogordo range, Trinity lay about 230 miles south of Los Alamos. The range, once grazing land, is now White Sands Missile Range. The booklet explains the test, the site, and the museum. It serves as a compact official history.
27712-sir-harry-hotspur-of-humblethwaite:
Anthony Trollope, author of Framley Parsonage, published this novel with Hurst and Blackett of London in 1871. Its hero is Sir Harry Hotspur of Humblethwaite, a mighty person in Cumberland, with twenty thousand a year derived from land.

Chapters introduce the heroine, Lord Alfred's courtship, vacillation, and George Hotspur, with a ball in Bruton Street and Lady Altringham. Later come the hunt becoming hot, the heroine's refusal to desert him, cousin George hard pressed, and Sir Harry's return. Emily Hotspur's sermon, George Hotspur yielding, and a vow never to be married lead to the end. Trollope writes a Cumberland tale of family, fortune, and courtship.
27777-lafayette:
Martha Foote Crow wrote this 1916 life of Lafayette for young readers in the True Stories of Great Americans series, published by Macmillan. It follows the French nobleman from boyhood through his service in the American Revolution and beyond.

Chapters cover Brandywine, Monmouth, Virginia, the two redoubts, and the surrender at Yorktown, then his imprisonment in Europe, an attempted rescue, and a triumphal tour of America. Crow presents Lafayette as a youthful idealist whose sword and name America repaid with a nation's heart. Illustrations include the council at Hopewell, the surrender of Cornwallis, and a carriage in which Lafayette rode.
279-photos-and-maps-of-trinity-atomic-te:
This file lists the photographs and maps of the Trinity atomic test site, courtesy of the White Sands Missile Range public affairs office. Each entry names its image: the base camp, the blast at ten seconds, and Oppenheimer and Groves in the crater. The gadget's lift into the hundred-foot tower appears twice.

Other images show Jumbo's unloading, the McDonald-Schmidt ranch house where the plutonium core was assembled, and a Manhattan Project patch. Road maps and a visitor site map complete the set, with the White Sands emblem. The list serves as a caption index to a visual record of July 1945.
28006-the-perpetual-curate:
Mrs. Oliphant wrote The Perpetual Curate, part of her Chronicles of Carlingford, opening with the claim that Carlingford is essentially a quiet place, with no trade properly so called. Its pleasant parties and superior people gather in Grange Lane for no reason but that they like it.

The center of life in Carlingford is the clergy, administrators of the commonwealth with defined, compulsory duties, and the minister of Salem Chapel is everything in his little world. Oliphant's novel of church, society, and provincial character is a classic of Victorian domestic fiction.
28289-the-essays-of-george-eliot-complet:
The Essays of George Eliot, complete, collected by Nathan Sheppard, New York, 1883, gathers Eliot's periodical essays, long anonymous in the Westminster Review. Sheppard, editor of Character Readings from George Eliot, opens with an introduction on her analysis of motives. He then prints ten essays: on Carlyle, woman in France, evangelical teaching, German wit, and German life.

Later essays treat silly novels by lady novelists, worldliness, rationalism, ornament, and Felix Holt's address to workingmen. Funk and Wagnalls published the volume. The collection shows Eliot the critic, sharp, learned, and moral, behind the novelist. It suits readers of Victorian letters.
28399-four-plays-of-gil-vicente:
Aubrey F. G. Bell edited Four Plays of Gil Vicente, Cambridge, 1920, from the first edition of 1562, with translation and notes. Vicente, Portugal's great early dramatist, wrote devotional pieces, comedies, tragicomedies, and farces, first printed at Lisbon by Ioam Alvarez, with leave of the Inquisition. Bell's volume gives four plays in Portuguese and English.

The plays are Auto da Alma, the Soul's Journey, Exhortacao da Guerra, an exhortation to war, Farsa dos Almocreves, the carriers, and a pastoral tragicomedy of the Serra da Estrella. Notes and a list of proverbs close the book. It suits students of Portuguese drama and early European theatre.
28488-tartuffe-or-the-hypocrite:
Moliere's Tartuffe, or The Hypocrite, in Jeffrey D. Hoeper's verse translation, opens with Madame Pernelle storming out of her son's house. She scolds Elmire, Mariane, Dorine, Damis, and Cleante in turn, and praises only Tartuffe, the holy man she believes guides the family to heaven.

The household disagrees: Dorine calls Tartuffe a false Capuchin who forbids every pleasure, and Damis resents his tyrannical power over the home. Moliere's comedy turns on that clash between professed piety and real hypocrisy, and on a family trying to unmask a fraud before he ruins them. The play remains a classic of French comic theatre.
28567-godfrey-marten-undergraduate:
Charles Turley's Godfrey Marten, Undergraduate, published in London in 1904, continues the schoolboy hero of his earlier book into university life. The night before Godfrey leaves for Oxford, his father gives him two hundred pounds a year, more than he can afford, and warns him to avoid debt and behave like a gentleman.

Godfrey arrives at Oxford as an exhibitioner of St. Cuthbert's, having lost his luggage, while his friend Fred Foster holds a scholarship at Oriel. Chapters follow freshers' matches, wine, a cricket match at Burtlington, essays, Nina's visit, the warden, the hedonists, and a tutorship, through to their last year. Turley writes a warm, humorous Oxford novel.
28597-a-man-to-his-mate:
J. Allan Dunn's A Man to His Mate, published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company of Indianapolis in 1920, opens on the San Francisco waterfront. Rainey meets a giant tapping his way along the Embarcadero, a blind man in dark glasses who asks the way to the sealing schooner Karluk. Rainey senses something watchful behind the glasses, even as he offers help and direction.

Later chapters follow target practice, a bowhead hunt, a divided company, and a show-down at sea. Peggy Simms, Honest Simms, Tamada, and Lund enter the action as rivalries simmer and break. Readers get a sea adventure of loyalty, suspicion, and mates tested under pressure.
28675-red-men-and-white:
Owen Wister's Red Men and White, published by Harper and Brothers in 1895 with illustrations by Frederic Remington, gathers Western stories. Little Big Horn Medicine opens with Crow chiefs in council, soldiers at Fort Custer, and settlers discussing a new stir in the tribe. Two cavalry lieutenants, Stirling and Haines, ride out debating whether the Crows will go on the war-path.

Stirling, fifteen years fighting Indians, trusts Crow reason, while young Haines holds the Eastern view. Cheschapah the agitator gallops past in feathers, while his mild father Pounded Meat greets them quietly. Specimen Jones, a serenade at Siskiyou, the general's bluff, and Salvation Gap follow. Readers get the West in Wister's early voice.
29-the-1990-united-states-census-incompl:
Tables from the 1990 Census of Population and Housing fill this partial file. State entries list total population by sex and age, with median age and related counts. The Alabama tables open the sequence shown here.

Readers should note the file's own label: it is incomplete, not the full census release. Even in part, it shows how the Census Bureau broke down each state's people. Researchers use such tables to track age structure and growth state by state. Even partial, the tables help local historians compare towns and counties in that census year.
29033-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote this third volume of Critical Miscellanies, with essay ten on Auguste Comte, published by Macmillan in 1904. The essay's contents run from Comte's introduction and the influence of Saint Simon through marriage, serious illness, and official work to the completion of his Positive Philosophy. Later sections treat J. S. Mill, the question of subsidy, money, and literary method, with Madame de Vaux and the Positive Polity.

Morley calls Comte the most eminent of the thinkers whom France's overthrown institutions turned toward social speculation, vastly superior to De Maistre, Saint Simon, and Fourier alike. The essay then weighs his law of the three states, his classification of sciences, and his religion of humanity. Readers get a masterly Victorian estimate of positivism, clear, critical, and fair.
29402-the-french-immortals-quotes-and-im:
David Widger compiled this companion volume, Quotes and Images: The French Immortals, gathering quotations and images from a shelf of French novels rather than reprinting the novels themselves. The contents list reads like a survey of nineteenth-century French fiction, from Rene Bazin's The Ink Stain and Therese Bentzon's Jacqueline to Charles de Bernard's Gerfaut and Paul Bourget's Cosmopolis.

Other titles include Jules Caretie's Prince Zilah, Francois Coppee's A Romance of Youth, Alphonse Daudet's Fromont and Risler, and Alfred de Vigny's Cinq Mars. Anatole France's The Red Lily, Pierre Loti's Chrysantheme, and Alfred de Musset's The Child of a Century also appear. Readers get a browsable treasury of French fiction in quotation, useful for sampling authors before choosing a full novel.
29468-the-story-of-don-quixote:
Arvid Paulson and Clayton Edwards retold the story of Don Quixote for young readers, with color pictures by Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis. The Hampton Publishing Company of New York printed it, with copyright in 1922 by Frederick A. Stokes Company. Its chapters follow the knight through the terrible and undreamt-of adventure of the windmills, with other events fit to be told in full.

A later picture shows Quixote sure that a boat had arrived by magic to carry him to some great knight. The retelling keeps Cervantes' humor and pathos in plain, child-friendly prose. Young readers meeting the knight for the first time will find a warm, well-illustrated doorway into a great classic.
29616-two-arrows-a-story-of-red-and-whit:
W. O. Stoddard's Two Arrows, a story of red and white, stands in Harper's Young People's Series beside Toby Tyler, Buffalo Bill, and the Flamingo Feather. Its opening chapter is called The Hungry Camp. Its theme runs through the book: mountain lands everywhere have always been wonderlands, full of things nobody has found, even in the oldest and best known ranges.

Stoddard writes a boys' tale of Indians and whites meeting in mountain country, with adventure, hardship, and friendship at its heart. The book belongs to an era of frontier fiction for young readers. Modern readers will find a period adventure, vivid in place, dated in outlook, and useful for studying its age.
29736-continental-monthly-vol-iii-no-iv-:
Volume three, number four of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy and dated April 1863, opens with The Wonders of Words. Its author notes that every nation keeps a tale of a golden age, when all was youthful, fresh, and lovely, before the gaunt shadow of sorrow that ever stalks beside us. An age of Saturnian rule, when gods conversed with men, frames the essay.

The issue mixes literary reflection with Civil War-era national policy, in the magazine's earnest, learned voice. Vanitas vanitatum, the essay sighs, is not mere blasé complaint but universal experience. Readers of Civil War magazines will find a thoughtful number from a journal that tried to join letters to the nation's crisis.
29748-the-duke-of-chimney-butte:
G. W. Ogden, author of The Land of Last Chance, wrote The Duke of Chimney Butte, printed in 1920 by Grosset and Dunlap with a frontispiece by P. V. E. Ivory. Its land gets rain seldom in summer, while winter wind sweeps snow into rocky canyons and levels butte tops with drift. Chapters open with the all-in-one, Whetstone the outlaw, an empty saddle, and feet upon the road.

Allurements of Glendora, the homeliest man, and the house on the mesa follow, with a voice saying there is no use running away from me. Ogden writes western romance with dry humor and range color. Readers of classic westerns will find a sturdy tale of a duke in a land of buttes.
2988-mark-twain-a-biography-complete:
Albert Bigelow Paine's complete Mark Twain: A Biography gathers the whole personal and literary life of Samuel Langhorne Clemens in one text. Paine dedicates the work to Clara Clemens Gabrilowitsch, who upheld his purpose to write history rather than eulogy, and thanks Howells, Twichell, and Goodman for years of help. The biography runs from Clemens's Missouri childhood through his world fame.

Later chapters follow Twain onto the amateur stage, playing Peter Spuyk in The Loan of a Lover at Hartford on April 26, 1876, with Helen Smith as Gertrude. Paine notes genuine dramatic talent in the Hartford company. The complete text lets readers follow one life without hunting across volumes, from river pilot to beloved author.
30073-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume 8, slice 3, of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica carries entries from Destructor to Diameter in alphabetical order. Its long destructor article weighs refuse-burning plants in detail, from chimney draught and forced draught to boiler placement, flue gases, and cost per ton. A Bristol case from 1892 prices a sixteen-cell Fryer destructor at 11,418 pounds, with foundations and chimney shaft broken out separately.

As one slice of a vast dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information, the file shows the Britannica method at work: signed, technical, and packed with figures, rules, and examples. Readers will find the period's engineering mind on full display, where a furnace is judged first by clean burning, and steam raising counts only as a second gain.
30115-tante:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick opens Tante in London, on the night Madame Okraska sings at the old St. James's Hall. Horse buses still ply an unwidened Piccadilly, the private motor remains a curiosity, and the bell of the muffin man passes through foggy streets and squares. Okraska, breaking a St. Petersburg to New York journey, gives her only London concert that winter, while eager listeners wait on cold stone stairs.

The Century Company published the New York volume in December 1911, under a 1911 copyright, and Sedgwick sets her social world with exact period detail. Next door, the Moore and Burgess Minstrels sound blatant and vulgar by distance, a little melancholy in the mirth. Readers who like novels of manners will find a London already passing, caught at the hour of one great concert.
30178-our-moslem-sisters-a-cry-of-need-f:
Annie Van Sommer and Samuel M. Zwemer edit a missionary volume that speaks for women in Moslem lands, as reported by women missionaries at the Cairo Conference. Their appeal, printed at the front, asks women's missionary boards across Britain, America, Canada, Europe, and Australasia to hear reports from all parts of the Moslem world. A mother and daughter from Tunis face the title page, grounding the plea in named places and lives.

Fleming H. Revell published the volume in 1907, and its chapters interpret what field workers claimed to hear and see, in lands the editors call lands of darkness. Modern readers should take the book as a period missionary source, not as a neutral survey, since its voice is that of its own movement. As history, it records how early twentieth-century missions framed their work among women.
30222-the-strand-magazine-vol-05-issue-2:
The Strand Magazine for March 1893, volume 5, issue 27, leads with A Game of Chess, translated from the French. King Philip II plays at chess in the Escurial Palace against Ruy Lopez, a humble priest of great skill and the king's particular favourite. Lopez kneels on a brocaded cushion while courtiers stand in constrained, painful attitudes, and orange groves perfume a magnificent morning outside.

Violet curtains barely soften the burning light, and the king's brow stays black as night, his eyes turning impatiently toward the door. Nobles stand in silence, trading meaning glances, as some great event weighs on the assembly. An illustration catches Lopez crying that the duke shall finish his game, promising a tale where chess, pride, and power meet at one board.
30836-seven-keys-to-baldpate:
Earl Derr Biggers wrote this 1913 mystery novel, published by Bobbs-Merrill, about a lonely inn and the people who keep arriving there. It opens in a railway waiting room at Upper Asquewan Falls, New York, where a young woman cries bitterly over a scrap of cambric. Billy Magee, watching her, wonders if she is beautiful, and his talk with her leads toward Baldpate Inn, shut up for the winter on its mountain.

Twenty-two chapters follow a lovelorn haberdasher, blondes and suffragettes, a professional hermit, a mayor, ghosts of the summer crowd, and melodrama in the snow. Keys, falsehoods, and a red card pile up as Magee tries to sort truth from play-acting. Biggers keeps the tone light and theatrical, and the puzzle turns on who holds a key, and why each visitor came at all.
31005-coquette:
Frank Swinnerton's 1921 novel is built in three books, Toby, Gaga, and Consequences. It opens on a winter Saturday night in a Hornsey Road flat, where street noise, closed shops, and a singer upstairs set the scene of ordinary London life. Sally, watching the road below from her window, belongs to the household at the center of the story.

The novel follows its people through domestic rooms, work, and close family ties rather than through grand events, letting small choices and social pressures shape what happens next. Readers get a plain, closely watched portrait of London home life in the early 1920s, told with attention to sound, light, and the small frictions of living close together.
3124-the-people-for-whom-shakespeare-wro:
Warner rebuilds the London audience that first watched Shakespeare, starting on the morning Elizabeth died, 24 March 1603. Sir Robert Cary rides unsent to tell James of Scotland, and the new king scatters knighthoods as he travels south, making twenty-eight at Theobald's alone. The anecdote sets the tone: a restless, rank-hungry, talkative England crowding into playhouses.

The essay then asks what such people brought to the plays: their habits, their news, their taste for bold speech and quick action. By sketching the crowd before the stage, Warner helps a modern reader hear Shakespeare's lines as his own hearers heard them, amid the noise and appetite of a capital changing monarchs.
31311-vocations-explained-matrimony-virg:
Vocations Explained, by a Vincentian Father and published by Benzinger Brothers in 1897, abridges Questions on Vocations. That catechism was approved by Cardinals Gibbons and Satolli, five archbishops, and twenty-two bishops, with the imprimatur of Archbishop Michael Augustine of New York.

In question-and-answer form it defines a vocation as a call from God to some state of life. The states are matrimony, virginity, the religious state, and the priesthood. Eighteen sections cover what a vocation is and why one must follow it, matrimony and mixed marriages, virginity, and the three counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience. They go on to marks and doubts of a religious vocation, parents' duties, vocations to the priesthood, and means of knowing one's vocation through prayer, humility, retreat, and counsel. The book is a compact guide to choosing a calling at the end of the century.
32206-the-utah-batteries-a-history-a-com:
Charles R. Mabey's The Utah Batteries: A History was published in Salt Lake City in 1900. It gives a complete account of the muster-in, sea voyage, battles, skirmishes, and barrack life of the Utah Batteries, with biographies of officers and muster-out rolls. Mabey, late sergeant of Light Battery A, Utah Volunteer Artillery, dedicates the book to the Utah batterymen who bravely fought for their country's flag on a foreign soil.

Mabey conceived the history after the Utah Battalion sailed from San Francisco to the Philippines. He kept a diary during the entire campaign and collected what other material could be used. Immediately upon arrival in Salt Lake City, he set the work in hand. Readers get a Spanish-American War unit history, written by a sergeant who served, from muster to muster-out, with rolls and biographies for the record.
32404-second-thoughts-are-best-or-a-furt:
Andrew Moreton's pamphlet, printed in London in 1729 for sixpence and reprinted at Oxford in 1841, improves a late scheme to prevent street robberies. Dedicated to King George II, it promises streets strongly guarded and gloriously lit. Any part of London, it claims, will be just as safe and pleasant at midnight as in daylight, with burglary made totally impracticable. Moreton also offers thoughts for suppressing robberies on all public roads of England.

The pamphlet, humbly offered for his country's good and submitted to Parliament, follows Moreton's earlier plan for a flourishing London. Its mix of lighting, watchmen, and road safety shows early Georgian faith in practical policing. Readers interested in crime, cities, and reform will find a short, bold tract that treats midnight safety as a matter of lamps and guards.
3253-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
This complete constitutional edition gathers Abraham Lincoln's papers and writings in full. Arthur Brooks Lapsley edited the set, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt. An essay on Lincoln by Carl Schurz and an address on Lincoln by Joseph Choate join the edition. The volumes run from early speeches to the presidency's final papers.

Volume one opens just after Lincoln's re-election, with an offhand speech to serenaders on the evening of 10 November 1864. It has long been a grave question, he begins, in his plain, careful way. Lincoln whole, in order, from early speeches to final papers: that is the set's plain promise, and it keeps it.
3259-countess-kate:
Charlotte M Yonge tells the story of Countess Kate in this 1902 Macmillan volume, joined with The Stokesley Secret. A frontispiece shows a man comforting a little girl on the stairs while a boy watches. That scene fixes the book's temper: a child in need of kindness, watched over by older eyes. Kate herself is the young countess of the title.

Yonge, a favorite Victorian writer for girls, builds her tale on rank, duty, and affection. A child lifted by a title must learn what the title obliges her to be. Rank, duty, and affection test a child lifted by a title, and kindness does the teaching.
32594-stalemate:
Basil Wells's Stalemate, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in November 1954, stages a duel between the last two fighters on a mile-wide island high above Earth. Gram Treb and Harl Neilson trade bullets, grenades, and taunts, each counting the other's cartridges, under United Nations supervision that has reduced a war to single combat.

Treb, twenty-nine, has already survived two such duels and buried comrades from three battles. The story weighs the rules of a duel between gentlemen against the rules of war between nations, asking whether men in war can still act as gentlemen at all.
32837-check-and-checkmate:
Walter Miller Jr. tells of John Smith XVI, new President of the Western Federation of Autonomous States, in this story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of January 1953, illustrated by Tom Beecham. Elected by more than six hundred million votes to one hundred and thirty, the president has no real name of his own and wears a golden mask of tragedy.

Two weeks after his inauguration he seeks his hardest campaign promise: a conference with Ivan Ivanovitch the Ninth of the East. Forty years of Big Silence divide them. A Hell Wall and interference stations have barred even radio contact between the halves of the globe. The interview is arranged, but victory here hinges not on the mightiest sword, but on lowly subterfuge.
32947-on-snake-poison-its-action-and-its:
A. Mueller, a Sydney physician, wrote this 1893 treatise to explain his treatment for snakebite by hypodermic injection of strychnine. The method, he notes in his preface, had already spread through the Australian colonies and was even used by lay people in urgent cases. Mueller sets out to show, in terms a moderately educated reader could follow, how snake venom harms the body and how his antidote was meant to counter it.

The book therefore mixes case experience with plain physiology, arguing that a poisoned patient could be steadied if the remedy reached the system in time. Its claims belong to nineteenth-century medicine and should not be read as present-day advice. As history, it captures a colonial doctor's confidence, his rivals and supporters, and a time when a single bold remedy could win wide use.
32986-thomas-stanley-his-original-lyrics:
Thomas Stanley's original lyrics gather the poems of a seventeenth-century poet praised by James Shirley for numbers that carry weight yet stay clear and terse. They are complete in their collated readings of 1647, 1651, and 1657, edited by L. I. Guiney and published in Hull in 1907. The edition gives an introduction, textual notes, a list of editions, an appendix of translations, and a portrait of Stanley, who lived from 1625 to 1678.

Its contents sort the lyrics by the editions that first printed them. The run goes from The Dream and Despair in 1647 to The Breath, The Night, and The Kiss in all original editions. Readers can thus trace how a poem changed across printings. Guiney's collation makes the book a scholarly tool as well as a pleasure to read. For lovers of Cavalier poetry, it remains the fullest guide to Stanley's short, elegant verse.
3306-at-suvla-bay-being-the-notes-and-sk:
John Hargrave, White Fox of The Scout, served with the 32nd Field Ambulance, X Division, in the Mediterranean Expeditionary Force. His notes and sketches of the Dardanelles campaign, written at Suvla Bay during the Great War, make this book. A dedication verse sets the contrast: the author and Minobi once played at Ali Baba on a green linoleum floor, and now camp near Lala Baba by the blue Aegean shore.

Hargrave sailed, as his verse says, in the good ship Argo to a war that was no game. The sketches that follow mix humor and horror at the front: wounded men, officers, and the daily grind of a failed landing. The book preserves a young ambulance man's Gallipoli, told while the campaign was still fresh and its outcome still in doubt.
33094-the-cutting-of-an-agate:
William Butler Yeats's Cutting of an Agate, published by Macmillan in November 1912, gathers essays on Irish literature, theater, and the life of the mind. Its first part offers thoughts on Lady Gregory's translations, with essays on Cuchulain and his cycle and on Fion and his cycle. The essays trace how old Irish heroes live again in modern telling. The second part, Discoveries, ranges more freely.

Later essays treat prophet, priest, and king, personality and intellectual essences, the musician and the orator, a guitar player, the looking-glass, and the tree of life. They then turn to old wives' tales, modern manners, and the drama of contemporary life. Yeats writes as poet and theater-maker, arguing that art must root itself in folk memory and in living speech. The book remains a key statement of the Irish revival's ideals.
33111-the-origin-of-the-family-private-p:
Frederick Engels's Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State argues that human society was not made once for all by divine will, but developed through changing institutions. It was translated by Ernest Untermann and published in Chicago in 1908. Untermann's preface attacks the pulpit, platform, and press suggestion that submission to superiors is imposed by God. It presents scientific investigation as showing group life taking different shapes, as organic life takes different forms.

Engels traces prehistoric stages, the family, the Iroquois gens, the Grecian gens, the origin of the Attic state, and gens and state in Rome. He goes on to the gens among Celts and Germans, to the rise of the state among Germans. His argument links family forms, property, and state power in one historical chain. The book remains a central text of Marxist anthropology, still read for its bold attempt to explain society's deepest institutions.
33305-lost-man-s-lane-a-second-episode-i:
Anna Katharine Green's Lost Man's Lane, a second episode in the life of Amelia Butterworth, was copyrighted in 1898. Green, author of That Affair Next Door and The Leavenworth Case, returns to her sharp-eyed spinster detective, whose curiosity and sense lead her into a new mystery. The tale's setting, a lane where a man is lost, gives it both a puzzle and a place.

Amelia Butterworth herself, shrewd and proper, carries the story, noticing what police miss and pressing on where others stop. Green's plotting is careful, her New York detail rich. For readers of early detective fiction, Lost Man's Lane is a pleasing return to a beloved amateur sleuth, with a mystery that rewards a keen eye.
33441-the-man-of-taste:
James Bramston's Man of Taste, a poem from 1733, is reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by F. P. Lock. The reprint, number 171 from the Clark Memorial Library in Los Angeles, was published in 1975, with general editors from the library and the university. Bramston's satire takes aim at the tastes, follies, and fashions of his age.

The poem suits readers of Augustan satire, offering a short, sharp portrait of a man whose taste is his pride and his flaw. Its tone is witty and critical, in the manner of Pope's age. For students of eighteenth-century verse, it is a useful, well-edited reprint of a minor classic, with notes to guide modern readers.
3350-the-wandering-jew-complete:
This file holds Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew complete, in a single text. A note on the author opens it: Sue lived from 1804 to 1857, and his path to fiction was unusual. Physicians and seamen have often made novelists, the note says, but rarely has one man trained in both callings won his greatest fame as a writer. Sue began as a physician and surgeon, then spent six years in the French Navy.

The novel that followed made him famous across Europe. A wandering outcast, a scattered family, and a Jesuit scheme for a vast inheritance drive its thousand pages. Readers who want Sue whole, without hunting through eleven separate volumes, will find the entire serial here, from its Paris opening to its final reckoning.
3389-literature-and-life-complete:
William Dean Howells gathers his thoughts on books, travel, and daily life in this full collection of essays. The table of contents runs from his defense of literature as a part of life to pieces on a Dutch hotel and Spanish prisoners of war. It also covers a summer colony and the streets of New York. Short stories and sketches sit beside longer critical essays, so the book shifts tone often.

What holds the mix together is Howells's plain, observant voice. He writes about a circus in the suburbs, a dime museum, a beach at Rockaway, and a horse show with the same care he gives to famous authors. The collection works as an introduction to his nonfiction and as a portrait of American life at the turn of the century.
33891-bartholomew-sastrow-being-the-memo:
Bartholomew Sastrow, a German town official of the sixteenth century, left memoirs that Albert D. Vandam turned into English in 1905. The book opens with murder, family trouble, and strife at Stralsund, then follows Sastrow through school at Greifswald and Rostock, hard years as a notary, and office in his home town.

Sastrow writes with blunt candor about lawsuits, town factions, and the new preaching of Martin Luther, who once wrote to his father. His pages give a ground-level view of a German town in an age of faith and feud. For modern readers, the memoirs feel direct, rough, and close to daily life.
33972-florida-an-ideal-cattle-state:
W. F. Blackman, president of the Florida State Live Stock Association, compiled this booklet on Florida as a cattle state, copyrighted in 1918. Requests for sound facts on Florida's chances for beef cattle had come from all parts of the country in growing numbers. Blackman gathered men of long, successful work in live stock to answer them.

Several writers had grown and sold cattle on a large scale in Texas before studying Florida conditions at close range. Professor C. V. Piper, a leading authority on southern grasses and forage crops, lent an address on that subject. The booklet makes a plain, hopeful case for Florida cattle.
34234-a-lonely-flute:
A Lonely Flute is a book of poems by Odell Shepard, published by Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York in 1917. A Coleridge epigraph gives the title: a voice now like all instruments, now like a lonely flute. The collection holds some thirty-seven poems.

The contents mix nature lyrics, road songs, and meditations: Nightfall, Birds of Passage, The Watcher in the Sky, and The Grave of Thoreau. Others include Spenser's Faërie Queene, a ballad of love and death, and poems to orioles and a goldfinch. The Proem says the eternal visions beyond the last dim star escape every song. It hears magic melodies still slumbering in the flute, and whispers answering beside the eternal sea. Laus Mariae begins with a name like a deep melody hallowed by sundown.
34472-origin-and-early-history-of-the-fa:
Origin and Early History of the Fashion Plate is a study of costume illustration. Its first figure shows the dress of Sigmund von Herberstein for the Polish embassy of 1517. Over his doublet and breeches he wears a brocade gown lined with silk. The study begins, that is, before the fashion plate proper existed.

From such early embassy portraits the book traces how dress came to be pictured for its own sake. It follows the costume book and the engraved figure toward the plate that later filled fashion journals. The work is antiquarian in method, plate by plate and source by source. For students of dress it marks the starting line: the long road from a record of what one man wore to pictures made to sell a style to thousands.
34512-rosalind-at-red-gate:
Rosalind at Red Gate, by Meredith Nicholson, was printed by Grosset and Dunlap from a copyright of 1907, with art by Arthur I Keller. Two mottoes front it: one from As You Like It, one from the Morte D'Arthur on a ring that shifts each hue. The teller takes a wire from Paul Stoddard on the Glenarm pier, a scrap that starts all the fuss. He is at rest in his friend's house at Annandale, at work on a book of Russian rivers.

Heads ahead name Mr Reginald Gillespie, a search of Tippecanoe Creek, and a fight on a house-boat. The carnival of canoes gives the front plate. A lady of shadows, a touch of dishonor, and an odd affair at Red Gate fill the run. Tale fans get lake, gate, and gallantry in Nicholson's bright hand.
34649-the-right-to-ignore-the-state:
Herbert Spencer argues here that a citizen may rightfully ignore the state altogether. The Freedom Press of London reprinted the chapter as a penny pamphlet in 1913. It comes from the 1850 edition of Spencer's 'Social Statics,' the title page states plainly.

Spencer omitted the chapter from his revised edition of 1892, the editors warn fairly. That omission shows a change of view, they grant, but to repudiate is not to answer, they argue. The anarchist publishers hold the arguments unanswerable, and their penny sheet kept a famous dropped chapter in circulation for radicals.
34857-harvard-stories-sketches-of-the-un:
Waldron Kintzing Post dedicated these sketches of the undergraduate to the Class of '90, his own. Putnam published the book at New York in 1895. His preface is a letter to classmates scattered far apart. The stories, he says, are only yarns and pictures of us boys, founded almost all on actual occurrences of college life. Some happened under his own notice; others he had from men whose names he never knew. No reader, he warns, should recognize himself in any character.

The preface walks the Yard in memory: Holworthy gazing down the green, University Hall's white walls, Massachusetts and her partner, and Jones who rings the bell. The river and the elms are still there. Post allows himself the higher traditions of the old place only once; the rest is rollicking. Such volumes fixed the image of Harvard for a generation that never saw Cambridge.
3567-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-compl:
Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne tells his full story of Napoleon in this complete edition of his memoirs, edited by Colonel R W Phipps in 1891. The contents run from prefaces for the 1836 and 1885 editions through volume one, covering 1769 to 1800, and on through the Consulate, the empire, and the fall. Bourrienne served as Napoleon's private secretary and knew him from youth.

No other single source gives so long an inside view of Napoleon's daily life, orders, and conversations. Readers should remember that Bourrienne writes as a former friend with his own grievances, so his judgments need care. Still, as a record of how power looked from the next desk, the memoirs remain essential reading on Napoleon.
3580-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant, Napoleon's first valet, tells the whole story of the emperor's private life in this complete edition, translated by Walter Clark in 1895. The preface notes that the work first appeared in French in 1830 and had never before been rendered into English, with the original volumes nearly out of print. The translator added notes, and the publishers added illustrations.

Constant's aim, in his own phrase, was to paint Caesar in undress: to show Napoleon at home, at table, and on campaign, away from state portraits. Readers get the full arc, from the Consulate household to abdication and farewell. The complete volume suits readers who want the valet's view in one place, without hunting through twelve separate parts.
3600-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-compl:
This complete edition gathers all of Montaigne's Essays, from the prefatory life and letters through Books One, Two, and Three. The preface presents Montaigne as a great French writer who deserves to rank as a classic in all countries, not only in his own land. His essays, the preface says, made his intellectual and physical self public property, as he took the world into his confidence on every subject.

Readers get the full range in one volume: custom, fear, friendship, cannibals, books, vanity, and experience. Montaigne studies himself to study mankind, and his digressions became a model for the essay ever after. The complete edition suits readers ready to live with Montaigne at length, dipping in or reading straight through.
36197-our-calendar-the-julian-calendar-a:
Our Calendar is a handbook of calendar reckoning by the Reverend George Nichols Packer. Miller published it at Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in 1893. Its title promises the Julian calendar and its errors explained. It shows how the Gregorian calendar corrected those errors. Rules for finding the dominical letter are given in it. The day of the week of any event can be fixed by them. The span runs from the days of Julius Caesar to the year 4000. A new and easy method of fixing Easter is offered.

A Hebrew calendar section shows the correspondence of Bible dates. Those events are matched with our present Gregorian calendar. Valuable tables and charts illustrate the whole work. Packer dedicates it to a Pennsylvania supreme court justice. That friend suggested the little volume and helped publish it. The book is a practical almanac maker's reference.
36378-ancient-manners-also-known-as-aphr:
Ancient Manners is the complete English translation of Aphrodite, the novel by Pierre Louys, privately printed at Paris for subscribers only. This large-paper edition was limited to one thousand copies. Zier illustrated the volume. The author's preface opens with Wagner's remark that the ruins of the Greek world teach how modern life might be made supportable.

The story is set in Alexandria. It follows the courtesan Chrysis and the sculptor Demetrios, who dreams and desires through five books. Chapters take in the garden of the goddess, the dinner, the orgie at Bacchis's, and Cleopatra. The last book moves through the supreme night to dust and pity. The novel made Louys famous as a stylist of antique desire, and this edition prints the whole text without cuts for its subscribers.
3649-the-dwelling-place-of-light-complet:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, tells the full story of Janet Bumpus and her mill town in this complete edition. The novel opens with a glacier image for industrial life, as helpless people are torn from the parent rock, crushed, and left stranded in strange places. Edward Bumpus, Janet's father, is severed from the firm granite of stable things and cast into a shifting world.

The complete story follows Janet from childhood through work, love, and political awakening, as strikes and speeches shake Hampton. Churchill writes a large novel of labor, faith, and class in New England. The complete edition suits readers who want the whole arc in one volume, from family loss to a young woman's stand.
36568-god-and-the-state:
Michael Bakunin argues first principles in God and the State, printed in New York by the Mother Earth Publishing Association. The edition calls itself the first American edition. A preface by Carlo Cafiero and Elisee Reclus stands in front, with a portrait of Bakunin.

Bakunin asks who is right, the idealists or the materialists, and he answers for the materialists. Ideas grow out of the facts of life, he says, not the other way round. The whole past of mankind, in thought, morals, and public life, mirrors its money history, he argues. Modern science backs this core claim, he holds, and calls it grand and firm.
3664-yvette:
Guy de Maupassant writes a novella about Yvette, a young woman in Paris society, and the men who circle her. The chapters are called The Initiation of Saval, Bougival and Love, Enlightenment, and From Emotion to Philosophy. The story opens as Jean de Servigny and Leon Saval leave the Cafe Riche on a fine night, choosing to walk rather than take a cab.

Saval, a newcomer to Yvette's world, learns its rules at Bougival and in Paris drawing rooms, where charm covers calculation. Maupassant writes with his usual irony about love, money, and reputation. The novella suits readers who enjoy his short fiction: a sharp, sad portrait of a girl whose beauty opens doors that lead nowhere kind.
3684-mr-crewe-s-career-complete:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, tells the full career of Mr Crewe in this complete edition. The story begins with Hilary Vane of Ripton, a lawyer, deacon, and trustee who boasts he never held office, yet whose word moves the state. Against Vane's quiet machine stands Crewe, a young reformer who desires only to make his state a utopia.

The complete novel follows Crewe from rallies and newspapers through legislative hearings to the test of his ideals in office. Churchill writes New Hampshire politics as a contest between friendship, interest, and principle. The complete edition suits readers who want the whole political story in one volume, from portrait to climax.
36873-a-fluttered-dovecote:
George Manville Fenn wrote A Fluttered Dovecote, illustrated by Gordon Browne. D Appleton and Company published this edition at New York in 1890. The narrator is Laura Bozerne of Chester Square, Belgravia, who calls herself a virgin and martyr. She opens by taking a fresh sheet of paper. The last was spotted with tears, and the blotting-paper took the glaze off and ran the ink. She means to write the history of her sufferings.

The world calls her young at eighteen, but she feels old, she says. Her life would fill thick volumes with thrilling incidents. Modesty confines her to the adventures of one single year. Memory the first is headed Mamma Makes a Discovery. She turns over her blotted diary, blistered with tears, as she writes.
37021-four-afloat-being-the-adventures-o:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote Four Afloat, being the adventures of the Big Four on the water, issued in New York by D Appleton and Company in nineteen oh seven. Barbour had earlier written Four in Camp and Four Afoot. He gave the book to J W A, skipper of many craft. A plate shows the launch Vagabond starting after another craft with a rush. Chapter one introduces a gasoline launch, four boys, and a dog.

Chapter two starts the Vagabond on its cruise. Wherein Dan Practices Steering and salt water chapters follow. Wherein Tom Buys Lobsters and Dan Disapproves brings comedy. In Which They Follow a Race and a stowaway discovery fill the middle. They outwit the captain of the Henry Nellis in a later chapter. A stern chase is not always a long chase, the tale promises. Boys get a summer cruise tale of seamanship and fun.
3739-a-far-country-complete:
Winston Churchill's full novel of modern America follows Hugh Paret from boyhood to middle age in one long arc. The book opens with Hugh calling himself a corporation lawyer by accident and promising an autobiography of a romanticist. It then tracks him through school, the law, railroad politics, sudden wealth, and a marriage strained by ambition, until success itself stands trial.

Readers get the whole story here rather than in parts, with the Hutchins family, their library, and their riverside houses marking each stage of the rise. Churchill keeps the moral question in view throughout, asking what a life spent getting is worth. The complete text suits readers who want to judge Hugh whole, from his first hopes to his final reckoning.
37485-boy-scouts-in-glacier-park-the-adv:
Walter Prichard Eaton wrote Boy Scouts in Glacier Park, with rights held from nineteen eighteen, a tale of two young easterners in the high Rockies. Photos by Fred Kiser show the Great Continental Divide and game trails. Eaton gave the book to Kiser as the best of companions on the high trails. Joe, one of the boys, gets bad news about his lungs at the start.

His friend Spider finds a way to pump Joe's lungs full of mountain air. The boys cross the continent with their faces glued to the train window and reach Many Glacier. They pitch tents, learn the diamond hitch, and cross Piegan Pass and Gunsight Pass. A ranger tells a grizzly tale by the fire, and Joe falls into a crack on Blackfeet Glacier. The book sells fresh air as a cure and the trail as a school.
3766-coniston-complete:
Winston Churchill's full Coniston novel tells a New Hampshire love story against the rise of machine politics. The book opens after Jackson's presidency with the Boss Era. It follows Cynthia Ware from childhood errands at the village store to womanhood at Miss Sadler's school. It also tracks Jethro Bass as he builds a political machine from favors, railroads, and loyal hounds like Jake Wheeler. Love, loyalty, and conscience pull Cynthia between Jethro's world and Bob Worthington's.

The complete text lets readers judge the whole design, from the tannery house years to the Boston parlors where Cynthia renounces and reconsiders. Churchill's moral stays constant, that popular rule is only as good as the virtue of its people. The novel suits readers who want one long American chronicle rather than a tale in parts.
37669-in-the-arctic-seas-a-narrative-of-:
In the Arctic Seas is the tale by a sea chief of the Royal Navy of the find of the fate of a lost knight and his men. Prints fill its form. A note tells how its spell was kept as first struck, with print faults set right in hush.

A front print shows his small ship as it steams out of the drift ice. Its full title tells its grief: the great chief who sailed to find the north west road was lost with all his men in the ice. This trip found the proof at last: bones, gear, and a writ note on a lone isle. The tale closes one of the great dark tales of the sea age.
3775-napoleon-bonaparte:
John Abbott wrote this popular life of Napoleon for readers who wanted the whole career in one stirring volume. The book follows the Corsican boy to Toulon, Egypt, and the coup that made him First Consul, then through Austerlitz, Jena, and the Russian snows to exile and Saint Helena. Abbott favors vivid scenes over dry analysis, with camps, courts, and battlefields drawn in warm, admiring colors.

A Spanish interlude shows the method, as a ragged stranger with a carbine eats a priest's whole supper and drinks to his host's health before the war resumes. The biography is partisan and old fashioned, but it carries a reader swiftly across twenty years of European upheaval. Those who want a first life of Napoleon, full of incident, will find Abbott a genial guide.
38137-stories-of-the-badger-state:
Stories of the Badger State, by Reuben Gold Thwaites, is a school history of Wisconsin published by the American Book Company in 1900. Its thirty-odd chapters carry the state from the mound builders to its own century.

The early chapters treat the mound builders, the life and manners of the Indians, the discovery of Wisconsin, Radisson and Groseilliers, and Joliet and Marquette. The Jesuit missionaries, a quarter-century of warfare, the commerce of the forest, and the old French days follow. Later stories cover the coming of the English, the Revolutionary War, the lead mines, the Winnebago and Black Hawk wars, territory and statehood, pioneer life, slave catching, and a great fire. The opening chapter describes the mounds of the Mississippi basin, most worn by rain and frost to two or three feet, a few still rising eighty feet or more.
38195-the-outcaste:
The Outcaste is a novel of India by F E Penny. Chatto and Windus published this special edition in London in 1912. It was sold only in India and the British colonies. The scene is the native state of Chirakul. Ananda, a convert to Christianity, stands at the centre of the cast. His friend Bopaul shares his caste, and Dorama is his wife.

Dr Wenaston heads the Maharajah's College at Chirapore. His sister Eola and Professor Twyford complete the English circle. The book is dedicated to students of Hindu theology and ethics. The first chapter opens at an aviation ground. A gust snaps an aeroplane's wings before a breathless crowd. The machine folds and drops, and the crowd believes the pilot dead. Eola's brother calms her: the man lives, though the machine is smashed.
3824-the-lamp-of-fate:
Margaret Pedler opens this family romance at Coverdale, where Hugh Vallincourt waits for news of a son and heir. For eight successive generations the first born of the Vallincourts has been a boy, so fixed a habit that no one doubts the ninth will follow suit. The house lies silent with disinfectant in the air, and hushed steps move upstairs while Hugh stares at lawns and leafless trees.

Later chapters carry the story to Devon lanes, where a boy called Coppertop rides a wagonette toward Storran of Stockleigh, past drivers who swish whips more at flies than at horses. Pedler asks what lamp guides children stumbling in the dark, quoting Omar Khayyam for her title. Readers who like generational sagas will find fate, family, and romance woven together.
38240-the-esperantist-complete:
The Esperantist was a monthly sheet for the new world tongue Esperanto. Volume one runs from November 1903 to December 1904. Mudie ran the sheet from the Esperanto Club in London. One copy cost four pence, or three shillings for a year. Its aim was to spread the made tongue for all lands.

Stead writes the lead piece on the tongue in number one. Bicknell gives an Italian summer in verse in that tongue. Motteau turns The Tempest into it for a taste of its range. Short prose deals with daily life and short hand in it. Tongue fans get the young cause in its own voice.
38460-checkmate:
Le Fanu, author of Guy Deverell, Wylder's Hand, and The Wyvern Mystery, wrote this novel of Mortlake Hall, issued by Downey and Company of Covent Garden in his own list of works. The contents run past sixty-five chapters. A certain Longcluse threads through them: he opens his heart, makes an odd confidence, follows a shadow, and sees a lady's note.

The story begins a mile and a half beyond Islington, at a singular and grand old house belonging to the Arden family, once distinguished in the northern counties. Martha Tansey and her story, Sir Reginald Arden, a catastrophe, and a man without a name appear in the early chapters. Moonlight walks, a midnight meeting, the Derby, and a garden party fill the middle, while Uncle David's suspicions, the night of the funeral, and Levi's apologue drive the tale toward its close.
3854-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
This complete text gathers all seven books of Madame de Montespan's memoirs of the court of Louis the Fourteenth. The translator's preface asks for a fairer hearing than harsh historians gave her. The memoirs were compiled in a vague, desultory way, with no regard for chronological order. Their value lies in self portraiture, as a cynical court lady whose beauty bewitched a king and whose sarcasm cut duchesses describes her own rise and fall.

War scenes balance the gossip, with orders to ravage Liege and Juliers, families in flight, castles sacked, and convents in flames, while Spanish and Dutch leaders rouse the people to resist. The complete memoirs suit readers who want the whole arc, from favorite to exile, in the favorite's own sharp voice.
38792-for-the-major-a-novelette:
A novelette by Constance Fenimore Woolson, author of Anne, published at New York by Harper and Brothers in 1883 with illustrations. The scene is Far Edgerley, a small village high on Chillawassee Mountain, six hundred feet above the busier Edgerley below with its cheese factories, sawmills, and stage line to the railway.

The mountain people look down on the lower town in more senses than one and prize their distance from traffic and cities. Against that setting Woolson sets Sara and her family, whose flower garden and quiet routines draw the visits of the Major of the title. The tale belongs to the local-colour fiction that made Woolson one of the noted American storytellers of her generation.
38981-the-chase-of-the-golden-plate:
Jacques Futrelle wrote The Chase of the Golden Plate. Dodd, Mead and Company issued it in 1906. Will Grefe drew its pictures. The book goes to three women Futrelle loved. Fama, Mayzie, and Berta stand named there. Part One is The Burglar and the Girl. A costume ball opens the chase.

Cardinal Richelieu and the Mikado step onto a balcony. They light cigarettes above Seven Oaks' door. A Dowager Empress of China waddles below. Geisha girls giggle behind an Indian warrior. The Czar of Russia sweeps in with rank's robes. D'Artagnan and the three musketeers swagger past. Mary Queen of Scots enters the throng as well. A stolen golden plate sets thief and girl running. Futrelle's light mystery in fancy dress shows the Thinking Machine author's playful side.
3900-court-memoirs-of-france-series-comp:
This vast file binds the whole court memoir series into one reading text of nearly eight million characters. Its contents list Marguerite de Valois, Cardinal de Retz, Madame de Montespan, and the Duchesse d'Orleans on Louis the Fourteenth. Saint-Simon, du Hausset, Campan, the Saint Cloud letters, and the Count de Grammont complete the set. Three centuries of French courts, from Valois queens to Napoleon's upstarts, stand in a single sequence.

A supper scene gives the flavor, as the Duke de Berry arrives to salute the king at table, all hearts open, and talk turns to post horses and roads. Readers who want the complete run, rather than single volumes, will find a library in one file, best dipped into by reign or by memoirist, since no one reads it straight through.
3918-serge-panine-complete:
This complete text gives all of Georges Ohnet's Serge Panine, crowned by the French Academy, with a general introduction to the series by Gaston Boissier's circle. The editor's preface presents the French Immortals as great romances since 1784. They are offered to American readers as a window on the inner life of a people whose greatness no turn of fortune could dim. Ohnet's novel of wealth, marriage, and speculation follows in full.

A ballroom passage shows its gossip machinery. Le Brede asks who a rich cousin of the Prince may be, and learns she owns a district in London and was kind to Serge Panine a year earlier. Her husband, shut in a Scottish castle and out of his mind, explains why she never married the Prince. Readers who want the whole novel will find ambition, ruin, and drawing room talk complete.
3922-the-red-lily-complete:
This complete text gives all of Anatole France's The Red Lily, with a preface on the author's life. Jacques Anatole Thibault, born in Paris in 1844 to a bookseller of the Quai Malaquais, was educated at College Stanislas, published poetry in the 1870s, and joined the French Academy in 1896. His critical writings fill four volumes of La Vie Litteraire, and his political articles fill Opinions Sociales.

The novel itself follows Therese through Florence, where morning thoughts dwell on walks, Virgins framed with angels, and children painted or carved who sing the Alleluia of grace. In the Brancacci chapel, her lover talks of Masaccio so vividly that she seems to see the adolescent master of masters. Readers who want France whole will find irony, art, and adultery in one long narrative.
3926-monsieur-madame-and-be-be-complete:
This complete text gives all of Gustave Droz's Monsieur, Madame and Bebe, the sketches crowned by the Academy in 1866. The preface traces Droz from Paris birth in 1832, son of sculptor Jules Antoine Droz, through the Beaux Arts and the Salon of 1857. From painting he turned to authorship under the name Gustave Z in La Vie Parisienne. His articles won favor as the work of an exquisite raconteur and sharp observer of intimate family life.

A domestic scene shows his method. A mother examines an embroidered garment, calls it lovely, and is interrupted by a knock and several voices, among them aunt Laura, a godmother, and Madame de P. with her thick lips ready for cheeks. Their glittering, ferreting looks intimidate the narrator. Readers who want Droz whole will find bachelor and married life in one comic volume.
3930-prince-zilah-complete:
This complete text gives all of Jules Claretie's Prince Zilah, with a preface by the Comte d'Haussonville of the French Academy. The preface calls Claretie the king of the chronicle, born at Limoges in 1840, educated at the Lycee Bonaparte, and destined for commerce before newspapers claimed him. Under names like Olivier de Jalin, Perdican, and Candide, he wrote for the Diogene, La France, L'Illustration, the Figaro, and the Rappel, and entered the Academy in 1888.

The novel's midnight scene shows its romantic machinery, as a Muscovite girl quiets hounds baying in the Himalayas kennel, unfastens their chains, and sends them bounding over the lawn in pale moonlight. She retraces her steps with the indifference her father might show ordering a spy shot. Readers who want Zilah whole will find Hungary, Paris, and a fate sealed by letters.
39330-immortal-youth-a-study-in-the-will:
Immortal Youth is a memoir study in the will to create by Lucien Price, printed in 1919. McGrath Sherrill Press of Boston imprinted the first printing of one thousand copies. A Rolland line from Colas Breugnon heads the book on sculptured souls that cannot burn. More copies could be had from the publisher for one dollar, the notice says.

The text opens in the third act of Wagner last music drama, with muted horns. Grandeur of a far off summons sounds in that flourish for the author ear. A young artist life and early death haunt this study of creative will. American letters keeps it as a tender period memoir of lost genius.
3934-zibeline-complete:
This file holds the whole of Philippe de Massa's Zibeline, with a life of its author. Alexandre Philippe Regnier de Massa, Marquis de Massa, was born in Paris in 1831. He took a cavalry commission after Saint Cyr, served in the Imperial Guards, and fought in the Italian and Franco German wars. He later wrote plays, a ballet with Petipa, and this brilliant romance of 1892.

A comic passage shows its machinery, as the actress Eugenie tells how Monsieur Desvanneaux announced her for a charity kermess. Under the mantle of charity, she says, the holy man paid court to her. His son in law honored her with an attack as well, arriving just as the father in law knelt to declare himself. Readers who want Zibeline whole will find gambling, gallantry, and Paris wit complete.
3938-a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-com:
This complete text gives all of Andre Theuriet's A Woodland Queen, crowned by the French Academy in 1890. The preface traces Theuriet from birth at Marly le Roi in 1833, through Bar le Duc and Paris law studies, to a Treasury career and then to fiction. His poems appeared in the Revue de Paris and the Revue des Deux Mondes, and his greatest novel excels in country nooks and polite rusticity.

A meeting scene shows his charm, as Julien the young mystic hears words that recall Saint Francis preaching to fish and conversing with birds. Timid before women, he raises his hat to leave, but Reine stops him, saying she must go to the sale of the Ronces woods. Readers who want the woodland romance whole will find inheritance, forest, and a singular girl complete.
3942-the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-ce:
Here is the whole of Alfred de Musset's Confession of a Child of the Century, with a preface by Henri de Bornier. The preface calls Musset, born of noble parentage in 1810 and educated at College Henri Quatre, the greatest poet of love modern times has produced, spontaneous, sincere, and emotional. At thirty he was already an old man, his passion burned out with his heart, seeking youth in artificial stimuli.

The novel's middle opens on Brigitte, seen one evening under lindens at a village entrance. Dressed simply and veiled, she caresses a stray white goat in a field, and the narrator plucks wild mulberry and steps up holding it out. The goat watches with apprehension. Readers who want Musset whole will find youth, jealousy, and a century's disillusion complete.
3946-monsieur-de-camors-complete:
This complete text gives all of Octave Feuillet's Monsieur de Camors, with a preface by Maxime du Camp. Feuillet, born at Saint Lo in 1821, entered for the law, joined the romantic school, and collaborated with Alexander Dumas and Paul Bocage before publishing Onesta and Alix in 1846. Posterity judges him leader of the idealistic school, with great imagination linked to analytical power, and a style neat, pure, fine, brilliant, and concise.

A night ride shows his plotting, as a doctor must content himself with essence of coffee and send to a village four leagues away for what the case demands. Camors hears this and answers that Trilby waits at the door, and with him he can do the four leagues in an hour. He takes the prescription traced on a pocketbook leaf, mounts, and departs. Readers who want Camors whole will find honor, ruin, and devotion complete.
3957-l-abbe-constantin-complete:
This complete text gives all of Ludovic Halevy's L'Abbe Constantin, with a preface by Legouve. Halevy, born in Paris in 1834 to author Leon Halevy and grandson of composer Fromenthal Halevy, left a lucrative civil service career when his patron the Duc de Morny died in 1865. He then gave himself to the theatre, and with Henri Meilhac formed a literary union of nearly twenty years before turning to fiction.

A ballet scene shows the novel's charm, as dancers advance with light trembling on spangled robes and Mrs Scott follows the evolutions with pleasure. Bettina grows thoughtful on perceiving a tall dark young man in a box across the house, and Miss Percival asks herself whether she must marry him and become a princess. Readers who want the abbe whole will find faith, Americans, and Parisian comedy complete.
3962-a-romance-of-youth-complete:
Francois Coppee's full novel follows Amedee, a young poet in Paris, from his early hopes to his first taste of fame and its costs. Time passes in leaps, marked by postmen, snow, and calendars, as the young writer finds friends among the city's long-haired literary set.

Amedee's sonnets win print in La Guepe and talk in the cafes, yet success brings rivals, pride, and tangled love. Coppee keeps the scenes plain and warm, with Paris streets, journals, and drawing rooms as the stage. The book suits readers who like a gentle story of art and youth. In it, a poet learns that praise is fickle and that a true life is harder to write than a fine verse.
39640-literary-fables-of-yriarte:
The Literary Fables of Yriarte presents Spanish fables in English dress. Devereux translated them from the Spanish. Ticknor and Fields published the book at Boston in 1855. The translator dedicated it to his Harvard class of 1829. The fables had served as a college text-book.

A preface explains the fable's power. Brief tales give weight to moral sayings. They direct the aim like the feather on a shaft. Yriarte's fables differ from the familiar stock. They were written for a special and pointed purpose. That purpose is criticism of writers and writing. The translator praises their terse simplicity. Yriarte was born in Tenerife in 1750. He lived at Madrid and died in 1791.
3967-cosmopolis-complete:
This volume collects the whole of Paul Bourget's Cosmopolis, with a preface by Jules Lemaitre. Bourget, born at Amiens in 1852, studied at the Lycee Louis le Grand and the Ecole des Hautes Etudes, meaning to devote himself to Greek philology. He gave up linguistics for poetry, criticism, and fiction. His essays on Renan, Taine, Amiel, Baudelaire, Leconte de Lisle, Dumas fils, Turgenev, the Goncourts, and Stendhal won praise for reading and meditation of rare depth.

The novel's middle turns on an anonymous letter. Poor Alba, reentering her chamber, wipes two large tears from pale cheeks and opens the infamous letter received the day before to reread it. She knows its perfidious phrases by heart, warning her she is compromised, more than a marriageable girl should be, by playing with Maitland the role she played with Goyka. Readers who want Cosmopolis whole will find Rome, honor, and ruin complete.
3971-jacqueline-complete:
Th. Bentzon, writing as Madame Blanc, tells the full story of Jacqueline, a young Frenchwoman caught between her father, her stepmother, and the men who seek her hand. A preface by Thureau-Dangin of the French Academy frames the novel as a study of a girl growing up under watchful adult eyes.

Jacqueline faces a proposed trip to Italy, tangled letters, and the hurt of being treated as a prize rather than a person. Her pride and her poverty leave her open to insult, and she must learn whom to trust. The novel stays close to her point of view, so readers feel each slight and each small win as she moves toward a choice of her own.
3975-the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-complet:
Rene Bazin's complete diary novel follows a young French scholar through months of study, family quarrels, and slow hope. He works on a thesis about the Junian Latins, freed slaves whose freedom Roman law did not fully accept, while his uncle presses him toward a safe law career in Bourges.

Dated entries carry the story from December days of worry to a May noon when a friend arrives to test his essay, and on to summer walks and fishing trips. Lampron and other friends lighten the record with humor and talk. The book charms by its plain daily form, letting a young mind argue, doubt, and grow in short entries that feel close to life.
3980-fromont-and-risler-complete:
Alphonse Daudet's complete Paris novel follows the house of Fromont, its brewer Risler, and Sidonie, whose ambition reshapes every life near her. Claire Fromont wonders what she has done to Sidonie, unaware of an old tie between her friend and Georges at Savigny.

Across four volumes of trade, marriage, and pride, the firm rises and falls with its people. Risler's kind heart, Sidonie's social hunger, and the Fromont family's honor collide in workshops, drawing rooms, and tenement landings. The full novel rewards patient readers with a broad, humane portrait of Paris work and family life in the late nineteenth century.
3985-gerfaut-complete:
Charles de Bernard's complete novel tells of Octave, Vicomte de Gerfaut, a gifted man whose pen counts for more in his age than a sword did in an earlier one. A feast shared with a friend opens the way to his story, told through castle visits, friendships, and a love that tests honor.

Gerfaut moves between Paris talk and the castle of Bergenheim, where Madame de Bergenheim weighs duty against feeling. Bernard mixes wit, courtly manners, and moral strain into a long tale of rank and heart. The full text suits readers who enjoy a classic French novel of love and honor, played out in drawing rooms, gardens, and long, careful talks.
3990-conscience-complete:
Hector Malot's complete novel follows Saniel, a hard-working Paris doctor whose pride, money troubles, and a fatal act with a knife drag him into guilt. Waking after two hours of sleep, tired and dull, he moves about his room in a daze before the memory of the knife returns.

Phillis, Glady, Brigard, and the law all press on him as he tries to manage testimony and to make amends. Malot keeps the story close to Saniel's mind, where each kind act toward Phillis wars with fear of being found out. The full novel is a steady study of conscience, showing how one deed can rule a life long after the deed itself is done.
3995-madame-chrysantheme-complete:
Pierre Loti's complete Japan novel tells of a French naval officer who marries, for a season, a young Japanese woman called Chrysantheme. By July, four officers of his ship live in like fashion on the same suburban slopes, arranged through the same agent, Kangourou.

Neighbors such as the merry Madame Campanule fill the visiting rounds, and Loti records homes, feasts, and temple days with a sailor's close eye. The full book moves from first landing to farewell, mixing charm, distance, and the sadness of a bond with a set end. It remains a vivid firsthand picture of Japan as seen by a French officer of the late nineteenth century.
3999-an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-compl:
Emile Souvestre's complete Paris journal follows a lodger in a top-floor room who wakes to birdsong and sun on the roofs. From that high perch he sees gardens, woods, and city streets, and turns each morning sight into a short note on life.

Uncle Maurice and other figures pass through the journal, which mixes diary entries with essays on fame, power, and kindness. The full text keeps the same mild, watchful tone from first page to last. It suits readers who like quiet books, where a butterfly at a window or a walk at dawn can open a whole train of thought.
40989-the-paston-letters-a-d-1422-1509-v:
Paston Letters, volume two of six, is part of the great edition of a Norfolk family archive. The letters run from 1422 to 1509, across the Wars of the Roses age. Pastons great and small write of land, lawsuits, marriage, and war in their own hands. Project Gutenberg holds the other five volumes of the new complete edition.

No other English family left so full a letter hoard from the fifteenth century. Rents, riots, sieges of Caister, and London news fill the gentry correspondence. Editors order the letters by date so a family saga builds letter by letter. Historians and general readers gain medieval England speaking plainly in its own words.
41024-the-paston-letters-a-d-1422-1509-v:
The Paston Letters, volume three, holds family letters from 1422 to 1509. The Gairdner edition of the letters runs to six volumes in all. Each volume stands as a separate text in the Gutenberg set. Volume three's letters come from the great Norfolk family's papers. Brackets and question marks stand as in the printed original text.

Damaged places in the old letters show as series of dots here. The year of each letter stood in a sidenote at the page top. That sidenote now stands merged at the head of each letter. Superscriptions in the old hands show by a carat mark in print. The Pastons wrote of land, law, marriages, and local rule in Norfolk. Their letters give a first-hand picture of fifteenth-century English life. Readers meet gentry affairs told in the writers' own plain words. This volume carries the family story deeper into that century.
4107-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's complete history of the Mayflower covers the whole voyage from July 15, 1620, to May 6, 1621. The ship was chartered about mid-June 1620 at London by Thomas Weston and Robert Cushman, acting for the Merchant Adventurers and the Leyden Separatists.

The full text joins charter, consort Speedwell, ship, officers, crew, passengers, quarters, provisions, and the ship's journal into one scholarly account. Ames writes from logs and letters, with appendices of lists and documents. Readers who want the Pilgrim story whole, in its fullest early form, will find this the standard Victorian history.
41081-the-paston-letters-a-d-1422-1509-v:
Volume four of the Paston Letters, 1422 to 1509, in Gairdner's edition, prints the family's correspondence in the standard six-volume set. The transcriber's notes explain the apparatus: years merged into the sidenotes at each letter's head, superscripts marked with a caret, damaged passages shown as dot series. Spelling oddities such as Jhon are original, not errors. Footnotes keep their printed numbering, keyed also to the index in volume six.

The Paston letters are the great surviving archive of an English gentry family's fifteenth century: land disputes, lawsuits, marriages, money, and local politics in Norfolk. This volume's letters carry the family's affairs through their middle decades, with abstracts where originals are lost. The Gutenberg set issues each volume separately, the general introduction in volume one released last, matching the printed order. Brackets, sic notations, and lists of misprints are preserved as printed.
41154-the-walking-delegate:
Walking Delegate is a novel of labour politics by Leroy Scott, published at New York in 1905. Doubleday, Page and Company issued the book in May of that year. Contents list chapters that follow an election fight inside a union.

The tale opens On the Saint Etienne Hotel and names its second chapter for the walking delegate himself. The Rise of Buck Foley, A Council of War, and Tom Seeks Help from the Enemy follow in order. Foley plays with two mice in one chapter, and the men are got in line in the next. The day after, new courage and new plans, and conferences with Mr Baxter close the contents shown in the head. Scott novel was an early American attempt to put union machinery and its bosses into serious fiction.
41296-rose-a-charlitte:
Rose à Charlitte, subtitled An Acadien Romance, is a novel by Marshall Saunders, the author of Beautiful Joe. Page and Company of Boston published it in 1898, with illustrations by Young. Saunders inscribed the story of the Acadiens to Theodore Harding Rand, a friend of the Acadian people and of her father.

The first book follows Vesper L. Nimmo, who receives a message from the dead and travels from Boston to Acadie. Chapters set scenes at the Sleeping Water Inn and introduce Agapit the Acadien. The opening chapter has a handsome young man by a fire insist that evil deeds do not die. Saunders, a Canadian writer famed for her animal story, here turns to the French-speaking Acadians of the Maritime provinces and their history, in a romance of return and memory.
41932-a-fair-mystery-the-story-of-a-coqu:
Charlotte Mary Brame wrote a tale of a fair coquette under a false name. In America she was known as Bertha Clay, a note says. Clay also wrote Dora Thorne and Beyond Pardon. The book's part fourteen is lost in the old print, a note warns. A voice and a face in the night start the tale.

A child's soft prayer at its mother's knee draws a sharp cry. Patty Brace lifts the white-clad child to her lap in tears. Brown curls rest on her breast as the scene's heart shows. Love that wounds and heals drives the long house tale. Such tales sold by the score to home readers then. Warm, grave turns fill each part.
42087-third-annual-report-of-the-kensing:
The Kensington Parochial Institute gave out its third yearly report for 1852, printed at Kensington in 1853. The vicar of Kensington, Archdeacon Sinclair, led the group as its head. A council of town men ran its work, with a priest as clerk. Gifts and dues came in through the fund holder on High Street.

The council tells members and town folk what the group had done that year. Its aim was to meet a growing want for sound books and good taste. Reading rooms, book rooms, and talks drew strong use, the report says. The council asks town folk to give more, so the work can grow. The report also claims such groups show how much a land wants to learn.
42442-the-wonderful-story-of-ravalette:
Dr P B Randolph, styled on his title page the Dumas of America, tells The Wonderful Story of Ravalette, issued by Sinclair Tousey of New York in 1863. The volume also holds Tom Clark and His Wife, their double dreams and the curious things that befell them therein, called the Rosicrucian's story. A line from Channing heads it: the fictions of genius carry the sublimest verities.

The introduction asks outright whether real magic exists, apart from stage jugglery and spirit photographs. Randolph scorns modern charlatans and counts most spectral reports as lies, yet holds that one case in a million may be true.
4264-the-golden-bowl-complete:
