Henry James's The Golden Bowl, complete in one volume, joins the two books of the 1904 novel. They are Book First, The Prince, and Book Second, The Princess. The Prince, a modern Roman in London, marries Maggie Verver. She is the daughter of the American collector Adam Verver.

Charlotte, an old friend of both, remains close to the family. The novel's drama is quiet and inward. Through Maggie's growing perception, James shows how a marriage that looks perfect can hide an old attachment. The famous golden bowl, bought in a Bond Street shop, stands for that hidden flaw. This text lets readers follow the whole arc without a break.
427-the-great-war-syndicate:
Frank Stockton imagines a near-future war between the United States and Great Britain in this speculative novel. A fishing dispute off Newfoundland lights the fuse late in the nineteenth century. Instead of fleets and armies, a private syndicate of rich Americans offers to run the war on business terms.

Stockton follows their strange machines, raids, and bargains as Britain answers in kind. The tale mixes satire with adventure, mocking both war fever and the faith that money can buy victory. It reads as an early what-if about private power, fought at sea and in the press.
4270-ragged-lady-complete:
William Dean Howells called his heroine a ragged lady, and this complete novel follows the Landers, a middle-aged couple spending their first summer at Middlemount. They do not know the roads, and their drives turn into small domestic comedies, as Mrs. Lander urges her husband to stop and ask the way while he presses rashly on.

Later parts move Mrs. Lander to a New York hotel she has known for years, where clerks, bell-boys, and waiters greet her by memory. Howells builds the novel from such social detail: marriage, money, and the habits of people who have lived long enough to be both fond and exasperated with one another.
42781-notes-and-queries-number-166-janua:
Number one hundred sixty six of Notes and Queries came out on Saturday, January first, eighteen hundred fifty three. The weekly billed itself as a shared space for writers, artists, and students of old records and family lines. It cost four pence a copy. This issue opens the seventh volume of the run.

Writers send in short notes on old books, plays, poems, and odd facts. Others pose questions and wait for answers in later issues. Topics here range from Bacon and Hamlet to folk tales and church records. A section covers new photo methods on paper. Readers who study how scholars traded facts before search tools will find the page lively.
42782-notes-and-queries-number-167-janua:
Notes and Queries number 167, for Saturday, January 8, 1853, is one issue of the London weekly for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. One copy cost fourpence, or fivepence stamped. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is when found, make a note of.

The notes hold a piece on the autograph of Edward of Lancaster, son of Henry the Sixth, by Sir Frederic Madden. Robert Bloomfield, a note for London topographers, and sermons by parliamentary chaplains follow. Minor notes treat Cremona violins, prices of tea, and the origin of the word molasses. Queries ask on Roman grave stones, chapel plaster, the word anywhen, and Sidney as a female name. Replies treat the Queen descent from John of Gaunt and Shakespeare readings. Scholars traded facts in these pages.
43012-opium-eating-an-autobiographical-s:
An unnamed habituate tells his own tale of opium eating here. Claxton, Remsen and Haffelfinger printed it at Philadelphia in 1876. Friends urged him to publish, thinking it would help the public. His preface warns readers not to expect De Quincey music in it.

He calls his tale a dull, trudging account of solid facts instead. Opium had bound and baked his mind hard, he owns plainly. He wrote now lest his mouth be sealed forever undelivered. An opening part treats his imprisonment before the habit tale proper. He begs the reader kind judgment of the chapters that follow in the small book.
43139-a-sweet-girl-graduate:
A Sweet Girl Graduate is a novel by Meade, in an edition dated 1891 with illustrations by Hal Ludlow. Its first chapter, called Going Out into the World, opens on a packed trunk. The trunk is new, with a canvas cover bound in red braid. Its owner's initials are worked on the top in large plain letters, three of them.

Those initials stand for Priscilla Penywern Peel, the heroine. The trunk is corded and strapped away, and Priscilla stands by her aunt in the little parlour of their cottage. The aunt thinks she has told the girl everything. Priscilla promises to write once a week and to try not to be nervous. Girls are not nervous nowadays, she asks, in the bright tone that carries her out of the house.
43149-waynflete:
Waynflete is a novel by Coleridge, published in London by Innes and Company in an edition dated 1893. A line from the novel John Inglesant heads the prologue: no one can doubt that the character of a country's people shapes the devil that country gets. The tale begins in 1785.

At ten at night on the fourth of October 1785, the master of Waynflete Hall sits at cards with Maxwell of Ouseley, his neighbour and his enemy. By the fire sits the squire's brother, the parson of the parish. Above the chimney hangs the portrait of the eldest son and heir, a fair boy with pleading eyes. The squire and vicar are big men of rough riding and hard drinking. Their visitor has the thinner face of a man used to defer. A card table, an enemy, and a portrait set the stage.
4361-memoirs-of-general-william-t-sherma:
William T. Sherman wrote these complete memoirs for his comrades in arms, volunteers and regulars alike. He notes that nearly ten years after the Civil War, no satisfactory history of it was yet open to the public. War Department papers were still being compiled, at a pace that might take a century.

What he offers is not a history of the war. Instead Sherman gives his own part in it, from early service through the great campaigns. He covers the marches that made his name. The complete text joins both volumes, giving the full arc of a general's career. It remains a first source for the Union war, blunt and detailed.
43940-baseball-joe-home-run-king-or-the-:
Lester Chadwick wrote Baseball Joe, Home Run King, or the greatest pitcher and batter on record, issued in New York by Cupples and Leon Company with copyright in nineteen twenty two. Chadwick had earlier written Baseball Joe of the Silver Stars and Baseball Joe in the Big League. A plate shows the longest hit ever made on the Polo Grounds. Chapter one is A Dangerous Plunge. Chapter two is A Surprise. The Baseball Joe series list stands in front.

Series volumes run from Baseball Joe of the Silver Stars through Baseball Joe Around the World. Joe Matson, Yale man and Giant pitcher, stands at his peak in this volume. Reggie Turns Up in chapter three, the contents promise. Games, rivals, and a pennant race fill the tale in Chadwick steady manner. Boys get clean baseball fiction from a long loved series, with Joe king at bat and on the mound.
4397-the-forsyte-saga-complete:
John Galsworthy wrote the Forsyte Saga as the chronicle of a wealthy English family across three generations, and this text joins its novels complete. The Man of Property opens at old Jolyon's house, at home among his kin, and follows the family through opera, dinners at Swithin's, and the projection of a new house.

Soames Forsyte, June, Bosinney, and old Jolyon carry the first novel's drama of property, art, and marriage. Later novels follow the family through war, divorce, and new generations. Galsworthy's saga is a portrait of an age, told through one family's houses, money, and loves, and it remains his best-known work.
4405-the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-e:
George Meredith's Shaving of Shagpat, complete in one text, is an Arabian entertainment in the manner of the Thousand and One Nights. Shibli Bagarag, a barber's nephew, must shave the magician Shagpat, whose enchanted hair holds a whole kingdom in thrall. The contents run from the thwackings and Bhanavar the Beautiful through the betrothal and the genie Karaz.

Later tales bring the well of Paravid, the talking hawk, the palace of Aklis, and the sword of Aklis. Koorookh, the veiled figure, the dish of pomegranate grain, and the flashes of the blade lead to the conclusion. The complete text lets readers enjoy Meredith's most fanciful book whole, tale nested within tale.
44074-meccania-the-super-state:
Meccania, the super state, is a satirical novel by Owen Gregory, first issued at London in 1918. Gregory inscribes it to a friend in token of twenty eight years of friendship. The contents open with a short account of a certain Ming and his journal. The narrator then becomes a foreign observer, and takes a first guided tour of a town called Bridgetown.

An introduction to the capital, a lecture by a professor with a toady's name, and chapters on culture in Mecco follow. A Meccanian apostle, a great festival, and the spread of the system fill the middle heads. Conversations and a scholarly discussion lead to the latest institution. A final chapter is called never again. Gregory's Meccania, a land of perfect order and state worship, mocks the machine state that the Great War had shown Europe.
4412-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-compl:
George Meredith's complete Ordeal of Richard Feverel joins all the books of the novel in one text. Sir Austin Feverel raises his son Richard by a scientific system, recorded in aphorisms, meant to keep the boy pure. The contents trace the system from the inmates of Raynham Abbey and Richard's fourteenth birthday through arson, juvenile stratagems, and Daphne's bower.

Later books bring the blossoming season, the magnetic age, and the system's encounter with wild oats. Richard's love, marriage, and ruin test his father's theory to destruction. Meredith's comedy of ideas remains sharp throughout, and the complete text lets readers follow the whole ordeal without a break.
44153-the-adventures-of-a-suburbanite:
The Adventures of a Suburbanite is a comic novel by Ellis Parker Butler, published by Doubleday at New York in 1911. Phelan drew the pictures. Its narrator tells how his wife Isobel was born in a flat, reared in a flat, and married from a flat. For two years after the wedding they lived in a flat, but he was no born flat dweller.

As soon as he could, he proposed moving to the country. Isobel hesitated, but weakly, and on the first of May they bought the place at Westcote and moved in. That very day neighbour Millington came over, glad someone had moved in at last. The last man had feared automobiles and would never ride with him. Hoping the newcomer was braver, Millington proposed a spin at once.
4420-sandra-belloni-originally-emilia-in:
George Meredith's Sandra Belloni, first called Emilia in England, is given here complete in one text. The novel follows Emilia, a young Italian singer, among the English ladies of Brookfield, who take her up as a musical prodigy and a social project. Its first book opens with the Poles' prelude and an expedition by moonlight.

Emilia plays the cornet in public, supplies the key to herself, and speeds her history to a big drum's march. Rival clubs, Wilfrid's diplomacy, and the government of Brookfield fill seven books. The complete text lets readers follow Emilia from first trial to goodbye, through sentiment, passion, and the comedy of English manners.
4426-rhoda-fleming-complete:
George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming, complete in one text, follows two Kentish sisters from Queen Anne's Farm into London's dangers. The first book introduces the Kentish family, the might of the money demon, and a text from scripture. The sisters meet, Edward and Algernon appear, and great news from Dahlia changes everything.

Later books bring the theatre, the farmer speaking, Rhoda and Robert, and an assembly at the Pilot Inn. Edward takes his course, Major Percy Waring enters, and the story moves toward expiation and conclusion. Meredith's novel is a Victorian study of seduction, honor, and forgiveness, told with his characteristic wit and moral force.
44319-miss-heck-s-thanksgiving-party-or-:
Ida Hamilton Munsell wrote a short tale about Myra Heck, a young Black woman who works as a maid in the small town of Rexville. The book is given to the womans club of Evanston, in Illinois, a group formed for mutual help. Myra has rare skill at house work, and good help is hard to find in town.

That skill gives Myra real power over the homes that hire her, and the tale treats her pride and bold dress with both humor and bite. Faults in her work are named in the text, yet her talent is clear. The title points to a Thanksgiving party at the heart of the plot.
4434-evan-harrington-complete:
George Meredith's Evan Harrington, complete in one text, follows a tailor's son who passes as a gentleman. The contents open above buttons, with the heritage of the son and the daughters of the shears. On board the Jocasta, the family and the funeral, and a gentleman on the road set the comedy moving.

Later chapters bring mother and son, an eccentric, the countess in low society, and doings at an inn. Ale shows one quality of wine, a cricket match is played, and Evan writes himself tailor, then calls himself gentleman. The complete novel is Meredith's comedy of class, birth, and love, told with high spirits and sharp observation.
4443-vittoria-complete:
George Meredith's Vittoria, complete in one text, joins all eight books of his Italian revolutionary novel. Signorina Vittoria, a singer on Monte Motterone, becomes a voice of the revolt against Austria. The contents run from the heights and the spy through Verona, the maestro's door, and the opera of Camilla.

Later books follow the flight across the mountains, the duel in the pass, the tobacco riots, and the five days of Milan. Through winter and a last meeting in Milan, Vittoria's song and her loves carry the history. The complete text gives Meredith's longest romance whole, with revolution as both backdrop and fate.
4452-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-co:
George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond, complete in one text, follows a boy fought over by his family into a life of adventure. Harry tells his story from Dipwell Farm through a taste of grandeur, a dear friend, and a tale of a goose. A free life on the road, Janet Ilchester, and an evening with Captain Bulsted follow.

Later chapters bring the great fog and the fire at midnight, a voyage on the Priscilla, and learned arguments with its captain. Harry's father, a brilliant adventurer and prince in exile, drives the plot through Bath, duels, and gipsy camps. The complete novel is Meredith's most rousing romance, told by a hero who loves his father and learns his faults.
4460-beauchamp-s-career-complete:
George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career, complete in one text, follows Nevil Beauchamp from champion of his country to radical candidate. The contents open with uncle, nephew, and baronial views of the present time, then show Nevil in action, Renee, love in Venice, and an awakening for both. A night on the Adriatic follows.

Later books bring Captain Baskelett, Dr. Shrapnel, Cecilia Halkett, canvassing, and the two passions. Beauchamp's fight for reform, his loves, and his quarrels with family fill seven books. The complete novel is Meredith's fullest study of principle in Victorian politics, witty, earnest, and unsparing.
4464-the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-w:
George Meredith called this novel a study in a well-known story, and the complete text tells it whole. It opens with a defense of the word fantastical, scorned by reviewers yet serviceable for nature and human nature alike. The wandering ship of the drunken pilot, mutinous crew, and angry captain fits the word, Meredith argues, as well as any poem.

The story itself retells the love affair of the socialist Ferdinand Lassalle and Helene von Donniges, with its brilliance, quarrels, and fatal duel. Meredith treats the pair as tragic comedians, grand and foolish at once. The complete novel is a compact masterpiece of irony, about ideals, vanity, and love.
4470-diana-of-the-crossways-complete:
George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways, complete in one text, follows Diana Warwick, witty Irish heroine, novelist, and talker, through London society. The contents open with diaries and diarists touching the heroine, an Irish ball, and the interiors of Redworth and Sullivan Smith. Hints of Diana's experiences, and what they led to, follow.

Later books bring the crisis, the conflict of the night, the authoress, and a drive in sunlight and moonlight. Diana's night-watch in the chamber of death, her dealings with Dacier, and the spectral crossways lead to triumph. The complete novel is Meredith's portrait of a brilliant woman, partly modeled on Caroline Norton, in a man's political world.
4476-one-of-our-conquerors-complete:
George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors, complete in one text, follows Victor Radnor, a self-made man of energy and charm, and Nataly, the woman he loves but cannot marry. The contents open across London Bridge, through the vague to the infinitely little, with old Veuve, a second bottle, and a London walk westward. An inspection of Lakelands follows.

Later books bring the dumbness of a household with one heart, a drive to Paris, a patriot abroad, and Nesta's engagement. Nataly in action, the burden upon Nesta, and the night of the great undelivered speech lead to the last chapter. The complete novel is Meredith's study of a conqueror undone by the very life he built.
4482-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-complete:
George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta, complete in one text, follows an old soldier and his young wife through society's judgment. The contents open with love at a school, Lady Charlotte, the tutor, and recognition. Shades of Browny and Matey advance and retire, and a mood of languor, a prattler's doses, and a bruised warrior follow.

Later books bring more of Cuper's boys, war at Olmer, old lovers and new friends, and a secret fished without angling. Along two roads to Steignton, Lady Charlotte's triumph, and the Ormont jewels lead to lovers mated and a conclusion. The complete novel is Meredith's comedy of an unequal marriage, told with wit and sympathy.
4491-celt-and-saxon-complete:
George Meredith's Celt and Saxon, complete as left in 1910, is his unfinished novel of Irish and English character. It opens with an excursion in a Celtic mind, following a young Irish gentleman of the O'Donnells, a Patrick, through talk, music, and family life. Mr. Adister, Caroline, and the princess set the social stage.

The second book brings Miss Mattock, a dinner party, Rockney, and the great Mr. Bull, with Celtic and Saxon views of him. Crossing the Rubicon, Captain Con's letter, and Mars convalescent close the text. Unfinished as it is, the novel shows Meredith's late wit on nations, manners, and the Irish question.
4537-sylvia-s-lovers-complete:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers appears here in its complete form, all three volumes in one file, published in London in 1863. It opens in Monkshaven, a whaling town on the north-east coast of England at the end of the eighteenth century. It follows Sylvia Robson, Philip Hepburn, and their rivals through courtship, war, and loss. The chapters run from Monkshaven and home from Greenland through the press-gang. They go on to engagements, ordeals, and wedding raiment.

Later volumes carry the story through happy days, evil omens, rescue from the waves, bereavement, recognition, and a closing turn of saved and lost. Gaskell writes with close care for dialect, sea work, and family feeling, and she lets small choices carry large consequences. Readers get the whole novel in one place, best read in order, as a rich Victorian tale of love, loyalty, and the price of a lie.
45549-the-air-mystery-of-isle-la-motte:
Craine wrote a boys flying tale printed in Cleveland and New York in 1930. Jim Austin and Bob Caldwell are the Sky Buddies, and their plane is christened Her Highness. Their book is the first of the set. A Canadian Mounted Policeman reins in his horse by the cockpit as the tale opens in southern Quebec.

Why are you fellows landing here, he demands of the two boys. Three mysteries, thundering waters, a mysterious find, and a capture fill the early chapters. A tail spin, a blaze, and the cry that the mail must go through raise the stakes. A cry for help and detectives close the contents. Isle La Motte in Lake Champlain gives the mystery its wild northern setting.
4600-a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-complete:
William Dean Howells calls this novel the first fruit of his New York life, after a quarter century in Cambridge and Boston ending in 1889. He frames the story through a literary adventurer and his wife, Basil and Isabel March, characters he had already used in Their Wedding Journey. Now older, they leave their adoptive New England for the commercial metropolis, where a new magazine offers work and risk.

In New York the Marches meet editors, writers, workers, and reformers, and a great strike tests their loyalties and their marriage. Howells writes social realism with humour and care, letting talk and daily life carry large questions about wealth, labour, and art. Readers get a rich portrait of Gilded Age New York, and of a middle-aged couple learning, sometimes painfully, how a new city changes old certainties.
4645-the-landlord-at-lion-s-head-complet:
William Dean Howells roots the novel in two weeks spent on Lake Champlain's western shore during the summer of 1891. From Vermont, across the water, he kept seeing a great peak that early French settlers named Le Lion Couchant, while plain Yankees called it the Camel's Hump. The peak struck him as a lion asleep, its head especially clear, and when his long-planned hotel story took shape, that sight supplied the book's name.

He fastened that name on the book before a word was written, and never wanted another. Whatever the finished story became, he felt sure no better name existed. The novel follows the landlord, his hotel, and the guests who pass through a New England summer world. Readers get a mature Howells novel about work, ambition, and manners, rooted in a Vermont mountain and a long-held idea.
4646-their-silver-wedding-journey-comple:
William Dean Howells follows Basil and Isabel March again in Their Silver Wedding Journey, in its complete form. The story opens with the Business End urging the editor to take a rest, since his wife wants him to go, his doctor agrees, and it is his Sabbatical year. Fulkerson adds a bait: March could send back copy for the magazine, though he need not write a line while gone.

Nine years have passed since the Marches took Every Other Week from Dryfoos, two years past the old seven-year Sabbatical term. The couple set out for Europe to mark twenty-five years of marriage, revisiting old places and old feelings. Readers get a gentle, observant Howells novel about a long marriage, travel, and middle age, told with humour and quiet wisdom.
46661-north-dakota-a-guide-to-the-northe:
Workers of the Federal Writers' Project wrote this guide to North Dakota, printed at Fargo in 1938. The State Historical Society sponsored the American Guide Series volume for the prairie state. Governor Langer writes the foreword, and the state director the preface, in its front matter list.

General information and annual events stand before the survey of the state itself. Contemporary North Dakota opens part one of the contents at page three. Tours keyed to a map at the front lead travelers through towns, buttes and badlands, in the great Depression project that set jobless writers to describing their own America state by state.
46950-the-adventures-of-bob-white:
The Adventures of Bob White is a children's nature story by Thornton Burgess, published by Little, Brown in 1919 with illustrations by Harrison Cady. Burgess was the author of Old Mother West Wind and the Bedtime Story-Books. His hero is Bob White, the quail, a handsome little fellow dressed in brown, white, and black. The book opens by praising cheerful work, in verse.

Bob White whistles rather than sings, and his clear, cheery call gladdens all who hear it. Farmer Brown's boy often stops to whistle back and always gets an answer. The other little people of the Green Meadows, the Green Forest, and the Old Orchard know and love him. A few, like Reddy Fox and Redtail the Hawk, love him as a meal they hope to catch. The story also teaches his value on the farm, eating weed seeds and insect eggs all summer long.
46952-the-adventures-of-old-man-coyote:
Thornton W Burgess wrote a children's nature story published at Boston in 1916, drawn by Harrison Cady. Burgess had written the Old Mother West Wind series and the Bedtime Story Books. Chapter one, the strange voice, opens the tale. Listen, says Jimmy Skunk, meeting Peter Rabbit on the Crooked Little Path where the moonlight is brightest. Peter is already listening with all his might.

His long ears turn toward a sound neither animal has heard before. Peter's teeth begin to chatter. Old Man Coyote's howl has come to the Green Meadows. Burgess taught natural history through animal talk. His bedtime stories ran in newspapers for decades.
4728-john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-comple:
Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., presents his memoir of John Lothrop Motley here in complete form, beginning with volume one. Holmes notes that the memoir rests on a biographical sketch prepared at the request of the Massachusetts Historical Society for its Proceedings. Questions involving controversies the Society could not enter are treated at length here, with details too long for a customary tribute.

The memoir opens in 1814 to 1827, with birth and early years to age thirteen. Motley's great-grandfather came from Belfast in Ireland to Falmouth, now Portland, Maine, in the earlier part of the last century. He married twice and had ten children, four by the first marriage and six by the last. Readers get the full Holmes memoir in one file, from childhood through historian, diplomat, and public man, in warm, old-fashioned prose.
47399-jack-the-young-cowboy-an-eastern-b:
George Bird Grinnell wrote a boys' tale of an Eastern lad on a Western round-up. Frederick A Stokes Company held the rights in New York in 1913. Four photos serve as pictures for the tale. Jack had starred as trapper, canoeman, explorer, and ranchman in prior books.

Chapters run from a tragedy at Powell's to cutting, branding, and riding circle. A bull fight, a buffalo tale, and a cowhand named Vicente add color. Grinnell knew the West at first hand and fills the tale with true work. Young readers gain a brisk guide to cow life told through a green boy's eyes.
47725-minnesota-the-north-star-state:
William Watts Folwell wrote Minnesota, the North Star State, for the American Commonwealths series, printed at Boston and New York in 1908. A map drawn by the author goes with it. The French period opens the contents, then the English dominion and Minnesota west annexed. Fort Snelling established, explorations and settlements, and the territory organized follow.

Territorial development, transition to statehood, and the struggle for railroads fill the middle. Arming for the Civil War, the outbreak of the Sioux, and the Sioux war come next. The sequel to the Indian war and honors close the list. The word Minnesota was the Dakota name for that large tributary of the Mississippi which flows from Big Stone Lake to Mankato, Folwell begins. A state gets its full history from its first university president.
4800-the-complete-poetical-works-of-perc:
The Complete Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley is the Oxford edition of 1914, edited with textual notes by Thomas Hutchinson, editor of the Oxford Wordsworth. Its preface says the edition contains all Shelley's ascertained poems and fragments of verse that have hitherto appeared in print. Hutchinson worked, as far as possible, on recognising the editio princeps, the first printed edition, as primary textual authority.

He was not content to reprint Mrs. Shelley's 1839 recension, or any later editor's. The present text results from a fresh collation of early editions, with rejected readings subjoined in footnotes. Wherever good reason appeared for superseding the editio princeps, as with Julian and Maddalo, the fact is announced and the substituted exemplar indicated in a prefatory note. Readers get Shelley's whole poetical work in a scholarly text, built from first editions rather than later reprints.
48392-chats-on-old-sheffield-plate:
Chats on Old Sheffield Plate is a collector's guide by Arthur Hayden. Fisher Unwin published the book at London, first in 1920 with a second printing in 1924. Hayden had written companion chats on old silver and old clocks. The book carries a frontispiece and fifty eight full page pictures, with five pages of makers' marks.

The opening chapter tells how silver plating by fusion was invented at Sheffield. Chapters then take up candlesticks, salt cellars, and cake baskets in turn. Tea and coffee sets, soup tureens, and centrepieces fill later parts. A closing chapter treats close plating, a cheaper cousin of the true Sheffield ware. Tables in the appendix give marks on old silver and on old Sheffield plate. The frontispiece shows a plated centrepiece of about 1775 to 1780, with wire baskets for glass dishes.
4860-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
This complete volume gathers John Lothrop Motley's history of the United Netherlands from 1586 to 1589, years when war, diplomacy, and invasion plots overlapped. It opens with Parma's river campaigns, Leicester's field command, and the death of Sir Philip Sidney after Zutphen, then moves through secret treaties and the Armada crisis.

The sweep covers Dutch towns held and lost along the Meuse and Rhine, English troops in Holland, and Spanish schemes against England and France. Motley keeps the focus on commanders and envoys whose choices linked all three countries. For readers who want the middle years of the revolt in one place, this span offers the full arc without hunting through separate parts.
4872-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Henry III of France's assassination reshapes Europe in this complete volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the Dutch response from 1590 to 1599. The Netherlands resolve to strike for freedom, organize a Dutch army, and surprise the castle of Breda by stratagem, opening a decade of steady recovery.

Across the span, Maurice's sieges, Spanish mutinies, and the politics of France and England intertwine, while Barneveld's diplomacy holds the republic's alliances together. Motley covers the whole arc in one place, from the shock of a king's murder to a republic confident enough to take the offensive. It suits readers who want the 1590s as a single story rather than scattered parts.
48732-les-mise-rables-v-2-5-cosette:
Victor Hugo's great novel Les Miserables reaches its second part, Cosette, in an authorized English translation by Lascelles Wraxall. The Boston edition came out in 1887. A picture shows Fauchelevent with the grave digger. The part opens not with Cosette but with the battle of Waterloo, told at full length.

Hugo walks the Nivelles road, Hougomont, and the plateau of Mont Saint Jean. He asks if Waterloo should be applauded at all. Then the tale turns to the ship Orion, where a convict number changes, and to Montfermeil, where a small girl alone in the dark meets a stranger. Thenardier at work and a doll on the stage mark Cosette's hard road to rescue.
4900-pg-edition-of-netherlands-series-co:
Charles V's abdication opens this complete edition of Motley's Netherlands history, and the scene sets the tone for all that follows. On October 25, 1555, the estates meet in the great hall of the Brussels palace. They have come to witness the emperor give up the rule he had long meant to surrender. Formal ceremony and deep feeling mark the day.

Motley describes the hall and the leading figures present. He weighs the character and career of Charles. Then he follows the emperor's retirement to Juste. The complete series carries the story through revolt, war, and republic building. For readers approaching Motley whole, this opening explains the empire the Dutch would soon defy.
4912-wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-cons:
John Richardson's tale of the Pontiac conspiracy opens with a survey of the American country still loyal to the English crown, preparing readers for scenes unfamiliar to Europeans. The novel then follows frontier conflict around the forts and forests where British authority met Native resistance after the French wars.

Wacousta, the mysterious figure at the story's heart, moves through sieges, disguises, and personal vendettas that bind the plot together. Richardson, who knew the frontier posts himself, gives the setting a soldier's detail. Readers get an early Canadian romance of war and revenge, written when the events were still within living memory.
49466-notes-of-a-private:
Notes of a Private, by John Milton Hubbard, recalls service in the Seventh Tennessee Regiment under Forrest. Hubbard rode with Company E in the cavalry corps of the Confederate army. His book bears a copyright of 1909 and was printed at Saint Louis in 1911.

Hubbard relies on his own memory for the sketches and portraits in these pages. The front matter prints his parole, signed at Gainesville, Alabama, in May 1865, and a note that he owned one horse. Chapters move from mustering in through raids and fights in five states. Davis Bridge, Corinth, Holly Springs, Fort Pillow, and Brices Cross Roads all figure in the tale. The book is given to Southern soldiers who stayed in the field to the end.
4966-waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-c:
Walter Scott's complete Waverley gathers the whole novel, from its playful deliberation over title and hero to Edward Waverley's adventures in the Jacobite rising of 1745. The preface weighs sounding surnames from history against sentimental ones, then sends its young English hero north to a Scotland divided by loyalty and rebellion.

Across the complete span, romance, war, and friendship test Waverley, and Scott's Scotland emerges in full color. The complete form suits readers who want the founding historical novel entire, without stopping between volumes. It remains the book that taught novelists how to set private lives against public history.
4969-the-belton-estate:
Anthony Trollope's Belton Estate opens with the remnants of the Amedroz family, after Mrs. Amedroz dies leaving Charles and Clara aged eight and six. Their father Bernard, lord of Belton Castle, is not vicious, not a gambler or drunkard, yet his peculiar character aggravates the children's loss in ways Trollope unfolds patiently.

Inheritance, marriage, and the estate itself become the questions on which the children's futures turn. Trollope studies how a flawed but not wicked parent shapes two lives. Readers get a domestic novel of property and affection, quieter than his political fiction but just as attentive to the moral weight of ordinary choices.
4973-frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-music:
Frederick Niecks's complete life of Chopin gathers the composer's whole story, from his ancestors and his father Nicholas's arrival in Poland to Frederick's birth, infancy, and family. Niecks opens with heredity itself, quoting Goethe on what a child owes father, mother, and grandparents, and Schopenhauer's formula for character and talent.

From those beginnings the biography follows Chopin through Paris, his loves, his publications, and his music, to the end of a short life. The complete form lets readers trace one artist from cradle to grave without gaps. It remains a standard life of Chopin, thorough, humane, and attentive to both the man and the musician.
4989-a-sweet-girl-graduate:
Mrs. L. T. Meade's Sweet Girl Graduate follows Priscilla Peel and her friends through college life at St. Benet's, from going out into the world to the delights of being a fresher. Chapters take in an unwilling at home, an eavesdropper, Miss Oliphant's room, St. Hilda's chapel, conspirators, and a trap that must be escaped.

Polly Singleton and pretty little Rosalind join the circle, and sealskin and pink coral mark the season's fashions. Meade writes for girls about friendship, study, and growing independence. Readers get a school story of the older kind, where college is both a place of learning and a training ground for character.
5000-the-notebooks-of-leonardo-da-vinci-:
Leonardo da Vinci's complete notebooks gather the master's writings on painting, sculpture, science, and invention in one place. The painting notes discuss the Last Supper's decay and restoration, while the sculpture notes trace the Sforza horse through thirteen manuscript passages, and other sections range across anatomy, water, flight, and machines.

Vasari's remark that Leonardo labored more by word than by deed frames the collection: the manuscripts are the work. Readers who want Leonardo whole, rather than in a single volume's slice, get the notebooks complete, with all their curiosity, observation, and unfinished brilliance intact.
50021-an-irish-precursor-of-dante:
Boswell wrote a study of an Irish precursor of Dante, printed in London in 1908 as number eighteen of the Grimm Library. The subject is the Vision of Heaven and Hell ascribed to the eighth century Irish saint Adamnan. Boswell gives the Irish text in translation beside the study. Dante's Commedia was preceded by a long series of visions of the otherworld, he shows, and the vision was a favourite subject with Irish writers of the middle ages.

Part one traces Adamnan himself: abbot of Iona, missions to Northumbria, talks with the Venerable Bede, and work in the Paschal dispute. His birth, parentage, and the meaning of his name are set out first. Students of Dante and of early Irish letters get the root stock of the heaven and hell journey here.
50195-practical-etiquette:
Practical Etiquette is a manual of good form by an author who signs only N C, published in Chicago by A Flanagan. This twentieth-thousand edition was copyrighted in 1899, entirely re-written and enlarged. The preface says it aims to answer every question of ordinary social life.

To speak with authority on good form, the author admits, is itself not good form, yet where opinions conflict she decides by common sense without citing authority. American custom, she notes, is now so uniform that good society is the same in West, North, East, and South. The chapters run from introductions, calls, and cards through notes of invitation and wedding invitations. Dinners, teas, receptions, and dancing parties follow, then conversation, chaperonage, dress, street etiquette, traveling, bicycling, and even telephoning. Table service, funerals and mourning, children's politeness, official etiquette, and business correspondence complete the code.
50865-the-german-pirate:
The German Pirate, His Methods and Record is a wartime exposé by an author signing as Ajax, published in London in 1918 by C Arthur Pearson. It charges German submarines with piracy and sets out case after case of merchant ships stopped, looted, and sunk in 1917.

A selection of cases opens the book: the Dutch steamer Gamma on February 1, 1917, then the Garnet Hill, the trawler Romeo, the Dauntless, and more through July. The first chapter, The Pirate as Thief, tells how the Gamma's crew were questioned while men took flour, hams, butter, and tools from her holds. The title pages quote Nietzsche and Bernhardi against the German case, framing the record as evidence for British readers.
50921-1-000-a-plate:
One Thousand Dollars a Plate is a science fiction story by Jack McKenty, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in October 1954, with illustrations by Beck. The scene is Mars, where a settlement lives under a pale sky. Even the travel books, the narrator jokes, praise the Canal Casino's new sign above the watery sunset.

The night sky redeems the planet: tourists stay up till sunrise with stiff necks. The craters of the moons show to the naked eye, and opera glasses pick out the buildings of the Deimos Space Station. When the Marsy Gras festival fires its skyrockets, Mars Observatory answers with fireworks of its own. McKenty builds his tale on that contrast between a drab colony by day and a splendid one by night, with a costly dinner promised by the title.
51278-grace-o-malley-princess-and-pirate:
Robert Machray set forth this tale of Grace O'Malley, princess and pirate. Cassell printed it in London and New York in 1898. Ruari MacDonald, redshank and rebel, stands as its named teller. Contents open with Grace saved from the sea in chapter one.

The princess begins her reign, a sword title deed follows next. The colonel of Connaught and the queen peace fill early chapters. Grace dances out of Galway and captures the Capitana ship. A chest of gold, a woman wile, and whispering rocks come. The siege raised and a dear victory mark the later chapters of the chronicle.
51438-hyde-park-from-domesday-book-to-da:
Hyde Park, from Domesday Book to Date is a history by John Ashton, published in London in 1896. Downey issued it with one map and twenty one illustrations. Ashton had written on social life under Queen Anne. His preface faults the only prior history of the park. Larwood's account stopped at 1825 as too near the present. Ashton sets out to carry the story from Domesday to his own day.

The contents begin with the forests round London and the manor of Eia. The manors of Hyde, Ebury, and Neate follow from Domesday. Henry the Eighth and Elizabeth take the park into royal hands. Deer, foxes, and the last shooting fill the first chapter. The Commonwealth sale and Cromwell's accident come next. A camp during the plague of 1665 and the Cheesecake House follow in order.
51686-marjorie-dean-post-graduate:
Pauline Lester's Marjorie Dean, Post-Graduate was published by the Burt Company in 1925. It opens the post-graduate series for girls of twelve to eighteen, whose companion volumes are Marjorie Dean, Marvelous Manager, Marjorie Dean at Hamilton Arms, and Marjorie Dean's Romance. Marjorie had already passed through Lester's high school and college series. The first chapter, On the Sands, gathers the young people on a moonlit beach. Hal Macy proposes a moonlight cruise in the Oriole.

Danny Seabrooke trades boasts with Hal over lifting Geraldine from the sand, and Jerry refuses the help with scorn. Lawrence Armitage strums a guitar and watches the squabble with amusement. The party's teasing covers Hal's plain devotion to Marjorie, who stays matter-of-fact. The series' pattern is set at once: friendship, mild rivalry, and clean fun, with the talk kept quick and the scenes short.
51698-the-little-man-who-wasn-t-quite:
Little Man Who Wasn t Quite is a science fiction story by William Stuart, from Galaxy of December 1961. Walker supplied the pictures for the magazine printing of the tale. Its narrator starts with Jonesy, skid row, and a man named Stanley in pieces. How much of Stanley was or wasn t there is the riddle at the core.

Skid row, the voice warns, holds horrors seen and unseen for the men who land there. Each man there keeps his own private collection of them, the narrator says. General opinion is to let them be, and the tale tests that cold wisdom. A half present man makes the horror literal in this grim short piece.
5181-inebriety-and-the-candidate:
George Crabbe's early volume pairs two poems: Inebriety, a mock-heroic poem on drunkenness, and The Candidate, a satire on a young man's hopes of preferment. Inebriety sings, with ironic grandeur, the spirit that stains the cheek and rules the head, following its votaries from winter drinking to ruined mornings.

Crabbe, later famous for realistic tales of village life, shows here his satiric beginnings. The two poems offer readers a lively example of Augustan wit applied to common vices, in verse that is both learned and sharply observant of human folly.
5186-kalevala-the-epic-poem-of-finland-c:
John Martin Crawford's 1888 translation presents the complete Kalevala, Finland's national epic, in fifty runes. It opens with the birth of Wainamoinen, follows his sowing, his contests. The fate of Aino follows, then the epic moves through Ilmarinen's forging of the Sampo, Lemminkainen's adventures, and the long tragedy of Kullervo.

Compiled by Elias Lonnrot from Finnish oral poetry, the Kalevala gave Finland a heroic past in song. Crawford's version was the first full English translation, and it remains a readable doorway into a world of singers, smiths, magic. The struggle for the Sampo, the wondrous mill of plenty, drives the epic.
51935-human-all-too-human-a-book-for-fre:
Part one of Nietzsche's Human, All-Too-Human, a book for free spirits, comes in Helen Zimmern's translation. It forms volume six of the Complete Works, the first complete and authorised English rendering, edited by Dr Oscar Levy. Foulis of Edinburgh and London issued it in 1909. Kennedy's introduction frames the book as the record of a crisis.

The contents run in nine divisions: first and last things, the history of the moral sentiment, the religious life. The soul of artists and authors, higher and lower culture, man in society, wife and child follow. A glance at the state ends the list, and an epode among friends closes the part. Kennedy contrasts the Wagner essay of 1876 with this book of 1878: the long essay gives way to aphorisms, some melancholy, some satirical, as Nietzsche shook off Wagner and Schopenhauer alike.
51938-daireen-complete:
Frank Frankfort Moore wrote this novel, and the Gutenberg copy notes a patch in its making. Chapters twenty to twenty-four came from a different edition, since they were missing from the 1889 print used for the rest. In those chapters, single quote marks stand where double marks are the rule elsewhere.

The tale opens with lines from Hamlet about an inheritor and the deeds of his lands. The Macnamara addresses his son with grand air, telling him he has forgotten what is due to himself. Due to his father and to forefathers who bled comes next, in a comic Irish scene of pride and drink.
5206-fires-and-firemen-from-the-eclectic:
This article from the Eclectic Magazine of May 1855, drawn from the Quarterly Review, reports on London's Fire Brigade through the annual reports of its superintendent, James Braidwood. It describes fire stations, their sentinel on duty, and the polished engines, gleaming branches, and shining chains kept ready for instant service.

The writer follows a brigade dash through crowded streets, horses foaming, to a burning house, where hoses, pumps, and daring firemen fight the flames before a cheering crowd. The piece offers a vivid contemporary portrait of Victorian firefighting, and of the men who attacked fire as hunters attack a wild beast.
5240-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's complete Confessions of Harry Lorrequer gathers the whole comic career of its young Irish soldier hero. From his arrival in Cork, with civic festivities and private theatricals, through detachment duty, life at Callonby, duels, priests' suppers, and love affairs, Harry recounts scrape after scrape in high spirits.

Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds the full novel from first chapter to last. Readers get Lever's early masterpiece entire: military humour, Irish character, and a hero whose confessions charm precisely because he never quite learns from them.
5245-tales-from-the-arabic-complete:
John Payne's complete Tales from the Arabic gathers his full translation of stories from the Breslau and Calcutta editions of the Thousand Nights and One Night. Those stories do not appear in other printed texts. Across three volumes, readers meet Asleep and Awake, the Ten Viziers, King Shah Bekht and his vizier, Noureddin Ali of Damascus, and the merchant of Cairo.

The collection closes with Sindbad the Sailor, including his sixth and seventh voyages. It adds tables of contents for the Calcutta and Boulac editions. Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds Payne's whole translation, offering a fuller Arabian Nights than the familiar versions provide.
52507-anthony-the-absolute:
Samuel Merwin wrote this novel, published by the Century Company in New York in 1914. Crosby illustrated the book for its first readers. The tale opens at sea on March 28th, in the voice of its hero, Anthony, writing as he travels.

Anthony told a titled fellow passenger that evening that the man was a fool, and holds he was quite right. The man presides nightly over a round table in the smoking-room, sipping coffee and liqueur. He holds forth on every subject as if each were his own, a judge in Malaysia with a monocle and a drooping eyelid.
52666-glimpses-of-ocean-life-or-rock-poo:
Glimpses of Ocean Life, or Rock-Pools and the Lessons They Teach, is John Harper's seaside natural history. T Nelson and Sons of London, Edinburgh, and New York published it in 1860. Harper drew the numerous illustrations himself, and the book opens with plates of the Pholas shell, the common brittle star, and the cross-fish. He dedicated the volume to Lord Brougham.

An opening quotation from Rhymer Jones sets the frame: natural history is the handmaiden of religion, showing how carefully every creature is fitted to its station. The chapters begin with the shore itself, then turn to the invisible world of the microscope, its infusoria and wheel animalcules. Harper wrote for the aquarium craze of the day, teaching holiday rock-pool hunters to see design and wonder in a bucket of seawater.
5300-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
Jean de La Fontaine's complete Tales and Novels gathers the whole collection in English verse translation, from Joconde through the cudgelled cuckold, the husband confessor, the cobbler. The peasant and his angry lord lead on through the magick cup, the falcon, the eel pie, Belphegor, and many more.

Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds the full text, with La Fontaine's life and preface opening the book. Readers get the tales entire: bawdy, witty, and moral by turns, in the translation that first made La Fontaine's tales widely available to English readers.
53027-a-treatise-on-tobacco-tea-coffee-a:
Simon Pauli's Treatise on Tobacco, Tea, Coffee, and Chocolate came out at London in 1746, in Doctor James's translation. It weighs four fashionable commodities on the principles of medicine and chemistry, checked by observation and experience. The title page promises full directions for knowing in what cases, and for what constitutions, each substance helps or hurts. A third claim argues that Chinese or Asiatic tea is the same plant as the European Chamaelaeagnus, or Myrtus Brabantica. Copper plates show the tea utensils of the Chinese and Persians.

The tobacco section follows Monardus: the plant, called Picielt by the Indians, came from New Spain, was grown in Spanish gardens for ornament, and grew famous for curing wounds. Pauli writes for Osborne in Gray's Inn, with sellers at York, Newcastle, and Bath. The Latin motto from Celsus bids the reader know the nature of the body first.
5355-guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-com:
Sir Walter Scott's complete Guy Mannering gathers the whole novel of astrology, smuggling, and a lost heir in the Scottish border country. From the astrologer's casting of a child's horoscope through the smugglers' plots, the laird's schemes, and the mystery of Harry Bertram's fate, the story runs its full course.

Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds the novel entire, from its introduction on Waverley's success to its final revelations. Readers get Scott's second Waverley novel complete, with its border characters, its humour, and its famous Meg Merrilies, in a single narrative.
5364-the-inside-of-the-cup-complete:
Winston Churchill's complete Inside of the Cup gathers the whole novel of rector John Hodder and his fashionable St John's parish. From the Waring problems and Mr Langmaid's mission through the primrose path and the riddles of the twentieth century, the story follows Hodder's growing discontent, his winter at Winterbourne, and his reconstruction.

Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds the novel entire, from its opening chapters to retribution and light. Readers get Churchill's full study of faith, wealth, and social conscience in early twentieth-century America, in a single continuous narrative.
5373-richard-carvel-complete:
Winston Churchill's complete Richard Carvel gathers the whole Maryland romance. It runs from Lionel Carvel of Carvel Hall and memories of childhood, through over the wall and under false colours, to London town, the Serapis, and I come to my own again.

Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds the novel entire. It follows Richard from boyhood at Carvel Hall through revolution, sea war, and love. Readers get Churchill's full historical romance in a single narrative, with Dorothy, the duke, and the cause itself carried to their conclusions.
5382-a-modern-chronicle-complete:
Winston Churchill's complete Modern Chronicle gathers the whole story of Honora. It runs from her glimpse of the world in Book One through the Olympian order, Stafford Park, and the new doctrine, to her later years. Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds the chronicle entire, following Honora through marriage, society, and self-discovery.

Churchill writes a novel of modern American life, in which heredity, temperament, and providence are weighed against a woman's own choices. Readers get the full arc of Honora's life, from provincial girlhood to the mirror held up in her maturity, in a single continuous narrative.
5387-the-celebrity-complete:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, tells this story through a friend who knew the title figure before fame ever touched him. The narrator recalls an ordinary young man from their New York days, then watches him turn into a celebrated author after moving west. Set among drawing rooms, summer resorts, and admiring social circles, the novel follows that rise from close quarters.

The humor comes from the gap between the man and his reputation. Admirers project genius onto him, hosts compete for his company, and the narrator reports it all with dry amusement. Readers get a light satire of literary fame, showing how quickly society can turn a writer into a public curiosity.
5396-the-crisis-complete:
Winston Churchill's complete Crisis gathers the whole Civil War novel, from its opening chapters on origins, the mole, and unattainable simplicity. Bellegarde, a quiet Sunday in Locust Street, and the party follow. Raw material, Abraham Lincoln, the crisis itself, and the armies of the West come next.

Unlike the separate volumes in this library, this record holds the novel entire, following Stephen Brice through St Louis, Sumter, and the war. Readers get Churchill's full portrait of a border city divided by war. A young man choosing his loyalties stands at its centre, in a single continuous narrative.
54097-black-is-white:
George Barr McCutcheon's Black Is White was published in London in 1915 by Everett and Company. McCutcheon was by then the author of Graustark and Brewster's Millions. His first chapter seats two very old men in a library, staring at a blue envelope on the table by the fire.

The envelope holds a wonder the old men cannot grasp: a wireless message, come out of the air from far out on the Atlantic. They have sailed the seven seas and crossed all lands, they boast. Yet a man speaking a thousand miles off, his words lying on a table, is a new thing under the sun. Even the maid who poked the fire came and went unseen while they stared.
5416-the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-compl:
Anthony Hamilton wrote the Memoirs of Count Grammont about the French courtier Philibert de Grammont, and Sir Walter Scott edited them with notes. This complete edition gathers all eleven chapters, from Grammont's arrival at the siege of Trino and his early education and adventures, through Turin and the French court, to his time in England. A biographical sketch of Hamilton opens the book.

The memoirs move from sieges and banishment to love affairs, court rivalries, and marriages among Grammont's circle. Hamilton tells it as a participant's story, witty and frank about the people he knew. Readers get the whole arc in one volume, a classic of court gossip and seventeenth-century life.
54303-john-holdsworth-chief-mate:
John Holdsworth, Chief Mate is a sea novel by Clark Russell. Sampson Low published this sixth and cheaper edition in London in 1889. Russell also wrote The Wreck of the Grosvenor and A Sea Queen. A list of his sea tales fills the front pages here. The contents open at Southbourne on the coast. To the Downs and Down Channel take the ship to sea. In the Atlantic and A Gale of Wind follow in order.

Taken Aback stands sixth among the chapter heads. In the Boats begins the survival story at chapter seven. The Second Day through the Seventh Day count the ordeal. The Tenth Day continues the count of days adrift. Russell's readers knew him for storm and wreck realism. The chapter heads alone tell a tale of a ship lost. Holdsworth's rank of chief mate puts him in command of the boats.
54583-brian-fitz-count-a-story-of-wallin:
Crake, a clergyman and fellow of the Royal Historical Society, wrote Brian Fitz-Count, a tale of Wallingford Castle and Dorchester Abbey published in London in 1888. Crake had already written the Chronicles of Aescendune, stories of Saxon England. This novel moves later, into the Norman world of castles, abbeys, and civil war in the reign of King Stephen.

The story opens on the evening of September 30, 1139, with Brian Fitz-Count pacing the ramparts above the Thames. Brian holds Wallingford by marriage to the Lady Maude, widow of Baron Milo Crispin, and his lands stretch from Wales to Cornwall. Chapters that follow bring a chase in the greenwood, prisoners, lepers, a new novice at the abbey, and an escape from Oxford Castle. Later pages reach a pestilence, a sanctuary, and a journey to the Holy Land. Readers get a rich picture of twelfth-century life told through one baron's household.
5460-an-egyptian-princess-complete:
Georg Ebers wrote An Egyptian Princess as a historical romance of ancient Egypt and Persia, translated from the German by Eleanor Grove. This complete edition gathers the whole story, from its Egyptian court beginnings to Babylon and the Persian royal household. The preface to the second German edition shows Ebers revising carefully, calling the book a corrected edition and comparing an author to a father sending a child out anew.

Nitetis, the Egyptian princess, stands at the center, caught between Egyptian custom and Persian power. Court intrigue, temple politics, rescue plots, and royal marriages carry the long narrative. Readers get Ebers's full romance in one volume, rich in historical detail and old-fashioned storytelling.
5466-the-sisters-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Sisters, translated from the German by Clara Bell, appears here in its complete form. Ebers dedicates the book to his friend Eduard von Hallberger, recalling twenty years of unbroken friendship and four earlier works published under Hallberger's care. This fifth book, partly written at Hallberger's home in Tutzing, was meant as a special token of thanks.

The romance itself follows sisters caught between Greek and Egyptian worlds in ancient Memphis, with palace life, temples, and family loyalty at its center. Ebers writes as a scholar as well as a storyteller. Readers get the full novel in one volume, detailed, earnest, and steeped in Egypt.
5472-joshua-complete:
Georg Ebers's Joshua, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, appears here complete. Ebers explains in the preface that he resolved the previous winter to finish the book, and that he had meant to dedicate it to his dear friend Gustav Baur. Baur died a few months earlier, so the book goes out instead to his memory, praised for a sunny nature and brilliant mind.

The novel retells the biblical story of Joshua, called Hosea in Egypt, from Egyptian court life through the Exodus toward the promised land. Ebers writes as a scholar of the ancient Near East. Readers get the full romance in one volume, earnest, detailed, and shaped by nineteenth-century biblical scholarship.
5482-cleopatra-complete:
Georg Ebers's Cleopatra, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, appears here complete in twenty-five chapters. The preface answers a doubt about love in the pagan world by pointing to Antony and Cleopatra, and to the Roman general's will expressing his wish to rest beside her. Ebers treats their love as historical fact, not modern invention.

The novel follows Cleopatra's Alexandria through Barine, her family, her attendants Iras and Charmian, and the Roman power pressing on Egypt. Art, politics, and romance interweave across the whole arc. Readers get Ebers's fullest Egyptian romance in one volume, rich in court detail and tragic momentum.
5493-the-emperor-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Emperor, translated by Clara Bell, appears here complete, gathering both parts of the Hadrian romance. Ebers explains in the preface that he planned the story fourteen years earlier, from lectures on Roman rule in Egypt. Scientific work delayed it, and only later did he set it in Hadrian's time, after treating the early monks in Homo Sum.

The novel follows Hadrian's Alexandria through architects, artists, stewards, and citizens, from building projects to baptisms and departures. Ebers grounds court and workshop in historical study. Readers get the whole imperial romance in one volume, broad, detailed, and full of Alexandrine life.
5499-homo-sum-complete:
Georg Ebers's Homo Sum, translated by Clara Bell, appears here complete. The preface traces it to Ebers's work on a history of the Sinaitic peninsula, where study of early Christianity led him through martyrdom accounts, ascetic writings, and lives of saints and monks. In Cotelerius's collection he found a narrative that seemed peculiar and touching despite its improbability, set at Sinai and the oasis of Pharan below it.

The novel follows hermits Paulus, Hermas, and their circle through temptation, remorse, and faith in the desert. Ebers writes as a historian of the first Christian centuries. Readers get the full romance in one volume, serious, atmospheric, and rooted in desert monastic life.
5507-serapis-complete:
Georg Ebers's Serapis, translated from the German by Clara Bell, appears here complete. It opens on a hushed Alexandrine night, with moon and stars watching over closed houses and shops, and an oppressive, fevered tension in the air. For some weeks, night itself has felt strained, as if the city waits for a blow.

The novel follows performers, priests, and citizens through the last days of the Serapeum, as pagan worship and Christian power collide in late Roman Alexandria. Hippodrome races, temple rites, and household escapes fill the long arc. Readers get Ebers's fullest late-antique romance in one volume, dramatic and richly peopled.
55122-the-athelings-or-the-three-gifts-c:
The Athelings, or The Three Gifts is a novel by Margaret Oliphant, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1857. It first appeared in Blackwood's Magazine. The first book, Bellevue, opens in a street. It is a spring afternoon, cheery but cold, and lamps and shop-windows shine through the ruddy twilight.

Down the suburban street walk two young women dressed entirely alike. One is very pretty, eighteen years old, with the sweetest girl's face imaginable under her simple bonnet. People smile when they pass her, unawares, and she thinks it is because everybody is amiable. The other is twenty, taller and paler, and as far from commonplace as can be conceived. Their brown merino dresses and cloaks match to the last ribbon and rosebud. Oliphant sets her tale of the three gifts among sombre lines of houses and smoky evergreens. The novel is an early work of a great Victorian storyteller.
5516-arachne-complete:
Georg Ebers's Arachne, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, appears here complete. It opens in deep silence over water and green islands, where palms and sycamores cast long shadows and waterfowl fly under flecked clouds. From that quiet landscape, the romance of artists in ancient Alexandria unfolds across its books.

Hermon the sculptor, Ledscha, Daphne, and their circle pursue art, love, and rivalry, with statues, fires, and night meetings marking the way. Ebers writes about making art with a maker's attention. Readers get the full novel in one volume, graceful, romantic, and steeped in the ancient city.
5529-the-bride-of-the-nile-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile, translated from the German by Clara Bell, appears here complete. The preface explains Ebers's view that Mukaukas is a title rather than a name, following de Goeje and Arab writers who apply it to Byzantine representatives facing Muslim power. He also notes Horapollo, the ancient writer placed in the seventh century, as part of his historical frame.

The novel follows Paula, Orion, Philippus, and their circle through Byzantine Egypt at the Arab conquest, with trials, prisons, river journeys, and love affairs. Ebers grounds romance in scholarship. Readers get the full novel in one volume, long, detailed, and full of Nile life.
5542-a-thorny-path-complete:
Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path appears here complete, opening in Heron the gem-cutter's Alexandrine studio. His daughter Melissa raises a green screen over the broad window, letting blinding autumn sunlight flood the room, until her father's impatient voice calls enough and his busy fingers return to work. An hour later, Melissa acts again without bidding, setting the household's rhythm.

The long novel follows Melissa, Andreas, and their circle through Caracalla's Alexandria, where Christians, gem-cutters, priests, and soldiers cross paths. Ebers writes a city under imperial pressure. Readers get the full romance in one volume, rich in craft, faith, and family feeling.
55478-the-game-birds-of-the-coasts-and-l:
The Game-Birds of the Coasts and Lakes of the Northern States of America is a sporting book by Robert Roosevelt, published by Carleton of New York in 1866. Its subtitle promises a full account of the sporting along the seashores and inland waters. It also compares the merits of breech-loaders and muzzle-loaders. Roosevelt's sporting works were issued uniform with this volume at two dollars.

The first chapter treats the game of ancient and modern days, its protection and importance, the proper shooting seasons, and the folly of batteries and pivot-guns. The second compares guns and gunnery, with a sharp review of a rival shooting book and a field trial. Bay-snipe shooting follows, with the birds, their habits, and their mode of capture. Later chapter summaries, preserved in the copy, reach the New Jersey coast.
5551-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, complete, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, tells a romance of old Nuremberg. It opens on the eve of Saint Medard's Day in 1281. Moonlight falls on the imperial free city, on the street from the Marienthurm to the Frauenthor, and on the Ortlieb mansion barred by house, watchtower, and a tall linden tree. Emperor Rudolph shelters in the city with secular and church lords.

The long novel follows the Ortlieb household, sisters, knights, and monks through medieval Nuremberg. Ebers writes the walled city in loving detail. Readers get the full romance in one volume, rich in family feeling and old German civic life.
5560-margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nurember:
Georg Ebers's Margery, complete, translated from the German by Clara Bell, tells a tale of old Nuremberg in its heroine's voice. The translator's note explains the book as a transcript into modern German of fifteenth-century Nuremberg language, avoiding period English imitation and merely shunning modern words. An introduction opens with a Venetian merchant's receipt, signed by an antiquary in the city of St. Mark.

Margery's story follows council families, brothers, suitors, and imperial visits across her young life. Ebers writes old Germany intimately, through daily detail. Readers get the full tale in one volume, charming, old-fashioned, and full of Nuremberg civic life.
55644-pedestrianism-or-an-account-of-the:
An unnamed writer, the author of a history of Aberdeen, set down Pedestrianism at Aberdeen in 1813. The book gives an account of the feats of famed walkers of the last and present centuries, with a tale of Captain Barclay's public and private matches. A closing essay treats training. The preface says the author meant at first to treat Barclay alone, then widened the plan to take in other walkers.

The author holds the subject weighty in a time of war, when the strength of the body is called on in the field. Greece trained its youth in gyms, and Rome by long marches and running. British troops at home, he charges, waste their time in idle rest on a plea of saving cost. The book is an early record of long-distance walking as a sport of bets and crowds.
5571-barbara-blomberg-complete:
Georg Ebers's Barbara Blomberg, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, appears here complete. It opens at the Golden Cross in Ratisbon, where sunlight plays on little round panes and a party of nobles, churchmen, and knights from the emperor's train comes out into spring breeze. Courtiers in the chapel start as a door bangs, and a corporal growls April weather.

The long novel follows Barbara, a singer who becomes Emperor Charles's love, through Ratisbon, Brussels, and married life, with Wolf, Pyramus, and court figures around her. Ebers writes music, favor, and family across decades. Readers get the full romance in one volume, sweeping and richly peopled.
5577-a-word-only-a-word-complete:
Georg Ebers's A Word, Only a Word, complete, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, opens with a boy's cry in a forest. Two hands clap, a gay laugh echoes, a wood pigeon joins in, and a startled jay spreads brown wings flecked with blue, soaring from pine to pine. Spring entered the Black Forest weeks before, May just ended, yet weather stays sultry as midsummer while clouds gather denser.

The long novel follows Ulrich from forest boyhood through soldiers, courts, and Spain to the Netherlands, with a single word carrying honor and fate. Ebers writes a sixteenth-century life in full. Readers get the complete romance in one volume, warm, adventurous, and richly peopled.
5583-the-burgomaster-s-wife-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Burgomaster's Wife, complete, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, opens with a dedication to Baroness Sophie von Brandenstein, his father's only sister. Ebers recalls her faithful friendship from childhood and his labor as her guest seventeen years earlier, arranging the material that became this book. She took friendly interest in notes of facts that seemed extraordinary, admirable, or amusing.

The novel follows Van der Werff's wife through the Spanish siege of Leyden, with rain, plague, secret councils, and civic courage. Ebers writes a city's resistance through one household. Readers get the full siege romance in one volume, earnest, detailed, and humane.
55849-truth-ve-rite:
Truth is a tale by Emile Zola, in English dress by Ernest Vizetelly, out in nineteen three. The tale opens in the first days of August of a hot year. A school man, his wife, and their small girl have come to a town to spend a month of rest past the kin of his wife. Two old wives of that house are named as those ladies by all the town.

A storm had marred the prize day of the past week, and a flood of rain fell that night. The sky stays low and thick at dawn. The ladies rise at six to be set for the church rite at seven. Their maid brings the drink pot and grumps that it will be cold, and not by her fault. The dame rails that the school man takes joy in late starts.
5587-in-the-blue-pike-complete:
Georg Ebers's In the Blue Pike, complete, translated from the German by Mary T. Safford, opens with a rough fellow's curse in a crowded street. He points out of doors, scarcely lowering his strange voice. Only two listeners understand him: a fading, sickly girl and the red-haired woman, a few years older, who leads him by a chain like a tame bear. Nuremberg magistrates had earlier cut out Cyriax's tongue.

The novel follows Kuni, Loni, and their wandering company through pilgrimages, taverns, and shrines, from Altotting toward Santiago di Compostella. Ebers writes outcast performers with sympathy. Readers get the full tale in one volume, rough, devout, and full of road life.
55948-the-abysmal-brute:
The Abysmal Brute is a prize-fight tale by Jack London, printed in 1913. The Century Company of New York brought the book out that year. London had writ The Call of the Wild and The Sea Wolf before. Sam Stubener, a manager of prize-fighters, opens the tale at his mail. Cranks, sports, and reformers all wrote to him with ideas to impart.

Dire threats, rabbit-foot fetishes, and lucky horse-shoes filled that mail. Quarter-million offers from irresponsible nobodies stood among the daily surprises. A razor-strop from a lynched man's skin had come to him once. A withered finger from Death Valley had reached him another time. Nothing could startle him again, he thought, till one letter came. It bore a postmark from an unheard-of office in Siskiyou County. An old fighter writes of a boy who can hit like a kick.
5599-the-story-of-my-life-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Story of My Life, from childhood to manhood, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, appears here complete, addressed to his sons in verse. Ebers urges himself to search the harvest of vanished years. His struggles upward to the light may guide his loved ones, and his errors may seem less black if they serve his children aright. The chapters then run from glancing backward through earliest childhood, festal days, Holland, and the Lennestrasse to art, revolution, Keilhau, and university.

The autobiography follows a Berlin boy to a scholar's manhood, through sculptors, schools, and 1848. Readers get Ebers's whole early life in one volume, warm, detailed, and full of nineteenth-century Germany.
56305-the-moon-considered-as-a-planet-a-:
James Nasmyth and James Carpenter wrote The Moon: Considered as a Planet, a World, and a Satellite, published by John Murray in 1874. Twenty-four plates of lunar views back the text. Carpenter had served at the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, and Nasmyth signs as an engineer. The preface says plainly what the book will not do.

Topography and the moon's paths through space are left to other works. The pair take up the face of the moon itself: its craters and marks, and the volcanic force they think shaped them. Years of watching through strong telescopes ground their claims. They link the moon's story to the broad scheme of how planets form, and hint the same laws hold for other worlds.
56325-sea-scouts-abroad-further-adventur:
Sea Scouts Abroad, further adventures of the Olivette, is a boys sea story by Percy Westerman. Westerman was a lieutenant in the Royal Air Force, as the title page states. His other tales listed at the front include The Submarine Hunters and With Beatty off Jutland. A press notice at the front says no boy alive will read his pages without a quickening of his pulses.

The Olivette is the craft of his Sea Scouts, met first in Sea Scouts All, which told how she was won. This volume takes the crew abroad in her for further adventures at sea. Westerman wrote for boys between the wars, when scouting and seamanship were paired in the public mind. His books turn drill, tides, and boat handling into plot, and this one sends its young crew beyond home waters to prove what they learned there.
56353-pyrometry-a-practical-treatise-on-:
A practical treatise on pyrometry, the measurement of high temperatures, comes from the author of Heat for Engineers. The technical problem is plain: ordinary thermometers fail where furnaces and molten metal glow in the works. Industry in steel, glass, and ceramics depends on knowing such heat exactly, in each of these trades.

A treatise of this kind surveys the instruments devised for the task, and it sets them out in their standard families. Thermoelectric couples, resistance devices, and radiation instruments form those families, as set out in the text of the treatise. The author wrote for engineers who must control heat in works practice, and he wrote it for use at work. Tables, calibration, and error sources matter more than theory here, in the professional literature that made high temperature industry a measured science.
5650-sketches-by-seymour-complete:
Sketches by Seymour, complete, gathers the comic illustrated sketches published in various versions about 1836. The editor's introduction explains that the copy used has no date and was published by Thomas Fry in London. Some of ninety plates bear only Seymour's name, and many read engravings by Wallis from sketches by Seymour. The printed book compiles five smaller volumes.

From confused chapter titles, readers may suspect the printer mixed up the chapters' order. This digital edition splits the complete book into five smaller volumes of manageable size. Readers get the whole comic collection, with plates and verse jokes, in one place.
56517-the-philosophy-of-auguste-comte:
The Philosophy of Auguste Comte is a systematic study of the founder of Positivism by Lévy-Bruhl, a teacher of philosophy at the University of Paris. Swan Sonnenschein published the authorized English rendering at London in 1903. Frederic Harrison, an Oxford fellow, wrote the opening words. The French book appeared in 1900 and was called an event in the Positive movement's story.

Harrison notes that a fresh stir came in 1903, when a statue of Comte was unveiled in the Place de la Sorbonne before a world gathering. Comte had then been dead forty-five years. A translation was urgently wanted, and Harrison was asked to present it. The study weighs Comte's whole lifework from inside the movement he founded.
5668-the-arabian-nights-entertainments-c:
The Arabian Nights Entertainments, complete, presents the Aldine Edition illustrated by S. L. Wood from the text of Dr. Jonathan Scott, in four volumes. The publishers' preface explains the series as artistic reprints of standard English fiction, well illustrated, with texts carefully chosen from approved editions and made as typographically perfect as possible. A small paper edition for America was limited to five hundred copies.

The complete set carries the Sultaness's thousand and one stories from first volume to last, with genii, lamps, sleepers awakened, and caliphs. Readers get the whole Arabian Nights in the handsome Aldine form, for reading straight through.
5674-hector-s-inheritance-or-the-boys-of:
Horatio Alger tells a school story built around a boy, a disputed fortune, and a fresh start away from home. The opening finds Mr. Roscoe alone in his grand house, turning over letters and telling himself that boldness may win him everything he wants. Hector soon learns a secret, leaves home, and enters Smith Institute, where the chapter titles promise a playground bully, lessons in Virgil, shared meals, and a coming clash.

Readers follow Hector as he tests himself among new schoolmates, stands up to pressure, and tries to earn his place rather than inherit it.
