The novel moves briskly from household scheming to classroom and playground scenes, and its plain moral is that steady work and courage count more than a family name or a sudden windfall.
5710-a-dissertation-on-horses-wherein-it:
William Osmer's Dissertation on Horses was printed in London in 1756. It argues from fact and philosophy that horses have no innate qualities. Their excellence, Osmer says, is mechanical rather than a matter of blood. Osmer sets himself against the common belief that fine breeding alone explains a good horse, and he builds his case on observed performance and reasoned principle.

Here is a window into eighteenth-century thinking about animals, sport, and nature versus training. The argument is bold for its time, since it questions pedigree in an age that prized it. Students of horse history, early science, and Enlightenment debate will find a short, pointed treatise that still raises a live question: how much of excellence is born, and how much is made?
57102-songs-of-the-common-day-and-ave-an:
Charles G D Roberts sings the farm year of the Maritimes in a book of poems issued at Toronto in 1893. William Briggs published it. He dedicates the work to Bliss Carman, his friend and kinsman.

A run of sonnets forms the heart of the book. Their titles read like a work diary: The Furrow, The Sower, The Mowing, The Potato Harvest. Frogs, salt flats, fir woods, and pea-fields follow. The summer pool and the cicada in the firs get their turns. Seven sonnets are reprinted from his earlier In Divers Tones to complete the set. The volume closes with an ode for the centenary of Shelley's birth. It first came out in a printing of two hundred copies. Roberts helped found a Canadian school of nature verse.
57556-doctor-rabbit-and-ki-yi-coyote:
Doctor Rabbit and Ki Yi Coyote is a children animal tale by Thomas Clark Hinkle, published in 1918. Rand McNally issued the book at Chicago as part of the Greenwoods series. Hinkle dedicates it to two children named by pet names in the front pages. Contents list the adventures of the doctor among his woodland patients.

Doctor Rabbit Gets a Call and In Fear of Ki Yi Coyote open the book in order. The Holes Under the Trees and Doctoring Billy Rabbit follow in the contents of the tale. Ki Yi Coyote Chases Doctor Rabbit and Doctor Rabbit Gets a Scare raise the danger in the list. Hinkle doctor is the wise rabbit of the prairie woods, forever outtalking the coyote who would eat his patients. His tales brought the Western animals into the nursery in the years when the Brer Rabbit tradition was passing into new hands.
57710-a-son-of-the-state:
Son of the State is a novel by W Pett Ridge, author of Mord Em'ly. The London edition is dated nineteen oh two. Chapter one opens under a round white September moon in a London street. Pitfield Street is lit from end to end by that moon, the tale begins. The gas lights in the shop windows look abashed and needless beside it.

Men on wooden seats read halfpenny evening papers as if it were day. At a music hall the early crowd streams out flushed with two hours of joy for twopence. The late crowd, waiting patiently at the doors, flows in to take their places. Shoppers reclaim the street after. A further crowd blocks the path outside a public house, gazing up at a lighted room.
58135-the-saint-s-everlasting-rest-a-tre:
The Saint's Everlasting Rest, a treatise of the blessed state of the saints in their enjoyment of God in heaven, was written by Richard Baxter and abridged by Benjamin Fawcett. This edition was published at Charlestown, Massachusetts, in 1811 by Armstrong. A front address speaks to the inhabitants of Kidderminster, magistrates and people, Baxter's own town.

The address recalls that the substance of the book was first preached in Kidderminster's parish church. Baxter's name and writings, it says, have made the town famous through the Protestant world. Fawcett's abridgment keeps Baxter's great subject: heaven as rest, urged on the reader as a motive for a holy life. Baxter's preface to another work is quoted in praise: such old and excellent writings should be brought out of oblivion and dust.
583-the-woman-in-white:
Wilkie Collins builds a sensation novel of identity, madness, and law in this multi-voiced tale. Walter Hartright, a drawing teacher, meets a woman in white on a midnight road. He then takes a post at Limmeridge House, where Laura Fairlie and her sharp sister Marian face a villainous count and a scheming husband. Many narrators tell the story in three epochs.

Collins writes with legal care, letting each witness add a piece, from lawyers to housekeepers to tombstones. The plot turns on switched identities, asylums, and a secret that must be proved. The novel endures as a founding mystery, where patience and resolve beat rank and gold.
58323-the-three-brothers-complete:
Mrs Oliphant wrote The Three Brothers, a novel in three volumes. Hurst and Blackett issued Volume One at London in 1870. Oliphant had written the Chronicles of Carlingford before this. Salem Chapel and The Minister's Wife bear her name too. Twenty-one chapters fill this first volume. Their Father opens the tale.

The Will and The New Career follow in turn. The Eldest Son and The Magician's Cave build the middle. Mrs Tracy's IOU and Ben's Reward add debts and gains. Millicent makes a new start late in the book. Laurie's Work and Kensington Gore close the volume. The tale starts with why the Renton sons went out poor. Rich boys cast loose need a cause, Oliphant says, and she gives it before the brothers' lives unfold.
58443-grania-the-story-of-an-island-comp:
Emily Lawless wrote Grania, the Story of an Island, for Smith, Elder at London in 1892. The complete tale runs in two volumes, and Lawless had won note with Hurrish before it. A plate shows the islands of Aran in Galway Bay. Lawless gives the tale to a friend who helped plan it from the start. That friend helped out its meagre scraps of Gaelic as the work grew.

The pair had agreed to try an Irish story without any Irish brogue in it. No figure on the small stage is supposed to speak a word of English. Aran, Lawless says, is a melancholy place, and the tale has caught its gloom in full. A flash of light on the sails of a fishing hooker opens the scene. Lawless gives island life, sea, and sorrow in grave, spare prose.
58449-the-military-sketch-book-vol-1-of-:
An unnamed line officer told tales of seventeen years in arms at home and abroad. His Military Sketch-Book came out in London in 1827. Volume one of two is this copy of the set. A press note at its front hails a work called The Lancers. A quote on verse heads it: a man who tells of field and fight.

Camp life, marches, fights, and fair scenes mix in his tales. Cheer and grief stand side by side in the sketch way. The book came from a hand that had marched those roads. Gear, grub, chiefs, and mess mates fill the day-to-day parts. War past fans get a rank voice of the old wars. Each sketch stands alone.
59082-the-sense-of-taste:
Two Columbia University psychologists, Hollingworth and Poffenberger, wrote The Sense of Taste, published by Moffat, Yard and Company in New York in 1917. The book belongs to the Our Senses series. Its editor opens with a general word on why the senses deserve study by ordinary readers.

The senses, he says, are living gateways between ourselves and a changing world. Through them come both our comfort in life and all our direct knowledge. The series aims to join sound technical knowledge with broad human interest, at a low price. Within that frame, this volume takes up taste: how the tongue and mouth sort sweet, salt, sour, and bitter, and how taste guides eating, health, and pleasure. It suits readers who want science written plainly.
5921-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Cervantes's Don Quixote, volume one complete, in the Ormsby translation, runs from a gentleman reader of romances to a knight carried home enchanted in a cage. Quixote is dubbed at an inn, rides out with Sancho, mistakes windmills and inns for giants and castles, meets goatherds and shepherds, and suffers penance in the Sierra Morena. Inn tales, a captive's story, and friends' schemes to bring him home fill the later chapters.

The pages offer the full first part of the great comic novel, where madness, friendship, and storytelling contend for the truth. Sancho's proverbs balance Quixote's ideals, and every adventure tests whether books or life teach better. The volume suits first-time readers wanting the whole arc, and rereaders who enjoy Cervantes's nested tales, debates, and laughter in one continuous journey.
5946-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Cervantes's Don Quixote, volume two complete, in the Ormsby translation, follows the knight from home interview to deathbed will. Quixote sallies again with Sancho, meets the Knight of the Mirrors, celebrates Camacho's wedding, descends into the cave of Montesinos, and laughs at Master Pedro's puppets. The duke and duchess stage enchantments, Sancho governs an island, Barcelona brings the enchanted head and the White Moon's defeat, and the knight returns home to die.

It offers the full second part, richer and stranger than the first, where Quixote knows his own fame and meets readers of his history. Sancho's government, Dulcinea's disenchantment, and the final shepherd dream give the comedy its depth. The volume suits readers wanting the whole arc, and it stands as the great sequel, where laughter and farewell share the final page.
59610-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of George William Foote's works on Project Gutenberg. Prisoner for Blasphemy leads the list. Flowers of Freethought fills two series there. Arrows of Freethought stands in the set. Bible Romances and Comic Bible Sketches join it. A life of Charles Bradlaugh stands in the roll.

The Book of God and Salvation Syrup appear as well. A sketch of Voltaire's life closes the list. Prisoner for Blasphemy tells Foote's own trials. Its chapters run from storm to summons to indictment. The Old Bailey and Newgate mark his road. Holloway Gaol and prison life fill the middle. A long night ends in daylight at the close. Flowers of Freethought gathers short sharp pieces. Old Nick and Sky Pilots stand among its heads. A freethought martyr's shelf gains a map in this plain index of banned and battled books.
5969-what-s-mine-s-mine-complete:
George MacDonald offers the full three-volume novel, which opens in a handsome London dining room that feels oddly lifeless. Nothing in it shows genuine choice, only fashion and class custom, from the mirrored oak sideboard to a dozen heavy chairs in fawn morocco. The room poses the book's question about what is truly one's own.

From that start the story moves to a girls' first walk, a village shop, work and wage, hills, a lake, and a clan Christmas. Later volumes carry Mercy, Alister, and their kin through love, loss, and new villages. This complete edition is described from its opening volume onward, without favoring any single part.
5976-thomas-wingfold-curate:
George MacDonald opens with Helen Lingard kept indoors by a swift gray November wind that turns every chimney into an organ pipe. She has spent the morning writing a long letter to her brother Leopold at Cambridge and has put off her walk in the neighboring park. By luncheon the wind has risen and rain threatens.

Helen is strong, healthy, and fond of wind, above all on horseback, yet she stands at her window looking over a balcony of shivering autumn plants to garden and meadows beyond. The novel follows this spirited young woman and the curate whose path crosses hers. Weather, house, and park set a vivid stage.
5999-guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-com:
Walter Scott's Guy Mannering, or The Astrologer, appears here complete, with illustrations listed for both volumes. Volume one shows the departure of the gypsies, Ellangowan and Carlavercock castles, Dominie Sampson in the library, and Dandie Dinmont at home. Volume two adds a party at Colonel Mannering's, smugglers attacked, and Pleydell as king.

Meg Merrilies directs Bertram to the cave, and Dirk Hatteraick is captured, while scenes on the Solway Firth frame the action. Scott mixes astrology, gypsy lore, smuggling, and lost heirs into a border romance. The complete text gathers the whole tale, from planetary signs to final reckonings.
60103-what-a-colored-man-should-do-to-vo:
What a Colored Man Should Do to Vote is a pamphlet for Black voters. It addresses colored men of voting age in the Southern states. As citizens, it opens, you cannot value your vote too highly. That vote expresses your choice of officers over your dearest interests. You should vote at every election, the pamphlet urges its readers.

Never sell your vote stands as its sternest command in capitals. The things that qualify a colored man to vote follow by state. Poll tax payment and registration certificates head the demands listed there. In Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi the rules stand set out plainly. Literacy tests and tax receipts guarded the ballot box against Black men.
60124-the-girl-of-the-golden-gate:
The Girl of the Golden Gate, a novel by William Brown Meloney, was published at New York in 1913. Its first chapter opens in a steamship agency on the Bund at Yokohama. The office is a hive of bustling travellers, eager to be gone. A stranger might think the whole white population of Yokohama meant to flee beyond the seas.

Meloney explains the scene: spring had come to the gateways of the Far East. It stirred the heart call to distant homelands, and broke the spell of the Orient for many. Others dream for ever of the day they will go back, and never do. The crowd holds a Chinese mandarin with his silky train, turbaned Sikhs, and Korean priests over their tickets. Into this stream of homeward bound folk the tale casts its heroine, bound for San Francisco and the Golden Gate.
6021-a-prisoner-in-fairyland-the-book-th:
Algernon Blackwood presents the book that Uncle Paul wrote. It opens with the motto that man is his own star, and that a soul able to render an honest and perfect man commands all light, all influence, and all fate. Our acts, the epigraph says, are our angels, good or ill, fatal shadows walking beside us.

Minks, Herbert Montmorency, appears as more than a secretary, even a private secretary, becoming a confidant in a tale of wonder. Blackwood blends childhood imagination with adult longing, letting fairyland press against ordinary rooms. The novel treats thought itself as a shaping power, bright or dark.
60282-african-colonization-by-the-free-c:
David Christy gave a talk on the settling of free Black folk from the United States in Africa, printed at Cincinnati in 1854. Christy spoke for the American Colonization Society in Ohio. His full claim is that such settling was a key aid to church work in Africa. He says he used the best sources he could find.

Critics had charged that the new towns in Liberia blocked the spread of the faith there. Christy sought facts on that charge in his work as an agent. He says the facts showed the towns in Liberia did more good than all other posts. His talk cites church reports and the African Repository. The piece shows how white church men of that age sold a plan now seen as flawed.
60463-frank-merriwell-s-diamond-foes-or-:
Frank Merriwell's Diamond Foes, or Straight Over the Plate, is a baseball story by Burt Standish in the long-running Merriwell series of books for young men. The front matter preserved here is the publisher's list of the series, which ran past a hundred titles. Frank and Dick Merriwell share the adventures, some on the diamond and some on the gridiron.

The publisher's notice boasts of a half million enthusiastic followers of the Merriwell brothers. It attests to the unfailing interest and wholesomeness of the tales. The brothers are lads of high ideals who play fair with themselves and with the rest of world. The stories, the notice says, are rich in fun and thrills in all branches of sport. They are high in moral tone and fire a boy's ambition to become a good athlete. Diamond Foes is the baseball entry for its season.
6049-works-of-john-bunyan-complete:
The complete works of John Bunyan, edited by George Offor, open with a memoir. It tells of a man born in poverty to ignoble parents, who followed his father's trade as a brazier and enlisted as a soldier. Returning from war, he gained an amiable, religious wife, and the memoir sets his story under texts about treasure in earthen vessels.

The memoir then asks how a youth ruddy and of fair countenance, unarmed except for faith, could meet a Philistine giant like Goliath. That question frames Bunyan's life as a whole. This complete edition gathers memoir, allegory, and treatises together, from Grace Abounding through Pilgrim's Progress and beyond.
60756-whitman-mission-national-historic-:
Whitman Mission National Historic Site, by Erwin Thompson, is a government handbook. The National Park Service issued it at Washington in 1964. It stands as number 37 in the historical handbook series. Waiilatpu, the site's Indian name, heads the tale. Marcus and Narcissa Whitman founded the mission there in 1836. They worked among the Cayuse Indians for eleven years. The handbook notes their aid to emigrants on the Oregon Trail. In the end the Whitmans were killed and the mission destroyed by the people they served.

Contents run from the call from the West to the massacre. The Cayuse, the mission children, and a community rising fill the middle. Preservation of the past closes the book, with a folio from digging at the site. Thompson thanks earlier Park Service and college hands for the groundwork.
60796-the-second-mate:
The Second Mate is a sea novel by Bedford Jones, published at Garden City in nineteen twenty three. Its scene is the tramp steamer Sulu Queen, bound south for Macassar and Singapore. The ship is falling apart, with loose plates, weak pumps, and a bad tail shaft. Her officers are drunk, drugged, or gone, save one man who does the work.

That man is Jim Barnes, the second mate, on whose labour all the rest draw pay. Her captain dreams on opium while her chief engineer lies dead drunk below. Lascar sailors, Chinese quartermasters, and a Malay serang fill out the strange crew. Nine passengers ride her, from an Arab merchant's family to two women missionaries. Coral reefs, the Celebes Sea, and night watches on the bridge set the stage.
60913-a-matter-of-taste:
Joseph Wesley wrote a science fiction tale that first ran in Worlds of If in January 1961. The tale is told as the oral report of claims adjuster Mark Atkinson. He works for Interstellar Insurance. His report bears a case number and a closing mark, and it tells of a claim on a far planet.

Atkinson lands on the fourth planet of Sunder's Pride, where the air can kill and the cold is deep. The men there trade with aliens who beat all human minds at mind control. Men die at set gaps of time, yet the post still makes a profit. Atkinson must judge the claim, the deaths, and the trade before he lets the navy step in.
60917-dialogue-between-john-and-thomas-o:
An unnamed Scots hand printed this talk between two working men at Paisley in 1842. Caldwell set the type for the author. John and Thomas chew over the Corn Laws, the Charter, and strong drink, in broad Scots speech.

Thomas opens by asking what will come of these terrible times. Want and hunger grow each day among them, and both men feel at a loss. John blames the Corn Bill in part for hurt trade and mass ruin. The talk hunts a cure for the present distress, as the title page promises. Cheap print like this carried the big fights of the day into mills and cottages in plain words.
6113-a-day-of-fate:
E. P. Roe calls A Day of Fate, in Shakespeare's phrase, some shallow story of deep love. Its first book runs from aimless steps and a June day dream through a shining tide and reality. Mutual discoveries, a Quaker tea, and the mystery of mysteries follow, with Old Plod and a bit of Eden along the way.

Moved, one of nature's tragedies, lightning and a subtler flame, and kindling a spark of life lead to my fate. The second book gives the day after, it was inevitable, returning consciousness, in the dark, a flash of memory, and love teaching ethics. Roe treats one day as the hinge on which a life turns.
61151-good-form-and-christian-etiquette:
Good Form and Christian Etiquette is a guide to conduct by Mrs. S. M. I. Henry. It was put out by the Review and Herald Publishing Company of Battle Creek, Michigan, with offices in Chicago, Toronto, and Atlanta. The copyright date is 1900, as the pack states. The preface sets out the aim of the book in the author's own words.

Let no one who reads this little book think that she has been laying down a lot of rules, the author says. The most she has tried is to point out some of the rules that thoughtful men and women have found needful to good social order. She adds what her long work for the unfortunate has shown: the things of conduct that ward off scandal and the casting out that follows it. The book joins good manners to Christian duty.
61224-spanish-john-being-a-memoir-now-fi:
Spanish John, by William McLennan and published in 1897, gives the memoir of Colonel John McDonell in complete form. McDonell won his nickname while a lieutenant in the Company of St James. That company served in the Regiment Irlandia in the service of the King of Spain. Its theatre of war was Italy in his early life.

The first chapter sets out with Angus McDonald of Clanranald for the Scots College in Rome. On the road the pair fall in with Mr O'Rourke and Manuel, and see strange company in Leghorn. Illustrations by Myrbach grace the volume in this edition. McLennan frames the book as the fruit of long talks over old days with his father. Scots exiles, Spanish service, and Italian campaigns give the memoir its sweep.
61445-a-house-divided-against-itself-com:
Mrs Oliphant wrote a novel in three volumes, here in its complete form. William Blackwood and Sons issued it at Edinburgh and London in the Roman year MDCCCLXXXVI. Frances and her father walk a hot, shadeless road to old Bordighera at the start. Olive woods and palm walls line the broad new path.

Mr Waring has lived in the Italian town for many years and hates hotel tourists. A band of English guests crosses his path and stirs his wrath at once. Fate seems set against him in small things and great, the tale observes. Family strain, pride, and place drive a grave tale of a house at odds.
61515-the-lawhorn-site:
The Lawhorn Site is an issue of The Missouri Archaeologist, volume 24, dated December 1962. Robert Bray of the University of Missouri edited the journal. A picture of artifacts heads the volume. The officers and trustees of the state archaeological society fill the front pages.

The volume reports the excavation of the Lawhorn site in Missouri. Such society journals recorded the amateur and university digging that built the archaeology of the Mississippi valley. Sherds, points, and burials are catalogued and drawn. The number shows mid-century American archaeology at work: local societies, university editors, and site reports shared in print.
6156-athens-its-rise-and-fall-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's complete Athens: Its Rise and Fall opens with a dedication to Henry Fynes Clinton. Clinton wrote the Fasti Hellenici, and Lytton thanks him for help drawn from that work. Chronology, Lytton argues, is not dry dates but explanation of events and philosophy of facts.

From Solon and Marathon through Miltiades, Themistocles, and Xerxes's invasion, the history runs to Cimon, Pericles, and the Peloponnesian War. Clinton's Fasti lights the scanty authorities where chronology best repairs gaps. This complete edition gathers all five books, from Athens's rise to its fall, in one arc.
6171-memorials-and-other-papers-complete:
De Quincey's complete Memorials opens with his address to the American editor of his works, anxious to place these papers in that house's hands exclusively in the United States. He seeks no further emolument, only acknowledgment of services already rendered.

The editor gathered a widely scattered collection, a task De Quincey found insurmountable from nervous depression, and shared profits without solicitation or legal claim. The complete edition adds Klosterheim, riddles, dialogues, and household wrecks. It is described from its opening address onward, gathering both volumes together. Both volumes join memoir, tale, and essay in one set.
61781-star-pirate:
Star Pirate is a science fiction story by Frederick Arnold Kummer the younger. It first reached print in Planet Stories in the summer of nineteen forty, the hosted note says. Its blurb tells of Vance McClean, an exiled star pirate. Return to Ceres means death for him, yet a cool million in palladium tempts him back.

The tale's narrator looks out from a small office building on Ceres by cold starlight. The mine shaft head stands a mile away, and the miners' huts are dark. The rich palladium vein has run out, so his uncle dismissed the workmen. Stacks of the metal wait in a wall safe behind him. He has lived on the asteroid for fifteen years, since the age of five. Earth is a haze of big buildings and green grass to him.
6179-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
Parker's complete Pierre and His People gathers five volumes. They run from The Patrol of the Cypress Hills and God's Garrison through A Prairie Vagabond, Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride, The Tall Master, and Antoine and Angelique. The general introduction for the 1912 edition sets each work beside its companions and his literary life.

Parker hopes the edition makes old friends warmer and new friends more understanding, noting most stories came from incidents or characters he knew or heard intimately, or found in historians. This complete edition is described from its contents and introduction, covering the whole far north cycle.
61801-mississippi-piney-woods-a-photogra:
Mississippi Piney Woods is Patti Carr Black's photographic study of folk architecture. The Mississippi Department of Archives and History published it at Jackson in 1976. It accompanied an exhibition at the Mississippi State Historical Museum. A grist mill at Lake Bounds in Clarke County fronts the cover. The Sam Hosey house near Moss, in Jasper County, is pictured early.

Black opens with Eudora Welty's dogtrot house from Losing Battles. The dogtrot, she writes, lives in every Mississippian's memory. Dogtrots and log houses spread across the state from the early nineteenth century. Folk architecture, she complains, has been largely ignored. Attention went to large mansion houses instead. Even antebellum was used only for affluent homes. Yet many pioneer-built houses predate the Civil War. Few survive in original form, and more fall daily; the study records them before they vanish.
6191-northern-lights-complete:
Parker's complete Northern Lights gathers five volumes a generation later than Pierre and His People. Volume one gives a lodge in the wilderness and Buckmaster's boy, volume two To-Morrow and Qu'Appelle, volume three swallows homeward and Marcile, and volume four famine, healing springs, and Orion.

The introduction notes railway, towns, and emigration ended the isolation and pathetic loneliness of Pierre's days. Visiting the far west again in 1905 after many years, Parker saw strange new life with modern energy and push. This complete edition is described from its contents and introduction, covering the newer north.
6194-mrs-falchion-complete:
Parker's complete Mrs. Falchion repeats the introduction of the three-decker days: begun in 1892 amid Pierre stories, finished in summer 1893, never serial, meant to be judged whole and taken at a gasp. Library sales outran public sales for every Parker novel until 1893.

A Methuen reader opposed the book, but Mr. Methuen, then Mr. Stedman, gave friendly confidence, certain it would arrest critics and public whether popular or not. Parker wishes he still had the original three volumes, which won almost unhoped success. This complete edition is described from its introduction, gathering the whole novel.
6201-cumner-s-son-and-other-south-sea-fo:
Parker's complete Cumner's Son and Other South Sea Folk gathers five volumes. They run from Cumner's Son itself through the High Court of Budgery-Gar, the Planter's Wife, a sable Spartan, and a pagan of the south. The introduction quotes his 1902 foreword to Donovan Pasha on twelve years of tales from lands well known to him.

First tales came from Australia and southern Pacific islands, where he lived and roamed in the middle and late eighties, given out with prodigality though not at first in book form. Canadian tales written far from their scenes ran alongside. This complete edition is described from its contents and introduction.
62081-the-timber-pirate:
The Timber Pirate is a Canadian novel by Charles Christopher Jenkins, copyrighted in 1922. McClelland and Stewart published it at Toronto. A prologue sets the scene in the Laurentians in winter. Night falls on a short sub arctic day. The departing sun throws glistening beams off the omnipresent whiteness. Silence lies oppressive over the snow. Only the splitting of frozen trees breaks it at intervals.

Twenty eight chapters follow from that still opening. Acey Smith and a strange pact on a train come first. A millionaire vanishes in chapter six. The hill of lurking death and the white monster of Nannabijou promise peril. A figure known only by initials gives orders in the middle chapters. Judgment of the lowly closes the tale at the meeting of the trails. Timber, money, and mystery drive the plot.
6210-the-trail-of-the-sword-complete:
Parker's complete Trail of the Sword gathers four epochs. They run from envoy extraordinary and renegade threat through friends in council, glass darkly, and porch of the world to water unto wine, hunters out, treasure house, and gift of a captive. Maiden no more closes the third epoch.

The fourth epoch tells a brother's blood crying from the ground, a trap set, an untoward messenger, tiger's claw to lion's mouth, gates of misfortune, and sword sheathed. The history of Jessica Leveret and Pierre Le Moyne of Iberville runs throughout. This complete edition is described from its contents, covering the whole trail.
6214-the-translation-of-a-savage-complet:
Parker's complete Translation of a Savage gathers three volumes. They run from his great mistake and difficult situation through out of the north, family name, and awkward half-hour to passing years, court-martial, every man's hour, and faith of comrades. Secrets of hearts, highway, chase of the yellow swan, and living poem follow.

The introduction notes the book was written in early autumn 1893 at Hampstead Heath. Parker often went there for composition air, to a residential place scarcely invaded by lodging-house keepers and rich in literary character. This complete edition is described from its contents and introduction, ending on the trail's edge.
6217-the-pomp-of-the-lavilettes-complete:
Parker's complete Pomp of the Lavilettes repeats the introduction of a book sold outright in 1896. It was the only such sale of his career, to Lamson and Wolffe of Boston after a gallant offer at Atlantic City. Its first appearance came under less than favorable conditions, though Parker believed its elements justified consideration.

He felt he might one day regain control, while immediate phenomenal sale seemed unlikely, unlike The Seats of the Mighty and The Right of Way, whose great sales he foresaw. General appeal in narrative and character marked those books. This complete edition is described from its introduction, gathering the Lavilettes whole.
62214-the-proposed-union-of-the-telegrap:
The Western Union Telegraph Company issued this statement at Cambridge in 1869. A proposed union of the telegraph and postal systems is its subject throughout. The contents open with a review of a paper by Washburne urging that union, answered point by point in the pamphlet.

A merited compliment to Professor Morse leads the review, with congressional aid next. Erroneous charges against the American telegraph system are answered in the third section, by the contents. Statistics of the telegraph in Europe and America for 1866, from official reports, arm the company's case against a government postal telegraph.
6222-the-trespasser-complete:
Gaston Belward leaves the north and rides to Ridley Court with Jacques Brillon, chasing a claim that will shape his whole life. Across eighteen chapters he tells his story, digs into his father's past, finds sponsors and foes, and stands at last between two worlds. Old papers, sealed bundles, and a family name found on a parchment pull him deeper into a heritage he can neither ignore nor easily own.

Parker wrote the novel in a Brittany garden in the summer of 1893, after a publisher asked him for a tale for an annual. The full arc moves from London fog and country roads to Paris rooms and hard choices about love and duty. It is a romance of inheritance, where a man's past keeps returning to test the life he tries to build.
6229-the-seats-of-the-mighty-complete:
Captain Robert Moray, once of the Virginia regiment and later of Amherst's, sets down the memoirs of his life in French Canada at war. From an escort to the citadel through prison cells, torture chambers, ramparts, and cathedrals, thirty chapters follow one officer through siege, captivity, and love. Doltaire, Bigot, Alixe, and Voban cross his path again and again, as governors and intendants plot above him.

Parker built the whole tale as a first-person memoir, with an imperial introduction and a prefatory note to guide the reader in. An appendix on the Scot in New France closes the book, tying its romance to real history. Read whole, it is a long arc of endurance, from a young soldier's first post to a final reckoning behind a tapestry in a battered town.
62346-in-black-and-white:
In Black and White is a volume of Rudyard Kipling's stories, issued as the fourth volume of his collected writings. Scribner of New York published this edition in 1909, under earlier copyrights. Most of the tales are set in India.

The tales include Dray Wara Yow Dee, Namgay Doola, The Judgment of Dungara, and The Finances of the Gods. Moti Guj—Mutineer and Without Benefit of Clergy stand among them. Others are In Flood Time, Georgie Porgie, Little Tobrah, and The Sending of Dana Da. From Many Inventions come On the City Wall and The Enlightenments of Pagett. The opening tale begins with a Kabul horse-dealer's patter to a Sahib. He offers almonds, raisins, grapes, and a pony of the rarest, thirteen three and fit for polo.
6236-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
Jersey's treacherous coast opens the tale, with tides that circle the Channel Isles and smash against rock and wall. From invasion through eleven years after, and on through France and Jersey again, Parker follows Guida, Philip d'Avranche, Ranulph, and Detricand across forty-six chapters of war, marriage, and revenge. Ships sail, courts sit, scaffolds rise, and island homes hold their own against empires.

The author wrote it as a break from his Canadian books, a romance of two kingdoms rather than one northern land. Read whole, the novel joins its parts: a French landing, a lieutenant's duty, a wife left spinning by the sea, and a Royalist hiding in plain sight. Its centre stays the island, small, proud, and ringed by a sea that forgives no error.
6241-the-lane-that-had-no-turning-comple:
Pontiac, a French Canadian parish under English rule, holds the whole of Parker's linked tales, from the Governor's visit to the last stories of hard winters and proud neighbours. Madelinette returns, redcoats march, a miller marries, Annette waits for Benoit, and Parpon the dwarf walks among them. Four volumes gather into one parish chronicle, with Medallion, the Cure, the Avocat, and the Seigneur presiding over its quarrels and kindnesses.

Read complete, the book shows a community over years, loyal to old France, obedient to new masters, and determined never to beg. Its tales move from sedition meetings to sickrooms, auctions, and chess games, always in the same lanes and kitchens. Parker gives Pontiac a full life, comic and grave by turns, in stories that stand alone yet gain weight together.
62466-the-prodigals-and-their-inheritanc:
Oliphant's novel opens on a family sentence being carried out. Chester has washed his hands of his two sons, and Tom is coming home tonight only to be sent off. His sister Winifred has sent the dog-cart to the station, and her father scolds the indulgence. There is a letter to Stafford, and a ticket waiting at the Cable Line office in Liverpool. Tom shall not have the journey money, lest he stay in London and spend it.

Winifred pleads that Tom is young and has done nothing very bad, only foolishness. Chester answers that the boys have taken him in, he who was never taken in before. Yet he agrees to see his son, so that all shall know how little is to be looked for from him. Methuen published the complete edition at London in 1894. The prodigals of the title must make their way without the inheritance.
6249-the-right-of-way-complete:
A courtroom holds its breath as a jury foreman squeaks out a verdict no one expected, and a woman laughs in a far gallery corner before the clerk calls for silence. Charley Steele, the counsel all eyes follow, has won through a discovery that turned dull blankness into crystal sight. From that trial the whole novel unrolls, through five years after, a woman in heliotrope, a river at night, and a parish that watches every move.

Read whole, the book follows Charley from law courts to Chaudiere, where Rosalie, Jo Portugais, the Cure, and the Seigneur shape his second life. Passion Plays, stolen crosses, trials, and partings fill sixty-one chapters, ending with an epilogue. Parker writes a long tale of guilt, grace, and a man learning to live straight after winning crookedly, or so it seemed at first.
6253-michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-sword:
Two dim records start the tale: Huguenot refugees admitted to communion at Southampton's Walloon Church, and the marriage of Angele Aubert to Michel de la Foret in August of the same year. Parker wonders what real lives lay behind those lines, and builds a romance of flight from France, refuge in England, and a court where swords and sermons contend. Lempriere the butler, Buonespoir the pirate, Leicester the favourite, and Elizabeth herself all cross the couple's path.

Read whole, the novel follows Michel and Angele from register entries to palace antechambers, sea chases, and a choice between sword and book. Parker calls it a letter from an ancient cabinet, faint with old perfume, and writes it as such, tender toward its sources and sharp toward court intrigue. It is a story of faith kept under pressure, and love that outlasts exile.
62583-the-theory-and-practice-of-argumen:
Victor Alvin Ketcham's Theory and Practice of Argumentation and Debate was published by Macmillan in 1914 and reprinted through 1917. Ketcham taught as assistant professor at Ohio State University. Part one, on practice, opens with the definition and importance of argumentation, then takes up the proposition. A good subject must interest, must suit the debater's knowledge, and must be debatable. The proposition should carry one central idea, stand in the affirmative, and use no ambiguous words.

Later chapters cover analyzing the proposition, the main issues, and evidence. Evidence comes from personal knowledge, interviews, letters, current and standard literature, and government documents. Ketcham directs students to record each fact on its own small card, complete in itself. The contents promise further parts on the brief, the argument itself, and delivery. The book served college debate teaching in the years before the First World War.
6260-donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-eg:
From a minaret, two watchers see pyramids, wells, hills, tombs of caliphs, and the Khedive's distant palace, while Cairo spreads below in palms, white stone, and bazaar noise. Housewives lounge on rooftops, harem women peer through lattice panels, and minarets rise like giant lamp posts over winding streets. This is the Egypt of Parker's fifteen tales, from a lamp held out to burn through orderlies, treaties, tyrants, and young lions of Dedan.

Read whole, the set follows Dicky Donovan and his circle through river towns, regiments, and palaces, as English rule meets Egyptian life. A grindstone, a drum, a flower of the flock, and the light of other days give the tales their names and their turns. Parker, writing after his Canadian years, treats Egypt as a second home ground, comic, tense, and fondly observed in equal measure.
6271-embers-complete:
Parker's poems run from Rosleen and Mary Callaghan through Kildare, far travel, and a light heart, to deserts, seas, and a courier star. Three volumes gather into one book of verse, with the world in making, the heart of the pioneer, the north trail, and the scarlet hills beside love songs and laments. Kings, woodsmen, and children share the pages, and England itself is praised as a mother of the north.

Read whole, the collection moves between Ireland, Canada, and the wider world, from a little house and spinning songs to Granada, Camden Town, and Juniper Cove. The poems stay short and musical, built on a single scene or refrain. They show the novelist in lyric mood, praising courage, mourning the dead, and finding, in a hill or a sea, a reason to go on.
6274-a-lover-s-diary-complete:
Two volumes of love poems make one diary, from a vision above the din to a passing envoy. The first half courts, pledges, and seals its love, through meetings, nests, shrines, and torches, with denial and captivity along the way. The second half dreams, surrenders, and divides, through wraiths, citadels, closed doors, and chalices, until morning comes and sacrifice gives way to reunion.

Parker writes the whole arc in short lyrics, each titled like a chapter in a life: the bride, the treasure, the decree, the darkened way, and the message. A poem for Tennyson and an envoy close the book. Read whole, it is a single feeling followed from first sight to last farewell and back again, earnest, musical, and unafraid of grand words for private pain.
6280-the-money-master-complete:
Jean Jacques Barbille, miller and moneymaster, calls his home peace and plenty at the height of his career, with pines, oak, and river for a setting. Five epochs follow him from a grand tour and a story of tomorrow through thirteen years after, a man from outside, misfortunes in train, and bells of memory at the last. Mills, farms, stores, kilns, and money lending build his empire, while Carmen, Zoe, and Sebastian Dolores pull it apart.

Read whole, the novel is a parish epic of getting and losing, told through a clerk of the court, a new cure, and neighbours who watch every turn. Parker follows one man's gifts, his philosophy, his shrug of who knows, and his final reckoning. It is a story of a French Canadian district in full, where prosperity proves as testing as poverty, and memory outlasts both.
6284-the-world-for-sale-complete:
A Druse girl runs rapids alone at low water while Tekewani calls from the bank, and two western towns watch a daring that no chief has matched. Ingolby, Jethro Fawe, and Fleda carry the tale through three books, from a whisper beyond and a prisoner freed to a sultan, a patrin's sentence, and beacons on the hills. Railways, town rivalry, and Romany pride braid together, and a blind man learns to smell a fine fall day.

Read whole, the novel earns its title at the last, as the world itself seems put up for sale and love must bid against pride and law. Parker writes Lebanon and its neighbour as one divided place, comic in its horse dealers and solemn in its courts. The complete tale moves from river daring to quiet rooms, and ends with patience, where sight returns only in the mind's eye.
62902-the-13th-district-a-story-of-a-can:
Brand Whitlock wrote The 13th District, a story of a candidate, for Bowen-Merrill at Indianapolis in 1902. Book one is named Of the People. It opens as a train swings into Grand Prairie depot, past a smoke-black shed. Cheers rise to meet Garwood, the candidate, loud past the roar of the wheels. Garwood lounges in the smoking car, his long legs stretched out, his face soot-black and damp with heat. Days of strain have left him worn to the bone.

Rankin, who ran his canvass, heaves up and slaps his shoulder in glee. Rankin had pulled off a last-day move at the Clinton convention. After twelve hundred and nine ballots, that move made Garwood the nominee for Congress. Whitlock builds a tale of votes, wiles, and the cost of a run for office in the Midwest.
6291-wild-youth-complete:
Askatoon, bright, clever, and composed, meets its match in Orlando Guise. His name is like no other that ever came that way, and he rides like a broncho buster born in the saddle. The Mazarines take possession, Louise names herself, and Orlando has adventures through bargains, gardens, and oriental ways. A moon not alone, a warning, Filion and Fiona with Patsy Kernaghan, and cross trails follow, until youth has its way.

Read whole, the novel spans two volumes of prairie life, where a town that sleeps with one eye open must deal with passion, pride, and kinship. Parker writes Askatoon as a character in itself, watchful and witty, against young people who will not be managed. The complete tale ends where youth, having fought its battles, claims the road it chose.
6295-no-defense-complete:
Goodbye, Dyck, a wild young Irish spirit calls, promising to meet his friend at the sessions or the assizes, a jest that soon turns grave. Dyck Calhoun, worst and best scamp of them all, drinks, games, and follows temptation until a tavern meeting, a quarrel, a duel, and the killing of Erris Boyne send him to prison. Mother and daughter wait, a father visits, and a letter from Sheila reaches him behind bars.

Read whole, the novel follows Dyck from prison release, grey at the temples after four years of an eight year term, into naval service, mutiny's hour, and the West Indies. A third book moves to Jamaica, where a planter's Christmas feast cannot hide old wounds and a governor must be faced. Parker writes a long tale of Irish high spirits, punishment, and a second life earned at sea.
6299-carnac-s-folly-complete:
A girl's voice calls Carnac to catch her on a summer day by a tumbling stream, where river drivers loose jammed logs with pike poles. From childhood and eleven years passing, the novel follows Carnac as manager, bargainer, and lover, through offers from Tarboe and Grier, a mother's counsel, and a goodbye. Vanishing from Montreal, he returns to find Junia gone west, and learns that a hotel book signature has barred the divorce he sought.

Read whole, the book runs three books deep, from timber woods to Quebec politics, candidacy, secret meetings, and a final way home. Luzanne Larue holds a terrible claim, Junia waits and nurses, and Tarboe dreams and works. Parker writes a Canadian life in full, where a young folly, signed in haste, must be answered across years of work, love, and public life.
63249-the-philosophical-theory-of-the-st:
Bernard Bosanquet wrote a philosophical theory of the state, published at London in 1899 and printed at Glasgow. A line from Rousseau's Émile heads the title page. The preface calls the work an attempt to express the fundamental ideas of a true social philosophy. Bosanquet criticizes and interprets well known thinkers only to set those ideas in clear light.

He abstains from practical applications except as illustration. Better grasp of first principles, he holds, would make practical problems handled more rationally. Party spirit, he says, has heated those problems too much for clear thought. His principles aim to free discussion from party prejudice. The book became a standard statement of British idealist political thought.
63856-s-o-s-aphrodite:
SOS Aphrodite is a science fiction tale by Stanley Mullen from Planet Stories. The story ran in the Summer nineteen forty nine issue of that magazine. Patrolman Steve Coran of the ISP trusts only one person in the tale. He trusts her only after strapping her in her bunk, the blurb says.

A sign across the street marks a Venus Transport contamination area, keep out. An ISP official warns Coran he will be in deadly danger from now. The foes are no lone pirates but a ring of saboteurs and killers. Rich and high placed men back them for aims of war and revolt. Coran laughs and asks why he was picked for the job.
64212-how-paper-boxes-are-made-a-practic:
How Paper Boxes Are Made, by Robert Salade, is a practical trade book printed at Lafayette, Indiana, in 1920. Salade also wrote on plate printing, die stamping, and making cutouts. His guide promises to teach the beginner to manufacture all kinds of paper boxes, and it carries 100 illustrations.

Early chapters cover plain set up boxes, the materials and machines used, and how to group machines to save time and labor. Later chapters turn to druggists' pill and powder boxes, round, oval, and dome topped, then to candy boxes plain and fancy. Special chapters treat the printing department of a box plant, embossing, gold leafing, and label work.
64882-the-servile-state:
Hilaire Belloc wrote this thesis book on the servile state coming again. Foulis printed it in London and Edinburgh in 1912. Restore property or restore slavery, no third course, he warns. A synopsis lays out the sections of the argument in front.

Definitions of wealth, capital, proletariat, and property open section one. Our civilisation was originally servile under pagan rule, section two. The faith dissolved that state for a time, section three. How the distributive state failed in England takes section four. Status in place of contract marks the servile state, a matter of kind not degree.
65303-recipes-hershey-s-baking-chocolate:
Recipes: Hershey's Baking Chocolate is a recipe booklet issued by the Hershey Chocolate Corporation, copyrighted in 1941. It teaches the home cook to use the company's baking chocolate blocks. Every recipe is built around that one product, measured in blocks and ounces.

Sauces open the book. Hot fudge sauce comes first: milk, two blocks of chocolate, sugar, corn syrup, and butter, cooked to the soft-ball stage and beaten creamy. It serves over ice cream or plain puddings. A foamy chocolate sauce follows, made with separated eggs and melted chocolate folded together, to be served at once. Such booklets were the chocolate maker's quiet sales force, turning a pantry staple into cakes, frostings, and drinks a family would ask for by name.
65379-selections-from-aunt-sammy-s-radio:
Selections from Aunt Sammy Radio Recipes and USDA Favorites was put out by the United States Department of Agriculture in August 1976. Aunt Sammy was a radio figure made by the department in 1926, the wife of Uncle Sam. Women across the land played her part on local stations.

Her show, Housekeepers Chat, mixed menus and recipes with talk on clothes, homes, and world news. By the end of the first year, forty three stations aired the show. The name faded in the Great Depression, and the show ended in 1946. This book pulls the best recipes and food ideas from that long run. Cooks get plain home dishes shaped by farm science and by what real homes had on hand.
65930-marcel-proust-an-english-tribute:
Marcel Proust: An English Tribute is a memorial volume of essays by English writers, collected by Scott Moncrieff. Thomas Seltzer published it in New York in 1923, soon after Proust's death. The contributors include Joseph Conrad, Arnold Bennett, Arthur Symons, and Clive Bell. Moncrieff, Proust's English translator, supplies the introduction.

Stephen Hudson gives a portrait, and Francis Birrell calls Proust the prophet of despair. Pieces treat the little Proust, Proust's women, and the character Gilberte. Compton Mackenzie writes a reader's gratitude, and Alec Waugh treats Gilberte in turn. The volume shows how fast Proust's fame crossed the Channel after his death.
6615-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-c:
Skinner's complete Myths and Legends gathers all his regional volumes into one vast shelf of American folk tales. Rip Van Winkle, Catskill gnomes, the galloping Hessian, and the storm ship on the Hudson lead the set. Tales from the Delaware, Puritan New England, and the South follow. So do tales from the Lakes, the Rockies, and the Pacific slope. No single region owns the book.

Read straight through, the set shows how each place in America grew its own ghosts, heroes, and warnings. Skinner's telling stays short, plain, and place-bound throughout. The complete volume is a treasure for lore lovers who want the whole map in one place, from coast to coast.
66197-notes-and-queries-number-199-augus:
Notes and Queries, number 199, is the weekly issue dated Saturday, August the twentieth, 1853. The London journal served literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of. The price was fourpence, or fivepence for the stamped edition.

Notes in this number treat Bacon's essays and early Philadelphia directories. Minor notes ask after the rights of women and green drinking pots of the Temple lawyers. Queries seek the source of Wellesley and the link between Celtic and Latin tongues. Replies cover the Rosicrucians and a line from the burial service. A section of photographic letters shows the journal keeping pace with new arts. Such numbers built the great Victorian store of small facts.
66199-notes-and-queries-number-205-octob:
Notes and Queries number 205 came out Saturday, October 1, 1853. The London weekly served literary men, antiquaries, and genealogists alike. Price fourpence, fivepence stamped, with Captain Cuttle motto on notes. Contents open with a groaning board story of Charles Second days.

Word awkward origin, an inedited poem, and Bale manuscripts follow. Charles Fox and Gibbon and Shakespeare correspondence fill the notes. Minor notes treat the Calf's Head Club and ducking stool lore. Queries ask General Monk birthplace and Noel family facts here. Replies treat prayer book editions, the crescent, and moon superstitions in the number.
66325-a-crowned-queen-the-romance-of-a-m:
A Crowned Queen is a state love tale by Sydney Grier, out in nineteen seven. A Blackwood house of Edinburgh and London brought out this third print. It stands second in his Balkan set of tales by its own leaf. Part one breaks a rest trip at a small Wales rail stop in the tale. Wright the coach man grumps that the train is late at that stop.

Lady word sent him at short note to meet that train in haste. Prodger the stop chief jokes he came too soon, not the train too late. Part names chart creed wars, a new hand at state craft, and crown men. A dad debt, a house pact, and dark ways fill the mid part names. Man whom the queen loves to grace heads a part in the list.
66788-in-and-about-drury-lane-and-other-:
Dr Doran wrote In and About Drury Lane and Other Papers, first printed in the Temple Bar Magazine. Richard Bentley and Son issued volume one in London in eighteen hundred eighty one. Doran knew the stage and its lore as few men did. His wit and store of tales fill the front note with praise.

The lead piece walks the lane and steps backstage at Drury Lane. A Boxing Day crowd in the slums gives way to a pantomime rehearsal. Master Betty, the boy actor star, gets a full study. Charles Young and William Charles Macready follow in turn. Home stage shows and lamp smell add color. French actresses close the roll of stage folk in this volume.
66898-dough-or-dynamite:
Dough or Dynamite is a western story by W C Tuttle. Tuttle had written Clean Crazy and Monkeying with Ancestors. The tale is told by Henry Peck, a hand at the Cross J ranch. He narrates in cowboy dialect throughout. The opening scene puts him in the corral with two partners. Muley Bowles and Chuck Warner are saddling a colt with him.

Telescope Tolliver rides in on a buckboard with a stranger. Archibald Ames is the visitor, and his name fits him inversely. Its length suggests his girth, and his surname his height. His dinky pants and libellous Stetson draw the crew's inspection. Chuck Warner, who can wiggle his ears like a mule, performs for him. Telescope explains the errand at last. Mister Ames has come west looking for local color. The cowboys' suspicion of strangers drives the comedy from there.
67312-as-others-see-us-being-the-diary-o:
As Others See Us, the diary of a Canadian debutante, was written under the pen name Goosequill and published at Toronto in 1915. A plate hints at romance to come: the diarist dreams of rescuing the man she loves. The diary opens on December 15, and she means to record the people, parties, and things she is going to enjoy.

Her hostess is Mumsie, her dead mother's friend, in a great city the girl names the City of Mammon. Silk dresses, ostrich plumes, and motors daze the village girl at first sight. A winter season of dances and teas begins in wonder.
6747-the-log-of-the-empire-state:
Geneve Shaffer, special representative of the San Francisco Examiner on a Chamber of Commerce tour of the Orient, logs three months of travel in The Log of the Empire State. She thanks her fellow travelers for help in gathering facts, and dedicates the book to her mother and your mother, in verse on folded hands and a valiant heart that beats on.

Ports, cities, and hosts of the Orient pass in brisk, journalistic entries, with a traveler's eye for color and commerce. Shaffer writes as a working reporter, not a tourist. The Log of the Empire State is a lively, period record of American business travel in Asia.
67532-the-confessions-of-the-celebrated-:
The Confessions of the Celebrated Countess of Lichtenau, turned from the German and printed at London in seventeen ninety-nine, purports to draw on the countess's own papers. The countess, born Minna Encken and later Madame Rietz, was held as a state prisoner in the fortress of Glogau. A portrait from a painting in another countess's hands heads the book. A covering letter sends the tale to a friend at Bath.

The letter says her beauty first won her notice, and her intrigues kept her power as her charms faded. Born a trumpeter's daughter, she served as a maid, then caught the eye of a young man of the highest rank at about age fifteen. He had her taught to read, write, dance, and draw, and taught her French himself. Her reach into politics, the letter warns, was felt by more nations than one.
6761-the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-f:
Smollett's complete Count Fathom joins both parts in one volume, with the author's preface and Maynadier's introduction. Part one runs from sage observations and a hero's infancy through military life, a mother's death, schooling, and schemes, to a partnership with a female associate and their first bold attempt. Part two carries the rogue's career to its end.

Read whole, the novel shows Fathom's rise, tricks, and fall in full, with Smollett's satire sharp throughout. The complete text suits readers who want the rogue's tale without a break. Ferdinand Count Fathom, complete, is a long, rich picaresque of an eighteenth-century schemer.
67837-millions-from-waste:
Millions from Waste, by Frederick Talbot, argues that trash is a source of wealth, and it was issued at Philadelphia and London in 1920. Talbot had written on railways, inventions, and the conquest of the sea by steam. Chapter one ties waste to commerce and national economy. A chapter on the German conquest of waste follows.

The war taught the world to salvage, and Talbot presses that lesson. Chapters take up salvage from the army swill tub and the recovery of military waste. Invention in waste recovery gets a chapter of its own. So do scrap saved from the sea and wealth won from slaughter house offal. Bones, blood, and condemned meat all yield value in his account. The book is a survey of a new industry born of war and want.
67998-beam-pirate:
George Smith wrote Beam Pirate, a science fiction tale first printed in Astounding Science-Fiction in October 1944. A headnote sets the plot: it was a pretty web that Akars spun aboard the Sun-freighter Cinnabar. Mass murder and piracy were in it. But he was not clever enough to allow for the plain-sounding asteroid charted as H277 Plus.

Jon Akars, petty officer of the freighter, backs away from the opened manifold of the air circulators. He feels hastily for the emergency mask at his belt. Any moment now the Venusian drug he dropped into the circulators will take effect. Without warning, men will drop at their posts, stiff and staring, yet keenly aware of all about them. Akars means not to be one of them. The prize is four kilos of precious metal Box Jordan found on an unknown world.
68230-the-impossible-pirate:
The Impossible Pirate is a short tale of a hunt in the space lanes. George Smith wrote it for a pulp book of the year 1946. Lieutenant Jeffries is called in by his chief of the Sun Police. The chief thanks him dry for the praise none can quite trust.

The task is to find Black Morgan, the pirate of the lanes. Jeffries has six months to bring proof that will hang the man. If he wins the hunt, a rise in rank waits at the end of it. If he fails, no blame will fall, for all have failed at the task. The chief owns he could not catch the man in his own tries. The tour will be a rest of sorts, with a hunt to keep the mind keen. That is the kind word with which the tale sends Jeffries out.
68411-bellarion-the-fortunate:
Bellarion the Fortunate is a romance by Sabatini, of a young rover in the Italy of swords and small states. It came out at Boston and New York in the mid nineteen twenties. Its rights were held that year by its hand, with all rights kept.

Its two books map a rise from naught to a knights spurs. A door step, a grey friar, and a door left ajar open his road. A safe place in a shrine, a high born girl, and the winds of fate lead to work in a great mans camp. A stale game at war, a marquis, and a word of dread fill the first book. Dogs that work a wonder, a famed free sword, and a siege close his rise.
68642-the-little-white-gate:
Florence Hoatson wrote these poems for children, and Harrap printed The Little White Gate in London in 1925. Margaret Tarrant drew the plates. Hoatson gave the book to her father, and the verse runs by the seasons.

Field and Garden opens the set, with poems for all the year round. The First Lamb, the first shoot, and the bulb house mark the spring. Buttercup gold, a poppy song, and the bird bath sing the summer. Fairies take the second part: fairies in Hyde Park, in the cupboard, and at a picnic. Home closes the book, with granny, aunts, mummy, and the boy next door in kind, small scenes.
69099-the-book-of-edinburgh-anecdote:
The Book of Edinburgh Anecdote is a collection of city stories by Francis Watt. Foulis published it in London and Edinburgh in 1912. A portrait of Lord Cockburn serves as frontispiece. The book is dedicated to Charles Baxter in memory of old days. Its chapters sort Edinburgh life by its great institutions. Parliament House and Lawyers opens the collection. The Church in Edinburgh and the town's college follow. Surgeons and Doctors get a chapter of their own. Royalty, men of letters, and artists come in turn.

The Women of Edinburgh and The Supernatural have chapters too. The Streets and The City close the list before the index. Illustrations show judges, archbishops, and painters of the city. Raeburn portraits appear among those plates. Watt gathers table talk of a capital's professions. The anecdote form keeps history at the level of persons.
6941-old-mortality-complete:
Scott's Old Mortality appears here complete, joining the two volumes into one romance. The editor's introduction traces its start to Joseph Train's breakfast with Scott in May 1816, when a parcel of traditions and a jesting letter signed Clashbottom gave birth to Jedediah Cleishbotham. A portrait of Claverhouse in Scott's den helped fix the tale's dark soldier hero.

The novel follows Morton among the Covenanters, from first rising to council, battle, and faction strife, with Burley at his side. This complete text carries the whole arc without a break, from the Galloway traditions that sparked it to the closing scenes of a divided Scotland. It is Scott's fullest portrait of faith at war with itself.
6944-the-heart-of-mid-lothian-complete:
Walter Scott's Heart of Mid-Lothian appears here complete, in the Tales of My Landlord second series arranged by Jedediah Cleishbotham. The editor's introduction tells how Scott began the novel almost before Rob Roy was done, and how talks with Longman failed in November 1817. Constable then took the sale in hand, and Scott promised his best volumes yet.

A Burns epigraph warns Scots that a note taking chiel walks among them and will print what he sees. The novel that follows is Scott's Edinburgh tale of law, prison, and family loyalty, told with humor and deep feeling. This complete text carries the story from its opening scenes through to its close without a break.
6964-telling-fortunes-by-tea-leaves-how-:
Cicely Kent teaches how to read fate in a teacup, with twenty illustrations to guide the eye. Her contents move from an introduction to tea leaf divination through practice, method, and general theories of reading the cup. She treats the art both as amusement and as a more serious study, with hints for diviners and remarkable instances of prophecy by the leaves.

Later chapters explain writing in the leaves, frequent symbols, and the Nelros cup, with two example readings of its signs. A dictionary of symbols, combinations and their meanings, and example cups with interpretations close the book. Kent opens on the earnest modern search for light on psychic matters, and she invites readers to try the cup themselves.
69769-the-boys-book-of-indian-battles-an:
Boys Book of Indian Battles and Adventures is a juvenile history issued by James Miller at New York in 1866. It holds ten engravings and anecdotes about the Indians of its tales. Its author is unnamed, billed as the author of Evenings in Boston and Ramon the Rover of Cuba. The book was entered for copyright in 1860 in the southern district of New York.

The preface says the character of the aboriginal inhabitants of the western continent is remarkable and striking. Still, that character has never been properly exhibited in a connected view before this book. Miller volume gathers battles and adventures into that connected view for boys. It belongs to the shelf of Indian books by which nineteenth century American boys formed their picture of the first peoples of their continent.
69826-monarchs-of-minstrelsy-from-daddy-:
Edward Le Roy Rice compiled Monarchs of Minstrelsy, a record of blackface stage acts from Daddy Rice to his own day, issued in New York in 1911. The rights were held by his wife Emma Rice, and he gave the book to his mother. Rice had written on minstrelsy in many short forms before he tried the whole field at once.

He says press pieces on the theme had stuck to old timers and to hearsay, with small care for facts. For men still living he used their own career sketches. For the dead he searched records and marked each claim with its source. The book aims to keep the names and fame of the top acts of the minstrel stage in story and picture.
7005-the-antiquary-complete:
Scott's Antiquary appears here complete, joining both volumes into one tale of a collector, a laird, and a beggar. The first volume's contents list an editor's introduction and twenty one chapters, with illustrations of the Antiquary and Lovel in the sanctum, Sir Arthur and Miss Wardour, and their rescue. Eddie Ochiltree's visit, Mrs Heukbane and Mrs Shortcake, and the ruins of St Ruth Abbey fill out the scene.

The second volume adds chapters on the funeral of the countess, Lord Glenallen and Elspeth, the Antiquary visiting Edie in prison, and the Antiquary arming. This complete text carries the whole story without a break, from Anselmo's shrewd and childlike opening to the closing revelations. It is Scott's warm comedy of old books, old stones, and new affections.
7025-rob-roy-complete:
Scott's Rob Roy appears here complete, joining both volumes into one Highland romance. The opening carries Wordsworth's verse on the good old rule, that they should take who have the power and keep who can. An advertisement recalls the editor's promise after the Antiquary to intrude no more, a promise broken like Benedict's vow to die a bachelor.

The complete text follows the young hero from his father's counting house into the world of Miss Vernon, Highland chiefs, and Rob Roy himself. Love, trade, family ruin, and outlaw honor tangle across both volumes without a break. This edition gives the whole novel as Scott first offered it, in full.
70280-the-story-of-the-congo-free-state:
Henry Wellington Wack, a New York lawyer, wrote The Story of the Congo Free State, issued by Putnam in 1905 with 125 art cuts and maps. A portrait of King Leopold the Second of Belgium fronts the book. Wack sets out the social, state, and trade sides of the Belgian system in Central Africa as he saw them.

Early parts trace Stanley's work, the founding of the state, and the Berlin Conference that set its trade rules. Later parts treat the Arab slave trade, wars against the Arabs, the Congo public force, and revolts of the Batetela. Trade, taxes, missions, schools, state lands, and the fierce press campaign in England and America fill the last third.
70450-the-boys-in-white:
Boys in White is the experience of a hospital agent in and around Washington, by Julia S Wheelock. The New York edition is dated eighteen seventy. A verse at the front calls the fittest place for man to die where he dies for man. In her preface Wheelock dates her service from September eighteen sixty two to July eighteen sixty five. She was in the hospitals round Washington in those years, she says.

She kept a journal of her experience, she writes, and parts of it appear here. It was kept for her own benefit, not for publication. Much was written late at night, wearied by labour and anxiety. She would fall asleep with the pen in her hand, she owns. Her object in going south was to help care for a wounded brother, she explains.
70500-gentlemen-please-note:
Randall Garrett wrote Gentlemen: Please Note, a science tale printed in Astounding Science Fiction in October, nineteen fifty-seven. The tale is cast as a letter dated the eighteenth of June, nineteen fifty-seven, from Trinity College, Cambridge. The writer asks his friend Sir James Trowbridge for help with old papers. Copies of letters sent to Isaac Newton as a young man are enclosed.

The letters hint that Newton may have hit on ideas close to Einstein's work on gravity and light. Doctor Henry Blake, a maths man, backs the claim from phrases in the texts. Newton's own replies are lost, so the writer hopes War Office files kept them. Garrett builds a puzzle from real names, lost files, and one bold guess.
70625-debts-hopeful-and-desperate:
Debts Hopeful and Desperate, a study by Ruth McIntyre, tells how money shaped the founding of the Plymouth Colony. Plimoth Plantation published it in 1963 with a grant honouring Ralph Hornblower. A letter of 1633 from the London merchant James Sherley to Governor William Bradford opens the book. Sherley holds that without their joint work, New England might yet have been scarce known.

The study follows the Pilgrims as they decide to emigrate and seek a patent and backing. London merchants invest, and in 1620 Pilgrims and merchants form a joint stock company. Against their patent, the Pilgrims settle at Plymouth, and the young colony struggles with hardship and debt. Disputes over accounts set colony and partners at odds for years. At last, in 1645, Plymouth's debts, hopeful and desperate, are discharged. McIntyre shows the colony as a business venture as much as a religious one.
70665-on-harelip-and-cleft-palate:
William Rose, a London surgery professor, wrote this book on harelip and cleft palate. Lewis printed it in London in 1891 from Gower Street. Rose gives the book to the memory of Sir William Fergusson. Fergusson was his teacher and friend for many kind years.

Rose says years of help to Fergusson taught him these operations well. He aimed to make the work complete and up to date. Colleague Albert Carless revised the book and wrote its growth chapter. Plates came by leave from Mason widow, Coles, and others named. William Rose held a surgery chair at King's College, London.
7091-the-yosemite:
John Muir's Yosemite, dedicated to Robert Underwood Johnson, lover and defender of forests and originator of the national park, opens with the approach to the valley. Muir thanks Whitney's Yosemite Guide Book and Bunnell for early history, then leads readers through winter storms, spring floods, snow storms, and snow banners. Trees of the valley, forest trees in general, and the big trees follow, with flowers and birds.

The South Dome, ancient glaciers and how the valley was formed, and how best to spend one's Yosemite time come next. Early history, Lamon, Galen Clark, and Hetch Hetchy Valley close the main chapters, with an appendix on legislation. Muir writes the valley as scientist, walker, and prophet of preservation.
71205-on-the-wings-of-fate:
On the Wings of Fate is a romance by Effie Adelaide Rowlands, sold as number 393 in the Eagle Series from Street and Smith of New York. The series put out a big new book each week. Its list claims copyright novels by authors famed wherever English is spoken.

The house warns buyers to shun cheap copies made by firms that paid nothing for the texts or plates. It tells readers to ask news dealers for the true line, or send to the house with four cents for postage. Rowlands tale stands in that line of modern romances, by the side of Mrs Georgie Sheldon long list. Readers of cheap love fiction of the day got a full length tale at a low price, fresh each week.
71378-profile-in-black-and-white:
Howard H Quint wrote a frank portrait of South Carolina and its race order. Public Affairs Press issued Profile in Black and White at Washington in 1958. Quint taught at the University of South Carolina at Columbia. A young Southern scholar did much of the research and first draft, unnamed.

Chapters run from the growth of race ties to the case from Clarendon County. The 1954 school ruling text stands in full at the back. White resistance, new nullification, and politics fill the hard middle parts. Readers gain a plain, brave survey of a state in deep change.
7140-the-great-conspiracy-complete:
John Logan's Great Conspiracy appears here complete, joining all parts into one history of its origin and course. The preface pledges historical accuracy, authentic facts, fair and impartial grouping, and true and just conclusions, without mincing words or refraining from calling things by their right names. Logan seeks no favor by fulsome praise on one side or undue denunciation on the other, of living or dead.

The history runs from obscure birth in the brooding brains of a few ambitious men of the Republic's earliest days. Through devolution it reaches nullification, armed rebellion, and still more recent and sinister developments. This complete text carries the whole argument without a break, from conspiracy's roots to freedom's assurance and the constitutional settlement that followed.
71502-american-politics-non-partisan-fro:
Thomas V Cooper and Hector T Fenton wrote American Politics, a non-partisan survey from the start to their day. The Fireside Publishing Company issued the fifteenth revised edition at Philadelphia in eighteen hundred ninety two. Cooper had sat in the Pennsylvania House and Senate. Fenton was a Philadelphia lawyer.

The gift page urges all citizens to take a share in public life. Book one traces each party line in turn. Whig and Tory roots in the colonies come first. Federal and anti-Federal strife follows fast. The fall of the Federals and the rise of Jefferson’s men fill next pages. Great speeches on great themes stand in the text. Tables of dates let a reader find a fact at a glance.
71550-under-dispute:
Under Dispute by Agnes Repplier, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1924, gathers twelve essays first printed in magazines such as The Atlantic Monthly, The Yale Review, and Harper's Magazine. Titles include The Masterful Puritan, Are Americans a Timid People?, The Divineness of Discontent, The Battlefield of Education, and The Idolatrous Dog. The opening essay reaches back to England's Civil War, where William Chillingworth, preaching at Oxford, called the Cavaliers publicans and sinners and the Puritans Scribes and Pharisees.

Repplier defends the Puritans as stern enthusiasts who coveted lofty things and paid any price for them, quoting William Brewster on the Mayflower's first terrible year. Her manner is urbane, combative, and fond of the telling quotation.
71769-a-tragedy-of-love-and-hate:
A Tragedy of Love and Hate, or A Woman's Vow, is a novel by Bertha Clay. It was printed at New York by Street and Smith, with copyright in 1899, 1900 and 1903. Clay also wrote The Duke's Secret, Dora Thorne and The Gipsy's Daughter. The book is number 153 of the Bertha Clay Library. The first chapter is named The Tragedy.

A little bird sings on a swaying bough above the water. Then the song seems to change to a dirge. Her dead face is turned to the bright sky while the flowers bloom around. The bird, the narrator hints, may have seen the deed done in the shade of the woods. From that dark opening the novel works back and forth through the love and hate of its title.
71777-of-yankee-granite:
Cameron wrote this account of the building of Bunker Hill Monument, and the Bunker Hill Monument Association printed it at Boston in 1953. John Silsbee Lawrence wrote the foreword. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology's alumni first sent the book out in 1952.

The prologue goes back to Saturday, June 17, 1775. A force of citizen volunteers held a fortified hilltop farm in Charlestown. They faced the trained troops of the world's strongest nation. When their scant powder gave out, they fell back in good order. One hundred forty of their number lay dead. The book tells how that fight's fame raised a granite shaft over the field, stone by stone.
71990-dante:
Edmund G Gardner revised his Dante primer in nineteen twenty-three, a book first published in nineteen hundred. Gardner states plainly that the volume is no new book on Dante. He gave it to Philip H Wicksteed, in deep affection and high esteem.

The chief changes fall in the parts on the poet's life and his lesser works. A list of books at the end was also brought up to date. Gardner says he would now stress Dante less as allegory and more as the sign and hero of Italy. He follows the Oxford Dante for the numbering of chapters in the Vita Nuova and the letters. Translations by Wicksteed and others aid him.
72714-the-evolution-of-climate:
Brooks, a fellow of the Royal Meteorological Society, wrote this study of how the earth's climate has changed through time. Benn Brothers printed The Evolution of Climate in London in 1922. Simpson, chief of the Meteorological Office, wrote the preface.

Factors of climate and the causes of its swings open the book. Brooks treats the long tale: warm ages, ice ages, and the grounds men have given for each.
