His tables need a plain type to read well, as the printer warns. In 1922 the science of past climates was young and hot with debate. This book set the proofs and the guesses in order for students of weather and of the earth's deep past.
7320-afghanistan-and-the-anglo-russian-d:
Theo. F. Rodenbough, brevet brigadier general in the United States Army, writes Afghanistan and the Anglo-Russian Dispute as an account of Russia's advance toward India. It rests on reports and experiences of Russian, German, and British officers and travellers. With a description of Afghanistan and the military resources of the powers concerned, and three maps, the book follows the road through the gates of Asia to the threshold of India.

British forces and routes face Russian forces and approaches in its chapters, with a review of the contest closing the survey. Rodenbough writes as a soldier-scholar, weighing armies, passes, and rulers, including Abdurrahman Khan, Ameer of Kabul. The book preserves a Victorian strategist's view of the Great Game.
73505-salute:
Thompson Burtis wrote a tale of the Border Air Service, told by a tall thin flyer who calls himself Slim Evans. Slim joined the Army Air Service in 1917 and stayed in, he jokes, since civil work pays too poor a wage. A feud of two air officers, one a regular and one a reserve, forms the tale he tells.

Slim warns readers not to damn a man too fast, nor to crown him a saint too fast. Years of flight have left him scarred, with a bad shoulder and few teeth left in his head. Grit, humor, and hard won doubt shape his voice from the first pages on.
73784-by-motor-to-the-golden-gate:
It tells of a drive by motor car across America to San Francisco. The book is filled with photographs and road maps. It is inscribed to the author's younger son, Bruce. Thirty three chapters carry the trip from New York to the Pacific.

The road runs through Albany, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Indiana to Chicago, then west through Rochelle, North Platte and the desert. The party meets Indians, fog, bad roads and the weight of public opinion on the way. The last chapters turn from story to counsel. One speaks to those who think of following in the same tire tracks. Another takes up clothes, food, equipment and expenses, with a daily expense account. A last one asks how far you can go in comfort.
7379-the-early-life-of-mark-rutherford-w:
W. Hale White wrote as Mark Rutherford, and this book tells the early life of that figure in his own voice. It opens in a provincial English family: sisters, a brother, and an elder sister lost in infancy. The brother, a painter of great promise praised by Ruskin and Rossetti, died young, passionate and hard to manage, and the loss shadows the whole household.

The memoir follows the boy's growth through family life, schooling, and the first stirrings of an independent mind. White writes plainly, without nostalgia, about affection, grief, and the slow discovery of a vocation. Readers meet the roots of the later Mark Rutherford books here: a dissenting, questioning spirit formed in an ordinary home, learning to see the world for himself.
739-henry-clay-s-remarks-in-house-and-se:
Henry Clay spoke these remarks in Congress on two great issues of the early republic. In the House on 19 January 1819 he addressed the Seminole War, questioning the course of war in Florida and the power claimed for it. In the Senate on 16 January 1837 he spoke on the Expunging Resolutions, asking what good could come from striking a censure from the record.

Clay's rhetoric is sharp and patriotic, pressing the Senate on its own powers and on the reach of the president. The speeches show the Great Compromiser at his most forensic, defending the legislature against executive overreach. They remain useful sources for the politics of Jackson's age and for Clay's own place in it.
73924-lancelot-biggs-cooks-a-pirate:
Lancelot Biggs is first mate of the Saturn, a hauler that hops between Earth and Venus, and Nelson Bond's story puts him in the galley. The narrator, Sparks, tells how Cap Hanson fires the ship's cook, Slops, whose whole art was tapioca three times a day. Then no other cook can be found in Sun City, an hour before blast-off. Biggs, who holds that cooking is simply a matter of chemistry, is the man left to prove it.

The story ran in Fantastic Adventures in February 1940. Bond writes broad space comedy: an iron-bellied captain, a crew ready to mutiny over one more dish of goo, and the long-suffering Biggs. What Biggs does when a pirate crosses his path is the joke the title promises.
7400-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
This volume holds the whole of Holmes's poetical works as collected in the 1893 three-volume set, in one place. It runs from the early poems of 1830 to 1836, through the additional poems of 1837 to 1848, and on into the songs, medical poems, and breakfast-table verses of his maturity. Old Ironsides, The Last Leaf, and The Chambered Nautilus all appear in their chronological company.

For a reader who wants Holmes entire, this is the natural starting point. The arrangement lets you watch a Boston doctor become a public poet, then a sage: occasional verse for dinners and jubilees beside lyrics that outlived their occasions. The famous poems gain from their neighbors, and the lesser ones show the working life of a poet who wrote for his city for sixty years.
74347-an-account-of-some-recent-discover:
An Account of Some Recent Discoveries in Hieroglyphical Literature is Thomas Young's report on the reading of Egyptian script, printed by John Murray at London in 1823. Young offers his original alphabet, as extended by Champollion, with translations of five unpublished Greek and Egyptian manuscripts. He dedicates the book to Humboldt, praising his candour in the distribution of literary justice.

The chapters open with the prevalent opinions on hieroglyphics. Investigations founded on the pillar of Rosetta follow. Further inferences are drawn from the Egyptian manuscripts. Young's results, he says, had been deduced some years since from the monuments, and then unexpectedly matched by work from another quarter. The book is a founding document of Egyptology, and a polite salvo in the race to read the stones.
7490-dryden-s-palamon-and-arcite:
John Dryden retold Chaucer's Knight's Tale in his own crisp and vigorous verse, and this school edition presents that retelling for study. Palamon and Arcite are two noble cousins imprisoned by Theseus. Both fall in love with Emily, and their rivalry, fought in tournament and sealed by fate, becomes one of English poetry's great love triangles. George E. Eliot edited the text with introduction and notes.

The preface notes the editor's hope: that through Dryden's verse, young readers will be introduced to Chaucer and learn to admire the old bard. The edition was made for secondary schools, where examination demands varied from college to college, and it explains Dryden's language and allusions as it goes. It is an ideal first meeting with both poets at once.
7535-a-book-of-old-ballads-complete:
Beverley Nichols's complete book of old ballads gathers the whole set in one volume, after the four separate volumes. The contents run wide. Hynd Horn, King Estmere, Barbara Allen's Cruelty, Fair Rosamond, and The Boy and the Mantle stand beside King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid, May Collin, and Thomas the Rhymer. Young Beichan, Clerk Colvill, and Gil Morrice follow.

Later pages add Child Waters, the Earl of Mar's Daughter, the Bailiff's Daughter of Islington, the Three Ravens, and the Wife of Usher's Well. Acknowledgments again show the book's range, from Tipperary through Kipling's Mandalay to Wilde's Ballad of Reading Gaol. For readers who want Nichols's ballads entire, this is the single volume to keep by the chair.
7558-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-m:
Madame Campan served Marie Antoinette as lady-in-waiting, and her memoirs are an insider's account of the French court before and during the Revolution. This volume gathers quotations and images from those memoirs, with the usual finder instruction: search any segment to reach its full context in the eBook. Campan writes from closeness, not from hearsay.

The entries show the court in crisis. There is advice that the king not separate himself from his army. There is the cry that all have been killed in their masters' service. The queen is allowed her candles and as much firewood as she wanted. Better to die than to implicate anybody, customs nearly equal to laws, and the gap between brilliant theories and simplest practice all recur. The collection gives the queen's last years in her servant's loyal, sharp-eyed words.
7605-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-comple:
The Caxtons complete gives Lytton's family picture whole, from preface to farewell. The preface warns that the plot is extremely slight and the incidents few, except those involving the fate of Vivian. Humor, used here for the first time in his work, carries much of the interest. Pisistratus Caxton narrates his family's life, becoming, as he feels, the type of a class daily increasing in modern civilization: one too many in the midst of the crowd.

The complete novel follows Pisistratus from school and home. It passes through Uncle Jack's schemes, Trevanion's politics, and Sir Sedley Beaudesert's polish. It follows the mystery of Vivian to the emigrant farewell in the new land. It is Lytton's longest, warmest domestic work, a family picture in the fullest sense, where the real plot is a young man's growth.
7608-zicci-a-tale-complete:
Zicci complete gives Bulwer-Lytton's whole supernatural tale in one volume. It opens where the first book opens, in the gardens at Naples on a summer evening in the last century. Gentlemen drink sherbet to music, and young Glyndon sinks into gloomy reverie. Merton, the Englishman who first addresses him, speaks for the reader's curiosity.

The complete tale follows Glyndon through his meeting with the mysterious Zicci, his love for Isabel di Pisani, and the fateful choice Zicci sets before him: marry Isabel or lose her forever. All the gentlemen present, the book notes, declared they could comprehend what the stranger described, having felt it themselves. Zicci is Lytton's early study of occult power and human desire, later reworked as Zanoni.
7614-eugene-aram-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Eugene Aram tells the whole tale of a scholar with a buried crime. Aram, a learned and gentle man, falls in love with Madeline Lester and hopes to marry her. His past, however, will not stay buried, and old associates return to Grassdale.

The complete novel follows Aram from quiet study through courtship, wedding plans, and arrest to trial. Lytton built the story on the real eighteenth-century scholar Eugene Aram, hanged for murder. The book asks whether learning and good conduct can atone for a deed done long before.
7623-pelham-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Pelham follows Henry Pelham from nursery to manhood. An only child of a Whig father and a fashionable mother, he learns the rules of good society early. Paris gambling houses, London tailors, and political factions school him further.

The complete novel mixes dandy comedy with a murder mystery. Pelham's polish proves a useful mask: behind it works a watchful mind. Thornton, Dawson, and Job Jonson cross his path as the inquiry tightens. Lytton's first great success, it made the dandy hero a figure of its age. Fashion and crime walk side by side through the whole tale.
7630-devereux-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Devereux is a tale of youth, exile, and return, composed when its author was almost a boy. The advertisement admits faults of construction that only a full rewrite could cure. It keeps instead the frank enthusiasm of early work, lightly pruned.

The complete novel follows its hero from London pleasure through disgrace, madness, and affliction to a hard-won recovery. A lost packet, a brother's suspicion, and years abroad shape his fate. Devereux stands as Lytton's early study of a life broken and remade. The hero's long road ends far from where it began.
76340-the-fairy-flute:
Rose Fyleman pipes for children in The Fairy Flute, printed in London, first published on October 6, 1921. Methuen made the book, here in a second edition of 1922. Fyleman had writ Fairies and Chimneys and The Fairy Green. She gives the book to all her nephews and nieces.

Short fairy poems fill the small volume. Consolation leads, then If You Meet a Fairy and Fairy Lore. Every Fairy Has a Star, The Fairy Lover, and The Fairy Tailor stand in the run. At Dawn, The Green Loch, and The Skylark vary the set with nature notes. In Bond Street brings the fairies to town. A fairy lullaby for a mortal, a canary, and a rainy morning keep the gentle, nursery tone.
7639-the-disowned-complete:
A soft May evening along a green English lane opens Lytton's The Disowned, where a young singer walks alone among woods and furze. The quiet scene soon gives way to a tale of birth, rank, and a family name cast aside, as a hero cut off from his kin must find his way back.

Across its full span the novel mixes romance, disguise, and sharp talk about pride and money. Old servants stay loyal, rivals press their claims, and letters reveal what polite talk hides. It stands as an early Victorian novel of love and social place, told at a broad, steady pace.
7649-ernest-maltravers-complete:
A gifted young Englishman grows from youth to manhood across Europe and back in Lytton's Ernest Maltravers, dedicated to German readers. The full novel joins the hero's growth in art and thought to love affairs, friendships, and the temptations of high society.

From Italian lakes to London salons, Maltravers meets poets, schemers, and women who test his ideals. The preface places it among the author's few novels of his own day, after the early Pelham and Godolphin. It remains a broad Victorian tale of talent, pride, and the search for a true life.
7658-kenelm-chillingly-complete:
An eccentric heir leaves a settled baronet's house for walking, talk, and odd trials in Lytton's Kenelm Chillingly, complete. Sir Peter and his well-taught wife give their son comfort and rank, yet the boy grows into a thinker who trusts ideals more than custom.

Across eight books he meets lovers, schemers, journalists, and plain country folk, debating real life against high aims at every stop. The novel blends comedy, philosophy, and romance, and ends as a portrait of a young man who seeks truth by stepping outside his class.
7671-what-will-he-do-with-it-complete:
In full, Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It?, written as Pisistratus Caxton, follows Guy Darrell, Lionel Haughton, Waife, and Sophy through fairs, London parks, and country houses. It opens at a Surrey fair and widens into a tale of lost sons, hidden kin, and fortunes made and spent.

Darrell's wealth, gained at the bar and by legacy, sets him among fine neighbors, while Mrs. Lyndsay and her daughter Caroline circle his house at Carlton Gardens. Across twelve books the novel blends comedy, satire, and pathos, asking what a man should do with talent, money, and a name.
7684-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
Twelve books carry Lytton's Harold from Godwin's house to Hastings field, following the last Saxon king through love, kin quarrels, and a fatal meeting with Duke William across the Channel. Edith, his beloved, stands beside councils, prophecies, and battles that decide a nation's fate.

Lytton built the romance on chronicles and his friend's library, aiming to make a remote age vivid for common readers. Battles, church politics, and oaths fill the tale, which treats the Conquest as a national turning point. It remains a landmark Victorian historical novel, rich in research and feeling.
7691-lucretia-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Lucretia, complete, pairs a dark tale of home training with its sunny twin, The Caxtons. Both test how early scenes and example shape later conduct, but Lucretia seeks its moral through awe and distress, where the other works through humor and warm feeling.

From a family group at the St. John house through conferences, Guy's Oak, and a second part set after revolution, the novel follows a girl whose lessons bend toward crime. Lytton notes readers judged the book by pain rather than purpose, a point the 1853 preface answers at length.
77095-the-history-and-adventures-of-the-:
The History and Adventures of the Renowned Don Quixote is Smollett's English rendering. The Spanish tale is by Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra, Spain's famed writer. Harrison and Company printed this four-volume set in London in 1792. Smollett set an account of the author's life before the tale itself. He gave the work to Don Ricardo Wall, Spain's secretary of state.

Wall had served as Spain's envoy at the court of Great Britain. Smollett dated his address from London in February of 1755. The life calls Cervantes at once the glory and reproach of Spain. His genius honoured his land, but his poor old age shamed it. Don Quixote and Sancho Panza ride on the road in the front picture. Books of chapters divide the knight's mad, noble quest through Spain. This old rendering kept the tale in English hands for years.
7714-my-novel-complete:
A winter night in Uncle Roland's tower opens Lytton's My Novel, complete, with Mr. Caxton turning a globe, his wife trimming a frock, and Pisistratus in bad humor by the fire. Roland reads a third volume, Squills ponders railway shares, and a family tale begins.

Across twelve books the Caxtons, Riccabocca, Randal Leslie, and Violante move through love, debt, exile, and politics. Frank grows smitten with a fair Italian, Randal watches with narrowed eyes, and the narrator debates his own craft. It is a long, witty panorama of English life.
77215-return-of-the-brute:
Return of the Brute is a war novel by Liam O'Flaherty. The Mandrake Press published it in London in 1929. The story opens at the battle front on a rainy night. Two soldiers share an outpost of a bombing section. Gunn has been dozing on the fire-step. Lamont keeps watch as sentry.

Lamont thinks he hears something crawling in the dark. Gunn listens and hears only rain and rats. The post holds eight inches of water. Gunn teases the young sentry gently. He takes the watch so Lamont can smoke. The talk is rough, cold, and tired. The scene sets the tone of trench life in the book.
7727-the-last-of-the-barons-complete:
Wars of the Roses fill Lytton's The Last of the Barons, complete, through Warwick the Kingmaker, Edward IV, and the scholar Adam Warner. From London courts to Middleham, from popular revolt to Barnet field, it tracks how great men rise, quarrel, and fall.

Lytton argues in his dedication that fiction can fill history's cold outlines with habit, motive, and thought. He uses careful guesswork where records fall silent. Sibyll, Marmaduke, Hilyard, and Richard of Gloucester carry the human cost. It is a broad, learned romance of fifteenth-century England, full of courts, camps, and scholars.
7735-paul-clifford-complete:
One novel with a robber hero stands out in Lytton's work: Paul Clifford, complete, written to attack prison discipline and a hanging code. Boys learn crime from felons in the yard, he argues, then men hang at the first chance, as if the state could hide its own blunders at Newgate's drop.

Across its full span Paul grows from a prison boy to a highwayman chief, moving between Bath assemblies, London taverns, and courtrooms. Lucy, Brandon, and Mauleverer pull him toward love, law, and rank. It remains a bold early Victorian protest novel, comic yet angry at heart.
7749-the-parisians-complete:
Lytton's The Parisians, complete, joins Kenelm Chillingly and The Coming Race as late works with one moral aim, his son's prefatory note explains. Early satire mocked false respect, later humor defended real bonds, but these three warn against popular theories that warp character and national life.

From salons and siege to letters between Isaura and her friends, the full novel follows Graham Vane, Alain de Rochebriant, and Rameau through Second Empire Paris into war. It blends romance, politics, and social satire into a wide picture of France at a turning point.
7756-godolphin-complete:
Lytton's Godolphin, complete, begins with a playful letter to Count d'Orsay, claiming a long-disowned hero who now begs his patron's name. Prefaces on self-criticism follow, then a tale of a gifted, restless man torn between Constance, Lucilla, and the claims of rank and wealth.

Across six volumes the hero moves through London drawing rooms and Roman palazzi, learning how feeling alone cannot guide a life, and how pride spoils what love might save. The novel pairs witty social scenes with earnest debate about virtue, love, and ambition, and stands among Lytton's most personal early romances.
7761-falkland-complete:
Lytton's Falkland, complete, restores his boyhood novel, once withdrawn for its morals yet widely read abroad in Tauchnitz editions. With his son's consent, the collected edition prints it again, noting that a book already in many hands should carry its history with it, not hide it.

In full, the tale follows Emily Mandeville, her husband, and Erasmus Falkland through journals, letters, and meetings that test marriage, conscience, and passion. It shows a young author already skilled at feeling and social talk, and a mature author uneasy with his own early work, a tension that makes the book doubly interesting.
7795-pelle-the-conqueror-complete:
Martin Andersen Nexo's Pelle the Conqueror, complete in Jessie Muir and Bernard Miall's translation from Danish, follows Pelle from boyhood through apprenticeship, the great struggle, and daybreak. Born in 1869 in a poor quarter of Copenhagen, Nexo was little known until the first part appeared in 1906.

The novel traces a poor boy's growth into a labor leader, through farm work, town shops, strikes, and hope for a fairer life. Its four parts form a single arc of Danish working life, praised as a major social novel of its age, and a portrait of dignity won through struggle.
78171-liberty-in-the-modern-state:
Harold Laski, professor of political science in the University of London, wrote this study of freedom, published by Harper and Brothers at New York and London in 1930. He defines liberty as the absence of restraint upon those social conditions that modern civilization requires for individual happiness. Four long chapters treat the nature of liberty, freedom of the mind, liberty and social power, and the outlook for liberty.

Laski argues that men are free when the rules they live under leave them without frustration in the realms they deem significant, and unfree when rules compel conduct they resent. Unlimited political power, he holds, always poisons its holders, who end by imposing their own canon of good on everyone else. Liberty therefore demands that rulers be limited and called to account, and Pericles was right that its secret is courage.
78204-the-privations-of-a-private:
The Privations of a Private is a war memoir by Marcus B. Toney, a Confederate veteran of Tennessee. A revised second edition appeared at Nashville in 1907. Toney dedicates the volume to the men who wore the gray and to his Masonic brethren. The title page lists the campaigns the book covers, from service under Lee and Jackson to prison life in the North.

Toney states his aim at the start. He means to follow the life of a Confederate private as he lived it and saw it lived by others. Chapters move through Bragg's invasion of Kentucky and the Chickamauga campaign. Later parts cover the Wilderness campaign and his time as a prisoner at Point Lookout and Elmira. Closing chapters treat the hardships of a citizen after the war and argue for a united citizenship.
7823-the-attache-or-sam-slick-in-england:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton's The Attache, or Sam Slick in England, complete, joins both volumes of the Yankee's English tour. The same 1843 letter sends Sam ahead to Edgeworth, warning that his humor needs indulgence while his original talk and queer views promise fun for his hosts.

From uncorking a bottle and a juicy country day through Ascot races, spies, patrons, and cow's tails, the full book satirizes England through American eyes. Sam's slang and shrewd asides cut both nations, making the complete edition a broad comic record of Atlantic manners in the 1840s, still sharp today.
7852-memoirs-of-aaron-burr-complete:
Matthew L. Davis's Memoirs of Aaron Burr, complete in two volumes, rests on forty years of friendship and Burr's full confidence. After Burr's return from Europe in 1812, he urged Davis to record his political life, and Jefferson's account of the 1801 contest in Congress pushed him to open every paper.

From law study and courtroom craft through the tied election, duel, and western schemes, the memoirs mix letters with Davis's own knowledge. With a motto of burying Caesar, not praising him, the work offers a partisan yet intimate portrait of a founder whom history has judged harshly.
78629-fires-of-fate:
Tuttle's Fires of Fate is a western of the Canadian border, by the author of Cultus Collins and the Ghost Gold. The head note gives the shape of it: a bunch of crooks along the border took long to learn that you can buck the Mounties just so long. They did not know a Montana cowpuncher stood in the ranks of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police.

Chapter one is The Resignation. Bud Conley, just fired by Inspector Grandon after one drunk bout on Monk Magee's hooch, spits his scorn for Magee: so low-down he could walk under a snake in a plug hat. Then Grandon names a complaint from Beaudet, and Bud whirls back to the desk to call it a lie to his face.
7878-passages-from-the-english-notebooks:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the English Note-Books, complete, joins both volumes of his private journals, dedicated to Francis Bennoch for hospitality that made England feel like home. The editor's preface notes Hawthorne's wish against biography and his extreme reserve, which kept strangers at bay.

Rather than a life written by another, these notes give Hawthorne's own record, day by day, through London, country houses, and travel. The complete text lets readers follow his English years whole, from first dinners and clubs to final departures, in prose at once shy, sharp, and observant of English manners.
7881-passages-from-the-french-and-italia:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the French and Italian Note-Books, complete, joins both volumes of his travel journals from France and Italy. It opens as before on January 6, 1858, with trunks packed at the Hotel de Louvre, cabs at dawn, and a cold drive to London Bridge station.

From Paris onward through Italian cities, Hawthorne notes pictures, churches, streets, and fellow travelers with a novelist's eye. The complete text lets readers follow one long journey without break, from first Channel crossing to final Italian days, in daily entries of observation and reflection.
78830-on-yacht-etiquette:
On Yacht Etiquette, by Captain Howard Patterson, is a small guide in the Rudder On series, bound in blue buckram and gold and sold for one dollar. Patterson led the New York Nautical College and once ran the school ship St Mary. The hosted text is the second edition, revised.

His full title promises what to do and how to do it, for any and all cases on board. Parts treat courtesies, discipline, ceremonies, and routine, plus the duties of officers. Notes sort flag forms, from the triangular club burgee to the swallowtail private signal of an owner. Rectangles mark flag officers. Yacht owners and crew of the sail age got a neat rule book for life afloat in good form.
78961-alias-whispering-white:
W C Tuttle wrote Alias Whispering White, a western tale told by a sourdough narrator. Tuttle had written The Hand of Providence and Pie for Magpie. The narrator and his pal Magpie take to a young mining engineer at once.

Franklyn Burt knows minerals well yet acts no better than the old hands. He pokes around their prospect and teaches them new tricks of timbering. Then a letter comes, the first since he arrived. He groans and curses over its news. Marion White, raised with him through school and college, is to marry a duke. Magpie jokes that they might push the old duke along. Feeling runs deeper than the joke.
78992-a-daily-rate:
Grace Livingston Hill's A Daily Rate was published at Philadelphia by the Union Press in 1900, under a Sunday-School Union copyright. Hill had written A Chautauqua Idyl and Katharine's Yesterday before it. The title marks the story's world of wages counted by the day, and its heroine's life is measured out in work, rent, and small hopes.

Chapter one is a birthday. Celia Murray, a saleswoman in a store, stands in the dim front room of Mrs Morris's boarding-house, watching for the postman. She is not really expecting a letter; she only wants to be near if one comes. Her half holiday went not to the parade but to mending worn garments in her cold third-story room, stitching down the row of them before the light failed. She called the work her dress parade, to keep her spirits up over it.
79556-the-gate-marked-private:
The Gate Marked Private is a novel by Ethel Dell, published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1928. Dell, who wrote under her married name of Savage for the copyright, had filled a long list of novels. The Way of an Eagle, Charles Rex, The Knave of Diamonds, Greatheart, and The Lamp in the Desert stand among them. The contents fall into two parts.

The first part opens with A Cock Pheasant, then Staple Farm, Little Staple, and Concerning Pigs. Matilda, Rosemary, The Real Reason, Original Sin, and Mary lead to The Discovery and Dick Dynamo. The second part turns to Three Friends, An Affair of Partnership, and Ravencombe, with Grievances, Punishment, Youth, and Christmas. A passage preserved in the copy sets the shooting scene. From the edge of the Long Copse on Staple Farm's northern boundary came the whir of wings.
79693-strait-is-the-gate-la-porte-e-troi:
Strait Is the Gate is a novel by André Gide, translated from the French by Dorothy Bussy. Macmillan of Canada published the translation at Toronto in 1924.

He warns that some might have made a book of it, but living it took all his strength. He lost his father before he was twelve years old. His mother then left Le Havre, where his father had practised as a doctor, for Paris. An apartment near the Luxembourg became their home. Miss Flora Ashburton, the mother's former governess, lived with them as companion and friend. Both women were gentle, sad, and dressed in mourning. The boy's health was delicate, and their one thought was to keep him from ailing.
8294-the-world-english-bible-web-complet:
This volume gathers the whole World English Bible, a modern English translation of the Scriptures made for free use by all. It runs from Genesis, with creation and the stories of Abraham and Moses. It moves through the histories, poems, and prophets of ancient Israel, then on to the Gospels, the letters of Paul, and the closing visions of Revelation. Sixty-six books stand in one sequence.

Because the text is in the public domain, it can be read, quoted, and shared without restriction, and its plain wording aims to be clear to ordinary readers. The complete edition suits anyone who wants the full Bible in a single modern rendering, whether for daily reading, study, or comparison with older translations.
8376-memoirs-correspondence-and-manuscri:
Lafayette's family published these memoirs, letters, and papers in 1837 as a legacy to the American people, and the volume gathers a life spent on two continents' revolutions. The young French marquis who sailed to join Washington became a general of the American war. He then returned to France to carry the same ideals into his own country's revolution, and later into its July days.

Letters to Washington, Jefferson, and friends, along with memoirs written in his own hand, show a man linking liberty across the Atlantic. Readers meet battles, prisons, and political quarrels, but also friendships that lasted decades. For anyone tracing how American and French freedom movements spoke to each other, Lafayette's own papers are the first source.
8460-marse-henry-an-autobiography-comple:
This complete edition gathers Henry Watterson's autobiography, Marse Henry, in full, from his early life through his long career as Louisville editor and political figure. Dedicated to Alexander Konta from Mansfield in 1919, the book opens with Watterson's verse on fame. That verse pictures fame as a mound of earth and faded printer's ink, and the book tells a life spent at the center of Kentucky journalism.

Watterson, founder of the Courier-Journal, knew presidents, generals, and editors, and his memoirs mix anecdote with opinion. The complete text suits readers who want the whole story in one volume, rather than the separate volumes. It remains a key source for newspaper history and for the politics of the post-Civil War South.
8505-normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its:
Gordon Home depicts Normandy, its scenery and romance, through its ancient towns, in this complete edition dated Epsom, October 1905. Contents move from some features of Normandy and the banks of the Seine to Rouen, the ancient capital. They continue to the cathedral city of Evreux and the road to Bernay, and to Lisieux and the romantic town of Falaise.

Home, both author and illustrator, gives a travel book of coloured and line illustrations, churches, streets, and landscapes. Readers get Edwardian travel writing at its most picturesque, before war changed the region. The volume suits armchair travelers and anyone planning a Normandy tour with a historic guide in hand.
8525-eve-s-diary-complete:
Mark Twain's Eve's Diary appears here complete, illustrated by Lester Ralph and presented as translated from the original. It opens on Saturday, when Eve is almost a whole day old, having arrived yesterday. She reasons that if there was a day before yesterday, she was not there, or she should remember it. She resolves to be very watchful now.

The complete diary follows Eve from first days in Eden through meeting Adam, naming the world, and learning love and loss, with Adam's diary entries balancing her own. Readers get Twain's comic Genesis in full, tender and funny, where Eden is seen through a woman's wondering eyes. The complete text suits readers who want the whole story, not a part.
8562-the-seaboard-parish-complete:
George MacDonald tells this long novel in the voice of a clergyman who has moved with his family to a parish by the sea. The narrator speaks straight to his readers, as if preaching, and mixes family scenes with plain talk about faith, duty, and daily conduct. His daughter Constance, called Connie, her birthday, illness, dreams, and watch-tower all thread through the early chapters.

Once the family reaches Kilkhaven, the story settles into parish life: the old church, Sunday evenings, sermons, neighbours, and small crises at home. MacDonald uses ordinary events, a letter, a journey, a sick room, to raise larger questions about trust and kindness. The complete text joins all the volumes, so the family's seaside years can be read straight through.
8726-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-compl:
Emile Zola's Rome, complete in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, follows Abbe Pierre Froment, author of New Rome, to the Eternal City to seek the Church's judgment on his book. Part one sets Pierre among the Boccaneras and the Romans of the Church: Cardinals Boccanera and Sanguinetti, Abbes Paparelli and Santobono, Don Vigilio, and Monsignor Nani. Part two turns to the Romans of new Italy, the Pradas and Saccos, and to the blood of Augustus in palaces, forums, the Appian Way, and St Peter's.

Later parts tour the Vatican, the Sistine Chapel, and the art of Michelangelo and Raphael, while Pierre's hopes for a rejuvenated Christianity meet Roman reality. Zola's naturalism fills every scene with crowds, food, vestments, and stone. The complete novel is long, but it rewards patience with a panoramic argument about faith, power, and Italy, and it stands as the middle panel of the Three Cities trilogy.
8795-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Dante Alighieri's Vision of Purgatory, illustrated by Gustave Dore and translated by the Reverend H. F. Cary, gives the complete second canticle, cantos one through thirty-three. Dante's bark lifts its sail over better waves, glad to leave so cruel a sea behind. Sings of the region where the human spirit is purged of sinful blot and prepared for ascent to Heaven. The mountain rises from a shore where souls arrive by boat, through terraces of pride, envy, wrath, sloth, avarice, gluttony, and lust.

At the summit lies the Earthly Paradise, where Beatrice replaces Virgil and Dante is washed clean for Paradise. Cary's verse and Dore's engravings make this the most approachable complete Purgatory in English. Readers who know the Inferno will find its necessary counterpart here: not eternal punishment, but hope, discipline, and the slow work of becoming fit for Heaven.
8799-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Dante's Vision of Paradise, illustrated by Gustave Dore and translated by the Reverend H. F. Cary, gives the complete third canticle, cantos one through thirty-three. Dante opens by praising the glory whose might pierces the universe, shedding more light in one part and less elsewhere. Confesses that he was a witness in Heaven of things beyond power to retell. From the moon's heaven upward, Beatrice leads him through spheres of light.

Saints, theologians, warriors, and mystics appear as flames, roses. Singing lights, until the final vision of the Trinity and the love that moves the sun and the other stars. Cary's translation and Dore's engravings have long served as the classic English gateway to Paradise. The complete volume lets readers climb the whole ascent in one journey, from earthly parting to a vision that words, Dante insists, can only approach.
8948-poems-on-serious-and-sacred-subject:
Printed at Chichester in 1818 at a private press, this small book of verse was not sold in shops but given as tokens of regard to the author's own friends. Its poems take up serious and sacred themes, above all death, faith, and the life of the soul. The opening piece, an epistle to a lady dated 1768, faces the fear of death head on.

The verse argues that guilt feeds dread, yet even the guiltless tremble at the grave, and it urges trust in God as the cure for fear. The tone is earnest and plain, not showy. As a private gift book, it offers a rare, close look at how one devout writer spoke to friends about the end of life.
9169-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-comp:
Émile Zola completed his Three Cities trilogy with Paris, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. This file gives the whole novel, not just one book. Its hero, Abbé Pierre Froment, sought faith at Lourdes and hope in Rome, and found neither. In Paris he faces a last choice between religion and life.

Vizetelly's preface states Zola's view plainly: Pierre stands for Man, torn between the Church and Reason. The novel's Paris scenes join plot to symbol. For readers of Zola, this complete text is the trilogy's fitting end, stern, vast, and humane.
9320-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-complete:
Ian Maclaren's complete Doctor of the Old School gathers all the Drumtochty tales in one volume. Contents include A General Practitioner, Through the Flood, A Fight with Death, The Doctor's Last Journey, and The Mourning of the Glen. Illustrations show Dr. MacLure, Sandy Stewart, and scenes of glen life.

Through these tales, MacLure rides by night and day, through snow and flood, to bedsides rich and poor. The glen mourns him as a friend, not just a doctor. The complete book remains a beloved classic of Scottish fiction, gentle, humorous, and full of heart.
9384-the-comrade-in-white:
Reverend W. H. Leathem wrote this devotional poem on Christ as the comrade in white. Its opening stanzas recall soldiers of the Cross in Holy War, who saw the Holy Grail borne on angels' wings as a pledge of Christ's presence. The chalice once held wine as emblem of sacrifice, and the Master still met his friends.

Later stanzas turn to soldiers now, fighting oppression, tyranny, and wrong, with Christ himself beside them, not just a relic. The veil lifts, and fellowship replaces vision. The poem remains a stirring Victorian hymn of faith in action, earnest and hopeful.
9450-samantha-among-the-brethren-complet:
Marietta Holley, as Josiah Allen's Wife, wrote Samantha Among the Brethren complete in 1890, dedicated to all women who work to bring brightness into dark lives. Its preface shows Josiah watching Samantha lift her inkstand to her literary corner with majestic gait. He asks what she will tackle now, and she answers: the Cause of Eternal Justice.

Josiah, uneasy, asks if there is anything else, and Samantha adds the meeting house in particular. The complete novel joins all parts into one comic epic of church, farm, and women's rights. It remains Holley's most beloved work, funny, earnest, and ahead of its time.
9600-the-works-of-john-greenleaf-whittie:
The Complete Works of John Greenleaf Whittier, in the Standard Library Edition, gathers his poems and prose as he himself revised them. The edition opens with volume one, Narrative and Legendary Poems, from The Vaudois Teacher to The Double-Headed Snake of Newbury. Whittier added head-notes on each poem's source and date, so readers can trace his art. Early poems once dropped from print return in an appendix.

Later volumes span nature, memory, faith, reform, and personal verse, with tales, sketches, and essays beside. The set aims to be full and retrospective, a life's work in order. A reader gets the whole Whittier in one edition, and the best path to a poet who sang for freedom and home.
9628-buried-cities-pompeii-olympia-mycen:
Jennie Hall's Buried Cities gathers her tales of Pompeii, Olympia, and Mycenae in one volume for young readers. Hall, a Chicago history teacher, opens by asking children if they love to dig for hidden treasure. Each city gets its own story of life, ruin, and rediscovery, with drawings and photos from original sources. Captions by a fellow teacher guide the eye.

Pompeii shows a Roman town caught by ash, Olympia a Greek games site, and Mycenae a kingly citadel of legend. Hall writes with clarity and warmth, made for school use. A reader gets three buried worlds in one book, and a fine first taste of archaeology as adventure.
9755-night-and-morning-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning, complete in one volume, gathers all five books plus a preface to the 1845 edition. Book one opens with an introductory chapter on sound learning, while later books follow Beaufort, Arthur, and their tangled fates through London and Paris. The complete contents run from book one's opening to book five's long close.

Taken whole, the novel traces ambition, guilt, and fortune across a generation, with Lytton's polished moral prose throughout. The single volume suits readers who want the full arc. A reader gets a major Victorian novel entire, rich in plot, place, and the price of pride.
9761-leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-compl:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila, or The Siege of Granada, complete in one volume, tells a romance of Moorish Spain's last summer. Book one opens in 1491, as Ferdinand and Isabel invest Granada beneath moonlit Sierra snows. Inside the city, groups linger to lutes and tales, half heedless of the siege. The enchanter and the warrior frame the tale's start.

Across five books, Leila's fate crosses kings, priests, and battles, from royal tents to the great assault. Lytton writes with rich, romantic color. A reader gets the whole Granada romance in one place, where a city's fall becomes a young girl's story.
9774-alice-or-the-mysteries-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, complete in one volume, opens in a Devonshire cottage in early April. Two ladies sit by open windows, before lawns gay with evergreens and first spring flowers. The sea, blue and calm, bounds the view through the trees. The cottage's owner, a woman past thirty yet looking younger, chose this remote spot to suit her quiet taste.

From this sequestered start, the novel's mysteries unfold across eleven books, through love, villainy, and Paris scenes. Lytton's prose favors polished romance and moral reflection. A reader gets the whole Alice in one place, a Victorian mystery of beauty, fate, and hidden pasts.
9924-viviette:
William J. Locke's 1916 novel centers on Viviette, a young woman caught between two brothers and their plotting. The opening chapters introduce the brothers, their conspirators, and a girl named Katherine, before famous duelling pistols bring the quarrel to a crisis.

When the crisis comes, Viviette herself takes the risk that decides matters, acting with courage the men around her lack. Locke writes with charm and a light irony, and the romance turns on character rather than action. Readers get an engaging story of love, honor, and a woman who refuses to wait.
a-book-of-old-ballads-complete:
Beverley Nichols selected and introduced A Book of Old Ballads, and the complete volume gathers all four parts of his set in one place. The acknowledgments trace most pieces to Percy's Reliques and to the English and Scottish ballads edited by Child and Kittredge, with Kipling's 'Mandalay' and Wilde's 'Ballad of Reading Gaol' included by permission.

The contents run in the four volumes' order, from 'Mandalay,' 'King Estmere,' and 'Barbara Allen's Cruelty' through 'The Heir of Linne,' 'Chevy Chace,' and 'Sir Patrick Spens' to 'Edward. Edward,' 'Hynd Horn,' and 'The Wife of Usher's Well. ' Kings, outlaws, mermaids, and betrayed lovers act out short dramas in verse, many in old spelling. An appendix names the source of every ballad, and colour plates illustrate favourites throughout.
a-cotswold-village-or-country-life-and-p: Joseph Arthur Gibbs describes a Cotswold village and country life in Gloucestershire. Flying westwards through the Thames Valley, he enters the Cotswolds and settles into village scenes. Chapters treat an old farmhouse, its occupants, and the pursuits of country people. Gibbs writes a fond portrait of rural England in its third edition form.
a-day-of-fate: Edward Payson Roe's 1880 novel, told by a printer narrator, follows aimless steps into a June day dream, a Quaker tea and a mystery of love. A bit of Eden, lightning and a subtler flame lead to a fateful choice, then to a second book of aftermath: weakness, failure, depths and a hope of hidden treasure. Letters, a meeting-house and Thanksgiving Day mark the road back.
a-dissertation-on-horses-wherein-it-is-d:
A Dissertation on Horses, by William Osmer and printed at London in 1756, argues against the reigning faith in blood. Osmer's title states his thesis in full: innate qualities do not exist, and a horse's excellence is altogether mechanical, not in the blood. By mechanical he means a matter of shape and build, the conformation of the animal, rather than the fame of its ancestors.

Inside, Osmer surveys the history of horse racing writing, the raising and use of horses among the nomad Arabs, and evidence that the ancient Nisaean breed survived in Turkey. Stories of the Godolphin Arabian, a foundation sire of English racing, test his argument on famous ground. The book reads as an early plea for evidence over pedigree worship, written while English breeding still ran largely on superstition about bloodlines.
a-doctor-of-the-old-school-complete: Ian Maclaren gives the complete Doctor of the Old School in one volume. Its parts follow a general practitioner through flood, a fight with death, a last journey, and the mourning of the glen. Dr. MacLure serves the people of Drumtochty with rough kindness and skill. The complete text gathers the whole beloved Scottish story in order.
a-far-country-complete:
Winston Churchill's complete novel tells the whole life of Hugh Paret in three books, narrated by Paret himself. He was a corporation lawyer, he begins, though by no means a typical one, and he calls his book the autobiography of a romanticist. The city of his rise, famous for sudden millionaires, stands behind every stage of the tale.

Book one makes the man, book two schools him in state politics and corporate power, and book three calls the account due. Marriage, ambition, friendship, and faith all pass under his own cross-examination. Churchill, once a national political figure, wrote the novel as an anatomy of American success and its spiritual price.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-complete:
William Dean Howells called A Hazard of New Fortunes the first fruit of his New York life. In his bibliographical note he tells how Basil and Isabel March moved with him from Boston in 1889. The Marches house-hunt through the commercial metropolis as he himself had done. A great street-car strike gave the story its public spine.

The Marches join a new magazine venture backed by the dry-goods rich Fulkerson and Dryfoos. Old Lindau, a one-handed German socialist, voices the era's anger at wealth. Howells weaves in the dreams of Henry George and Edward Bellamy, then current hopes for a fairer economy. Love plots cross class lines while the strike turns violent. The novel is his largest canvas: a comedy of housing and publishing stretched over a tragedy of labour.
a-journal-of-a-tour-in-the-congo-free-st: Marcus R. P. Dorman journals a tour in the Congo Free State. Dorman, author of a history of the British Empire in the nineteenth century, writes of political thought and popular ignorance. His Congo journal adds travel observation to that scholarly background. The book records firsthand notes from a troubled colonial state. Readers see trade, rule, and daily life through a traveler's eyes.
a-lover-s-diary-complete: Gilbert Parker's A Lover's Diary, complete, joins both volumes of his verse diary of love, first given to the public in 1894. The first volume ascends from vision and meeting to pledge; the second descends through dreams, a bride, a wraith and surrender into division, vanishing and a closed door. Reunion, overcoming and an envoy close a long arc from first sight to memory.
a-modern-chronicle-complete:
Winston Churchill's A Modern Chronicle, complete in one file, tells the whole career of Honora Leffingwell across three books and forty-one chapters. Born at Nice, the consul's daughter is raised in St. Louis by Uncle Tom and Aunt Mary. What's in Heredity? asks the first chapter. Perdita Recalled and Concerning Providence answer with her childhood.

Book One carries her through school to a glimpse of the world and the Olympian order of country houses. Book Two marries her to Howard Spence and installs her at Quicksands, among the great unattached. Book Three follows her divorce, her work on the Chiltern biography, and her union with Hugh Chiltern. Paris closes the chronicle, with Mr. Erwin seeking her there. Churchill, America's best-selling novelist of manners, made Honora a national mirror: ambition, wealth, and a woman's freedom priced in full. The complete text is the record entire.
a-prisoner-in-fairyland-the-book-that-un:
A Prisoner in Fairyland, by Algernon Blackwood and published in 1913, is the book that Uncle Paul wrote, as its subtitle promises. Blackwood, listed as the author of Jimbo, John Silence, and The Centaur, continues the story begun in The Education of Uncle Paul. His dedication offers the tale to a little mouse of his invention, whiskers up at the thunder, and a French poem on flying thoughts opens the door.

Uncle Paul, a man whose imagination never grew up, finds his way back into the world of children's thoughts, where ideas travel like starlight from mind to mind. A railway journey, a Swiss village, and a house full of children supply the earthly frame. Blackwood writes fantasy as metaphysics for the nursery: what adults call imagination, children experience as a country, and a grown man may be its prisoner by love as much as by enchantment.
a-romance-of-youth-complete:
Francois Coppee's A Romance of Youth stands whole in this English edition, a tale of a Paris childhood. Little Amedee, a widow's son, grows up beside the Gerard family. The engraver works at his copper plate while his daughters play around him. Shared dinners and a pasteboard doll fill the boy's happiest hours.

Maria makes Amedee her little husband in the children's endless games of calls and families. Years turn the game toward truth as the children reach youth. Work, poverty, and first ambition widen Amedee's Paris beyond the beloved rooms. Coppee builds the novel from kindnesses rather than adventures. Old neighbors and small mercies return to steer the ending's joys and regrets. Readers who take the story whole feel its design best: youth remembered as a warm world that time enlarges and breaks.
a-study-of-the-topography-and-municipal-: Ralph Van Deman Magoffin studies the topography and municipal history of Praeneste in this Johns Hopkins study of September and October 1908. The first chapter maps the domain, walls and gates, the triumphal gate, water supply, temple of Fortuna Primigenia, epigraphical topography, fora, and sacred way. The second chapter asks whether Praeneste was a municipium or a colony, then lists its officers, regulations, and quinquennales in alphabetical and chronological order.
a-sweet-girl-graduate:
L. T. Meade's A Sweet Girl Graduate, dated 1891 on its title page, sends Priscilla Peel to college. Priscilla Penywern Peel, nearly nineteen, packs her new trunk at Penywern Cottage. Her aunt Raby charges her to write weekly and not be nervous. Prissie answers that girls are not nervous nowadays.

At St. Benet's she tastes the delights of being a fresher, Meade's word for a first-year student. Eavesdroppers, conspirators, and a mysterious episode test her honesty. Polly Singleton and pretty little Rosalind supply the friendships and the fashion. A black self and a white self, one chapter's title, names her inner debate. Meade wrote pioneering fiction about women's education. Her graduate is sweet but not simple: the novel takes a girl's degree, and her character, seriously in an age that doubted both.
a-thorny-path-complete:
A Thorny Path in complete form gives the whole Alexandria novel by Georg Ebers in one long text. Ebers begins in the studio of Heron, a gem cutter, where his daughter Melissa raises and lowers a heavy screen against the autumn sun. From that quiet workshop the story widens to temples, race courses, prisons, and the court of Emperor Caracalla, whose visit hangs over the city.

Melissa's family is pulled into danger piece by piece. A brother loves across a faith line. A father and son are seized and sent to the galleys. An emperor notices the girl herself. Christian friends, above all the freedman Andreas, work to shield them. Sacrifice crowds, imperial feasts, and a final day of mass killing close the arc. Duty and pity carry the tale.
a-ward-of-the-golden-gate:
Bret Harte opens in San Francisco during the rainy season, when pioneer roofs drum under downpours and the wooden sidewalks of Clay and Montgomery streets float like pontoons. His prologue sets a wet, young city of mud and tide. Into this San Francisco comes the ward of the title, a young woman held in trust by older hands.

Nine chapters follow her guardians, her money, and the men who circle both. Harte mixes romance with the speculations and scandals of a boom city still close to its gold-rush youth. His local color — rain, sand hills, the Mission road — does much of the work, and the plot turns on loyalty tested by greed.
a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-complete:
André Theuriet's complete novel appears here with a preface by Melchior de Vogüé of the French Academy and a sketch of the author. The sketch gives his outline. He was born at Marly-le-Roi on October 8, 1833, trained in law, and long served as a treasury official. The Academy crowned him in 1890 for Reine des Bois, this very book. Three books of three chapters each carry the whole tale.

An unfinished will and the heir to Vivey open the story in the woods of eastern France. The dawn of love, love's indiscretion, love by proxy, a strange dark secret, and love's sad ending follow in the chapter titles, closing with love healing the broken heart. Theuriet writes pastoral France with a poet's patience for season and place.
a-word-only-a-word-complete:
A Word, Only a Word in complete form gives the whole novel by Georg Ebers in one text, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers opens in a Black Forest valley just after May, where the boy Ulrich laughs at book learning and cries that a word is only a word. Ruth, beside him, answers that not all words are alike, and the tale spends its length proving her right.

Ulrich grows through flight, art, and war. A smith helps a persecuted Jewish doctor escape by night, and Ruth's family scatters. The young man studies painting, rides with artists, sails for Venice, and serves as a soldier under the name Navarrete from Lepanto to the Netherlands. In a camp crowd he finds his lost mother working as a fortune teller. Spoken words, names, and oaths carry every turn.
a-young-folks-history-of-the-church-of-j: Nephi Anderson writes a history of the Latter-day Saints church for young folks, published by the Deseret Sunday School Union at Salt Lake City in 1916. Frontispieces show Joseph Smith the prophet and Hyrum Smith the patriarch. The address to parents and teachers argues that studying their country's history breeds patriotism. Studying church history, it says, will implant in boys and girls love for its heroes, loyalty to its principles, and appreciation of its achievements.
adventure-of-a-kite: Harriet Myrtle tells a short tale for young children in which a kite, once flying free, meets mishaps and new sights on its way. The story moves from cottage and field to the wider world outside, using simple scenes that a child can follow with ease. Short chapters, clear action, and a gentle tone make it an early reader about curiosity, accidents, and coming safely home.
afghanistan-and-the-anglo-russian-disput:
Theophilus F. Rodenbough, a brevet brigadier general in the United States Army, wrote Afghanistan and the Anglo-Russian Dispute as a military survey of Russia's advance toward India. He built it, his title page says, on reports and experiences of Russian, German, and British officers and travellers, with three maps and other illustrations.

Five chapters move through the gates of Asia to the threshold of India, then weigh the British forces and routes against the Russian forces and approaches. A closing review judges the military situation around Afghanistan, the buffer both empires watched under its ruler Abdurrahman Khan. For readers of the Great Game, it is a period briefing written when invasion routes were argued in earnest.
alice-or-the-mysteries-complete: Edward Bulwer Lytton tells the whole of Alice, or the Mysteries in this complete text, from the Devonshire cottage of its opening to the closing settlements of love, fortune, and revenge. The long romance follows Ernest Maltravers, Alice, Evelyn, and the scheming Lord Vargrave through English and Parisian society. Readers get the full arc of secrets, ambitions, and reconciliations in one volume.
an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-complete:
Emile Souvestre's garret journal is presented whole in An Attic Philosopher in Paris, Complete, the full English text of Un Philosophe sous les Toits. The book first appeared in 1850 and was crowned by the French Academy. Its narrator, a poor scholar in a Paris attic, keeps a diary of days spent among workpeople, neighbors, and the small chances of the streets below his window.

Inside, one entry tells how he quietly furnishes and heats the bare room of Perrine, the poor bandbox maker, then feasts her family on chestnuts and cider in their own home. Other entries follow a bookbinder's death, a clerk's ambitions, and the philosopher's own temptations to envy. Souvestre argues by example that attention and kindness are a poor man's philosophy. Readers taking the journal whole get nineteenth-century Paris from its rooftops down, written with a warmth that made the book a school prize across France.
an-egyptian-princess-complete:
Georg Ebers's An Egyptian Princess, complete in Eleanor Grove's translation, opens with the Nile in flood and Rhodopis's salon at Sais. Cambyses of Persia demands Pharaoh Amasis's daughter Nitetis in marriage, and the court smiles over its dread. Psamtik's jealousy, Bartja's love for Sappho, and the Greek world of Rhodopis fill the Egyptian books. The princess sails to a husband unseen.

Persia receives her into the hanging gardens and a court that fears her as a spy. Cambyses descends through cruelty toward madness; the trial of the bow and the king's seizure close his story. Bartja and Sappho's marriage crowns the epilogue, where Ebers bids his readers farewell. Grove translated the romance from the German of an Egyptologist who knew his ground. Herodotus supplied the frame; Ebers supplied the hearts. The complete novel is nineteenth-century historical fiction at its most learned and humane.
arachne-complete:
Arachne in complete form holds the whole Delta novel by Georg Ebers in one text, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers opens in the flood season of 274 BC at Tennis, a weaving town ringed by Nile water. Hermon, a gifted young sculptor, wants fame above all else, and his choices pull gods, patrons, and lovers into conflict across the full book.

Book 1 sets the still, bright landscape of islands, palms, and papyrus, then follows Hermon through rivalry, love, and blinding loss. Ledscha, wronged and patient, plans a revenge shaped by old island hiding places. A burned house, a rescued statue of Demeter, and a palace arrest raise the stakes late in the tale. Royal courts at Alexandria close around the artist, and pride meets its price.
at-sunwich-port-complete:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this comic novel of a small English seaport, issued with drawings by Will Owen. Sunwich is a sleepy harbour town of shipmasters, stewards, and quay-side gossips, and Jacobs knew the breed from his own dock-office years. Captain Hardy, his son, and the wily ex-steward Mr. Wilks stand near the centre of its feuds and courtships.

Twenty-five chapters string together tavern talk, family quarrels, and small schemes that keep going wrong. A captain hides his movements, a steward swears he only did what he was told, and marine circles savour every rumour. Jacobs writes the comedy in rich dialect and deadpan narration, letting vanity and obstinacy collide until the port's tangled affairs settle into marriages and uneasy peace.
at-suvla-bay-being-the-notes-and-sketche:
John Hargrave served with the 32nd Field Ambulance during the Dardanelles campaign of the First World War, and At Suvla Bay gathers his notes and sketches from that service. Hargrave, known to Scouts as White Fox, sailed with the Mediterranean Expeditionary Force. His unit landed at Suvla Bay on the Gallipoli peninsula. A short glossary of Turkish place words opens the book.

Chapters trace enlistment, the long voyage out, and arrival under shell fire. Hargrave sketches dugouts by Salt Lake, ambulance work, and the men around him. Characters and small adventures matter more here than generals' plans. He writes with a scout's eye for camp craft and landscape. Readers get a stretcher-bearer's ground-level view of a campaign famous for heat, thirst, disease, and stalemate.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-complete:
Athens: Its Rise and Fall, complete in five books by Edward Bulwer Lytton, tells the whole arc of the Athenian city in one history. Lytton dedicates the work to Henry Fynes Clinton, whose Fasti Hellenici fixed the chronology of Greece. Chronology, he argues, is not a dry list of dates. It is a philosophy built from facts, the frame that repairs scanty ancient authorities.

Book I lays the ground in early Attica. Book II runs from Solon's legislation to Marathon. Book III follows Miltiades, the rise of tragedy, and Xerxes' great invasion. Book IV builds the empire after the Persian war, from Themistocles' walls to the death of Cimon. Book V closes with Pericles, the truce, and the Peloponnesian War's first years, ending at its author's chosen summit in 429 BC.
autobiography-of-friedrich-froebel-c-tra:
Friedrich Froebel tells his own life in this autobiography, translated and annotated by Emilie Michaelis and H. Keatley Moore. The Syracuse edition of 1889 came from C. W. Bardeen, a publisher of pedagogy. Its motto is Froebel's own call: come, let us live for our children. Michaelis headed the Croydon kindergarten, and Moore examined music for the Froebel Society, so both translators worked inside his movement.

Froebel recounts a lonely childhood, university study, and slow arrival at his calling. One passage recalls the moment unity in nature and life stood clear to him: nothing in either realm failed to show the same law, though in varied degrees. French, English, German, and Swedish philosophy feeds the awakening. The book is the founder's own account of the thought that produced the kindergarten and its gifts.
barbara-blomberg-complete:
Barbara Blomberg in complete form presents the full novel by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers opens at the Golden Cross in Ratisbon, where Emperor Charles V keeps his rooms and a burgher's daughter sings. Barbara Blomberg's voice lifts her into the emperor's favor, and favor at that court is never a private matter for long.

Book 1 follows her through chapel performances, rehearsals, and summonses at changing hours meant to hide an affair behind her singing. Courtiers like Granvelle reckon how to use her, while the knight Wolf loves her in the open. Later volumes carry her to Brussels, marriage, and sons, and to the long kept secret of a child by the emperor who was taken from her. Ambition, music, and a mother's loss shape the whole arc in one text.
beauchamp-s-career-complete:
George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career, complete in fifty-six chapters, follows a naval hero who enters politics. Nevil Beauchamp, nephew of the Earl of Romfrey, wins glory in the Crimean War. He then adopts the radical teaching of old Dr. Shrapnel. Standing for Parliament at Bevisham, he preaches reform to voters who want favours instead.

Nevil's heart is divided between Renée, a French girl he loved in Venice, and Cecilia Halkett, an English heiress. His uncle's baronial pride fights his democracy at every step. Canvassing, duels of honour, a contested apology, and a disputed election fill the middle. The closing chapters, Without Love and The Last of Nevil Beauchamp, bring his death. Meredith wrote a demanding, witty novel about heroism wasted on a world of compromise.
boy-scouts-on-a-long-hike-or-to-the-resc:
Archibald Lee Fletcher wrote Boy Scouts on a Long Hike, copyrighted by M A Donohue of Chicago in 1913, though the record credits G Harvey Ralphson. Fletcher's Beaver Patrol bets it can hike twenty-five miles a day, past boys who call them tenderfeet. An Alabama camp and a runaway balloon change the plan.

The balloon drops its man into the Black Water Swamps, where no foot has trod. Duty above all things sends the patrol in on his trail. An oasis in the swamp and a rescue in the nick of time reward the march. Jo Davies's homecoming and a guilt question thread the early chapters. The patrol earns its well-done at the close. Scout endurance is the real subject here.
britannica-1911-absolute:
Absolute receives a philosophy entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word, from Latin absolvere, to loose, means in general independent, self-existent, unconditioned. Limited monarchy and the absolute failure of common speech show its loose range before the technical senses begin.

Logic sets absolute terms against relative ones, father implying son, though the entry argues every defined term is relative at bottom. The great use is the Absolute of metaphysics: the all-inclusive unity that explanation climbs toward, named also First Cause and God. Four verdicts sort the theories: it does not exist, it exists for thought only, it exists but is unthinkable, or it exists and is conceived in Unity, Being, and Truth. Spencer's absolute ethics gets a passing note.
britannica-1911-acmite:
Acmite, also called aegirite, is a mineral of the pyroxene group. It is essentially a sodium and iron silicate. Mineralogists call it a soda-pyroxene. Its crystals are monoclinic, like ordinary pyroxene. Their cleavage angles are nearly the same. Its optical behaviour differs, though. Its double refraction is negative. Its pleochroism is strong. Pleochroism means showing different colours in different directions. Its extinction angle is small. The crystals are elongated. They are blackish green or dark brown.

Occurrence gives the mineral its interest. Acmite marks igneous rocks rich in soda. Nepheline-syenites and phonolites are such rocks. It was first found near Kongsberg in Norway. Slender crystals there sit in granite veins. Some crystals run a foot in length. Its name comes from a Greek word for a point. The pointed crystal ends suggested that name.
britannica-1911-acolyte:
Acolyte comes from a Greek word for follower. It is the last of four minor orders in the Roman Church. The long 1911 entry argues the office began at Rome. Pope Cornelius listed forty-two acolytes there in 251. They already held an established place. Carthage is the only African see where they are clear. The Eastern Church never had the office. Armenians alone borrowed it from the West.

Duties and later history fill the account. Acolytes carry candlesticks in procession. They light the lamps of the church. They administer wine and water for the Eucharist. The order became a step to the priesthood. Every candidate had to pass through it. Yet laymen did the actual work almost everywhere. That was true by the time the entry was written.
britannica-1911-aconite:
Aconite is a genus of plants in the buttercup family. People know its members as monkshood or wolfsbane. About sixty species grow in northern mountains. One sepal forms a helmet over the flower. That hood gives monkshood its English name. Two petals hide under the hood on long stalks. Each petal carries a hollow spur of honey. Tall stems bear showy racemes of blue or yellow blooms.

Poison dominates the long entry. Common monkshood roots are sometimes mistaken for horse-radish. Their juice numbs and tingles the lips. One Indian species yields the famed bikh poison. Its alkaloid is called the most deadly poison known. Gardeners still plant aconites as hardy ornaments. The entry details the drug's action on heart and nerves.
britannica-1911-acre-state:
Acre, also spelled Aquiry, is a river of Brazil. It is the chief tributary of the Purus. It rises on the Bolivian frontier. Its course runs east and then north. The name also covers a district on that river. Rubber forests made the region valuable. Bolivians settled it between 1870 and 1878. Brazilian rubber collectors invaded in the next decade. Their rubber flowed to Manaus and Para markets.

Conflict followed the money. Bolivia set a custom-house at Puerto Alonso in 1899. It taxed rubber exports through that post. Settlers declared a republic of Acre that July. Brazil reduced them by the next March. Disorders dragged on for three more years. The Treaty of Petropolis settled the boundary in 1903. Brazil bought the rubber territory outright.
britannica-1911-acuminate:
Acuminate means sharpened or pointed. The word comes from Latin acumen, a point. Botany and ornithology use it most. It denotes a leaf narrowing into a point. Such narrowing is called lance-shaping in plain terms. The point generally forms at the tip. A leaf may narrow at its base instead. Bird feathers can be acuminate as well.

Poets stretched the word once, the entry notes. William Cowper used it for sharp, keen despair. Other writers kept the material sense strictly. Sir Thomas Browne used the pointed meaning. So did Bacon and Bulwer in their works. Readers of older natural history meet the term often. It describes shape only, never sharpness of mind. That one poetic exception stands alone.
britannica-1911-adam-juliette:
Juliette Adam (born 1836) was a French writer. Her maiden name was Juliette Lamber. She was born at Verberie in the Oise. An unhappy childhood came from her parents' quarrels. She told that story in a memoir of her youth. Her first marriage in 1852 was to a doctor. Her book of 1858 defended women writers. It answered Proudhon's views on love and marriage.

A second marriage changed her stage. In 1868 she married Edmond Adam, a senator. Her salon drew Gambetta and republican leaders. They opposed the conservative reaction of the seventies. In 1879 she founded the Nouvelle Revue. She edited it for eight years. Her foreign-politics notes attacked Bismarck relentlessly. She preached revanche against Germany throughout.
britannica-1911-affre-denis-auguste:
Denis Auguste Affre, who lived from 1793 to 1848, was archbishop of Paris in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born in the Tarn and trained for the priesthood at Saint Sulpice. There he taught church doctrine from 1818 and rose through church posts. In 1840 he was raised to lead the church in Paris.

He kept clear of party politics and gave his strength to pastoral care. His time is chiefly recalled for its tragic end in June 1848. Hoping to make peace, he climbed a barricade with a green branch in hand. He had spoken just a few words when shots rang out around him.
britannica-1911-agate:
Agate, in the 1911 Britannica, is a stone entry on a massed form of silica, chiefly chalcedony. It is not a single mineral species. Theophrastus said the name came from the river Achates in Sicily, where the stone was first found. Most agates sit as nodules in old lava rocks. They fill holes left by vapour in the molten mass, layer on layer.

Cut across, such a stone shows fine parallel bands, hence banded or striped agate. Water rich in silica seeped through the rock and coated the inside of each hole, and shifts in that water made the bands change. Bands of chalcedony trade places with layers of quartz and at times opal. One Brazil geode lined with amethyst weighed 35 tons at a show in 1902.
britannica-1911-agglomerate:
Agglomerate is a rock term for coarse stuff thrown out by volcanoes. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from the Latin for forming a ball. The rock sense rules the entry. Blocks of fire born rock sit mixed in a finer ground mass. Fine ash beds, called tuffs, are its smoother kin.

Agglomerate is coarser and less even than ash. It gathers near the mouth of a blast, not far afield. Showers of fine ash may coat a whole country thinly. Big blocks fall close to the crater that threw them. When a vent dies, its throat often chokes with such debris. Packed hard, that fill becomes agglomerate rock. For that cause these rocks mark old crater sites. Some blocks reach thirty or forty feet across. They are chunks of the strata the volcano burst through.
britannica-1911-aigrette:
Aigrette, defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, comes from the French word for the egret, the lesser white heron. An aigrette is the tufted crest, or head-plumes, of that bird. Such plumes were worn to decorate a woman's head-dress. The term also covers any similar ornament made in gems or other materials.

Certain ranks of officers in the French army wear an aigrette as part of their dress. From that feathery shape, the word spread by analogy into several sciences. It names tufts on the heads of insects and the feathery down of the dandelion. It also names the rays of light seen at the ends of electrified bodies, and the rays that stream from the moon's edge during a solar eclipse. One small word thus links fashion, natural history, and physics.
britannica-1911-albertite:
Albertite, a variety of asphalt, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It takes its name from Albert county in New Brunswick, where it is found. The mineral is jet-black in colour. It carries a brilliant, pitch-like lustre, shining much like fresh pitch when a surface catches the light.

A chemical analysis is printed in the entry, showing the substance to be overwhelmingly carbon, with hydrogen next and small shares of oxygen, nitrogen, a trace of sulphur, and a little ash. Its behaviour under heat sets it apart from ordinary asphalt. Albertite softens slightly in boiling water but fuses only imperfectly when heated further. It is also less soluble than ordinary asphalt in oil of turpentine. Those stubborn qualities made it a distinct variety worth naming rather than a mere local curiosity.
britannica-1911-albite:
Albite, a mineral of the felspar group, is described scientifically in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It belongs to the plagioclase division of the felspars. Chemically it is a silicate of sodium and aluminium, and it crystallises in the anorthic system, the least symmetrical crystal arrangement. Like all felspars it has two cleavages, one perfect and one weaker, meeting at a measured angle.

Fine lines run across the perfect cleavage face, caused by twinning under what mineralogists call the albite law. The mineral's hardness is given as six, and it is usually pure white, which explains its name from the Latin albus. Albite is an essential part of many acid igneous rocks such as granite and diorite, and it also forms secondarily in schists and limestones. Fine crystals line Alpine granite crevices, and varieties such as pericline are distinguished at the close.
britannica-1911-analcite:
Heat drives the water out of analcite with ease. Chemically the mineral is a water-bearing silicate of sodium and aluminium. Before the blowpipe it melts into a colourless glass, and acids pull it apart, leaving jelly-like silica behind. It often lines pockets in basic volcanic rocks like basalt, in company with other zeolites; the Tertiary basalts of northern Ireland yield many fine pieces.

Analcite is a common mineral of the zeolite group, growing in crystals of the cubic system. Its usual shape carries twenty-four faces, shown alone or joined with the cube, and crystals are often colourless, clear, and glassy to look at. One odd trait sets it apart: though cubic in form, it bends light weakly in two ways, a puzzle studied since Brewster's work in 1826. Kinds from Norway and the Clyde valley close the entry, cluthalite among them, an altered form of the mineral.
britannica-1911-anglesite:
Anglesite is a mineral consisting of lead sulphate, crystallising in the orthorhombic system alongside barytes and celestite. Dr Withering first recognised it as a mineral species in 1783, having discovered it in the Parys copper-mine in Anglesey, and Beudant gave it the name anglesite, from that locality, in 1832. Anglesey crystals, once found abundantly on dull limonite, are small and brownish-yellow from limonite staining.

Crystals from other localities, notably Monteponi in Sardinia, are transparent and colourless with a brilliant adamantine lustre. Nearly two hundred distinct crystal forms have been figured, making many specimens hard to decipher without measuring their angles. The mineral is soft, with hardness three, but very heavy, and it shows distinct cleavages. It occurs as isolated crystals in lead-bearing lodes, and in Australia and Mexico as large masses mined as lead ore, the pure mineral carrying sixty-eight per cent lead.
