britannica-1911-angulate: Angulate is an adjective meaning shaped with corners or angles. It comes from the Latin angulus, an angle. Botany and zoology both use the word. It describes the shape of stems in plants. It also describes leaves in plants. In zoology it describes the shape of wings. The entry is a brief dictionary-style note, giving the word's origin and the fields where the term does its work.
britannica-1911-anhydrite:
Anhydrite is a mineral of anhydrous calcium sulphate. It differs from gypsum in one key way. It contains no water of crystallisation. Its crystals follow the orthorhombic system. Three perfect cleavages run parallel to its symmetry planes. Distinct crystals are somewhat rare. The mineral usually appears as cleavage masses. Its colour is white, sometimes greyish or bluish. A pearly lustre marks its best cleavage.

Salt deposits commonly hold anhydrite alongside gypsum. A salt mine near Hall in Tirol yielded it first, in 1794. Stassfurt, Aussee, and Bex also produce typical specimens. Depth matters for finding it unchanged. Near the surface, absorbed water alters it into gypsum. Varieties receive their own names in the entry. Fibrous masses are called tripe-stone. A scaly granular kind, vulpinite, is cut and polished. Bergamo in Lombardy supplies that ornamental stone.
britannica-1911-ankerite:
Ankerite is a mineral of the rhombohedral carbonates. Dolomite is its close chemical relative. It differs from dolomite in composition. Iron and manganese oxides replace part of the magnesia. Its general formula reflects that substitution. Normal ankerite has a fixed stated formula. Its physical characters resemble dolomite and chalybite. Perfect rhombohedral cleavage defines its breakage. Hardness and specific gravity ranges are given.

Colour varies from white to reddish. Iron-ore deposits hold ankerite with chalybite. The mineral belongs to the dolomite-chalybite series. Loose names like brown-spar apply to that series. Pearl-spar and bitter-spar are also used. W. von Haidinger recognised the species in 1825. He named it after M. J. Anker. Anker was a Styrian mineralogist of the period. Leonard James Spencer signs this compact mineralogical notice.
britannica-1911-annabergite:
Annabergite is a mineral of hydrous nickel arsenate. Its formula includes eight water molecules. It crystallises in the monoclinic system. Vivianite and erythrite share its crystal form. True crystals are minute and capillary. They are rarely met with in practice. The mineral usually forms soft earthy masses. Encrustations are its common presentation. A fine apple-green colour marks it characteristically.

The old name was nickel-ochre, from 1758. Brooke and Miller proposed annabergite in 1852. The name honours Annaberg in Saxony. That town is one source locality. Nickel ores host the mineral naturally. It forms as their alteration product. One variety replaces nickel partly with calcium. Creetown in Scotland yields that variety. Dudgeonite is its name, after its finder. Leonard James Spencer signs the notice.
britannica-1911-anorthite:
Anorthite, a stone of the feldspar group, is set out in a 1911 Britannica earth entry. It stands as one end stone of a long chain of kin stones. Its mix is a blend of lime, alumina, and silica in set parts. Its crystals form in the sloped box system of stone lore. Like all feldspars it splits in two planes, one clean and one less so.

Hues run white, grey, and red, with light that shifts from clear to dim. Its hard grade sits near that of quartz in the scale. It forms a chief part of dark fire rocks such as gabbro and basalt. Fine crystals come from blocks cast out of Mount Vesuvius in past blasts. Rose gave it its name in eighteen twenty three for its sloped form.
britannica-1911-anthracite:
Anthracite is a 1911 Britannica article on a hard kind of coal. The word comes from a Greek term for coal. Anthracite is the name for coals that give off no tarry fumes when heated. They burn with a smokeless flame that is nearly without light.

Other names carry the same sense. Stone coal is one, though it differs from the German Steinkohle. In Scotland it is called blind coal, and in Ireland, Kilkenny coal. The poor anthracite of north Devon is used only as a pigment. It is known as culm. That same term marks the rock strata where such coal is found. Like strata in the Rhenish hill country are called the Culm Measures. In America, culm serves as an equal term in trade. Fuel readers get the names and marks of a prized coal.
britannica-1911-apatite:
Apatite is the subject of a mineral article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Apatite is a widely spread mineral. When found in large masses it has great worth as a source of phosphate. Werner first marked it as a species in 1786. He named it from a Greek word meaning to deceive. It had often been mistaken for other minerals, such as beryl or amethyst. Its chief part is calcium phosphate.

The article explains that fluorine or chlorine forms a key part of the mineral. Two chemical kinds are marked out, one with fluorine and one with chlorine. The fluorine kind is much the commoner of the two. The two elements can replace each other in shifting shares. Apatite often forms fine crystals, sometimes a foot or more in length. Its crystal form is the best example of one class of six sided symmetry.
britannica-1911-aphrodite:
Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty, is the subject of a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She is the match of the Roman Venus. Her myth and cult were in root Semitic, the article holds, but she soon became Greek in form and took a seat among the gods of Olympus. Some hold that an older Greek goddess of love was drawn into her.

The article first weighs her eastern first form and then asks how far its marks show in the Greek goddess. Among the Semitic peoples a chief goddess was served under many names. She was the Assyrian Ishtar, the Phoenician Astarte, the Syrian Atargatis, and the Babylonian Belit. One school holds that all of them were at root moon goddesses. That view has not won wide assent, the article notes, since the moon in Semitic myth is a male god.
britannica-1911-apophyllite:
Apophyllite, a stone classed with the zeolites, is set out in a 1911 Britannica earth entry. It acts like those stones when heated, yet holds no alumina in its mix. Its bulk is a wet mix of potash, lime, and silica. A trace of fluorine shows in most finds. Heat drives its water off at a high point, and damp air gives part of it back in time.

Its name, set in eighteen oh six, comes from Greek words for leafing off. Heat makes the stone flake as its water leaves. Crystals form square posts or sharp peaks with a pearl shine on the base cut. That shine gave it an old name, fish eye stone. It turns up in holes in basalt rock with kin stones.
britannica-1911-aragonite:
Aragonite, a twin-born mineral, is laid out in a stone entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is one of two forms of carbonate of lime in nature. The other form is the more common mineral called calcite. Aragonite grows in crystals of the orthorhombic system of form. Plain single crystals of it are rare in the ground.

Most of its crystals are twins grown through one another. Three twins can join to fake a six-sided prism shape. The stone is clear, white, or tinged with pale yellow. Glass-like shine marks its faces to the eye at once. No clean split sets it apart from its kin calcite. It is harder and heavier than calcite, and bends light two ways. Aragon in Spain gave the mineral its name.
britannica-1911-arete: Arête, a French term used in Switzerland for a sharp mountain edge, is defined in this short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The word comes from an old French form and from a Latin word for an ear of corn or a fish-bone. It denotes the sharp, bayonet-like edge of a peak such as the Matterhorn. Two steep sides meet in a long rising ridge. The word now denotes any sharp mountain edge worn bare by frost above the snowline.
britannica-1911-argyrodite:
Argyrodite is a mineral famed as the stone in which germanium was found. The 1911 Britannica entry credits C. Winkler with that find in 1886. The stone is a silver sulpho-germanate in its make up and form. It grows in cubes with eight or twelve faces in its crystals. Twin crystals show up oft in the mines where it is found.

First finds came from a silver mine at Freiberg in Saxony. Crusts of small, dim crystals there were classed wrong at first. Finer crystals from Bolivia later proved the true cubic form of the stone. Its hue is iron black with a purplish tinge on the face. There is no cleavage, and its weight for its size is high.
britannica-1911-associate: Associate is defined in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from Latin words meaning to join to. It names one who is united with another, and so, in general, a companion. In a narrower use it names a lower member of a body, such as an associate of the Royal Academy, or a degree below that of fellow. In English law the associates were officers of the supreme court. Their work was to list the cases, enter the verdicts, and hand records to the parties.
britannica-1911-ate:
Ate is a short myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a figure in Greek myth who stands for rash and ruinous folly. She is named as a daughter of Zeus and of Strife. Even Zeus was once tricked by her into a hasty oath.

The entry tells how Zeus then threw her out of Olympus for good. She stayed on earth, where she works harm and mischief among men. Mild prayers follow behind her and try to mend the harm she does. Later writers made her a punisher of sin as well. The entry closes with a list of books on the idea in Greek thought.
britannica-1911-athlete:
The 1911 Britannica article on the athlete explains a word from Greek games. An athlete was one who fought for a prize. The term now means anyone strong in body. It once covered contests in music and riding too. It narrowed to gymnastic contests. Later it meant the paid class of athletes.

The article contrasts old and new. Men of good birth once fought for glory alone. By the fifth century before Christ a paid class had arisen. Thinkers and doctors alike condemned the trade. It was said to harm mind and body. The article describes the strict training. A trainer set the diet and anointed the body. Food ran to cheese, figs, and bread, then to meat. The contests were running, leaping, wrestling, and boxing.
britannica-1911-augite:
Augite is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a key rock-forming mineral. Its name comes from a Greek word for lustre or shine. It is now used for the dark kinds in one pyroxene line. They run dark green, brown, or black in hue.

Black short stones of augite are common in many basalts. When the rock rots to clay, the black stones are left free. Such loose finds from Bohemia sit in most stone collections, the text says. A rock made almost wholly of augite is called augitite. The mineral also turns up in changed rocks, such as the crystal limestones of Tirol. There a green kind called fassaite is found.
britannica-1911-aulnoy-marie-catherine-l:
Marie Catherine de la Motte, Baronne d'Aulnoy, a French author who lived from about 1650 to 1705, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was born at Barneville in Normandy. Her aunt was a famed wit, called the tenth Muse by her circle. In 1666 she married François de la Motte, who became Baron d'Aulnoy.

With her mother, she plotted a charge of high treason against her husband. When the plot was exposed, the two women fled in haste to England. They moved on to Spain in 1679, and later won leave to return home by secret services. Her fame rests on her fairy tales, printed in three volumes in 1698. The set held twenty-four tales, among them the Blue Bird and the White Cat. Most of her tales drew on Basile's Pentamerone, an older Italian store.
britannica-1911-autunite:
Autunite is a mineral among the uranium micas. Calco-uranite is its alternative name. It differs from torbernite in one element. Calcium replaces copper in its composition. Chemically it is a hydrous uranium calcium phosphate. Eight or twelve water molecules attach. It closely resembles tetragonal torbernite in form. It actually crystallises in the orthorhombic system. It is optically biaxial, unlike torbernite.

Its crystals are thin plates of square outline. Perfect micaceous cleavage parallels the basal plane. Pearly lustre shows on that plane. Sulphur-yellow colour distinguishes it at a glance. Torbernite is emerald-green by contrast. It is a soft, light mineral relatively. Pitchblende and other uranium minerals accompany it. Silver, tin, and iron ores host it too. St Symphorien near Autun gives it its name. Falkenstein and St Day are other localities.
britannica-1911-axinite:
Axinite is a mineral made of a complex aluminium and calcium boro-silicate, with iron and manganese partly standing in for its metals. Haüy named it in 1799 from the Greek for axe, after the thin wedge shape of its crystals. Its usual colour is clove-brown, rarely tinged violet.

Fine glassy crystals come from Le Bourg d'Oisans in Dauphiné, found with albite, prehnite, and quartz in schist rock. Other homes include Cornwall, the Harz, Maine, Pennsylvania, and Japan, in large crystals. Unlike tourmaline, its fellow boro-silicate, axinite favors basic rather than acid eruptive rocks. Hard and clear enough when at its best, the Dauphiné crystals are sometimes cut as gemstones.
britannica-1911-azurite:
Azurite, or chessylite, is a mineral of basic copper carbonate whose vivid blue sets it against the emerald-green of malachite, a near relation holding more water. Pliny knew it as caeruleum; Beudant gave the modern name in 1824 for its azure colour, while chessylite, from 1852, honours Chessy near Lyons, source of the best crystals.

Its crystals are monoclinic, glassy, and translucent, with a lighter blue streak. Azurite forms in the upper parts of copper ore deposits where water with carbon dioxide and oxygen alters sulphide or native copper. It is common in all copper mines, sometimes in huge masses, as in Arizona and South Australia, and holds 55 per cent copper. It can itself alter into malachite, and massive pieces are sometimes cut and polished for ornament.
britannica-1911-bahia-state:
Bahia is an Atlantic state of Brazil, a vast land of 164,650 square miles drained in large part by the São Francisco river. Much of it is arid plateau, the chapada, standing 2,300 to 3,000 feet above the sea, crossed by rough limestone and bare gneiss highlands on the way to the coastal plain.

Climate follows the land: hot and dry inside, hot and wet on the coast. Cattle raising once ruled the interior but droughts and yearly burning of the fields nearly killed it. Farming zones grow sugar, cotton, tobacco, cacao, coffee, and tropical fruits, while exports add hides, rubber, fibre, diamonds, and cabinet woods. The people, largely of mixed descent, numbered 1,919,802 in 1890.
britannica-1911-baker-sir-samuel-white:
Baker, Sir Samuel White (1821-1893), was an English explorer. He was born in London in 1821. His father was a West India merchant. Office work proved Baker unsuited to commerce. He married in 1843 and sailed for Mauritius. Ceylon drew him onward in 1846.

In Ceylon Baker founded a mountain settlement. Nuwara Eliya became a health resort. He brought English emigrants there himself. Choice cattle breeds came with them. The settlement soon succeeded well. Hunting trips filled his Ceylon years. The Rifle and the Hound told that story in 1853. Later he supervised a Dobrudja railway. It linked the Danube with the Black Sea. In 1861 his great African tour began. He sought the sources of the Nile. He hoped to meet Speke and Grant. At Gondokoro in 1863 he met them instead.
britannica-1911-ballymote:
Ballymote is a market town of County Sligo, Ireland, 14 miles south of Sligo on the Midland Great Western railway. Its population in 1901 was 997. The town served farm trade in its district and had carriage-building works.

Old remains give the entry its interest. A strong castle, built in 1300 by Richard de Burgh, earl of Ulster, saw fighting in 1641 and 1652. Ruins of a Franciscan house, famed as a seat of learning, stand nearby. The 1911 Britannica entry prizes one fruit of its monks: the Book of Ballymote, from about 1391. That book is a mixed store of history, family lines, and romance in prose and verse. It is held by the Royal Irish Academy.
britannica-1911-bambute:
Bambute was the name used in the 1911 Britannica for a pygmy people of the Semliki Forest, on the western border of the Uganda Protectorate between Lake Albert and Lake Edward. The entry treats them as a branch of the pygmy peoples of equatorial Africa, akin to the Batwa described farther west. Average height is given as 4 feet 9 inches.

The people are described as nomad hunters who build only huts of sticks and leaves. They hunt the largest forest game with a tiny bow and poisoned arrows, and no other weapon. Sir Harry Johnston is quoted for their gift of drawing: with a sharpened stick they could sketch the beasts and birds they knew in sand or mud.
britannica-1911-banate:
Banate, a corruption of Panaiti, their real name, are a North American Indian people now usually called the Bannock. They are of Shoshonean stock, and whites sometimes knew them as the Robber Indians. Their former range was southern Idaho and eastern Oregon.

By 1911 they were split between the Fort Hall and Lemhi reservations in Idaho, and numbered about 500. The 1911 Britannica entry says they were generally friendly with the whites. Two exceptions are marked: serious outbreaks in 1866 and again in 1877–78. The entry is very short, giving name, stock, range, present reservations, and rough numbers, and little more.
britannica-1911-barrington-shute:
Shute Barrington (1734–1826), an English bishop and youngest son of the first Viscount Barrington, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Educated at Eton and Oxford, he held some smaller church posts before rising quickly through the bench of bishops. He became bishop of Llandaff in 1769, in his mid-thirties. He was moved to Salisbury in 1782 and then to Durham in 1791, where he stayed for the rest of his long life.

Belief and writing fill the rest of the short entry. Barrington was a strong Protestant, yet he was ready to grant Roman Catholics every degree of toleration short of political power and an established place for their church. He published several volumes of sermons and tracts setting out his views. He also wrote the political life of his brother, William Wildman Barrington, the second viscount.
britannica-1911-barytocalcite:
Barytocalcite is a rare mineral described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. When the entry was written it had been found only at Alston Moor in Cumberland, in the north of England. There it occurs as spreading groups of white, transparent crystals lining cavities inside the Mountain Limestone. That single locality, and the crystal groups in hollow rock, give the short entry its opening facts about where and how the mineral appears.

Measurement and chemistry follow. The crystals belong to the monoclinic system and are usually prismatic or blade-shaped. The mineral's hardness is 4, and its specific gravity is 3.65. It has perfect cleavages at angles close to those of calcite, a resemblance the entry warns about. Chemically it is a double salt of barium and calcium carbonates. That sets it apart from bromlite, in which the two carbonates are mixed rather than combined in fixed form.
britannica-1911-bassano-jacopo-da-ponte:
Jacopo da Ponte Bassano (1510–1592), a Venetian painter born at Bassano, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was educated by his father, himself an artist, and finished his studies at Venice. On his father's death he returned to Bassano and settled there for life. His usual subjects were peasants and villagers, cattle, and landscapes, with some portraits and historical designs.

Qualities of the work are weighed carefully. His figures are called well designed. His animals and landscapes show simple nature, strong local colour, and fresh flesh tints, with sound chiaroscuro, the modelling of light and shade, and perspective. His style shifted over his life, first copying his father, then drawn to Titian's lightness and colour, and finally settling into his own manner. Many supposed originals are copies by his sons or others. His Nativity altar-piece at Bassano is highly rated.
britannica-1911-bathgate:
Bathgate is a burgh in Linlithgowshire, Scotland, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies nineteen miles west of Edinburgh by the North British railway, and its people numbered 7549 in 1901. The district around it is rich in the stuff of mines: limestone, coal, ironstone, shale, and fireclay, all of them worked when the entry was made. Silver had once been mined there as well, in earlier times.

Work and an old marriage carry the entry. Town works made paraffin, paper, glass, chemicals, flour, and whisky, and freestone was quarried nearby. The burgh also served as a centre for the farm produce of its district. It became a burgh of barony in 1824 and a police burgh in 1865. Its past reaches much further back: Bathgate formed the dowry of Marjory, daughter of Robert Bruce, when she wed Walter, the hereditary steward of Scotland, in 1315.
britannica-1911-batholite:
Batholites, from Greek words for deep and stone, are great masses of intrusive rock, in the geological account given by the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In lands of old rocks, wide granite areas were forced up in a liquid state under great pressure. The molten rock wedged apart the beds around it, sent tongues into cracks, and floated off blocks of the strata. Those blocks still lie in the granite, changed by its heat.

How the space was made is the open question. One school held that batholites are cone-shaped masses rising from great depths and eating up the beds above them, partly melting the blocks they hold. The other school called them laccolites, cake-shaped masses pressed into weak planes in the upper crust. The bulk of the proof, the entry says, favours the laccolite view, though many granites plainly took in much foreign rock as they rose.
britannica-1911-bathvillite: Bathvillite is a naturally occurring organic substance described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is an amorphous material, without crystal form, opaque and very friable, so it crumbles with ease. Its colour is fawn-brown. It is found filling cavities, hollow spaces, in the torbanite or Boghead coal of Bathville in Scotland, the place that gives the substance its name. Its specific gravity is 1.01, barely above that of water, and it is insoluble in benzene, so that liquid will not dissolve it.
britannica-1911-bauxite:
Bauxite is a substance treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a mineral and as the chief ore of aluminium. Berthier described it in 1821 as a water-bearing alumina from Les Baux, near Arles in the south of France. The name bauxite was fixed later, in 1861, after that first home, and the stuff has long been mined there. It is never found in crystals. It occurs as earthy, clay-like masses, often in small round grains, and its colour runs from white through yellow and brown to red as the iron in it changes.

Impurity is the entry's warning. Tests for trade show bauxite varies widely. Alumina runs from about a third to over three-quarters of the mass, with water, iron oxide, and silica.  The entry thus presents bauxite less as one pure mineral than as a family of like ores.
britannica-1911-bello-horizonte:
Bello-Horizonte, also called Minas, is a city of Brazil and capital of the state of Minas Geraes since 1898. It stands about fifty miles north-west of Ouro Preto, joined to the Central of Brazil railway by a short branch line. Its people in 1906 were reckoned at 25,000 to 30,000.

Unlike most capitals, Bello-Horizonte was built on purpose. The state laid it out on an open plateau and fitted it with public buildings, gas, water and tramways before the government moved from Ouro Preto. The transfer cost about a million pounds. Growth came fast afterwards, and the entry counts it among Brazil’s most attractive state capitals.
britannica-1911-benitoite:
Benitoite is a mineral found in 1907 near the headwaters of the San Benito river, in San Benito county, California. Professor G. D. Louderback described it. Chemically it is a titano-silicate of barium, and it crystallises in the hexagonal system, with a hardness of six and a half.

The stone may be colourless or blue, the colour changing within a single piece up to a deep sapphire blue. The blue kind is cut as a gem and can be mistaken for blue spinel, though its softness gives it away against spinel and sapphire. It shines strongly, bends light well, and shows two colours by direction: pale along its main axis, dark across it.
britannica-1911-benson-edward-white:
Edward White Benson (1829–1896), archbishop of Canterbury, was born at Birmingham, son of a manufacturing chemist of some note. At King Edward’s school he sat beside Westcott and Lightfoot, and Trinity College, Cambridge, followed for all three. His mother’s death in 1850 left him near penniless with young brothers and sisters to keep.

Benson became a fellow of Trinity, taught at Rugby under Frederick Temple, and in 1859 opened Wellington College as its first headmaster. Church posts rose steadily until Canterbury itself. As archbishop he kept close, warm ties with the Eastern churches and the wider Anglican communion. His writings include an essay on the cathedral, charges and sermons, and his sons Arthur, Edward and Robert all became authors.
britannica-1911-beryllonite:
Beryllonite is a mineral phosphate of beryllium and sodium, with formula NaBePO4. It occurs as complex orthorhombic crystals and as broken fragments. The 1911 Britannica entry places it in a granitic vein at Stoneham, Maine. There it lies with felspar, smoky quartz, beryl, and columbite. Professor E. S. Dana discovered it in 1888. He named it for its large beryllium content.

The crystals run from colourless to white or pale yellow. They are transparent, with a glassy lustre, and cleave perfectly one way. Hardness is 5.5 to 6, and specific gravity 2.845. A few stones have been cut and faceted as gems. Their refractive index is no higher than quartz, so they lack brilliance. The entry is short and purely mineralogical.
britannica-1911-bessieres-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Bessières (1768–1813), Duke of Istria, was a French marshal born near Cahors. He served briefly in the Constitutional Guard of Louis XVI. He fought Spain as a non-commissioned officer. In Italy in 1796 he caught Bonaparte's notice at Roveredo. After Rivoli he carried the captured colours to the Directory in Paris. In Egypt he won further credit at Acre and Aboukir.

At Marengo in 1800 he led a brilliant charge for the Consular Guard. He became a marshal of France in 1804 and led the Imperial Guard's cavalry. The 1911 Britannica entry praises his cool judgment and dauntless courage. A musket ball killed him in 1813, days into the new campaign. Even Spanish priests, it says, held masses for his soul. A note on his brother Bertrand closes the article.
britannica-1911-bibracte:
Bibracte was an ancient Gaulish town, now the site of Mont Beuvray near Autun in France. It stood on a hilltop 2,500 feet above sea level. Digging there has uncovered a vast area of 330 acres. A rampart of stone and wood, three miles long, rings the site. Inside lie houses, a temple of the goddess Bibractis, and workshops. Iron and bronze workers and enamellers all had shops there.

The 1911 Britannica entry makes Bibracte the capital of the Aedui in Julius Caesar's time. Augustus later moved its people to his new town, Augustodunum, modern Autun. His aim, the entry says, was to break the free native traditions of the hill town. A second, far more obscure Gaulish town near Reims bore the same name. Excavation reports by Bulliot and Déchelette are cited at the close.
britannica-1911-biot-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Biot (1774–1862) was a French physicist, born at Paris on 21 April 1774. He served briefly in the artillery after his schooling. In 1797 he became professor of mathematics at Beauvais. In 1800, with Laplace's backing, he took the physics chair at the Collège de France. At an unusually early age he entered the Academy of Sciences, in 1803. In 1804 he rose with Gay-Lussac on the first balloon ascent made for science.

With Arago he measured an arc of the meridian in Spain from 1806. They had already studied how gases bend light together before that survey. Other geodetic work kept him busy for years after. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his honours, including commander of the Legion of Honour in 1849. He never won the Academy secretaryship he sought. Election to the French Academy in 1856 consoled him somewhat. His son Edouard, a sinologist, closes the article.
britannica-1911-biotite:
Biotite is an important rock-forming mineral in the mica group. Hausmann gave it the name in 1847, honouring the French physicist J. B. Biot. Biot had found in 1816 that the magnesia micas were optically uniaxial, or nearly so. Biotite is the iron-bearing member of that family, and its iron content varies widely. Its make-up mixes aluminium, magnesium, iron, and potassium silicates. Small shares of other elements appear in the full formula.

Like other micas it splits perfectly in one direction, the 1911 Britannica article notes. Its colour is dark green or brown, and thick crystals turn deep black. Its strong pleochroism, showing different colours by direction, helps mark it out. Though common worldwide, it has little trade value, the entry says. Its sheets are small, dark, and not transparent enough for industry. Fine smoky-black sheets fit for use come from Renfrew County in Ontario.
britannica-1911-bipartite:
Bipartite, from the Latin bi-, two, and partire, to divide, means having two parts. In general use it marks anything in two matching parts or in duplicate. The 1911 Britannica entry walks the word through four sciences in a few lines. In geometry a bipartite curve has two distinct branches. The article points to figures under the parabola heading for that case. In botany the word fits leaves split in two near the base.

A bipartient factor is a number whose square exactly divides another number. In zoology Bipartiti was Latreille's name for a group of meat-eating beetles. The entry is a short glossary note covering all four senses. It gives the Latin roots and one sense per field. No examples beyond those senses are supplied in its brief text. The word itself is the subject here.
britannica-1911-birch-pfeiffer-charlotte:
Charlotte Birch-Pfeiffer (1800–1868) was a German actress and dramatic writer, born at Stuttgart. Her father was an estate agent named Pfeiffer. She trained at the Munich court theatre and began leading tragic roles in 1818. In 1825 she married Christian Birch, a historian from Copenhagen. She kept acting after the marriage. From 1837 to 1843 she managed the theatre at Zürich. In 1844 she joined Berlin's royal theatre for good.

She stayed at that Berlin house until her death in August 1868. Her close knowledge of stage craft fitted her to dramatize popular novels well. The 1911 Britannica entry counts her plays, adapted and original, at twenty-three volumes. Many still held public favour when the entry was written. Her novels and tales filled three more volumes in collected form. A note on her daughter Wilhelmine von Hillern, a novelist, closes the piece.
britannica-1911-bismuthite:
Bismuthite is a somewhat rare mineral made of bismuth trisulphide, Bi2S3. It forms crystals in the orthorhombic system. It is isomorphous with stibnite, meaning it shares stibnite's crystal form, and looks much like it. Its crystals grow as loose bundles of needles without end faces. Masses of it show a leafy or fibrous build instead. A perfect cleavage runs along the needles' length. The colour is lead grey leaning to tin white, often tarnished yellow.

Hardness is only 2, while specific gravity runs 6.4 to 6.5, the 1911 Britannica entry gives. It occurs in Cornwall and Bolivia, often with native bismuth and tin ores. At Brandy Gill in Cumberland it sits in white quartz with molybdenite and apatite. Cronstedt knew it in 1758, and Beudant named it in 1832. The entry warns its name is easily confused with bismite and bismutite. Bismuth-glance is offered as a safer name.
britannica-1911-blanqui-louis-auguste:
Louis Auguste Blanqui (1805–1881) was a French revolutionary writer who spent much of his life in prison for his republican views. Born at Puget-Théniers, where his father was sub-prefect, he studied law and medicine but chose politics. He fought in the July Revolution of 1830 and kept preaching republicanism under Louis Philippe.

Jail terms followed one after another. For his part in the Société des Saisons rising he was condemned to death in 1840, the sentence cut to life imprisonment. Freed in 1848, he attacked the new order at once and drew ten more years in 1849. He escaped custody in 1865, worked against the Empire from abroad, and returned under the amnesty of 1869.
britannica-1911-blessington-marguerite:
Marguerite, Countess of Blessington, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Clonmel in Ireland in seventeen eighty nine, she was the daughter of a small landowner. Her youth was marked by want and by her father's harsh ways. At fifteen she was forced to wed a captain.

The entry tells how that first husband died in a debtors' prison in eighteen seventeen. The next year she wed Charles John Gardiner, earl of Blessington. Known for beauty, charm, wit, and open handed ways, she shared his rich tastes. Those tastes left his estates deep in debt. In eighteen twenty two the pair went abroad for some months.
britannica-1911-bokhara-state:
Bokhara, or Bukhara, is a state of central Asia under Russian protection, lying along the middle Oxus River. It stretches between 37 and 41 degrees north, with Russian districts to the north, the Pamirs east, Afghanistan south, and Khiva west. Counting Karateghin and Darvaz, its area is about 85,000 square miles.

The west is a plain watered by the Zarafshan through countless canals, where farming lives only in very fertile oases. Sand desert and dry steppe cover the rest of the lowland. The middle lands rise to plateaus near 4000 feet, cut by rivers running to the Oxus, with cooler, wetter, fertile valleys. The long entry goes on through the eastern highlands, the people, the emir's rule, and the state's trade and history.
britannica-1911-boracite:
Boracite is a mineral picked out for its odd optical behaviour, first seen in 1787 at Lüneburg in Hanover. Its small, sharp-faced crystals sit in numbers inside gypsum and anhydrite in salt deposits there. In outer form they are cubic, with the same symmetry class as blende and tetrahedrite.

Crystal shape shifts with which face rules: tetrahedron, cube, or rhombic dodecahedron, and twin crystals occur. The stones are clear to milky, glassy in shine, colourless or white but often tinged grey, yellow, or green, and hard, at 7 on Mohs' scale. Haüy noted in 1791 that the crystals are strongly pyroelectric, taking a positive charge at four corners when heated and a negative charge at the four opposite corners. Later pages work through the optical puzzles in full.
britannica-1911-bouillotte:
Bouillotte is a French card game of the poker family, hugely popular during the Revolution and again for some years from 1830. Three, four, or five may play, with a piquet pack cut down to fit the number at the table. Counters or chips are used, as in poker.

Each player first puts one counter into the pot, and each in turn may raise it, while those who will not match the raise must drop out. Three cards are dealt to each, and with four players a thirteenth card, the retourne, is turned up. Players must then bet, call, raise, or fold, and on a call the hands are shown. Hands are ranked by brélans, sets of three or four of a kind, with special rank when the turned card matches. If no set is held, the highest count of pips wins.
britannica-1911-briquette:
Briquette, a small form of the French brique, brick, is a solid fuel also sold as patent fuel: small coal pressed into blocks with a binding stuff. The entry walks through the making step by step. The small coal, washed first if needed, is dried until moisture falls to at most 4 per cent and crushed if the pieces run coarse.

Next the coal is worked in a pug mill with 8 to 10 per cent of gas pitch, heated to between 70 and 90 degrees until it turns plastic. Moulded and squeezed at one half to two tons per square inch in a machine with a turning die-plate. Cold blocks, usually 7 to 20 pounds each, come out hard and break less in handling than loose coal. Boilers at sea and on locomotives burn most of them, and South Wales, rich in steam-coal dust, is the British centre of the trade.
britannica-1911-brochantite:
Brochantite is a mineral species made of a basic copper sulphate, with the formula Cu4(OH)6SO4, crystallising in the orthorhombic system. Its crystals are usually small, needle-like or prism-shaped, with a perfect cleavage along one face. They shine with a glassy lustre and run in colour from emerald green to blackish green, with specific gravity 3.907 and hardness between 3 and a half and 4.

First found with malachite and native copper in the copper mines of the Urals, it was named by A. Levy in 1824 after Brochant de Villiers. Several supposed species, konigine from the Urals, brongniartine from Mexico, krisuvigite from Iceland and warringtonite from Cornwall, later proved to be this same mineral. Other homes named include Roughten Gill in Cumberland, Rezbanya in Hungary and Atacama in Chile, where look-alike atacamite keeps it company.
britannica-1911-bromlite:
Bromlite is a mineral of the aragonite group, an isomorphous mixture of calcium and barium carbonates in varying shares, written (Ca, Ba)CO3. That mix sets it apart from barytocalcite, a true double salt of the same carbonates in equal parts. Like aragonite it crystallises in the orthorhombic system, but simple crystals of it are not known.

Every crystal is a complex twin shaped like a double-ended, false six-sided pyramid, much like witherite's but sharper, its faces striped across and split down the centre by a twin seam. Under polarised light a cut section shows six differently aimed individuals arranged in twelve segments. The mineral is translucent and white, sometimes pink-tinged, with specific gravity 3.706 and hardness 4 to 4 and a half. Only two homes are known, both in northern England: the Fallowfield lead mine near Hexham, and Bromley Hill near Alston, where it runs in veins with galena.
britannica-1911-bronte:
Bronte is a town in the province of Catania, Sicily, on the western slopes of Mount Etna, 24 miles north-north-west of Catania directly and 34 miles by rail. It held 20,366 people in 1901, a large town by the standards of the island's interior. Two grants, centuries of rule apart, frame its short history in the entry.

The emperor Charles V founded the town. Its extensive estate first belonged to the monastery of Maniacium, or Maniace. In 1799 Ferdinand IV of Naples granted town and estate as a dukedom to Nelson. The British admiral, a gift that tied the Sicilian town's name to a famous sea victory's hero. Those facts, place under Etna, population, founding and the Nelson dukedom, make up the whole brief notice.
britannica-1911-bronzite:
Bronzite is a member of the pyroxene group of minerals, standing with enstatite and hypersthene in that group's orthorhombic series. Rather than a species of its own, it is really an iron-bearing variety of enstatite. Through partial change it has gained a bronze-like half-metallic shine on its cleavage surfaces. That shine gives it its name.

Enstatite is magnesium metasilicate, with the magnesia partly replaced by ferrous oxide: up to about 5 per cent in plain enstatite, from about 5 to 14 per cent in bronzite. With still more iron the mineral passes into hypersthene. A special change called schillerization splits the iron out as fine films along cleavage cracks, producing the metallic sheen, stronger still in hypersthene. Bronzite runs green or brown, with specific gravity about 3.2 to 3.3, and it occurs in basic igneous rocks such as norites, gabbros and peridotites.
britannica-1911-brookite:
Brookite is one of three forms in which titanium dioxide is found in nature. The other two are rutile and anatase, which share its makeup but not its form. Rutile and anatase grow in one crystal system, while brookite grows in another. The name was given in eighteen twenty five in honour of Henry James Brooke. Brooke was an English student of minerals.

The entry sorts brookite crystals into two types by shape and colour. The more common type is thin and flat, with many small bright faces. Such stones are a rich red brown and let some light through. The second type looks like six sided double pyramids and is black. Its name in that form is arkansite. The stone has no clear split plane.
britannica-1911-brucite:
Brucite is a mineral made of magnesium hydroxide, crystallising in the rhombohedral system. It was first described in 1814 as native magnesia from New Jersey by A. Bruce, an American mineralogist. F. S. Beudant named the species after him in 1824. The same name had earlier been used for the mineral now called chondrodite.

It is usually found as platy masses, sometimes of considerable size. The plates show a perfect cleavage along their surface. White, at times tinged grey, blue or green, it runs from transparent to translucent. A pronounced pearly lustre marks its cleavage faces. In look and softness it resembles gypsum or talc. Its optical character sets it apart, though: it is uniaxial with positive birefringence, while gypsum is biaxial. The fibrous variety nemalite holds iron oxide in place of part of the magnesia.
britannica-1911-caillie-rene-auguste:
René Auguste Caillié, a French traveller who lived from 1799 to 1838, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a baker in Poitou, and tales of travel fired him as a boy. At sixteen he sailed for Senegal. The fixed aim of his life became the hidden city of Timbuktu.

To reach it he learned Arabic and lived for months among the Moors as a convert. He then joined a caravan in the guise of an Arab from Egypt. Ill health held him for five months on the road, yet he pushed on. In April 1828 he entered Timbuktu and stayed two weeks. He crossed the Sahara to Morocco and got home safe. A British officer had reached the city first but was slain on the way out.
britannica-1911-calcite:
Calcite is the subject of a mineral entry in the 1911 Britannica. Calcite is a stone made of calcium carbonate in nature. It forms crystals in one set system of shapes. Save for quartz, no mineral is spread more widely. Its crystals show great range and fine form. In bulk it forms marble, limestone, and chalk. Those rocks come in part from shells and coral remains.

The name is new next to the stone itself. It was first used in 1836 for one odd form. By about 1843 it had its present sense. A clear kind called Iceland spar was much studied. Work on that spar led to laws of split light rays. The stone splits with ease in three lines. Its hardness, weight, and fizz in weak acid mark it well. Four main habits of crystal form are then set out.
britannica-1911-capronnier-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Capronnier (1814–1891) was a Belgian stained-glass painter. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born in Brussels in 1814. He died in the same city in 1891. He had much to do with the modern revival of glass-painting. His first fame came from study of the old methods. He restored old glass with great skill. He also made copies for the Brussels archaeological museum.

Capronnier made windows for churches in many cities. Brussels, Bruges and Amsterdam all hold his work. Orders came to him from France, Italy and England too. At the Paris Exhibition of 1855 he won a medal. It was the only medal given for glass-painting that year. The entry is brief, and it rests his name on two things. One is his mastery of old workmanship. The other is the wide reach of his church windows.
britannica-1911-carbohydrate: Carbohydrate is a general name in chemistry for a family of compounds. This 1911 Britannica entry defines the class in a single sentence. The compounds are written by the formula Cx(H2O)y, carbon joined with the elements of water. They are essentially products of the vegetable world. The sugars belong to the class, and so do the starches. Gums and celluloses are named as members too. The entry sends readers to the articles on those substances for detail. Nothing beyond the formula and the member groups is stated.
britannica-1911-carcagente:
Carcagente is a town of eastern Spain. It stands in the province of Valencia. It lies near the right bank of the river Júcar. Two railways meet at the town in a junction. Its population in 1900 was 12,262. This 1911 Britannica entry describes its setting and trades. The town is picturesque and of considerable antiquity. Roman remains have been found in its neighbourhood.

Groves of orange, palm and mulberry trees surround Carcagente. Many Moorish houses stand within the town. Their old blue-tiled cupolas contrast with modern factory chimneys. Silk mills and linen factories have opened in recent times. Rice growing is an important local industry. The moist, warm climate of the low Júcar valley suits it well. The entry gives the town's rivers, groves and mills. It leaves a picture of old houses beside new industry.
britannica-1911-carloforte:
Carloforte is a town of Sardinia, in the province of Cagliari. It is the capital of the small island of San Pietro. That island lies off the west coast of Sardinia. It measures about 6 miles by 5 miles. The town's population in 1901 was 7693. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its history and trades. The town stands on the east coast of the island.

Charles Emmanuel III of Savoy founded Carloforte in 1737. He planted a colony of Genoese settlers there. Their dialect and costume still prevail in the town. In 1798 Tunisian raiders attacked the place. They carried off 933 inhabitants as slaves that year. The captives were ransomed after five years. The place was then fortified against fresh attacks. Carloforte is now a centre of the tunny fishery. Manganese mines also work in the island.
britannica-1911-carnot-lazare-hippolyte:
Lazare Hippolyte Carnot (1801–1888) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French statesman, the second son of the general Lazare Nicolas Carnot. Born at Saint-Omer, he spent his early years in exile with his father and returned to France only in 1823. Barred from active politics, he turned to writing, publishing translated Greek chants and an account of Saint-Simonian doctrine, and he helped run the movement's journal, Le Producteur.

Elected deputy for Paris in 1839, Carnot sat with the Radical Left against Louis Philippe. In February 1848 he backed the republic, and Lamartine made him minister of education in the provisional government. He pushed for free, required primary schooling and for girls' secondary schooling, but his defence of religious teaching angered both sides and forced his resignation that July. He later opposed Napoleon III and ended his career as a senator for life.
britannica-1911-carnot-lazare-nicolas-ma:
Lazare Nicolas Marguerite Carnot (1753–1823) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French general and engineer from Nolay in Burgundy. Trained at Mézières, he joined the Corps de Génie in 1773 and rose to captain ten years later. He wrote on machines and balloons, and his prize essay on Vauban won praise from Prince Henry of Prussia. A quarrel over fortification theory landed him in prison before the Revolution pulled him into politics.

Elected a deputy for the Pas de Calais, Carnot became the army's chief organiser on the Committee of Public Safety. The entry credits him with drafting nearly every military paper the committee issued during the wars of 1792 and 1793. He helped steady the north-eastern frontier after the defeat at Neerwinden and shared in Jourdan's victory at Wattignies. The account presents him as the tireless staff officer behind France's defence.
britannica-1911-carrier-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Carrier (1756–1794) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French Revolutionist born at Yolet, near Aurillac in Upper Auvergne. He worked as a country attorney and in 1792 was chosen deputy to the National Convention. He belonged to the Cordeliers and Jacobin clubs and was known as an influential member of both. He helped set up the Revolutionary Tribunal and voted for the death of Louis XVI.

In October 1793 the Convention sent Carrier to Nantes to crush the revolt there by the severest measures. He formed a band called the Legion of Marat and filled the jails with prisoners. Trials soon gave way to mass killing: victims were guillotined, shot, or cut down in the prisons. Worst of all, prisoners were loaded onto vessels with trap-door bottoms and sunk in the Loire. These drownings, the Noyades of Nantes, anchor the entry's account of his mission.
britannica-1911-carucate:
Carucate is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry defining an old English measure of land. The word comes from the medieval Latin carrucata, from carruca, a wheeled plough. A carucate was a unit of area based, in all likelihood, on the ground that a team of oxen could plough in a year. Land measures of this kind tied the size of a holding to the work a plough team could do on it.

The entry adds the fiscal use of the term. “Carucage” names a tax levied on each carucate of land, so the measure served the tax collector as well as the farmer. Readers who want the wider system of early land units are sent to the article on the Hide, the better known measure of the same family. In a few lines the entry gives the word's root, its probable basis, and its use in taxation.
britannica-1911-cassiterite:
Cassiterite, the main ore of tin, is laid out in a stone and mine entry in the 1911 Britannica. Its name comes from the Greek word for tin. The stone is tin oxide and forms four sided or eight sided prisms. Twin forms with sharp notched joints are common in finds. Thin forms in Cornwall bear names drawn from nails and needles. Loose grains in stream beds are called stream tin.

Pure stone may be white, but most finds run brown or black from iron in the mix. A red form and a gummy shine form get note as well. The stone is hard and very heavy for its size. That weight lets wash work split it from light rock with ease. It turns up most in veins in granite rock.
britannica-1911-caste:
Caste is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a form of social organisation. The word comes from the Spanish and Portuguese casta, lineage. Behind that stands the Latin castus, pure. The entry warns that writers have applied the name loosely. Many large scale systems have been called castes, in praise and in blame. Before the word spread through Europe, it was tied to the Brahmanic division of Hindu society into classes. The matching Hindu word is varna, colour.

Because the Indian notion itself is vague, the borrowed word often means little. The entry tests borderline cases. Palgrave claimed that the colleges of workmen in Roman Britain were castes in practice, since the son had to follow the father's trade. The entry answers that such bodies look more like early craft guilds. The piece works as a caution on the word itself.
britannica-1911-cavaignac-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Cavaignac is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French politician born at Gourdon in the Lot. His department sent him as deputy to the Convention. There he joined the party of the Mountain. He voted for the death of Louis XVI. The Convention kept him busy on missions in the provinces. He repressed opponents of the revolution with rigour in the Landes and the Gers.

At Bayonne he and Jacques Pinet set up a revolutionary tribunal. Charges of cruelty were brought against him in 1795, but the Convention dismissed them. He later held minor offices and served Murat's government at Naples in 1806. During the Hundred Days he was prefect of the Somme. At the Restoration he was proscribed as a regicide. He spent his last years at Brussels, where he died in March 1829. The entry then turns to his sons, Godefroi and General Eugène Cavaignac.
britannica-1911-cerargyrite:
Cerargyrite is a mineral article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about silver chloride, a key ore of silver. The name is a Greek form of the older name hornsilver. Gesner used that name as far back as 1565. The word joins the Greek for horn and for silver.

Till 1841 and 1842 the term also covered the bromide and the mixed chloro-bromide of silver. Chemists then split those off under their own names. The pure chloride came to be called chlorargyrite, though the older name is still often used for it alone. A fourth kin stone, with iodine in the mix, has also been found. The article holds that the group name fits the whole set better. All four look much alike and differ in essence only in what they are made of.
britannica-1911-cerussite:
Cerussite is a mineral made of lead carbonate and a key ore of lead, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its name comes from a Latin word for white lead. Old names in use were lead spar and white lead ore. The present name dates from eighteen forty five.

The mineral forms crystals in one system and often grows as twin crystals. Three crystals joined can make a six rayed star shape. Crystals are common and have bright, smooth faces. The mass form is dense and grainy, at times fibrous. It is most often clear or white, with a bright shine like a gem. It is very brittle and breaks with a shell like curve. Its hardness and weight are given in the entry.
britannica-1911-cette:
Cette, a seaport in the south of France, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands south west of Montpellier in the department of Herault. About thirty two thousand people lived there at the count in the entry. After Marseilles it was the chief trade port on the south coast.

The old town climbs the foot of Mont Saint Clair, a hill on a tongue of land. A canal links the lagoon of Thau to the harbour basins. New quarters lie across the canal on two islands. A breakwater guards one of the safest harbours in France. Courts, a bank branch, a hospital, and schools of trade and sailing are listed. Canals join the town to Lyons and to Bordeaux. Wine and brandy lead its exports, while wine, grain, and coal lead imports.
britannica-1911-chabazite:
Chabazite is a mineral in the zeolite group, covered here in a 1911 Britannica entry on its form and makeup. The stone forms white to flesh red crystals with a glassy shine. Its crystals look much like cubes, so early writers called it a cubic zeolite. Twinned crystals are a key mark, and one flat form was named phacolite for its lens shape.

Inside, the entry gives the hardness, weight, and light effects of the stone in plain terms. Heat drives off water and changes how light passes through it. The text also lists named forms such as haydenite and acadialite and tells where they occur. It notes the stone is most often found in holes in basalt rock.
britannica-1911-chansons-de-geste:
Chansons de geste, the epic tales of old France, are the subject of a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name means songs of deeds. These long poems held a prime place in French letters from the eleventh to the fifteenth century. Their core is a chain of deeds drawn from the past. Round that core the poems group in sets called cycles.

Wandering singers known as jongleurs may have chanted such poems as early as the ninth century. The first that still stands is also the most famed, the Song of Roland. Its date is placed between 1066 and 1095. The entry traces how the form sprang from a blend of German spirit and Roman shape. That blend fed the new Christian world of France.
britannica-1911-charente:
Charente is an inland department of south-western France, and a survey entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its land and waters. It covers 2,305 square miles and held 351,733 people in 1906. Most of it is hilly, with the highest ground, over 1,000 feet, in the granite north-east.

The entry divides the department into the cold lands of the north-east and the warmer lands elsewhere, where heights run lower. Large woods cover much of the north. The river Charente drains most of the department, joined by the Tardoire, Touvre, and Ne. The climate is mild but moist, and farming thrives, with more than half the surface under the plough.
britannica-1911-chasles-victor-euphemien:
Victor Euphémien Philarète Chasles (1798-1873) was a French critic and man of letters. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces a hard boyhood shaped by Rousseau ideas. His father had voted for the death of Louis XVI in the Convention. The boy was placed with a printer to learn manual work first.

A plot in 1815 landed him in prison for two months. Work in London on classic editions followed his release from jail. Back in France he spread study of English authors to wide readers. He also brought Nordic and Russian writing to French notice early. Chairs and library posts came as he wrote some fifty volumes.
britannica-1911-chihuahua-state:
Chihuahua is a northern frontier state of Mexico, bounded by the United States, Coahuila, Durango, Sinaloa and Sonora. Its area is 87,802 square miles and its people rose from 260,008 in 1895 to 327,784 in 1900. Much of the surface is a high plateau sloping toward the Rio Grande, while the Sierra Madre breaks the west into fertile valleys. A dry sandy plain runs inland from the Rio Grande for 300 to 350 miles.

Rain is scarce and water shortage checks farming, though soil and climate suit wheat, corn, beans, cotton and grapes where irrigation works. Stock raising matters in the western hills, but mining is the chief industry, with gold, silver, copper, mercury, lead and coal. More than one hundred silver mines yielded an estimated 4,500,000 dollars a year at the end of the 19th century. The Mexican Central railway crosses the state from north to south.
britannica-1911-chlorite:
Chlorite, a group of green minerals like mica, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. The name was given in 1798 from a Greek term for a green stone. These minerals are water bearing mixes of alumina, magnesia, and iron. Many kinds and forms have been set out, but they are hard to tell apart.

Like the micas, chlorites split in clean flat sheets along one face. Their flakes bend but do not spring back, a point of split from true mica. They most often come as soft scaly masses of a dark green hue. In make up they hold near thirteen parts water in a hundred. They hold no alkalis, and alumina forms a fifth of their mass.
britannica-1911-church-rate:
Church Rate was the name of a tax formerly levied in each parish in England and Ireland for the benefit of the parish church. Money from the rates paid for divine service, repairs to the fabric and the salaries of church officials. Churchwardens made the rates with parishioners duly assembled in vestry or church after proper notice. Arrears could be recovered in the church court, or before two justices when sums were small.

The rate fell as a personal charge on occupiers of land or houses, and compulsion proved hard to apply in practice. Nonconformists objected in conscience to supporting the Established Church, and in mostly Catholic Ireland the grievance was felt most sharply. Agitation led in 1868 to the Compulsory Church Rates Abolition Act. Rates then became voluntary only, and non-payers lost any say in how the money was spent.
britannica-1911-chute:
Chute, a French word for a fall of water or the like, pronounced as shoot, names a channel or trough down which objects may slide. Timber, coal or grain move down such a channel from a higher to a lower level. The word also covers a channel cut in a dam or river for floating timber. In Louisiana and on the Mississippi it names a side channel of a river, or a narrow way between an island and the shore.

A second use belongs to sport rather than trade, set apart from the working channels. The water-chute, or water tobogganing, is a Canadian pastime now popular in London and elsewhere. A steep wooden slope ends in a shallow lake at its foot. Flat-bottomed boats run down the slope, gather speed fast, and dash into the water.
britannica-1911-cleft-palate:
Cleft palate is a split in the roof of the mouth present from birth, explains a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on surgery. It is often linked with hare lip. A baby with the flaw cannot suck, so an operation is needed. The flaw often runs in families.

The best time to operate is between two weeks and three months of age, the entry says. Closing the cleft early aids feeding and growth. It also likely saves the voice from the odd tone tied to a flawed roof. That tone can persist even after a late repair. A key advance came from a plan to push the two halves of the palate together to the mid line. Once the palate is dealt with, the lip can be repaired with ease.
britannica-1911-clinoclasite:
Clinoclasite is a mineral article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a rare mineral made of a basic copper arsenate. It grows in the monoclinic system and has a perfect cleavage along the basal plane. That cleavage sits at a slant to the faces of the crystal, and from this the name comes: Greek words for to incline and to break give clinoclase, or clinoclasite. The crystals are deep blue and most often stand in radiating half round groups.

The article gives the mineral's marks: it is soft, and its specific gravity is 4.36. It was once found with other copper arsenates in the mines of the St Day district of Cornwall. Clinoclasite is a mineral of secondary birth, formed in the upper parts of veins as copper ores and mispickel decay.
britannica-1911-cochin-state:
Cochin was a feudatory state of southern India, under Madras in rank, with an area of 1,361 square miles. British Malabar, Coimbatore and Travancore bounded it on most sides. The Arabian Sea lay to the west. One part of the Chittore taluk sat apart from the main land, ringed by British ground.

The entry divides the state into three zones. Forested hills of the Western Ghats formed the east. A central belt of uplands and plains sloped down toward coast lagoons. A flat shore strip formed the west. It then traces the rajas and their tribute. Tribute was fixed at two lakhs in 1818. Prosperity grew under Sir Sri Rama Varma, who came to the throne in 1895.
britannica-1911-colbert-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Colbert (1619–1683) was a French statesman born at Reims, where his father and grandfather were merchants. He claimed descent from a noble Scottish family, though proof is lacking. His youth passed in a Jesuit college and in the offices of a banker and a notary. Before he was twenty he gained a post in the war office.

Kinship with Michel Le Tellier opened that door. Colbert inspected troops and did like work for some years. His skill, force and tireless labour then made him Le Tellier's private secretary. Wealth and sway soon followed. The long entry traces his rise and his harsh rule in detail. One dark thread runs through the later part. Men were pushed toward sentence to the oar in great numbers. Even men freed by time served were seldom let go.
britannica-1911-colemanite:
Colemanite, in the 1911 Britannica, is a mineral entry on a water bearing calcium borate found in California. It forms bright crystals with one flat cut, clear and glassy to diamond bright in shine. The stone holds just over half boron trioxide by weight. That makes it a key source of trade borates and boracic acid.

The mineral was first found in 1882 in Death Valley, in Inyo county. A year later richer beds turned up near Daggett, set in sandstone and clay. Large masses have since been worked there and in Los Angeles county. The entry sets two kin stones beside it. Priceite, soft and chalk like, lies in beds in Oregon, and pandermite comes from Asia Minor in nodules up to a ton. A last note takes up ulexite, the cotton ball borate.
britannica-1911-colima-state:
Colima is a small Pacific coast state of Mexico, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a geography entry. It lies between Jalisco and Michoacan, and with its offshore islands its area is only a little over two thousand square miles. That makes it the second smallest of the Mexican states. Its people grew from about fifty five thousand in 1895 to sixty five thousand in 1900.

Most of Colima lies within a narrow, flat coastal plain. Beyond it the land rises north east into the foothills of the Sierra Madre. Two rivers and their branches drain the state and serve widely for irrigation. Tidewater lagoons add to its malarious character, and one large lagoon is the centre of a salt industry. The soil is fertile, the entry says, but poor transport held back production beyond local needs. The climate is hot and humid on the coast.
britannica-1911-columbite:
Columbite is the subject of a mineral entry in the 1911 Britannica. Columbite is a rare stone made of iron and niobium. Manganese and tantalum can take their place in part. In this stone a new element was found in 1801. Charles Hatchett found it and named it columbium. He named it for America, the source of his sample. The stone is also called niobite in some texts.

Its crystals are black and shine like dull metal. Twin crystals are not rare in the stone. It splits cleanly along one face when struck. Its hardness and weight are given as set marks. More tantalum makes the stone weigh more per bulk. Stones rich in that share are called tantalite. Sites in Bavaria, the Urals, and the United States are named. Two linked stones from Norway and Finland close the entry.
britannica-1911-comte-auguste:
Auguste Comte is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which calls him a French Positive thinker. He was born on the nineteenth of January 1798 at Montpellier. His father held a post as a tax officer for the district.

The article stresses his fierce will and his scorn for mere rank. At the polytechnic school in Paris he joined a revolt against a master, and the school was shut down. Sent home, he chose to go back to Paris in 1816. There he lived on very little, giving maths lessons to pay his way. He took Benjamin Franklin as his model of a wise life. The text follows his lean years as a young thinker in Paris.
britannica-1911-conglomerate:
Conglomerate, in petrology, is a coarse rock made of rounded pebbles set in a finer mass. The word comes from a Latin verb for rolling into a ball. Roundness is the key mark of the rock. Sharp-fragment rocks of like build are breccias, not conglomerates. The two kinds hold split meanings for the geologist who reads them.

Pebbles gain their round shape in two ways. Weather wears them down in place. Streams and sea waves grind them in travel as well. Hard rocks form most pebbles, granite, gneiss and sandstone among them. Quartzites and flints stand among the hardest of all. They thus fill conglomerates in high share. The banket rock of the Transvaal gold reefs gives a rich case. Gold sits in its mass and in its pebbles alike. Age marks other named kinds, some of them shot through with dolomite.
britannica-1911-connellite: Connellite is a rare mineral, described in a brief science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It forms tufts of fine needle shaped crystals of a rich blue colour. It grows with other copper minerals such as cuprite and malachite. Its presence in Cornwall was noted in 1802. Arthur Connell first tested its makeup in 1847, and the mineral bears his name. Outside Cornwall it had been found only in Namaqualand.
britannica-1911-copalite:
Copalite, also called copaline, fossil resin or Highgate resin, is a natural organic substance found in the London clay at Highgate Hill. It occurs as rough pieces of a pale yellow colour. Fresh broken, it gives off a resinous, aromatic smell. Heat at a modest level drives it off as vapour.

It burns with ease and gives a yellow, smoky flame. Near no ash stays behind when it burns. The hosted entry is short and holds no more than those marks. Name, place, colour, smell and burning form its whole stock of facts. A reader gains a field note for one London clay find, and no claim past what the piece itself can show.
britannica-1911-corday-d-armont-marie-an:
Marie Anne Charlotte Corday d'Armont, who lived from 1768 to 1793, was the Frenchwoman who killed Marat, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells her story. Born near Séez in Normandy, she came from a noble but poor family and counted the dramatist Corneille among her forebears. She was educated in a convent at Caen, then sent to live with an aunt.

In that quiet life Corday saw almost no one, and she spent her lonely hours reading the philosophes, above all Voltaire and the Abbé Raynal. Plutarch was another favourite, and from his pages she most likely drank in the idea of classic heroism and civic virtue that drove her famed act. When the Revolution broke out she studied politics in Girondin papers. When that party fell in 1793, many of its leaders fled to Normandy and made Caen their base.
britannica-1911-cordite:
Cordite, the smokeless powder used by the British army and navy, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is made as round rods or strings of set thickness. The soft paste is pressed through holes in a steel plate, and that string-like form gives the powder its name. Thin rods serve revolver shells, and thick rods serve heavy guns.

The mix was first fixed by a board led by Sir Frederick Abel in 1891. The first mark held much nitro-glycerin, gun-cotton, and a little mineral jelly. A later mark, called Cordite MD, cut the nitro-glycerin and raised the gun-cotton. It burns a bit slower, gives more speed, and keeps heat lower in the gun. The rods bend without breaking and shed water well.
britannica-1911-corrosive-sublimate:
Corrosive Sublimate is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a mercury compound. It is also called mercuric chloride in the text of the entry. The stuff is a white solid made by more than one path. Trade makes it by heating a mix of mercury salt and common salt.

The vapour then sets into small diamond-shaped crystals of white. It melts at a heat of 288 degrees and boils at 303. It melts in cold water only a bit, and more in hot. In spirits and in ether it melts with great ease. It joins with many other salts to form double salts. The entry ends by noting its weight in the healing art. There it serves as an astringent, a caustic, and a germ killer.
britannica-1911-corte:
Corte is a town of central Corsica, north east of Ajaccio. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 4,839 people in 1906. The upper town clings to a steep rock. Below that rock two rivers, the Tavignano and Restonica, meet. The rest of the town spreads on both banks below. A citadel built by Vincentello d'Istria crowns the rock. Courts and a college serve the district from Corte.

Houses of two patriots stand out in the entry. Pasquale Paoli lived in one while Corte was his seat of rule. That rule ran from 1755 to 1769. In the other, the wife of Giampietro Gaffori held the house against the Genoese in 1750. Statues honour both men in the town. Corte was the heart of the fight against Genoa in the 1700s. Paoli set up a university there. Marble pits nearby feed trade, along with wine and timber.
britannica-1911-covellite:
Covellite is a mineral made of cupric sulphide, with the formula CuS. It forms in the hexagonal system. It occurs in nature less often than copper-glance, its orthorhombic kin. Crystals of it are very rare. The mineral most often forms in compact and earthy masses. It also coats other copper sulphides with a blue film.

Dark indigo-blue colour is its hallmark mark. Old German miners called it indigo-copper for that hue. Its name honours N. Covelli, who in 1839 found its crystals on Vesuvian lava. There the mineral formed where two volcanic gases met and acted on each other. In most cases it grows in copper veins by the change of other sulphides. Chalcopyrite, copper-glance and erubescite all feed its growth. Named homes include Sangerhausen in Saxony, Butte in Montana and Chile. It is soft, at one and a half to two in hardness.
britannica-1911-creosote:
Creosote is a product gained by distilling coal, bone oil, shale oil, or wood tar. Beech wood tar is the chief source named in the entry. Its name joins Greek words for flesh and for to preserve. The stuff is drawn from the distillate by means of alkali. It is then freed with acid, filtered, and distilled again in stages.

When pure, creosote is a colourless, oily liquid that bends light strongly. It was first got in eighteen thirty two by Reichenbach from beech tar. It is in the main a mix of phenol, cresol, guaiacol, and kindred bodies. It has a strong odour and a hot taste on the tongue. It burns with a smoky flame when lit in the open. It dissolves sulphur, phosphorus, resins, and many acids and colours.
britannica-1911-crevillente:
Crevillente, a town of eastern Spain in the province of Alicante, is given a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the railway between Murcia and Alicante, among the eastern foothills of the Sierra de Crevillente, with a little over ten thousand people in 1900. The town is an old one, with flat roofed Moorish houses set in gardens of cactus, dwarf palm and orange trees, broken by masses of rock. 

The land round it is dry by nature, yet two springs near by water it, springs that differ sharply in warmth. The district is famed for its melons and also yields wine, olives, wheat and esparto grass, while its workshops make coarse cloth, esparto goods, oil and flour.
britannica-1911-crocidolite:
Crocidolite is a blue fibrous mineral of the amphibole group, close in kinship to riebeckite. Klaproth described it in 1815 as blue ironstone, and Hausmann gave it its present name in 1831 for its nap-like look. In chemical terms it is an iron sodium silicate. Its likeness to asbestos won it the name Cape Asbestos. Its chief home is Cape Colony, where it occurs with magnetite and other iron ores.

As the mineral alters, alkali leaves it, its iron rusts, and silica settles between its fibres. The hard stone that results takes a silky shine when polished. In blue it is sold as hawk's-eye, and in rich golden brown as tiger-eye, a fashionable South African cat's eye. A table of analyses compares the fresh mineral with both altered stones. A further product of the same change, mixed silica and iron hydrate, is called griqualandite.
britannica-1911-crocoite:
Crocoite is a mineral made of lead chromate that crystallizes in the monoclinic system. It matches the paint chrome-yellow in composition and serves at times as a paint itself. The entry calls it the only chromate of any note found in nature. It was found at Berezovsk near Ekaterinburg in the Urals in 1766. Beudant named it in 1832 from the Greek word for saffron, after its colour.

Its crystals are a bright hyacinth red, translucent, with a shining surface that dulls in light. The streak is orange-yellow, the hardness low, and the weight high for its size. Fine crystals come from Brazil, Luzon, and Mashonaland, and gold often occurs with the mineral. The finest known, long slender prisms three or four inches long, came from the Adelaide Mine at Dundas in Tasmania. Kindred minerals at Berezovsk include phoenicochroite and vauquelinite, named for the chemist who found chromium in crocoite.
britannica-1911-crystallite:
A crystallite is a rudimentary, imperfect form of crystallization, found where a thick medium blocks the movements that build full crystals. Quickly cooled volcanic rocks, pitchstone and obsidian among them, are full of such bodies. Under the microscope their glassy base holds minute crystals and crystallites in great numbers. Crystallites can also be grown by letting a sulphur solution dry slowly on a slide.

The entry names their forms as they grow. Small round globulites may join into bead-like rows called margarites, or swell into longulites, baculites, and hair-fine trichites. The largest may turn suddenly into true crystals with double refraction. Microliths, by contrast, already hold crystal properties and belong to known minerals. Spherulites are radiate clusters of such microliths, often spreading out from an early crystal face. Vogelsang first drew wide notice to these bodies, and took globulites as first stages toward crystals.
britannica-1911-cuprite:
Cuprite is a 1911 Britannica article on a mineral that is a key ore of copper. Cuprite is made of cuprous oxide. It crystallizes in the cubic system. Copper makes up most of its weight. Haidinger gave it the name cuprite in 1845, from the Latin word for copper.

Older names were red copper ore and ruby copper. Those names set it apart from the other native copper oxide. That one, cupric oxide, was known as black copper ore. Well-formed crystals of cuprite are common in the ground. They most often take the shape of the regular octahedron. At times they join with the cube or other forms. A few Cornish crystals show a rare form with twenty-four faces. Rock and ore readers get the name, the make-up, and the crystal habit in short order.
britannica-1911-danburite:
Danburite is a rare mineral, a calcium and boron silicate that crystallizes in the orthorhombic system. C. U. Shepard found it in 1839 at Danbury in Connecticut and named it for that place. Its crystals are prismatic and closely mimic topaz in form and angles. They run from transparent to translucent, and from colourless to pale yellow. The stone is hard, at seven on the scale, and its specific gravity is 3.0.

At Danbury the mineral sits in dolomite with microcline and oligoclase. Large crystals four inches long have come from veins in granite at Russell in St Lawrence county, New York. Smaller, well-formed crystals occur on gneiss at Mount Scopi and in the Vals Rhine valley in Switzerland. Splendid crystals have lately been got from Japan. Find-spots and crystal form make up the entry. It lists no use for the stone beyond the cabinet of the collector.
britannica-1911-enceinte:
Enceinte, from the Latin for “girdled within,” is a French term used in fortification for the inner ring of works around a town. The entry is careful to part it from the like-sounding word for “pregnant,” which comes from a girdle loosened. Strictly, the enceinte was the unbroken line of bastions and curtains forming the “body of the place.”

In modern fortification, the entry says, the enceinte is usually simply the innermost unbroken line of fortifications. The word has a wider architectural use as well. In that use an enceinte is the close or precinct of a cathedral, an abbey, or a castle. The notice is short, a word-book entry for engineers and architects.
