It gives the strict old sense, the looser modern sense, and the precinct sense, and it warns against the false friend that shares its spelling.
britannica-1911-epaulette:
Epaulette, a French word from épaule, a shoulder, is properly a shoulder-piece. The name was applied to the shoulder-knot of ribbon to which a scapulary was tied, worn by members of a religious order. Its military use likely came from the metal plate that guarded the shoulder in the armour of the 16th century.

The use of the epaulette to mark grades of rank began in France in 1759, at the suggestion, it is said, of the duc de Belle-Isle. By the late 18th century it had become a solid ornament, a flat shoulder-piece running out into an oval plate with a thick fringe of gold or silver for officers. The entry gives its wear by service and date. British naval officers above sub-lieutenant wear it, while the British army gave it up about 1855.
britannica-1911-epidiorite:
Epidiorite, in petrology, is a typical member of a family of rocks made chiefly of hornblende and felspar, often with epidote, garnet, sphene, biotite, or quartz, and usually layered in structure. The term covers much the same ground as “amphibolite” and “hornblende-schist.” These rocks are metamorphic, changed by heat and pressure. Though their make-up is like diorite, they were formed from more basic rocks such as diabase, dolerite, and gabbro.

They occur among the schists, slates, and gneisses of the Scottish Highlands, the north-west of Ireland, Brittany, the Harz, the Alps, and the ranges of eastern North America. The rocks are dark green, weather brown, and in many places carry gold in quartz veins. Fresh, they are tough and hard, and well suited for road-mending stone.
britannica-1911-epidosite:
Epidosite, in petrology, is a typical member of a family of metamorphic rocks composed mainly of epidote and quartz. The rocks are pale yellow or greenish yellow, hard, and somewhat brittle. They may arise in more than one way, from several kinds of parent rock. Some began as epidotic grits and sandstones. Others are limestones changed by contact with hot rock.

Most epidosites, though, are kin to epidiorite and amphibolite, local forms of rocks that began as basic intrusions or lavas. The sandstone kind occur with mica-schists and sheared grits and often keep traces of their layered start. The third group forms bands, veins, and streaks inside epidiorite masses. When streaked and varied in colour, epidosite has been cut and polished as an ornamental stone for brooches and simple jewelry. The rocks now and then carry visible specks of gold.
britannica-1911-epidote:
Epidote is a mineral species made of a basic calcium, aluminium, and iron silicate, crystallizing in the monoclinic system. Good crystals are common and usually prism-shaped. Much about the mineral shifts with the iron in it, from 5 to 17 percent of ferric oxide. Colour, optical behaviour, and weight all vary with that share.

The hardness is 6.5, and the colour is green, grey, brown, or nearly black, most often a marked yellowish-green or pistachio-green, whence the old name pistacite. The name epidote is one of Haüy's crystal names, from a Greek word for “increase.” Epidote is a plentiful rock-forming mineral of second-hand origin. It occurs in crystalline limestones and schists, and as a weathering product of felspars, micas, and other minerals in igneous rocks.
britannica-1911-erubescite:
Erubescite is a native copper iron sulphide valued as a copper ore, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It forms crystals in the cubic system. Most often it shows as joined cubes, or as dense and grainy masses. A fresh break shows a bronze or copper hue.

In damp air that hue soon fades to bright blue and red tints. Those tints gave it names like purple copper ore and horse flesh ore. Its own name comes from a Latin word that means to grow red. The stone is soft for a metal ore and leaves a grey black streak. Other names in use are Bornite and, in French works, phillipsite. Both names had served for other stones first.
britannica-1911-erythrite:
Erythrite is a name used twice over, for a cobalt mineral and for a substance in chemistry, and this 1911 Britannica entry treats both in turn. The mineral is a compound of cobalt and arsenic with water. It forms blade-shaped crystals in radiating groups, bright crimson in colour with a strong shine, though light dulls both in time. More often it shows as a soft crust of peach-blossom pink, long known as cobalt-bloom.

The finest crystals come from Schneeberg in Saxony, and the crust form has been found in Thuringia, Cornwall, and other places. The second erythrite is a kind of alcohol with a sweet taste, found free in a common alga and bound up in many lichens. The name in both uses comes from a Greek word for red.
britannica-1911-estate:
Estate is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word came through Old French from a Latin term for state or condition. It once named the state in which a man lives, a sense now kept mostly in poetry. The plainer word state has taken over most of its old ground.

Two fields kept the word in daily use. The first is the law of property, and the entry gives it most room. In the widest sense, a man's estate is all that he owns. Land and linked interests form his real estate, and the rest is personal estate. In strict legal use, an estate is an interest in land. That idea, the article says, lies at the root of English land law. A second field, constitutional law, is also named. Readers get a guide to a word that shapes how property is owned and described.
britannica-1911-etiquette:
Etiquette names the rules of behaviour kept in society, above all the formal ceremony of courts. The entry also covers the procedure of organized bodies, with precedence and promotion in view. Professions such as law and medicine keep their own codes. Those codes guard the dignity of the profession and shield its members from injury. The word is French, from the Old French estiquette or estiquet, a label or ticket.

Its deeper root is Teutonic, from sticken, to stick or post up. Cotgrave glosses the French word as a billet given for the holder's benefit. It could serve as a form of introduction. It also meant a notice posted at the gate of a court of law. The entry notes that the path from label to ceremonial rule seems plain. The New English Dictionary, though, finds the history not clearly established.
britannica-1911-eunuch-flute:
Eunuch Flute, also called the Onion Flute or mirliton, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a wind instrument in use in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Its sound is akin to the comb music of the nursery, and it is still made as a toy. In French its names mean the eunuch flute and the onion flute.

The body is a wooden tube that widens slightly into a bell at the end. A very fine membrane, like an onion skin, closes the top end, stretched tight as a drum skin. The player sings into a round hole pierced a couple of inches below that membrane. The voice sets the membrane vibrating, which strengthens the sound and gives it a bleating tone. A movable cap guards the membrane. Mersenne, who drew and described it, said the vibration improves and charms the voice.
britannica-1911-fate:
Fate, in Roman mythology, is fatum, the spoken word of Jupiter and the unchanging will of heaven. The plural form, Fata, meant the destinies of persons or of cities. It then came to name the three goddesses who controlled those destinies. The Fata Scribunda were goddesses who wrote down a man's destiny at his birth.

Fata could also be singular, and popular and ceremonial speech used masculine and feminine forms, Fatus and Fata. The Fates also bore the name Parcae. Their attributes matched those of the Greek Moerae, the three goddesses of destiny in Greek myth. The entry is short, giving the Roman term, its plural use, and its Greek parallel in a few lines.
britannica-1911-felsite:
Felsite is a term geologists use for fine grained igneous rocks of acid makeup. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the term was common in England above all. Grains are too small to judge with the naked eye in most cases. Felspar and quartz make up most of the rock in tiny parts.

The rocks are pale, hard, and apt to split in a sharp way. Some hold larger quartz crystals set in the fine ground. Others show banding, round growths, or small air holes in places. Many scholars had dropped the broad term as too loose. Finer names split the group by what the microscope can show.
britannica-1911-fife-military-flute:
Fife, the small flute of the army band, is the subject of a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In its first form it was a plain tube blown from the side. In army use it is a small shrill flute that plays with the drum. Its pitch sits between that of the full flute and the piccolo.

The piece tells how six finger holes and strong blowing gave the fife its scales. Newer forms add four, five, or six keys to the plain tube. Old writers in France and Germany are quoted on its tone and use. The Swiss first paired it with the drum on the march. By the mid fifteen hundreds, drum and fife came with each hundred foot troops in English hosts.
britannica-1911-flandrin-jean-hippolyte:
Jean Hippolyte Flandrin (1809-1864), French painter, was born at Lyons in 1809. His father, trained for business but drawn to art, ended as a miniature painter for want of early teaching. Hippolyte was the second of three sons, all painters. His younger brother Paul became a leader of the modern French landscape school. The eldest, Auguste, taught at Lyons. After study at Lyons, Hippolyte and Paul saved their money and walked to Paris in 1829.

In Paris the brothers entered the studio of Ingres, who became their lifelong friend as well as teacher. Poverty pressed Flandrin until 1832. That year the Grand Prix de Rome, won by his Recognition of Theseus by his Father, freed him. Five years at Rome followed, and pictures sent home raised his fame. His St Clair healing the Blind was painted for Nantes cathedral. The entry follows his rise in the school of Ingres.
britannica-1911-flannelette:
Flannelette is a cotton cloth made to imitate flannel. The word seems to have been first used in the early eighteen-eighties. A Daily News reference of 1887 calls it a poverty-stricken article. By the time of this entry it was in wide use for underclothing, night gear, dresses, dressing-gowns and shirts. It is usually woven with a much coarser weft than warp. Its flannel-like face comes from raising or scratching up that weft.

Some kinds are raised on both sides, with long or short nap as the purpose needs. Plain dyed cloths and woven stripes and checks make a large trade. Almost any heavy cotton cloth can be turned into flannelette. The entry notes its cheapness for poorer buyers and the fire risk of flimsy kinds. A patented fire-resisting sort was sold as Non-flam. It was made in Britain, Europe and the United States.
britannica-1911-fontenay-le-comte:
Fontenay-le-Comte is a town of western France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Vendee. It stands 30 miles north-east of La Rochelle, on the state railway between that town and Saumur. Its population in 1906 was 7,639 in the town and 10,326 in the commune. Fontenay is an ancient, straggling town a few miles south of the forest of Vouvant. It spreads on both banks of the river Vendee, at the point where the river becomes navigable.

The church of Notre-Dame, built from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century, has a fine spire and a richly carved west entrance. The church of St Jean is its fellow. Several old houses survive, above all the Hotel de Terre Neuve of 1595-1600, rich in decoration and tapestry. Fontenay was the birthplace of many notable men. A Renaissance fountain, given by the king, also marks the town.
britannica-1911-fouque-friedrich-heinric:
Friedrich Heinrich Karl de la Motte Fouque was a German romantic writer. The hosted text opens in mid-article, with his introduction to A. W. Schlegel, who published his first book, Dramatische Spiele von Pellegrin, in 1804. His next work, Romanzen vom Tal Ronceval of 1805, showed his loyalty to the romantic leaders more plainly. In 1806 he versified a sixteenth-century romance of medieval chivalry as the Historie vom edlen Ritter Galmy, a knight's tale in verse.

Fouque's Sigurd der Schlangentoter of 1808, a hero play, was the first modern German dramatization of the Nibelungen saga. It drew wide attention and shaped later versions of the story, among them Hebbel's Nibelungen and Wagner's Ring. His interests split between medieval chivalry and northern mythology. In 1813, the year of the rising against Napoleon, he fought again with the Prussian army.
britannica-1911-franklinite:
Franklinite is a mineral of the spinel group, made of oxides of iron, manganese, and zinc in shifting shares. It forms large octahedral crystals, often with rounded edges, and also granular masses. The colour is iron-black with a metallic lustre, the hardness 6, and the specific gravity 5.2.

It looks much like magnetite but can be told apart because it is only slightly magnetic. Large amounts occur with zincite and willemite in crystalline limestone at Franklin Furnace, New Jersey, where it is mined as a zinc ore carrying 5 to 20 per cent of the metal. Once the zinc is drawn out, the residue serves in making spiegeleisen. The entry also notes the related zinc mineral gahnite found at the same place.
britannica-1911-frossard-charles-auguste:
Charles Auguste Frossard (1807-1875), French general, was born on 26 April 1807 and entered the army from the École Polytechnique in 1827, posted to the engineers. He served at the siege of Rome in 1849 and at Sebastopol in 1855, rising to general of brigade. In the Italian campaign of 1859, as general of division and chief of engineers, he caught the eye of Napoleon III.

In 1867 the emperor made him chief of his military household and governor to the prince imperial. Frossard was among the few senior men who in 1866-1870 foresaw war with Germany and tried to prepare for it. Offered a corps or the chief engineer post in 1870, he chose the II Corps. He held Spicheren on 6 August until German reinforcements and the absence of other French corps forced him back, and he shared the surrender of Bazaine army at Metz. He died in August 1875.
britannica-1911-fullerton-lady-georgiana:
Fullerton, Lady Georgiana Charlotte (1812–1885), an English novelist and philanthropist, was born at Tixall Hall in Staffordshire on the 23rd of September 1812. She was the youngest daughter of the first Earl Granville, and in 1833 she married Alexander George Fullerton. Her first novel, Ellen Middleton, appeared in 1844. In 1846 she entered the Roman Catholic church, three years after her husband had done the same.

Her later novels include Grantley Manor in 1847, Lady Bird in 1852 and Too Strange not to be True in 1864. After her only son died in 1854 she gave herself to works of charity. With Miss Taylor she founded the religious community of the Poor Servants of the Mother of God Incarnate. She died at Bournemouth on the 19th of January 1885.
britannica-1911-gallarate: Gallarate is a town of Lombardy in Italy, in the province of Milan, 25 miles north-west of that city by rail, with 12,002 people in 1901. The town is of medieval origin and is remarkable mainly for its textile factories. It is a railway junction for Varese, Laveno and Arona, on the Simplon route. Six miles west stand the electric works of Vizzola, the largest in Europe, drawing 23,000 horse-power from the river Ticino.
britannica-1911-galois-evariste:
Evariste Galois (1811-1832) was a French mathematician, born on 25 October 1811 and killed in a duel on 31 May 1832. The 1911 Britannica entry is brief, and it points readers to his papers rather than telling his life. An obituary by his friend Auguste Chevalier appeared in the Revue encyclopedique in 1832.

His collected works came out in the Journal de Liouville in 1846, and about fifty of those pages deal with when algebraic equations can be solved by radicals. The entry credits Galois with greatly enriching that branch of algebra. It also credits him with the notion of a group of substitutions, sending readers to the articles on equations and on group theory. A fuller edition of his works, with an introduction by C. F. Picard, appeared at Paris in 1897.
britannica-1911-garrote:
Garrote is an execution article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The garrote was a device used in Spain and Portugal to put condemned criminals to death. The Spanish word behind the name means a cudgel, a stout stick. The entry describes the machine and the ceremony around it in grim detail.

The prisoner rode to the scaffold on horseback or in a cart, wearing a black tunic. A procession of priests attended him to the place of death. He was seated and fastened to an upright post by an iron collar. A knob, worked by screw or lever, then broke his spinal column. In the older form, a cord was tied round the neck with a stick set between. Twisting the stick tightened the cord until the man was strangled. The article closes by noting the English crime called garrotting, a violent form of robbery.
britannica-1911-gavotte:
Gavotte, in the 1911 Britannica, is a dance and the music written for it. The word came into French from the Provencal gavoto. Properly, the entry says, it is the dance of the Gavots, the people of Gap, a district in the Upper Alps in the old province of Dauphine.

The dance itself is brisk and lively in character. The entry sets it beside the minuet: much alike in kind, but quicker and less stately. From the dance, the name passed to the matching form of musical composition. The whole notice is a few lines long, giving the word's home, the dance's temper, and its musical afterlife, with a pointer to the article on dance for more.
britannica-1911-gazette:
Gazette, in the 1911 Britannica, is a name for news-sheets or newspapers carrying an abstract of current events. The entry centres on the London Gazette, the English government's official organ. It appears every Tuesday and Friday.

Its contents are official acts: proclamations, orders in council, army and navy promotions, appointments to state offices, and rules that acts of parliament require to be published there. Bankruptcy notices and partnership dissolutions appear too. By the Documentary Evidence Act of 1868, a copy of the Gazette is prima facie evidence of royal proclamations and government orders. Edinburgh and Dublin have their own gazettes, and most countries publish like journals. The entry ends with gazetteer, once a writer for gazettes, now a geographical dictionary.
britannica-1911-geffroy-mathieu-auguste:
Mathieu Auguste Geffroy (1820–1895) was a French historian, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his turn to northern history. He was born in Paris and studied at the École Normale Supérieure. He then held history posts at various lycées. His French thesis of 1848 dealt with the political and religious pamphlets of Milton.

That thesis showed his pull toward foreign history, the entry says. He fitted himself for it by mastering the Germanic and Scandinavian languages. In 1851 he published a history of the Scandinavian states. The work was praised for its clear arrangement and sound facts. A long stay in Sweden later gave him rich documents. They served a political and social history of Sweden and France at the end of the eighteenth century.
britannica-1911-gilsonite: Gilsonite, also called Uintahite, is a form of asphalt found in the Uinta valley of Utah. The short 1911 Britannica note names it after Gilson of Salt Lake City. It occurs in masses several inches across near Fort Duchesne. The stuff is black, breaks with a curved glossy face, and turns soft and plastic when warmed. Output in 1905 came to 10,916 short tons, and it dissolves freely in hot oil of turpentine.
britannica-1911-girard-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Girard (1765-1850), known as Le Pere Girard, was a French-Swiss educationalist born at Fribourg. The 1911 Britannica entry says he was the fifth of fourteen children, and showed his gift for teaching early, helping his mother with the younger ones. Trained for the priesthood at Lucerne, he taught in convents, notably at Wurzburg in 1785-1788.

In 1798 he published a scheme of national Swiss education, full of Kantian ideas. He taught at Fribourg from 1805 to 1823, then at Lucerne until Jesuit hostility drove him on, retiring to write his books on education. His work on teaching the mother tongue ran to a ninth edition by 1894. The entry says Switzerland hailed him as a second Pestalozzi, praising his way of waking children's minds rather than cramming them with rules.
britannica-1911-glauconite:
Glauconite is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a green mineral. In chemistry it is a hydrous silicate of iron and potassium. It occurs most in green sands and muds. Those deposits are gathering now on the sea bottom. They form at many different places in the seas. The wide spread of these sands was first made known by Challenger naturalists. They occur in the Mediterranean as well as the open ocean.

They have not been found in the Black Sea. Nor have they been found in any fresh water lakes. These deposits are not truly abyssal in nature. They are of land origin, the text stresses. The mud and sand come from the wear of continents. Marine currents transport that material out to sea. Most of the mass is quartz, felspar, and mica. Calcite in it probably always comes from shells. Many other minerals occur in smaller shares.
britannica-1911-granite:
Granite, a name adapted from an Italian word meaning grained, is the group name for a family of igneous rocks, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. True granites are rich in silica and made chiefly of quartz and felspar, with some mica, hornblende, or augite, and have a fully crystalline build. In popular use the term is given to almost any hard crystalline rock that looks like granite.

Syenites, diorites, gabbros, and even some limestones are bought and sold daily as granites, the article notes. True granites are common rocks, above all among the older layers of the earth's crust. They vary much in colour, white, grey, pink, greenish, or yellow, chiefly by the state of their felspars. Many show large crystals of felspar, well seen on polished faces, and in the field granite occurs in great masses covering wide areas.
britannica-1911-granulite:
Granulite, a name for certain rocks, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term for a little grain. Rock men use it for two distinct classes of stone, and the schools of two nations split on the sense. In the French use it names a granite that holds both kinds of mica.

That use has not won general ground, the article says. To German scholars, and to most in England and America, granulite means a banded, fine-grained rock remade by heat and pressure. It consists mainly of quartz and feldspar in very small rough crystals. It most often holds a fair number of tiny round pale red garnets as well. The rocks are close kin to the gneisses, with near the same minerals, but they are finer in grain and weaker in their banding.
britannica-1911-graphite:
Graphite is a mineral made of the element carbon, described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. In chemical terms it is the same as diamond. Yet the two differ a great deal in their outward traits. Graphite is black and lets no light through, while diamond is clear.

Graphite is one of the softest of all minerals, and diamond the hardest. Graphite carries electric current well, while diamond does not. It never forms full crystals, only thin six sided plates and scales. The flakes bend but do not spring back. The stuff feels greasy and soils all it touches. Its name, given in seventeen eighty nine, comes from a Greek word for to write. That is because it is used to make pencils.
britannica-1911-grate:
A grate is the iron or steel frame that holds a fire in a home. The word comes from a Latin term for a hurdle. When coal took the place of logs, the old fire irons no longer fit the task. Coal burns in small lumps and gives a fierce, close heat. The fire had to be held in a small space. A basket or cage came into use for that end.

In time the basket gave way to the small grate of iron and fire brick set into the wall. That form then stayed in common use in England. Bright steel grates were much used in the early 1800s but took hard work to keep clean. Black grates that could be freshened with black-lead took their place. The Adam brothers drew many fine grate designs shaped like baskets.
britannica-1911-gravelotte: Gravelotte is a village of Lorraine between Metz and the French frontier. It is famed as the scene of a great battle on the eighteenth of August eighteen seventy. There the Germans under King William of Prussia fought the French under Marshal Bazaine. The field runs from the woods by the Moselle above Metz to Roncourt, near the river Orne. Other villages that played a large part lie north of Gravelotte. They include Saint Privat and Sainte Marie aux Chenes.
britannica-1911-greenaway-kate:
Kate Greenaway (1846-1901) was an English artist and book illustrator, daughter of the wood-engraver John Greenaway, born in London on 17 March 1846. The 1911 Britannica entry has her studying at South Kensington, at Heatherley's life classes and at the Slade. From 1868 she exhibited water-colours at the Dudley Gallery.

Her early fame came from Christmas cards, whose quaint beauty won an extraordinary vogue. Her subjects were young girls, children, flowers and landscape, drawn with artless simplicity, freshness and humour. The entry says the welcome they met came from more than love of novelty. Work for children's books followed, with Little Folks from 1873, and drawings for the Illustrated London News from 1877. Encouraged by H. Stacy Marks, she held to her own manner against friends who urged a conventional one.
britannica-1911-greenockite:
Greenockite is a rare mineral made of cadmium sulphide. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes small, bright, honey yellow crystals. They form in six sided shapes with unlike ends. Their faces show deep lines across, and their shine ranges from glassy to resin like.

Crystals had been found only in Scotland when the entry was made. Sites near Glasgow held them in hollows of basalt rock. Lord Greenock found a key set in 1840 during rail tunnel work. The mineral took its name from him in honor. Elsewhere it shows only as yellow dust on zinc ores that hold some cadmium.
britannica-1911-gretry-andre-ernest-mode:
Andre Ernest Modeste Gretry (1741-1813) was a French composer, born at Liege on 8 February 1741, the son of a poor musician. The 1911 Britannica entry has him a choir boy at St Denis, then a pupil of Leclerc, Renekin and Moreau. Hearing an Italian opera company at work taught him more than any master.

Longing to finish his studies in Italy, he composed a mass in 1759 whose dedication paid his way. Five years in Rome under Casali followed, though he confessed his harmony and counterpoint stayed moderate. His intermezzo La Vendemmiatrice won universal applause at the Aliberti theatre. A borrowed score of Monsigny then decided him for French comic opera. He left Rome on New Year's day 1767. The long article follows the Paris career that made him the master of opera comique.
britannica-1911-greuze-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Greuze (1725-1805) was a French painter, born at Tournus in Burgundy on 21 August 1725. The 1911 Britannica entry says he is generally called self-taught, but only in a limited sense. His father thwarted his bent; the Lyonnese portraitist Grandon encouraged it, and won the father over.

Greuze followed Grandon to Lyons, then to Paris, and worked from the living model at the Royal Academy's school. His first picture, a father explaining the Bible to his children, met doubt about whether it was truly his. Further works of the same class settled the question and won him the connoisseur La Live de Jully's support. The long article treats the sentimental family scenes that made his fame, the heads of young girls, and the eclipse of his reputation in later life.
britannica-1911-hakodate:
Hakodate is a town on the south of the island of Yezo in Japan. For many years it was held to be the chief town of the island. Sapporo later took that rank in form. Hakodate had 84,746 people in 1903. The town is built along the north-west base of a rocky point. The point forms the east side of a wide bay and joins the mainland by a narrow neck of sand.

The top of the rock, called the Peak, bears a fort. Hakodate was one of the first ports opened to foreign trade. Its bay is land-locked, deep, and easy to enter, with good ground for anchors. The Russians once used it as a winter port. Chief goods sent out are beans, peas, sea goods, sulphur, furs, and timber. Salt fish, oil, and oil-cake are among the goods brought in.
britannica-1911-hecate:
Hecate is a goddess in Greek mythology. Her name means she who works from afar. Her origin is disputed among scholars. The accepted view makes her Hellenic. Farnell argued she was imported from Thrace. Homer never mentions her at all. Hesiod makes her the daughter of the Titan Perses and Asterie. That passage may be a later Orphic interpolation.

In Hesiod she holds power over heaven, earth and sea. Wealth and daily blessings flow from her hand. War, games, cattle, hunting and law-courts all feel her influence. She is often identified with Artemis as a moon-goddess. Farnell treated her instead as chthonian, an underworld power. She presides chiefly over magic and spells. Circe and Medea are her sorceress daughters. Torch in hand, she helped Demeter search for Persephone. Theocritus invokes her in his famous love incantation.
britannica-1911-hennequin-philippe-augus:
Philippe Auguste Hennequin (1763–1833) was a French painter, born at Lyons and trained as a pupil of David. He won the Grand Prix and left for Italy. Unrest at Rome in the Revolution forced him back to Paris, where he painted the Federation of the 14th of July. In July 1794 he was accused before the revolutionary tribunal and jailed, then accused and jailed again, in danger of death.

His chief work, done in 1801, is Orestes pursued by the Furies, now in the Louvre. In 1802 he was one of four painters in the contest Gros won with the Battle of Nazareth. Napoleon later set him to paint scenes from the German campaigns. After 1815 he settled at Liège and painted the Death of the Three Hundred in defence of that city. In 1824 he moved to Tournay as head of the academy, and worked on until his death in May 1833.
britannica-1911-himly-auguste:
Himly, Auguste is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French historian and geographer of the nineteenth century. Born at Strassburg on the twenty-eighth of March 1823, Himly studied at home and took a course at Berlin. In Paris he swept the boards, coming first in exam after exam, among them the Ecole des Chartes. His doctoral thesis on Wala and Louis the Pious, printed in 1849, set him in the front rank of French scholars in Carolingian history.

Soon after, Himly turned his powers to geography. In 1858 he took a post teaching geography at the Sorbonne and gave the rest of his life to the subject. His great work, a history of how the states of central Europe took their shape on the land, came out in two volumes in 1876. He died at Sevres in 1906.
britannica-1911-humite:
Humite is the name of a group of minerals made of magnesium, silica, and fluorine. The 1911 Britannica article sets out the three kinds in the group. They are chondrodite, humite, and clinohumite, each with more magnesium than the last. The three look much alike, in shades of honey yellow, brown, and red. Their shine runs from glassy to resin-like, and they can be told apart only by fine tests on their crystals.

The name marks Sir Abraham Hume, whose gem stock is kept at Cambridge. It was given in 1813 to bright yellow crystals found in limestone blocks thrown out by Vesuvius. All three kinds have since been found at that site. The entry also names finds in Sweden and Finland. Large red crystals occur with magnetite at an iron mine near Brewster, New York.
britannica-1911-hydrate:
Hydrate is a chemistry article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a class of compounds that hold the parts of water. In its broad sense the term covers salts that carry water locked in their crystals. Such salts are called hydrated, and when the water is driven off they are called dry or anhydrous.

The article draws a line within that broad sense. In a tighter sense the term names compounds built on the hydroxyl group. Those are more often called hydroxides. Lime slaked with water is given as the stock case. The piece sets out how the form of these compounds shifts with the strength of the base metal in them. It notes a split in kind as well. Forms drawn from non metals act as acids. Forms drawn from metals act for the most part as bases.
britannica-1911-infante: Infante is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is the Spanish and Portuguese form of a Latin word for a young child. It is a title for sons of the ruler of Spain and Portugal. Daughters bear the matching title infanta. The eldest son in Spain does not bear it, since he holds a higher title. Other royal kin can gain it only by grant from the ruler.
britannica-1911-isabey-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Isabey, a French painter who lived from 1767 to 1855, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Nancy, he took lessons at nineteen from Dumont, miniature painter to Marie Antoinette, and then became a pupil of David. Employed at Versailles on portraits of two dukes, he gained a commission from the queen.

That commission opened a long list of orders from the successive rulers of France, down to his death in 1855. Backed by Josephine and Napoleon, Isabey arranged the ceremonies of their coronation and prepared drawings for the official record of it. Louis the Eighteenth paid him for that work, and Isabey painted that king's portrait in 1814. He kept royal favour under the Restoration and helped arrange the coronation of Charles the Tenth. The July monarchy gave him a post with the royal collections, and Napoleon the Third granted him a pension.
britannica-1911-jeannette:
Jeannette was a borough in Westmoreland county, Pennsylvania, some 27 miles east of Pittsburgh. The 1911 Britannica note gives its growth in plain counts. It held 3,296 people in 1890 and 5,865 in 1900. By 1910 the count had risen to 8,077, with many born abroad.

Trains on the Pennsylvania line served the town each day. An electric line linked it with Pittsburgh and with Uniontown. Gas from the ground lit and heated its homes and shops. Work centred on making glass, table ware, and goods of rubber. The town was laid out in 1888 and formed as a borough the next year.
britannica-1911-kennett-white:
White Kennett (1660–1728) was an English bishop and antiquary, born at Dover in August 1660. He was schooled at Westminster and at St Edmund's Hall, Oxford, where as an undergraduate he issued several translations of Latin works, Erasmus's In Praise of Folly among them. In 1685 he became vicar of Ambrosden in Oxfordshire.

A few years later he came back to Oxford as tutor and vice principal of St Edmund's Hall, where he gave a strong push to the study of antiquities. George Hickes taught him Old English. In 1695 he published his Parochial Antiquities. In 1700 he became rector of St Botolph's, Aldgate, in London, and in 1701 archdeacon of Huntingdon. A sermon in praise of the first duke of Devonshire won him the deanery of Peterborough in 1707. He then joined the Low Church party and fought the Sacheverell movement with vigour.
britannica-1911-khiva-khanate:
Khiva is a khanate article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Khiva was once an important kingdom of Asia, by 1911 a much reduced state. It depended on Russia and clung to the delta of the Amu-darya, the Oxus River. Its frontier ran down the river's left bank toward Lake Aral.

The entry measures the land with care. The khanate ran 200 miles from north to south and 300 at its widest. The watered oasis covered some 5210 square miles, the steppes far more. Each part held an estimated 400,000 people, the steppe folk being nomads. Russia's Transcaspian territory pressed against its southern line. Readers get the frame of a shrunken desert state: river, oasis, steppe, and a watchful empire at its edge.
britannica-1911-kleber-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Kleber was a French chief of hosts who lived from seventeen fifty-three to eighteen hundred. He was born at Strasbourg, where his father was a builder. He trained for work on fine builds, then won a place at a war school by aid to two lords in a brawl. Low birth blocked his rise in a realm host.

Back in France he oversaw builds, then joined the new hosts in seventeen ninety-two. Skill won him fast rank. He beat the kings men in the west and shone at Fleurus. He went with the host to Egypt, took towns in the east, and held a port town as its head.
britannica-1911-kunzite:
Kunzite is a clear, lilac-coloured form of the mineral spodumene, used as a gem-stone. It was found in 1902 near Pala, in San Diego county, California, close to ground known for fine rubellite and lepidolite. Dr C. Baskerville named it after Dr George F. Kunz, the New York gem expert who first described it. Tests by R. O. E. Davis proved it a spodumene.

Kunzite is found in large crystals, some as heavy as 1000 grams. Its hues run from a soft rosy lilac to a deep pink, and it is strongly dichroic, showing two shades by the light's path. Near the surface it can lose colour in the open air. Under the Röntgen rays, under radium, or under ultra-violet light, it glows with a strong phosphorescence.
britannica-1911-la-charite:
La Charité is a town of central France, in the department of Nièvre. It stands on the right bank of the Loire, 17 miles N.N.W. of Nevers, on the Paris-Lyon-Méditerranée railway. In 1906 it held 3990 people. The town keeps the remains of a fine Romanesque basilica, the church of Sainte-Croix, of the 11th and early 12th centuries. Its nave was rebuilt late in the 17th century.

The town owes its fame to its priory, founded in the 8th century and made a dependency of the abbey of Cluny in 1052. The priory became the mother of many houses, some in England and Italy. La Charité was fought over hard in the wars of religion of the 16th century,. Its trades are hosiery, boots and shoes, files and iron goods, lime and cement, and cloth, and it deals in wood and iron.
britannica-1911-la-porte:
La Porte is a city of Indiana, the county seat of La Porte county, 12 miles S. of Lake Michigan and about 60 miles S.E. of Chicago. It held 7126 people in 1890, 7113 in 1900 and 10,525 in 1910. Five railways serve it, two of them electric. The city lies in the midst of a rich farming region, and the shipping of farm and orchard produce is one of its chief trades. It has many factories besides.

La Porte stands in a region of fine lakes, among them Clear, Pine and Stone lakes. That setting has given it a strong name as a summer resort. The lakes also yield a large supply of clear ice, which is shipped to the Chicago markets. The town was settled in 1830, laid out in 1833, made a town in 1835, and first chartered as a city in 1852.
britannica-1911-laccolite:
A laccolite is an intrusive mass of igneous rock with a cake-like form, named by Grove K. Gilbert from the Henry Mountains of Utah, where they run 1 to 5 m. across and up to about 5000 ft. thick. It spreads along bedding planes like a sill, but over a small area with much greater thickness; its top is domed, its base flat, and it thins fast at the edges.

The shape comes from the toughness of the injected rock, usually of intermediate, alkali-rich kinds such as the trachytes, which flow far less freely than basalts. Basalts spread into thin flat sills instead. The strata above are lifted and bent, often cracking so dikes run into the fissures; the rocks below stay flat. British geologists have widened the term to other intrusions, such as the gabbro masses of the Cuillin Hills in Skye.
britannica-1911-lafontaine-sir-louis-hip:
Sir Louis Hippolyte LaFontaine (1807–1864), Canadian statesman and judge, was born at Boucherville in Quebec on the 4th of October 1807. He was educated at the Collège de Montréal under the Sulpicians and called to the bar of Lower Canada on the 18th of August 1829. In 1830 he was elected to the House of Assembly for Terrebonne and became an ardent supporter of Papineau against the governor's administration.

LaFontaine did not approve his leader's violent methods. After the fighting at Saint Denis he petitioned Lord Gosford to summon the assembly and act to stem the revolutionary course of events. When rebellion broke out again in 1838 the constitution of 1791 was suspended and LaFontaine was briefly imprisoned, while Papineau went into exile. At that crisis the French Canadians turned to LaFontaine as their leader, and under him they kept up their opposition to the special council of crown nominees.
britannica-1911-lanjuinais-jean-denis-co:
Jean Denis Lanjuinais (1753-1827), born at Rennes, stands in this 1911 account as a French lawyer turned lawmaker. A strong college record made him a doctor of laws and barrister at nineteen. He advised the Breton estates, taught church law at Rennes from 1775, and first made his name pleading against an old feudal right over pigeons.

Sent to the states-general of 1789, he called for an end to nobility and helped set up the civil order for the clergy. Back in the Convention from September 1792, he held moderate ground, fought the Mountain hard, and stayed loyal to the republic. The hosted text breaks off mid-sentence at his refusal to vote on the king's fate, so his later career is not present here.
britannica-1911-lanzarote:
Lanzarote is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes an island in the Atlantic Ocean, part of the Spanish Canary group. It is the most easterly island of that chain. Bare hills cover most of the land, and all of it shows its fire born past.

The entry gives the size of the island and a count of its people. A huge eruption in seventeen thirty remade half the island and wrecked nine villages. A port with two forts gives safe anchorage on the south east coast. Fresh water is so scarce that the people once had to leave the island. Camels serve as the beasts of burden in the dry heat.
britannica-1911-laterite:
Laterite, in the study of rocks, is a red or brown surface deposit of clay or earth, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains how it forms. It gathers on the surface of rocks through their breaking down, and is very common in tropical regions. The name comes from the Latin word for a brick.

The entry says the deposit is usually soft and crumbly, but hard lumps and bands rich in iron often occur in it. Its beds run up to thirty or forty feet deep, often soft below while the top is hard. That laterite is simply rotted rock is shown by its keeping the veins and outlines of the parent rock below.
britannica-1911-laurahutte: Laurahutte is the subject of a short village article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Laurahutte is a village in Germany, in the Prussian province of Silesia. It stands southeast of Beuthen, on a railway line. It has a Protestant church and a Roman Catholic church. Its chief note is its huge iron works, which employ about six thousand hands. In 1900 its people numbered over thirteen thousand.
britannica-1911-laureate:
Laureate comes from the Latin laurea, the laurel tree sacred to Apollo. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the laurel crown as honor for poets and heroes. In English the word came to mean marked by glory of any kind. Laureate letters once meant dispatches that announced a victory in war.

In England the term narrowed to the poet laureate office over time. Ben Jonson first held a post much like it under Charles I. Dryden gained the title by formal patent in 1670 with pay. Holders from Shadwell to Tennyson are listed in order in the entry. Southey, Wordsworth, and Tennyson restored honor to the post.
britannica-1911-leadhillite:
Leadhillite is a rare mineral made of lead compounds, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its crystals most often take the form of six sided plates. At times they form sharp diamond shapes. A clean split face shows a strong pearly shine. The crystals are most often white and let light pass.

The mineral is soft, with a set weight range given in the entry. Study of its crystals and light traits points to three distinct kinds. All three look the same from outside, and they may grow together in one crystal. One kind has long gone by the name susannite. Leadhillite forms as a later mineral in lead veins that have been changed by air. It is also found in old Roman lead slag.
britannica-1911-ledru-rollin-alexandre-a:
Alexandre Auguste Ledru-Rollin, a French politician who lived from 1807 to 1874, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Fontenay-aux-Roses in February 1807. His grandfather was a famed quack doctor of an earlier reign. He had just begun practice at the Paris bar when the July revolution came.

For ten years he defended republicans in the great political trials. In 1841 he was elected deputy for Le Mans almost without opposition. His fiery election speeches brought a trial and a prison sentence. He won his appeal on a point of form and escaped both. By 1846 he had given up his court post for politics alone. He stood as the known leader of the working men of France. His power lay more in the country than in the chamber. Finding no support in the press, he founded his own paper, La Réforme.
britannica-1911-lefebvre-desnoettes-char:
Charles Lefebvre Desnoettes, a French horse general born in seventeen seventy three, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He joined the army in seventeen ninety two and served on the northern and river fronts. Six years later he was captain and aide to General Bonaparte.

At Marengo he won a step up, and at Austerlitz he rose to lead a regiment. He fought in the Prussian wars that came next. In eighteen hundred and eight he was made a general and a count. Sent into Spain, he led the first siege of Saragossa, which failed. The field of Tudela showed his skill far better. Late that year British horse troops took him at Benavente. He stayed held in England for more than two years.
britannica-1911-lennox-charlotte:
Charlotte Lennox, a British writer who lived from 1720 to 1804, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. She was the daughter of a colonel who served as a deputy governor of New York. She went to London in 1735. Left with no support at her father's death, she began to earn her living by writing.

Lennox tried the stage with no success and wed in 1748. Samuel Johnson held her in high regard, ranking her above Carter, More, and Burney. Her chief works list The Female Quixote, a novel of 1752, and a study of Shakespeare's sources. In that study she argued he spoiled the tales he borrowed. Her comedy The Sister closed after one stormy night.
britannica-1911-lignite: Lignite, from the Latin lignum, wood, is a coal that has not fully formed. The entry is a single short passage. Its colour is most often a brown shade. Wood grain still shows in it, a mark of the wood it came from. For the rest, the entry points the reader to the main account under Coal. That cross-point is all the hosted text holds beyond the name, the colour, and the wood mark.
britannica-1911-limburgite:
Limburgite is a dark volcanic rock that looks much like basalt. One trait sets it apart: felspar is lacking in the normal stone. The name comes from Limburg in Germany and the Kaiserstuhl rocks there. Olivine and augite form its chief mass. A brown glassy paste binds them.

Augite runs green, brown, or violet in this rock. Olivine runs pale green, clear, or yellow. Small fresh augite grains crowd the paste. Iron oxides rich in titanium and apatite play small parts. Felspar shows at times but never in bulk. Nepheline is rare as well. Large hornblende or mica grains mark some stones. Hauyne marks the Cape Verde kind. Finds spread from the Rhine and Bohemia to Scotland, Spain, Brazil, and Kilimanjaro. Flows, sills, and dykes all carry it. Augitites, its close kin, lack olivine.
britannica-1911-limonite:
Limonite, or brown iron ore, is a water-born iron stone. Its Greek name points to meadows, where it forms as bog ore in wet ground. No crystal shape marks it. Fibrous, lumped, or earthy forms are the rule. Knobbed and stalk-like shapes show at times. Brown and yellow shades rule its colour.

Its streak is always a brown shade. That trait splits it from haematite, with a red streak, and from magnetite, with a black one. Hardness sits just over five. Weight runs from 3.5 to 4 times water. Old iron stones turn into limonite as air and rain work on them. Pyrites rot into it, at times keeping their first shape. Iron-rich waters lay it down, at times with help from living things. Rich beds sit in the Lias, Oolites, and Lower Greensand of England. Some ores hold near thirty per cent iron.
britannica-1911-lord-advocate: The Lord Advocate is the chief law officer of the crown in Scotland. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica casts him as head of all public trials there. He acts as chief accuser in crime cases and speaks for the crown in court. A solicitor general and deputes aid him. His reach is far wider than that of the matching officers in England. The post seems to date from the early 1500s. In 1597 he gained the right to bring charges on his own charge sheet.
britannica-1911-louvet-de-couvrai-jean-b:
Jean Baptiste Louvet de Couvrai is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French writer and politician. He was born in Paris in 1760, a stationer's son. He worked as a bookseller's clerk in his youth. He first won notice with a bold novel of love. That book, on the knight Faublas, came out from 1787 to 1789. Its heroine was based on a jeweller's wife he knew.

That woman left her husband and wed Louvet in 1793. His next novel dealt with the case for divorce. It also backed the marriage of priests, a hot topic then. All his work served the aims of the Revolution. He tried to stage a play of his at a Paris theatre. The entry follows his pen and his politics to his death in 1797.
britannica-1911-lycurgus-the-logothete:
Lycurgus, called the Logothete, was a Greek leader in the War of Independence. A life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his dates as 1772 to 1851. He was born on the isle of Samos and schooled at Constantinople. He took the set path of a Phanariot Greek in Turkish service.

He served two rulers of Walachia as secretary, treasurer, and chancellor in turn. Back on Samos from 1802, he fell under Turkish doubt and was jailed, then fled and was pardoned. When the war for freedom broke out, he led Samos to declare itself free and was made its ruler. His raid on Chios with too small a force brought a massacre on that isle in 1822. His own folk cast him down for that failure, though he rose again in part.
britannica-1911-magistrate:
Magistrate, from the Latin magistratus, first meant a public office, and then the man who holds it. In a broad sense it names a man set to run the law, or one with large power in law or rule. Men speak in this sense of the first magistrate of a king's realm, or the chief magistrate of the United States. In its more common use, though, the word fits lesser officers of the law.

Those lesser officers may be unpaid, as justices of the peace are, or paid, as stipendiary magistrates are. A paid magistrate is named in London under an act of 1839. He is named in boroughs under an act of 1882, and in some districts under an act of 1863 and special acts. In London and in boroughs he must be a barrister of at least seven years' standing.
britannica-1911-malachite:
Malachite is a copper ore of fine green hue, at times polished as a gem. Its stone entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name comes from the Greek word for mallow, a green leaf plant. Old writers may have classed it with other green stones they named loosely.

The stone is a basic copper carbonate formed by weather on copper ores. It is found in the upper parts of ore beds, oft as a crust. It can take the shape of the stone it replaced in the ground. Most masses are lumpy, stalk like, or fibrous, not fine crystals at all. Rare small dark green crystals of a slanted form do occur at times.
britannica-1911-mallarme-francois-rene-a:
François René Auguste Mallarmé, who lived from 1755 to 1835, was a French revolutionary born at Nancy. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the twenty-fifth of February 1755, the son of a lawyer. He was raised for the law and held a district post at Pont-à-Mousson. In the Revolution he was sent by Meurthe to the Assembly and then to the Convention. There he joined the Mountain and voted for the death of Louis the Sixteenth.

Mallarmé led the Convention on the thirtieth of May 1793. His weakness the next day much aided the rising that cast out the Girondists. On mission in Meuse and Moselle he won a grim name. He had girls at Verdun put to death for giving flowers to Prussian troops. After the fall of Robespierre he changed sides with the Thermidorians.
britannica-1911-manganite:
Manganite is a mineral formed of manganese oxide joined with water. The 1911 Britannica article says its crystals grow as prisms with deep lines along their length. They often bunch in bundles. The colour runs from dark steel grey to iron black, with a bright, near-metal shine. Its streak is a dark red-brown. The stone is soft for a metal ore, and it splits cleanly in one plane.

In acid the mineral dissolves and gives off chlorine gas. The best crystals come from Ilfeld in the Harz, where it lies with calcite in veins through porphyry. Other finds are named in Thuringia, Alsace, Scotland, and Michigan. As an ore of manganese it is far less rich than pyrolusite. Its name was given by Haidinger in 1827. French writers call it by a Greek-based name that means unprofitable, since it serves poorly for bleaching.
britannica-1911-marie-antoinette:
Marie Antoinette was queen of France, ninth child of a great empress and her husband the emperor. Born at Vienna, she was raised under a plain and strict rule. Her schooling was shaped with one end in view: a French match planned by her mother, and a tutor was set over her for that task.

Her wedding to the heir of France at Versailles was meant to crown a grand plan of state. It was to bind Austria and France in a firm pact. That aim, her youth, and the deep rot of the French court made her place a hard one, the 1911 Britannica entry says. A royal mistress with full sway over the old king led a strong cabal at court. In less than a year that cabal felled the chief minister and shook the pact.
britannica-1911-marie-galante:
Marie Galante, an island in the French West Indies, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies sixteen miles south-east of Guadeloupe, of which it is a dependency. The island is nearly circular and covers 55 square miles. A rocky limestone plateau fills its centre, rising in the east to 675 feet. From that height the land falls in wooded terraces to the sea.

The shores are rocky, and there are no harbours. The roadstead off Grand Bourg is hard to reach because of reefs. The climate is healthy and the soil rich, with sugar, coffee, and cotton the chief products. Grand Bourg is the largest town. Columbus discovered the island in 1493 and named it for his ship. French settlers came in 1648 and suffered attacks from the Dutch and British. Since 1766 France has held the island almost without break.
britannica-1911-marquette:
Marquette, a city and port in Michigan in the United States, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the seat of Marquette county, on the south shore of Lake Superior. The census of 1910 counted eleven thousand five hundred people. The city stands on a bluff a hundred feet above the lake, amid rounded hills.

Its fine air makes it a loved summer resort, and a large park crowns a headland to the north. Marquette is best known as the shipping hub of a rich iron-ore district. Great ore docks line its front, and trade through the port runs to millions of dollars a year. Foundries, rail shops, and stone quarries add to its work. The town took the name of Jacques Marquette, and became a city in 1871.
britannica-1911-massillon-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Massillon, a French bishop and preacher, was born at Hyeres in sixteen sixty three. His father was a royal notary of that town. At eighteen he joined the Congregation of the Oratory and taught in its colleges. In sixteen ninety three he was asked to preach a funeral oration. That speech was the start of his fame as a preacher.

Massillon left a quiet abbey to head a famed seminary in Paris. He soon won a wide name and preached at the court of Versailles in sixteen ninety nine. He became bishop of Clermont in seventeen seventeen. Two years later he joined the French Academy. In his own age his fame matched that of Bossuet. His sermons stress conduct more than points of dogma.
britannica-1911-matriarchate:
Matriarchate, meaning rule of the mother, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The term names a supposed early and low form of family life in primitive societies. On this theory, the child's father was unknown. The mother therefore came before the father in key respects. Descent and inheritance ran through her line.

The theory holds that this order was once universal in prehistoric times. It did not give women personal power, the article stresses. They were treated as mere chattels, yet they were the sole known relatives of their children. The custom of tracing descent through the female still survives in places. The article cites Fiji, the Bechuana, Senegal, and the Tuareg as cases. A short bibliography points readers to works by McLennan, Bachofen, and Westermarck.
britannica-1911-meissen-margraviate:
Meissen is a German margraviate treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its lands are now merged in the kingdom of Saxony. The mark centred on the castle of Meissen on the Middle Elbe. King Henry the Fowler built that castle about the year 920.

It was raised as a defence against the Slavs of the east. In 965 the eastern mark was split, and Meissen stood as one of five. The emperor Otto the Third gave the margrave's office to Ekkard in 985. His brother and sons held the mark after him and widened its bounds. When the second Ekkard died in 1046, the mark was divided anew. Counts of Weimar and Brunswick held Meissen in turn thereafter. In 1089 the mark passed to Henry of Wettin. His house later gave Saxony its kings.
britannica-1911-melaconite:
Melaconite is a mineral made of cupric oxide, also known as black copper ore, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes it. It looks strikingly unlike cuprite, the red copper ore, which is cuprous oxide. Crystals of melaconite are rare and take the form of thin triangular or six-sided scales.

More often the mineral comes as a dull iron-black mass, earthy or powdery to the touch. Its name comes from Greek words for black and dust, given by Beudant in 1832. The crystallised kind from Vesuvius was later named tenorite, a name now in common use for the species. The crystals soil the fingers easily. They have been found only at Vesuvius, where they coat lava, and in Cornwall. The commoner forms occur in copper mines as a coating on other copper ores.
britannica-1911-mesquite:
Mesquite, a tree of dry lands, is explained in a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is native to the southern United States and ranges south through Mexico to Chile. It can reach forty or fifty feet in height, with a short trunk and a loose head of crooked branches.

Its great trait is a main root that dives deep in search of water. That root lets the tree live where no other woody plant can grow. Its size above ground hints at how deep the water lies below. Where water sits within fifty feet, the plant grows as a tree. Where roots must go past sixty feet, the stems stand just two or three feet high. The heavy wood lasts near for ever in soil and serves for fence posts. Sweet pods give food to local people.
britannica-1911-mignonette:
Mignonette, a small garden bloom loved for its scent, is the topic of a plant entry in the 1911 Britannica. Its French name means little darling in that tongue. Cowper called it a fragrant weed in his verse of the day. The plant grows low and spread out, scarce a foot in height. Soft green leaves clothe its twiggy stems in a dense mass.

Spikes of small blooms cap the ends of its many branch tips. Those blooms are plain and easy to pass by eye at first look. Their scent in the air betrays them at once to the nose. The plant may spring from North Africa in the wild state. Seed came to England from Paris in seventeen forty two. New garden forms grow more stout with bolder bloom heads.
britannica-1911-minute:
Minute is a word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sorts out the split senses and sounds of one short English word. As one word it means very small, or keen and exact in detail. As a noun it names the short written note of what a meeting did.

The entry adds the use for a state memo that gives leave for a step. The same word names a sixtieth part of an hour of time. It also names a sixtieth part of a degree in the measure of a circle. That use came from star men of Babylon by way of Greek texts. Latin phrases for first and second small parts gave us both words.
britannica-1911-molinier-auguste:
Auguste Molinier, a French historian who lived from 1851 to 1904, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Toulouse in September 1851. He trained at the school of charters in Paris and left it in 1873. Posts followed in great libraries, at the Mazarine, at Fontainebleau, and at St Genevieve, where he became librarian in 1885.

Molinier knew old handwriting well and had a deep grasp of archives and manuscripts. He soon took a first place among scholars of medieval France. His leaving thesis listed the acts of Simon and Amauri de Montfort, a key help for the tale of the Albigenses. He then led a new edition of the great history of Languedoc, with notes on feudal rule and on the land in the middle ages. He also edited chronicles and pilgrim routes for learned bodies.
britannica-1911-monazite:
Monazite is a mineral made of a dry phosphate of the cerium metals, with small amounts of thorium and yttrium. The thorium share runs from one to ten per cent. The mineral has real trade worth as a source of thoria. Thoria is used to make the Welsbach and other mantles for gas lights that glow. The cerium in monazite is also used, to a small degree, in pharmacy.

The article gives tests of monazite from three places: Burke county in North Carolina, Arendal in Norway, and Emmaville in New South Wales. The tests list the shares of phosphorus, cerium, lanthanum, and other parts in each sample. The weights come out near five times that of water. The text notes that thoria and silica are often present in equal parts by weight of their units.
britannica-1911-monzonite:
Monzonite is a group name for a kind of igneous rock. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the name from Monzoni in Tirol. The rocks look like granite and run dark grey in color. Their grain runs from fine to fairly coarse in most samples.

Two feldspars in near equal shares mark the group apart. Granites and syenites lack that even split of the pair. Crystals of one kind sit inside large plates of the other. Quartz is scarce, though a quartz bearing branch exists. Green augite and bronze mica plates fill much of the mass. White flecks of apatite and dark ores dot thin slices. The Tirol rocks vary much from face to face. Chemists place the group midway between acid and basic rocks.
britannica-1911-muscovite:
Muscovite is a rock forming mineral of the mica group, and a mineral entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its nature and name. It is also known as potash mica, a compound of potassium, hydrogen, and aluminium. As the common white mica, it can be split into thin clear sheets of large size. Such sheets were once used in Russia for window panes.

From that Russian use came the name Muscovy glass for the mineral. The name Muscovite itself was proposed by Dana in 1850. The mineral forms crystals in the monoclinic system. Well shaped crystals are rare, and they take the form of rough six sided prisms or plates. Thin scales with no clear crystal outline are far more common. Its most marked trait is a perfect cleavage along the base plane.
britannica-1911-mysore-state:
Mysore is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a native state in the south of India, ringed by British ruled land. The state splits into two zones of marked contrast in look and life. Hill country in the west bears one name, and open plains bear another.

The entry maps three great river systems that drain the state to one bay. No river there can bear boats, but dams turn flow to farm use. Huge earth dams hold back water to feed long ditch lines. Hill streams are banked at each good spot to form chains of tanks. One tank spills its excess down to fill the next in line.
britannica-1911-napoleonite:
Napoleonite is a type of rock also called corsite, after the isle of Corsica where it is found. The 1911 Britannica entry treats it as a form of diorite with a rare round build. Its grey base looks like plain diorite at first glance. Set in that base are round lumps one or two inches wide.

Each lump shows rings of light and dark bands in neat zones. Crystals fan out from the core in a clear star-like plan. The pale parts are rich in feldspar, while dark parts hold hornblende and pyroxene. Cut and ground smooth, the stone makes a fine trim piece for small goods.
britannica-1911-nazarite:
Nazarite, more rightly Nazirite, was the Hebrew name for a special kind of devotee, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The marks of such a person were unshorn hair and no wine. Full rules for the vow are given in the book of Numbers. Every product of the grape vine is barred there.

The person must also not go near a dead body, even that of a close kin. The law in its present form came late, the entry says, and set rules for a known custom. It treats the vow as lasting for a set time only. It gives rites for a vow broken by chance taint, and a closing rite. At the end the person cuts off his hair and burns it on the altar, then returns to common life.
britannica-1911-note:
Note, a word from the Latin nota, meaning a mark or sign, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. In music, a note is the sign that stands for a sound in written form. The word also names a short memo on papers or speeches. That use seems to have begun in law, in land transfer work.

The piece gives much space to notes between states. In that field a note is more formal than a letter, not less. Such notes pass between envoys and foreign ministers on weighty points. At times a mere swap of notes has the force of a pact. The text sets out joint, same form, and round robin types.
britannica-1911-novelli-ermete:
Ermete Novelli, an Italian actor and playwright born in Lucca in March 1851, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the son of a prompter. He first appeared on stage in 1866. Between 1871 and 1884 he played character and leading comedy parts in the best companies. By 1885 he had a company of his own.

Novelli won great success in Paris in 1898 and again in 1902. In 1900 he set up a new theatre in Rome, the Casa di Goldoni. It was modelled on the Comédie Française. He turned Gaboriau's Monsieur Lecoq into a play for the stage. Alone and with others, he wrote several comedies and many monologues. Readers get a short, factual sketch of a leading Italian stage figure of his day.
britannica-1911-omelette:
Omelette, at times written omelet in English, is a French word whose past is traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its tale shows the odd changes a word can take. The root is a Latin word for a small plate. That became a French word for a thin plate, and a wrong split of the phrase reshaped it step by step.

Later forms slid through shifts of sound to the word seen in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The first sense seems to be a pancake of thin flat shape. Omelettes are made with eggs beaten up lightly. Milk, flour, herbs, cheese, or mushrooms may go in as the cook needs. They are cooked fast in a buttered pan and served at once.
britannica-1911-onteniente:
Onteniente, a town of eastern Spain in the province of Valencia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the right bank of the Clariano river, a small stream that feeds the Júcar. A rail line from Játiva to Villena serves the town. The count in 1900 was 11430 people.

A parish church there stands out for its tall square tower. A palace of the dukes of Almodovar adds a second mark. A large modern suburb spreads outside the old town, which was once walled. Traces of those ramparts can still be seen in places. Local hands make linen and woollen cloth, paper, brandy, furniture, and earthenware. Trade in grain, wine, and oil fills out the work of the town.
britannica-1911-ordinate:
Ordinate is the subject of a short maths article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The hosted text opens with the tail of the article on the word ordinary in church and civil law. It then turns to the maths term itself. In the system of co-ordinates set out by Descartes, the ordinate names one distance for a point.

The article defines the ordinate as the distance of a point from the flat axis. That distance is measured in line with the upright axis. A diagram in the text shows a point and its ordinate as a drawn line. The word, the text notes, was first used by Rene Descartes. Readers who need the term for geometry get a brief, exact sense of what it measures and how it is drawn.
britannica-1911-oubliette:
Oubliette, a French term from a word for forget, names a hidden cell or pit in a castle or prison in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. One kind could be reached only by a trap door from a cell above it. The other kind was a secret shaft that led to the moat or river. Bodies of men meant to vanish could be dropped down that shaft.

Viollet le Duc drew one such pit at the castle of Pierrefonds in France. The entry warns that many so called oubliettes were in truth drains or waste outlets. Yet they may at times have served the grim use all the same.
britannica-1911-ozokerite:
Ozokerite, or ozocerite, is a mineral wax that can be called crude native paraffin, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short science entry. Its name joins Greek words for smell and for wax. The stuff burns, and it is found in many lands in varied purity, with finds named in Scotland, Northumberland and Wales and in some thirty countries in all.

The only sources of trade supply in the entry's day were in Galicia, at Boryslaw, Dzwiniacz and Starunia, on both flanks of the Carpathians. Such deposits are thought to form as petroleum slowly dries and sours in cracks, leaving its paraffin behind as a vein leaves its mineral. In the ground the wax ranges from very soft to as hard as gypsum. Its colour in Galicia runs from light yellow to dark brown, and it often looks green by the play of light.
britannica-1911-palette: Palette names the thin flat board on which painters lay and mix their paint. The 1911 Britannica note traces the word to French and Latin words for a spade or flat blade. Such boards may be made of wood, china ware, or like stock. The word also names the slotted box that holds the small stones for mosaic work. By extension it names the set of hues one painter tends to use. A thin bent knife for the board gets its own name in the note.
britannica-1911-pallavicino-ferrante:
Italian writer Ferrante Pallavicino, born at Piacenza in sixteen eighteen, is given a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from an old Italian family. He was well schooled at Padua and joined the Augustinian order young. He lived chiefly in Venice.

For a year he served as a field chaplain on campaign in Germany. Soon after his return he put out sharp satires on the Roman court. He also mocked the Barberini house, and Rome set a price on his head for it. A Frenchman lured him from Venice and betrayed him near Avignon. After fourteen months in prison he was beheaded there in sixteen forty four. His tamer works came out after his death.
britannica-1911-papeete:
Papeete is the capital of Tahiti in the Pacific and the chief port of the French lands in Oceania. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 4,280 people, of whom 2,500 were French. The town stands on the north-west coast of the island. A reef guards its harbour, with two gaps for ships to pass. Five mountains rise behind the town.

The entry walks through what a visitor would see. The richer parts look French, with a cathedral, barracks, an arsenal, and public offices. A botanic garden is also named. The Chinese quarter and the native market stand in sharp contrast to the settler streets. Of the two harbour gaps, the Papeete one runs about seven fathoms deep. The Taunoa gap is wider but not as deep.
britannica-1911-para-state:
Para, or Grao Para, a northern state of Brazil, is the subject of a regional entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the third largest state of the republic, with an area of 443,922 square miles. The entry gives it 445,356 people in 1900. The three Guianas and the Atlantic bound it on the north, and Amazonas on the west.

The Amazon valley finds its outlet to the ocean through the centre of the state. North of the river lies the Guiana plateau, dry in parts behind its frontier ranges. South of it the land rises in forested terraces toward the great central plateau of Brazil. Save for the Guiana highlands and some grassy plains, the state is densely forested. Its low levels are webbed with rivers, lakes, and linking channels. The Amazon itself crosses the state for about five hundred miles.
britannica-1911-parisite:
Parisite is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a rare stone with a mixed build. It holds rare earth parts with lime in a salt form. It is found in crystals alone, of a six sided form. Most take the shape of sharp twin peaks capped by flat ends.

The faces of the peaks are lined across. A clean split runs flat through the stone. The hue is hair brown, and light can pass through it. Light that has crossed a crystal shows a marked band of hues. That band is a sure test for the stone. For years the sole known source was a famed emerald mine at Muzo in Colombia. A man named Paris found that mine in the early last age. There the stone sits with emerald in dark rock.
britannica-1911-pegmatite:
Pegmatite, a rock name first used by Hauy for masses of graphic granite found in veins, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Such rock is made of quartz and alkali feldspars grown into each other as crystals. Naumann later used the name for coarse veins rich in quartz, feldspar, and muscovite. These veins branch through granite and the rocks around it.

Many pegmatites grow very coarse grains. Feldspar blocks can run to feet or even yards across. Rare minerals turn up in them in large amounts and in fine crystal form. The text stresses that their minerals were the last to part from the parent rock. That fact helps explain their rich and odd mix.
britannica-1911-peridotite:
Peridotite is the subject of a rock entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a deep formed rock made in large part of olivine, with little or no feldspar. Such rocks are the most basic of their class, with much iron oxide and magnesia in them. That makeup gives them dark colours and high weight for their size.

They weather with ease and are changed into serpentine, the entry explains. In that change water is taken up and joins with the minerals inside. In some forms, called dunites, olivine far outweighs all other minerals. It appears in small rounded grains without good crystal form. The entry is for readers with training in geology.
britannica-1911-perlite:
Perlite is the subject of a rock entry in the 1911 Britannica. Perlite, or pearlstone, is a glassy volcanic rock. When struck with a hammer it breaks in round bits. Those bits oft show a pearly shine on their faces. Thin slices under the lens show why it breaks so. Small cracks run through the glassy stuff in curves. Those cracks oft form rings one inside the next. The rings bound the small spheres the rock falls in.

Pearly shine comes from light bounced off air films. Long straight cracks cut across the ring groups. Decay can fill those cracks with rust like stuff. That fill makes the cracks stand out to the eye. The glass can turn dull and fine grained on cracks. In split light the glass shows no hue shift as rule. A kind of opal shows the same ring crack form.
britannica-1911-perovskite:
Perovskite is a mineral article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a stone made of calcium titanate. A small share of the calcium is most often swapped for iron. In layered rocks its crystals take the form of cubes, at times trimmed at the edges and corners by many small faces. In eruptive rocks the crystals are eight-sided and tiny.

Though cube-shaped, the crystals bend light in two ways, so the article calls them pseudo-cubic. Their look under polarised light is much like that of boracite, and they show signs of complex twinning. The colour runs from pale yellow to blackish brown, and the crystals range from clear to opaque. The piece gives a high light-bending index, a hardness of about five and a half, and a weight four times that of water.
britannica-1911-perquisite:
Perquisite is a word of law and office use explained in a note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes from a Latin word for a thing gained by careful search. In strict use it names the gains that come to the holder of an office over and above the set pay of the post.

In law it names chance gains, such as heriots, fines, and reliefs, that fall to a lord of a manor above the yearly rent of his copyholds. In loose use it names the small chance gains that custom lets servants keep. These are goods the master has used or no longer needs.
britannica-1911-petalite:
Petalite, a mineral species made of lithium, aluminium, and silica, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its crystals in form come close to those of spodumene, a kindred mineral of like make up. It splits with ease along one flat plane in the stone. For the most part it occurs in flat splitting masses, not in lone crystals.

That flat habit gave it its name, from a Greek word for a leaf. The stone is colourless or at times reddish in tint. It ranges from clear to cloudy in its passage of light, with a glassy shine.
