It was first found in 1800 as splitting masses in an iron mine on the island of Utö. That isle lies in the Stockholm archipelago in Sweden. A clear glassy kind called castor turns up in granite holes on Elba.
britannica-1911-pharmacosiderite:
Pharmacosiderite is a mineral made of iron, arsenic, oxygen, and water, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. Its crystals take the form of small, sharp cubes of an olive or grass green hue. For its cubic form it was early known as cube ore in English and in German.

Hausmann gave it its present name in 1813, from Greek words for arsenic and for iron. The faces of its cubes are lined in line with one diagonal, the text notes. A strange trait is that a crystal placed in ammonia turns from green to red in minutes. Placed in dilute acid, the red crystal turns green once more in the test. The mineral is of secondary origin and is found on quartz in the upper parts of copper veins.
britannica-1911-phillipsite:
Phillipsite is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a stone of the zeolite group. It is a wet mix of potash, lime, and other earth parts, the text says. Its make-up shifts a bit from case to case. One kind with less silica goes by a like name.

The stones form cross-shaped twin shapes of some complexity. They are most times smaller and more glassy than those of harmotome. Round groups with a fibrous build are also common finds. The kind was set up by Levy in 1825 and named for William Phillips. It forms in the hollow spots of volcanic rock. The Giant's Causeway and Rome are two spots named.
britannica-1911-phyllite:
Phyllite is a group of rocks formed from clay rich sediments changed by heat and pressure, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines the group. The Greek name comes from a word for leaf, since the rocks split into leaf like plates. In most cases phyllites are altered clays or shales. They consist chiefly of quartz, chlorite, and muscovite.

Phyllites show a strong parallel grain, known as schistosity. They stand midway in a series of changed clay deposits. Clay slates lie on one side of them, and mica schists on the other. Slates share much the same makeup but are finer grained. Slates also split far more cleanly. In phyllites, white mica is more common than in slate, and its crystal plates grow larger. The entry helps readers place a common rock in its family.
britannica-1911-picrite:
Picrite is a dark rock rich in the base called magnesia. The 1911 Britannica entry takes its name from a Greek word for bitter. Bitter salts form from that base, which explains the odd name. The rock is made chiefly of olivine and of augite in bulk. Hornblende, biotite, and feldspar may join the mix in smaller shares.

In the ground these rocks lie with dolerites and kin rocks. They form in sheets or sills thrust between older beds of stone. In the hand they look dark green to black at first sight. Much olivine makes them rot fast when air and rain strike them. They turn deep green and brown as they break down in place.
britannica-1911-plebiscite: Plebiscite is a vote of all electors in a country on one set question, a term borrowed from the French. Its entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the best known French case as the vote of eighteen fifty two. That vote confirmed the coup of eighteen fifty one and made Napoleon the Third emperor. In Roman law a plebiscitum was a decree passed in the assembly of the plebs, led by a plebeian magistrate in that body.
britannica-1911-prehnite:
Prehnite, a mineral made of calcium, hydrogen, aluminium, and silica, is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It forms crystals that are flat in shape, yet they seldom stand alone and distinct. They pack close in barrel shaped or round groups with a sparkling surface. That form, with a pale oil green colour, makes the mineral easy to know.

Prehnite lets light pass and shines like glass, with a hardness a bit over six. It is classed at times with the zeolites, since it occurs where they do. Its small share of water leaves only at a red heat, so it is not water of crystallisation. The mineral fills hollow spots in basalt and like rocks as a later growth. Fine pieces come from Scotland, New Jersey, and the Lake Superior copper country.
britannica-1911-protectorate:
Protectorate, a tie between two states in which one holds sway over the other, is the subject of a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The control may be great or small, plain or veiled. The word itself is new in this sense, the entry notes. The thing it names is as old as power.

Strong states have long ruled weak ones while still calling them free. Such a cloak grants power with less cost and less blame than plain seizure. The league held by Athens about 467 before Christ is given as an early case. States called allies in name had to bring their great suits to Athens. Rome too draped its rule in soft words, such as client and free city. The piece gathers cases from all ages.
britannica-1911-pyrargyrite:
Pyrargyrite is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a stone made of silver in a salt form. It is known as dark red silver ore. It is a key source of the white metal. A close kin stone holds the same build with a swap of one part. That kin is called light red silver ore.

Both stones were named as red silver ore by a great old writer in fifteen forty six. For long they were held as one kind. Fine tests of both in eighteen hundred and four split them for good. Both form crystals of the same class and the same grade of matched form. That class is the one seen in the gem tourmaline. The crystals are most times full and clean in shape, in prism form.
britannica-1911-pyromorphite:
Pyromorphite is a mineral made of lead, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At times it is found in such bulk that men mine it as an ore of lead. Its crystals most often form six-sided prisms with flat ends. Some crystals curve like small barrels, and round lumpy masses also occur.

The stone is a close twin of apatite and of mimetite in form. It is so like mimetite to the eye that only tests in the lab can tell the two apart. Old names for the pair were green lead ore and brown lead ore. Its hues run to bright shades of green, yellow, or brown, with a resin-like shine. The name joins Greek words for fire and form. A fused chip takes a faceted shape as it cools and sets.
britannica-1911-pyroxenite:
Pyroxenite is the subject of a rock article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pyroxenite is a rock made chiefly of minerals of the pyroxene group. Named kinds rest on which mineral leads, such as augite or bronzite. A close kin group is made chiefly of hornblende. A Greek based name for the whole dark series is also given.

The article says these rocks come in most cases from melted rock. Some forms sit in very old rock masses in Scotland. They are kin to gabbros, from which they differ by lacking felspar. They also sit close to rocks that hold olivine. In the field they most often occur with masses of gabbro and kindred rocks. They form thick veins or patches inside those masses. Sites in Shetland, America, New Zealand, and Saxony are named. In time the rocks can decay into serpentine.
britannica-1911-rate:
Rate is a broad term for a share, a standard, a grant, or a tax. The 1911 Britannica article notes that in England the word names the levy of funds for local ends. Such funds stand apart from taxes raised for the needs of the state. Local rule is paid for by charges on lands and houses, based on their yearly letting worth. The local board works out what sum beyond its income it needs, and levies a rate to meet it.

The first rate in England was that for poor relief. Most rates since rest on the poor rate and are levied with it. The highway rate came next. Later acts added rates for police, schools, lights, burial grounds, and more. The parish list of values forms the base for the charge. That list gives the gross rent a place might fetch, less the cost of repairs and dues.
britannica-1911-regnault-de-saint-jean-d:
Michel Louis Étienne Regnault de Saint Jean d’Angély (1761–1819) was a French politician, and his rise in the Revolution opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Saint Fargeau on the third of December 1761. Before the Revolution he was a lawyer in Paris. He also held a post in the naval provostship of Rochefort.

In 1789 the Third Estate of Saint Jean d’Angély sent him to the States General. His eloquence made him a marked figure in the Constituent Assembly. He boldly attacked Mirabeau in debate there. He also settled the dispute over the ashes of Voltaire, by a decree that they belonged to the nation. At the time of the king’s flight to Varennes, his proposals showed a marked moderation.
britannica-1911-renaudot-theophraste:
Théophraste Renaudot (1586–1653) was a French physician and philanthropist, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells of his work for the poor. He was born at Loudun and studied surgery in Paris. At only nineteen he took his doctor degree at Montpellier, it seems by favour. After a time of travel he began to practise in his native town.

In 1612 Richelieu called Renaudot to Paris. The call rested more on his charity work than on his medical fame. He was made physician and councillor to the king. He was asked to set up a scheme of public assistance for the poor. Many blocks were put in his way by rivals. He went back to Poitou until 1624, as commissary general of the poor. Six years passed before he could begin his Paris work in earnest.
britannica-1911-retinite: Retinite is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a class of fossil resins. The name comes from the Greek word for resin itself. The term covers resins dug most often from beds of brown coal. They look much like amber at first glance. Yet they hold little or none of the acid found in true amber. The broad name serves a use, since no two finds prove quite alike.
britannica-1911-rhodochrosite:
Rhodochrosite is a mineral article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rhodochrosite is a mineral made of manganese carbonate. It crystallizes in the same system as calcite and shares its form. True crystals are somewhat rare; it is found more often in solid or rounded masses.

The entry gives the tests by which the mineral is known. When pure it holds a large share of manganese in its makeup. Iron often takes part of that place, and other metals appear in small amounts. Its hardness is rated at four, and its weight varies within set bounds. The colour is usually rose red, though it can shade to grey or brown. The name itself comes from Greek words for rose coloured. Manganese-spar and dialogite are given as other names. The article serves collectors who need a stone's clear marks.
britannica-1911-rhodonite:
Rhodonite, a mineral of the pyroxene group, is the subject of a science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is made of a manganese compound and takes its name from the Greek word for a rose, after its rose-red colour. It most often occurs in masses that can be split or packed tight, though its crystals can form thick flat shapes. Iron and calcium often take the place of part of the manganese.

The article gives its hardness and weight and names two kinds, one rich in calcium and one that holds zinc. The stone is prone to change, forming dark veins and patches as it breaks down. Those black marks can strike the eye in the compact stone, which is cut and polished for ornament. In the Urals, good coloured stone was dug in large amounts from clay-slate ground.
britannica-1911-richards-alfred-bate:
Alfred Bate Richards (1826-1876) was an English journalist born in Worcestershire. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his schooling at Westminster and at Oxford. His first book, Oxford Unmasked, attacked abuses at the university in plain terms. Dramas and poems followed before he turned to army papers in 1848.

Strong imperial views marked his writing throughout his career. He foresaw a Canadian Pacific railway decades before it was built. In 1855 he became first editor of the London Daily Telegraph. He pushed hard for volunteer rifle corps in its pages as well. A corps of one thousand working men in London took him as colonel.
britannica-1911-rodin-auguste:
Auguste Rodin, a French sculptor born in 1840, is profiled as a living artist in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Paris and showed a taste for his art early. He went first to the classes of Barye, but did not fall too far under his sway. From 1864 to 1870 need drove him to work for Carrier-Belleuse.

There he learned to master the hard craft side of sculpture. His own bent showed as early as 1864 in his Man with a Broken Nose. After the war he found no work in Paris and went to Brussels for six years. In 1877 his Bronze Age went to the Salon, and in bronze in 1880 it won a medal and was bought by the state. From that time he gave himself in chief to a vast work, the Portal of Hell, drawn from the Inferno of Dante.
britannica-1911-roederer-pierre-louis-co:
Pierre Louis Roederer (1754–1835) was a French politician and economist, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his early work. He was born at Metz on the fifteenth of February 1754, the son of a magistrate. At twenty five he became a councillor at the parlement of Metz. In 1787 he was asked to draw up a list of remonstrances for that body.

That same year Roederer published a treatise against internal customs houses. The work set out at length the laws of commerce and the theory of customs duties. In 1788 his pamphlet on deputation to the states general won wide notice. It stated liberal principles with bold force. On the strength of it, the Third Estate of Metz chose him as a deputy. His path into the politics of the Revolution was thus set.
britannica-1911-roulette: Roulette, a term in mathematics, is defined in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. A roulette is the path traced by a point on a curve. The curve rolls along another curve that stays fixed. Pascal used the name for the cycloid, the simplest case. A cycloid is traced by a point on a circle rolling on a straight line. The trochoids and epicycloids are also simple roulettes. The entry points readers to a book on roulettes and glissettes.
britannica-1911-sabatier-louis-auguste:
Sabatier, Louis Auguste, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French church thinker. Born at Vallon on the 22nd of October 1839, he read at Montauban. He also studied at Tubingen and Heidelberg in his youth. From 1864 to 1868 he held a pastor post at Aubenas.

He then took a chair in church teaching at Strassburg in France. His strong French feelings in the war of 1870 got him expelled in 1872. After five years of work he set up a church faculty in Paris. He rose there to the post of dean of the faculty. His chief books are named, led by a work on the Apostle Paul. A late work on faith and the spirit came out after his death.
britannica-1911-san-vicente:
San Vicente, the capital of the department of San Vicente in Salvador, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 30 miles east of San Salvador on the river Acahuapa. That river is a left-hand tributary of the Lempa. The city's people numbered about 18,000 in 1905. It sits in a volcanic region rich in hot springs and geysers.

The volcano of San Vicente, the highest in the department, rises above 7,000 feet. Indigo and tobacco plantations surround the city. Its commerce is considerable, and much of it passes at the All Saints' fair each November. Local making includes shoes, hats, cloth, silk, spirits, and cigars. The city was founded in 1634 on the site of Tehuacan, an old Indian city. For one year, 1839 to 1840, it was the capital of the republic.
britannica-1911-scolecite:
Scolecite is a mineral of the zeolite group in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In chemical terms it is a hydrated silicate of calcium. It ranks as a lime zeolite beside natrolite and mesolite. It usually occurs as needle-like crystals massed in fibrous bundles.

Its crystal faces meet at angles near those of natrolite, yet the systems differ. An optical test parts them, since scolecite crystals do not darken evenly lengthwise. The mineral is colourless or white, clear, and glassy in lustre. It forms as a secondary mineral in old volcanic rocks. There it fills the hollow bubbles of weathered basic lavas. Fine spreading groups of its prisms come from Iceland and from India. The name is Greek for a worm, the article explains. Its crystals sometimes curl like worms when heated before the blowpipe.
britannica-1911-scrutin-de-liste: Scrutin de Liste is a brief term article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French way of electing national deputies. Under this system the voters of a whole department vote for all the deputies to be chosen in that department, much like the general ticket in the United States. The article sets it against the scrutin d'arrondissement, under which voters in each small district choose only the single deputy for that district. For more, the entry points the reader to the article on representation.
britannica-1911-senate:
Senate is defined and traced in an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Latin senatus, from a root tied to age, as in senex, old. In plain terms it first meant a gathering of old men, the heads of the chief families. From there it came to mean the upper council in a state.

The entry sorts out close but unlike bodies. It links the Greek gerousia at Sparta to the same thought. It warns that the council set up by Cleisthenes at Athens was a wholly different body. The word fits first the great council of Rome. It is then used for the second house in France, Italy, and the United States. The piece is a firm base for study of how states are ruled.
britannica-1911-sheffield-plate:
Sheffield plate is copper coated with silver for table and house ware. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how the craft was found by chance. The process is now dead, but the goods still bear the town name. Much of the ware was in fact made in Birmingham.

In 1742 a workman overheated a knife handle of mixed metals. The silver fused and clung to the copper as a skin. Thomas Bolsover saw the trade value in that mishap at once. His ware looked like silver but cost less and wore stronger. He stuck to small goods such as snuff boxes at first. Joseph Hancock then made the plate first and shaped it after. That one shift opened the craft to goods of every size.
britannica-1911-sillimanite:
Sillimanite is a rock-forming mineral, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is made of aluminium silicate, the same mix as cyanite and andalusite. Yet it parts from those two in crystal form and in its traits to eye and hand. Its crystals grow as long slim needles with no end faces.

The needles often pack in fibrous or dense masses, which gives the stone its other name, fibrolite. The name sillimanite honors Benjamin Silliman the elder. Its color runs from greyish white to brown, with a glass-like shine. It splits clean in one plane along the length of the needles. The stone is a mark of gneiss and of schist rocks. Old tools of the dense form are found in west Europe, much like tools of jade.
britannica-1911-smaltite:
Smaltite is a mineral made of cobalt and arsenic, and the 1911 Britannica entry sets out its basic traits in a few short lines. It forms in the cubic system, most often as cubes or mixed cube forms, though good crystals are rare. More often it is found in dense or grainy masses, white to grey in tone, with a bright metal shine and a dark grey streak.

The entry also gives its hardness and weight, and notes that iron and nickel can take the place of some of the cobalt. As nickel grows, the mineral grades into a close kin form. It turns up in veins with ores of cobalt, nickel, copper, and silver, and its name comes from smalt, the blue color it helped make for glass and fine ware.
britannica-1911-sonsonate:
Sonsonate, the capital of the department of the same name in Salvador, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Sensunapan and on the rail line from San Salvador to the Pacific port of Acajutla, thirteen miles south. Its people numbered about 17,000 in 1905.

The article calls it the centre of a rich farming district and one of the busiest factory towns in the republic. Its workshops turned out cotton cloth, pottery, mats and baskets, boots and shoes, sugar, starch, cigars, and spirits. Through the port it sent out coffee and sugar. Grain came in through the same port for sharing out to all parts of the interior. Short as the entry is, it gives the town's trade in full.
britannica-1911-soracte:
Soracte is a 1911 Britannica article on a mountain in the province of Rome, Italy. It is a narrow, isolated ridge of limestone. It lies south-east of Civita Castellana. Its length is about three and a half miles. The highest summit stands 2,267 feet above sea level.

Just below the summit stands a monastery. It was moved there from the top in 1835. It was founded about the year 748 by Carloman, son of Charles Martel. The altar holds fragments of carved work from that early period. Until modern times, Trinitarian monks occupied the house. On the actual summit stands a church. From its lonely place, the mountain commands a magnificent view. Soracte is a striking object in the landscape. It can be seen from Rome itself. Horace names it in verse, white with high snow. Virgil names it too, as the article goes on to show.
britannica-1911-southgate:
Southgate is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town district in Middlesex, England. It lies nine miles north of Saint Paul's Cathedral in London, on the Great Northern railway line. In 1901 it held 14,993 people.

The article paints a leafy outer suburb of the capital. Christ Church, built in Early English style, was the work of Sir Gilbert Scott. Its stained glass came from designs by Sir Edward Burne-Jones and Dante Gabriel Rossetti. Near New Southgate station stood the Colney Hatch asylum for the county of London. That large hospital for the insane opened in 1851 and grew much larger in later years.
britannica-1911-southworth-emma-dorothy-:
Emma Dorothy Eliza Nevitte Southworth (1819-1899) was an American novelist, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives her life and output. She was born in Washington on the day after Christmas and studied in a school kept by her stepfather. In 1840 she married Frederick Southworth of Utica. After 1843 she kept herself by teaching, and her first story appeared in a Baltimore paper.

Her first novel, Retribution, ran as a serial and came out in book form in 1846. It was so well taken that she gave up teaching and wrote steadily for the periodicals, above all for the New York Ledger. Her novels ran to more than sixty in number. Some were translated into German, French, and Spanish. The entry lists titles from The Deserted Wife of 1850 onward.
britannica-1911-staurolite:
Staurolite is a mineral made of aluminium, iron, and silica, found in dark red-brown crystals. The 1911 Britannica article notes that the crystals are most often impure. They can hold as much as thirty or forty parts in a hundred of quartz and other matter. The crystals take the form of six-sided prisms. Twinned pairs that cross each other are common and mark the stone at sight.

That cross shape gave the mineral its name, from Greek words for a cross and a stone. Old names for it meant stones of the cross in French. It looks much like garnet and has been called grenatite. Clear worn pebbles in Brazil are at times cut as gems. The stone is a mark of schist rocks and of rocks changed by heat. Fine twins occur in Brittany and in parts of the United States.
britannica-1911-sterling-antoinette:
Antoinette Sterling is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. She was an Anglo American singer who died in 1904. She was born at Sterlingville in New York state. She studied with three famed teachers of song. Two of those teachers bore the Garcia name. After two years of song in America she crossed the sea. In 1873 she came to England to sing. Her first show there was at Covent Garden.

She rose fast to favour among contraltos of the day. Her greatest wins came as a singer of ballads. Three songs that she made famed are named here. She was a woman of deep faith and zeal. Her name was oft linked to works of charity. She wed a husband in the year 1875. She died in January of the year 1904. Her son wrote the story of her life in 1906.
britannica-1911-stilbite:
Stilbite is a mineral article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a member of the zeolite group. The mineral is a hydrated calcium aluminium silicate, with a small share of the calcium often replaced by sodium. The colour is usually white, sometimes red, and the perfect cleavage has a strong pearly shine. That shine gave the mineral its name, from a Greek word meaning to shine, bestowed in 1796.

The article records the naming history and where the mineral occurs. After heulandite was split off in 1818, the name desmine was proposed, and German writers still use it. Fine finds include Iceland's volcanic rocks, pink crystals near Bombay and Poona, and brick-red crystals in Scotland.
britannica-1911-strontianite:
Strontianite, a mineral made of strontium carbonate, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It takes its name from Strontian in Argyllshire, where it seems to have been known as early as 1764. It was not seen as a distinct mineral until later. Study of it led to the discovery of the element strontium. It forms crystals in the orthorhombic system, akin to aragonite and witherite.

Well-formed crystals are rare, since the mineral more often grows in radiating, fibrous, or granular masses. Its colour is white, pale green, or yellowish brown. Calcium sometimes replaces part of the strontium. It occurs in metal-bearing veins in lead mines in Scotland, Yorkshire, and Saxony. It is also found in marl in Westphalia and in limestone in New York. Its uses include making red fire for fireworks and refining sugar.
britannica-1911-suite:
Suite, in music, is a group of dance tunes, most in twin form, of a fair and trim type. It forms the chief shape of tool music in the first years of the seventeen hundreds. It points the way to the form that came next. As Bach knew it, the set holds four main moves.

Light moves slip in past the third move and past the last. The first move is slow and rich in flow, with short notes past the first bar. The next has two kinds, French and from Italy, in twin pace. A slow third move, held as Bachs most plain and deep small works, comes next.
britannica-1911-syenite:
Syenite is a geology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pliny first used the name for rocks like the hornblende granite of Syene in Upper Egypt. That stone was widely used in ancient times for building work and monuments. Werner later gave the name to a like looking rock near Dresden.

Now, the entry says, syenite is the group name for a class of coarse grained deep rocks. They are made chiefly of an alkali feldspar and a dark iron bearing mineral. In the hand they look much like hornblende granite and are hard to tell from it. The key difference is that quartz is absent or scarce in syenites. The chief feldspar forms nearly half the rock and is often veined with a second kind.
britannica-1911-sylvanite:
Sylvanite is a 1911 Britannica article on a mineral that is a key ore of gold. Sylvanite is a telluride of gold and silver. Its crystals belong to the monoclinic system and are often rich in faces. They are often twinned, which gives branching forms like written characters.

From that look, the mineral was early known as graphic gold. It was also called white gold. Its colour is tin-white, with a bright metallic shine. The name sylvanite comes from Transylvania. There it occurs with native gold in veins through porphyry. Places named are Offenbánya and Nagyág, near Déva. It is also found at several places in Boulder county, Colorado. The text adds notes on its hardness and weight. Ore hunters get a gold mineral known at a glance by its script-like crystals.
britannica-1911-sylvite:
Sylvite is a mineral made of potassium chloride, first seen in 1823 as a crust on lava from Vesuvius. The 1911 Britannica article says fine crystals were later found in the salt beds of Stassfurt in Prussia. They were found as well at Kalusz in Austrian Galicia. The crystals grow in the cubic form and split cleanly along the cube faces. They look much like crystals of common salt, the piece notes.

Fine tests show a lower grade of symmetry than salt has. The crystals have no planes of symmetry, though they keep the full set of axes. They are colourless or at times bright blue, and clear to the eye. The stone is soft and light for a mineral. Like salt, it lets heat pass through it with ease. Its name comes from an old drug name for the salt, tied to the chemist Sylvius.
britannica-1911-syndicate:
Syndicate is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a word with use in both university and business life. At first it meant a body of syndics, or officers. At Cambridge it still names the body in charge of the University Press. In commerce, a syndicate is a body of persons who join to carry through a money deal or a shared venture.

Syndicates are often formed to buy or take over an undertaking, the entry explains. They hold it for a short time, then sell it on to a company. The profits are then split and the syndicate breaks up. Some syndicates rest on agreements that make them plain partnerships, with each member liable in person. More often in the entry's day, they were formed as companies under the law.
britannica-1911-taste:
Taste is the sense that responds to things dissolved in the mouth. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica locates the sense in the tongue. The word comes from Latin terms for touching sharply. By likeness it also names a feel for beauty in art.

Three kinds of feeling meet in the tongue, the entry says. Taste, touch, and warmth each have their own paths. The back of the tongue and its tip taste most keenly. The mid tongue and hard palate have no taste at all. Small flask shaped bodies in the skin do the tasting work. Two scholars found those taste bulbs in 1867. Nerves link the bulbs to the brain through named cords.
britannica-1911-tavernier-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Tavernier is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris in 1605, he was a French trader who helped open trade with India. His father and uncle were map makers and engravers from Antwerp.

The article follows his travels from boyhood on. By sixteen he had seen England, the Low Countries, and Germany. Years in Hungary and Italy gave him court polish and a taste for war. In 1631 he reached Constantinople and went on to Persia. Later trips took him to India, to the court of the Great Mogul, and to the diamond mines. He made six long trips in all, dealing in gems and fine goods for great princes.
britannica-1911-tergeste:
Tergeste is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an ancient city of Istria. It is the modern Trieste, at the head of the Adriatic Sea. Its port gave Pannonia and Dalmatia an outlet for their trade. That trade was the source of its weight, then as now.

The place is first named about the year 100 before Christ, as a village. Tribes from the inland hills attacked it some fifty years later. Augustus built a wall and towers there in his Dalmatian wars. In time it became a Roman colony with a wide tract of land. The church of San Giusto stands on the site of a Roman temple. Old carvings are built into its front wall.
britannica-1911-termite:
Termite is a zoology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Termites are a group of insects with four wings that grow outside the body. In many of them, though, no wings ever appear at all. The wings are near one size, long, narrow, and paper like. At rest they lie flat on the back, so only one wing shows.

After a short time the wings are shed, leaving small stumps, the entry says. The mouth bears strong jaws for biting. Termites were once classed with one order of insects and later moved by scholars. They now form an order with one small, obscure family, with about three hundred species known. The entry warns that the common name white ants misleads. Termites differ greatly from true ants and are rarely white.
britannica-1911-ternate:
Ternate is a small island in the Malay Archipelago, off Halmahera. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica shapes it as near round, some 25 square miles. A triple coned volcano of 5,400 feet makes up most of it. Blasts from that peak have often been destructive. The town of Ternate holds only 3,000 people. Its harbour is good, yet trade and shipping stay small.

The town heads a Dutch residency of vast reach. That residency covers island groups from Halmahera to New Guinea. Its whole area runs to 155,800 square miles. Some 108,415 people lived under it in 1905. Direct Dutch rule touches only a few islands. Elsewhere the sultans of Ternate and Tidore govern for the Dutch. The island's folk are Malay in race and Muslim in faith. Lost trade routes left the place a shadow of its past weight.
britannica-1911-terre-haute:
Terre Haute, a rail city of Indiana, is placed in a city entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands high on the east bank of the Wabash River. Chicago lies far north and Indianapolis east by rail from it. In 1910 its folk came to over fifty-eight thousand in count. Wide streets, paved and shaded by oaks and elms, mark the town.

The state normal school there dates from the year 1870. Its library held some fifty thousand books by the year 1909. Rose Polytechnic Institute, founded in 1874, stands in the city too. It teaches machine, power, civil, and chemical craft and building art. A school for girls at St Mary-of-the-Woods lies west of town. A gift library of thirty thousand books serves all readers.
britannica-1911-theralite:
Theralite, a rare group of rocks, is defined in a 1911 Britannica article on rock science. These rocks are made of nepheline, basic plagioclase, augite, and olivine. The name comes from a Greek word meaning to pursue. The group was sought for a long time to round out a set of basic rocks.

The text lists traits seen under close study. The feldspars tend to be basic and zoned, and the pyroxene may be green or brown with much titanium. Olivine is most often found in large amounts. Named sites span Bohemia, the White Sea, Madagascar, and Montana. A close group, the teschenites, is also noted near the end.
britannica-1911-thorianite:
Thorianite is a rare mineral found in the gem gravels of Ceylon. The 1911 Britannica entry names Holland as the man who found it first. It shows as small, heavy, black cubes, much worn by water in streams. Dunstan gave it its name for its great wealth of thorium in bulk. Near seventy parts in a hundred are oxide of thorium, it says.

Oxides of uranium and of rare earths join the mix as well. Helium gas is present in the stone, the entry notes with care. Its radio action is a bit less than that of pitchblende ore. Chemists have probed it in hope of finding new elements in it. Two workers in 1908 claimed hints of new kinds of matter there.
britannica-1911-tlaxcala-state:
Tlaxcala, an inland state of Mexico, is set out in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Puebla bounds it on the north east and south. The state of Mexico lies to the west. It covers just over fifteen hundred square miles.

The land sits on the great high plain of Mexico, about seven thousand feet up. Hills rise in the west and south, topped by the fire peak Malinche. Three rail lines cross the state, and the capital bears the same name. The state is close in size to an old native republic. That small state held its freedom against the Aztec realm till the Spanish came. Its folk then fought Cortes, then joined him as firm allies.
britannica-1911-tonalite:
Tonalite is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a rock of the diorite class. The rock was first set out from Monte Adamello near Tonale. That site lies in the Eastern Alps. It can be called a quartz diorite in plain terms. Two dark minerals, biotite and hornblende, occur in near equal shares. The main pale mineral is plagioclase felspar. A small share of orthoclase may also be present.

Kinds rich in orthoclase have drawn other names over time. Some called them quartz monzonites or adamellites. The text backs grano diorite as the better term. That name is much used in America for such rocks. The rocks sit between granites and diorites in their make up. The entry notes how the dark grains grow and cluster. It also notes how they break down to chlorite and epidote.
britannica-1911-torbernite:
Torbernite is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a mineral with uranium in it. It is one of the stones called the uranium micas there. In make-up it is a wet mix of uranium, copper, and phosphate. Its crystals form square plates, most times very thin in build.

The stone splits clean along its base, with a pearly shine there. Its bright grass-green hue is a clear mark of the kind. It is soft in grade, and its rays outdo some pitchblende samples. It was first seen in 1772 at a town in Saxony. The best finds come from two spots in Cornwall, England. The name honours Torbern Bergman, a famed chemist of Sweden.
britannica-1911-trachyte:
Trachyte is a group of volcanic rocks in the science of petrology. The 1911 Britannica entry takes its name from a Greek word for rough. Tiny steam holes oft pit the rock and make its face rough. That rough face gave the whole group its lasting name in science. The chief stone in the mix is sanidine, a glassy feldspar.

Hauy first gave the name to rocks of this kind from Auvergne. For long the term was used in much too wide a sense. It once took in rocks now classed as rhyolites and andesites. Trachytes are oft called the volcanic kin of the plutonic syenites. Their feldspar shows in two sizes, large crystals set in fine ground.
britannica-1911-treilhard-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Treilhard, a French leader in the great change born in seventeen forty two, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Brives, he won fame in Paris as a court speaker. He was sent to the great meeting of seventeen eighty nine as a deputy.

In that first body he showed great skill in the work to remake the Church. He helped plan the taking of church lands for the state. Barred, like all that body, from the next house, he led the court for crime in Paris but lacked firm grip. The voters of his district then sent him to the Convention. There he joined the group called the Mountain and voted for the death of Louis the Sixteenth. He sat on the guard board for public safety too. The life shows law skill at the heart of a coup age.
britannica-1911-variscite: Variscite is a green mineral made of aluminium, phosphorus, oxygen, and water, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. Breithaupt named it in 1837 for its find place in the Saxon Voigtland, once called Variscia. It most often forms as a crust or in round lumps. A dense lump form found near Old Camp Floyd in Utah about 1894 was named utahlite. Its fine apple green hue led to its use, cut and polished, as a stone for ornament.
britannica-1911-waste:
Waste is a term of English law with more than one sense, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sorts four chief ones. The word comes through French from a Latin word for vast and bare. In one sense it is the waste of a manor. That is the part of a manor held in common by all, set apart from the own lands of the lord.

A second sense joins the words year, day, and waste. That was a right of the crown by an old law. The king took the gains of the free lands of men found of grave crime for a year and a day. He held a right of waste in the third sense on those lands as well. Past that span the lands went back to the lord of the fee.
britannica-1911-wavellite: Wavellite is a mineral made of a watered phosphate of aluminium. It forms crystals in the orthorhombic system, but clear single crystals are rare. It is found for the most part in round or half-round masses with a rayed structure inside. The stone lets some light through and ranges in hue from grey or white to green and yellow tints. Its hardness is three and a half, and its weight is 2.32 times that of water. Dr W. Wavell first found it near Barnstaple in Devonshire late in the 1700s.
britannica-1911-witherite:
Witherite is a mineral described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is made of barium carbonate and forms its crystals in the orthorhombic system. The crystals are all but always twinned in groups of three. That gives them a false six-sided form, much like the two-pointed crystals of quartz, with rough faces lined with fine marks.

Its colour is dull white or at times grey, and it is a heavy stone for its size. The mineral is named for Withering, who in 1784 saw that it was not the same as barytes. It is found in veins of lead ore at Hexham, at Alston, and near Chorley, and in a few other places. Water with lime sulphate in it turns it by slow work to barium sulphate. It is the chief source of barium salts and is mined in bulk in Northumberland.
britannica-1911-wollastonite:
Wollastonite is a rock forming mineral, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short science entry. In chemical terms it is a calcium metasilicate, and it belongs to the pyroxene group, though its cleavages set it apart from the other members. Its crystals are usually long in one direction and flattened in another, hence an early name, tabular spar.

The mineral is named after the scientist Wollaston. It usually occurs in white cleavage masses. Its hardness and its weight are given in figures, and it is a characteristic product of the change that heat and contact work in rock. It occurs above all, with garnet and diopside, in limestones that have been recrystallized. Crystals are found in blocks thrown out by Vesuvius. At Santa Fé in Mexico, a large mass carries ores of gold and copper.
buried-cities-pompeii-olympia-mycenae-co:
Jennie Hall wrote tales of three lost cities for boys and girls, in one full book. Hall taught history and English at the Francis W. Parker School in Chicago. Drawings and photos from first sources fill the pages. A foreword asks young readers if they like to dig for hid wealth, and tells of a boy who found an Indian grave in his sand cave.

Pompeii, Olympia, and Mycenae form the three parts. House tales bring Pompeii close: the house of Vettius, with its two seal stamps, money chests, and twenty rooms. Temple walks bring Olympia close, with its Hermes and child Dionysus. Grave gold brings Mycenae close, with Schliemann's queens and their crowns. Dig truth told as tale is the book's whole method. Friends of the late author helped end the picture work, as the front note owns.
campaign-pictures-of-the-war-in-south-af:
A. G. Hales, special man for the Daily News, wrote letters from the Boer War front, in a book of 1901. Cassell put it out at London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne. Sir John Robinson, head of the Daily News, gets the book in a long warm word.

Robinson had found Archibald Forbes, the best war pen of his age, Hales grants. The same hand gave Hales his chance, sought for twenty years. What Forbes owes that hand, Forbes's own life tale must tell; what Hales owes, he tells here. Front life in the South Africa war of 1899 to 1900 fills the letters: march, camp, and fight seen by a press man at the guns. The dear name in his mind, he owns at the close, is his patron's.
carnac-s-folly-complete:
Carnac's Folly, complete, by Gilbert Parker, holds his three book Montreal novel in one text. Parker begins in childhood and passes eleven years in a chapter. Carnac Grier grows up between two inheritances. One is his father John Grier's lumber empire, run at our price. The other is his own gift for painting, and a secret French marriage to Luzanne Larue that he cannot avow or undo.

Book II brings him home to a read will and a refused divorce. Book III sends him into an election, with Tarboe at the mills and Junia waiting on one ambiguous letter. A blue paper, a challenge, and a woman's letter decide the end. Parker's Canada is bilingual, commercial, and romantic at once. Carnac's folly is the classic Parker trap: a moment's surrender, a lifetime of paperwork, and honor demanding payment in public.
caste:
W. A. Fraser's novel, copyrighted in 1922, opens at Poona in India. The Mahratta princes Sindhia, Holkar, and Bhonsla plot against the British. The Peshwa's adopted son broods over his future. That son, Dandhu Panth, known as Nana Sahib, came home from Oxford dressed and mannered like an English gentleman, yet wearing the sacred thread of a Brahmin.

Hodson, the Resident, alone doubts the change, and the plot tightens around spies, decoity, and the dancer Bootea, who risks herself to save lives. Barlow, a British officer, is pulled between duty and protection. Fraser builds his tale on caste, loyalty, and the gulf between outward polish and inward resentment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-miri: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Miridite describes an abbatia nullius in Albania, where a Benedictine abbey dedicated to St. Alexander once stood, now destroyed. By decree of October 1888 the abbey with two parishes formed the nullius, together with five parishes from the diocese of Ljes. Three parishes from Sappa were added in 1890, and five more from Ljes in 1894. The country, then under Turkish rule, held Muslims, Greek schismatics and 16,550 Catholics, served by secular and regular clergy under an abbot chosen from the secular clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acolyte:
An acolyte, from Greek akolouthos, follower or attendant, holds the Latin church's fourth and highest minor order, just below a subdeacon. His chief offices are to light the altar candles and carry them in procession. He also carries them at the solemn singing of the Gospel, prepares wine and water for the Mass, and assists the sacred ministers at Mass and other public services.

At ordination the bishop presents him with an unlit candle and an empty cruet, with words expressing those duties. Altar boys are often called acolytes and perform such duties. The first authentic document naming acolytes is a letter of Pope Cornelius to Fabius of Antioch in 251, enumerating the Roman clergy. Later statutes, like the Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua of Gaul about 500, set out the same ritual.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acquapendente:
Acquapendente is an Italian diocese directly under the Holy See, with seven towns in Rome province. Until 1649 it stood under the church rule of Orvieto. That year, after Cristoforo Girarda, Bishop of Castro, was murdered in a plot, Innocent X ordered Castro destroyed in punishment. He raised Acquapendente to an episcopal city by a bull of 13 September 1649.

Its bishops still keep the title post Castrenses, after Castro. The first incumbent was Pompeo Mignucci of Offida, formerly Archbishop of Ragusa, who took possession on 10 January 1650. The diocese counts 13 parishes and 80 churches, chapels, and oratories, served by 47 secular clergy and 35 seminarians, among 19,350 people. Sources include Ughelli, Cappelletti, and Gams.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adoro-te-devo:
Adoro Te Devote, meaning I adore thee devoutly, is a hymn sometimes called Rhythmus or Oratio S. Thomae, written about 1260, though the date is uncertain. It belongs to neither the Office nor the Mass of the Blessed Sacrament. It appears in the Roman Missal, in thanksgiving after Mass, with 100 days indulgence for priests, later extended to all the faithful by a decree of 17 June 1895.

It also appears commonly in prayer and hymn books and has sixteen English verse translations. The Baltimore Manual of Prayers prints the Latin text with English translation. Either of two refrains follows each quatrain, though originally the hymn lacked any refrain. The entry cites Mone, Daniel, and Julian for manuscripts, refrains, and first lines of English versions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrien-rouque:
Adrien Rouquette, born in Louisiana in 1813 to French parents, died among the Choctaw Indians in 1887, their missionary. His youth's great passion was devotion to the Choctaw. Sent north in 1824 to turn his mind from his Indian associates, he went to France in 1829 and finished collegiate studies at Paris, Nantes, and Rennes, earning his baccalaureate in 1833.

Back in New Orleans, he shunned worldly pleasures, spending much time alone or among Indian friends. After studying law in Paris and preferring literature, his first poetic essay, Les Savannes, appeared in France, then edited Le Propagateur Catholique in Louisiana. Ordained priest in 1844, he served fourteen years at New Orleans Cathedral, where his eloquence crowded the building. In 1859 he left civilization and spent twenty-nine years as missionary among the Choctaw on Bayou La Combe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alberico-de-r:
Alberico de Rosate, also called Rosciate, was a fourteenth-century Italian jurist, an expert in law, who died in 1354. Born of humble parents in the village of Rosate near Bergamo, he studied law at Padua and took a doctorate, though he never taught. He spent his life at Bergamo as a lawyer active in public affairs, serving the Visconti rulers of Milan. In 1340 he travelled as envoy to Pope Benedict XII at Avignon.

In his later years Rosate turned to legal writing, and his works won him a high name among practical jurists. His commentaries on the Digests and the Codex, the great Roman law collections, were printed again and again, as at Lyons in 1517 and 1545-48. His Opus Statutorum, a work on statutes, and his Dictionarium, a store of legal maxims arranged as a dictionary, were likewise reprinted often.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-berrug:
Alonso Berruguete, the Spanish Michelangelo, mastered painting, sculpture, and architecture. He was painter Pedro Berruguete's second son and pupil. His family chose law for him and got him a Valladolid office, held for years after he turned to art. Michelangelo's fame reportedly drew him to Italy after his father's death.

In Italy he competed against Sansovino for a bronze Laocoön cast. At Florence he finished Filippo Lippi's unfinished altarpiece for San Geronimo's nuns. Back in Spain in 1520, Charles V made him chamberlain and court artist. Charles gave him Madrid, El Pardo, and Alhambra work. In favour under Philip II, he grew rich, married well, and bought Ventosa near Valladolid. At Valladolid he spent six years on San Benito's high altar, working with Filipe de Vigar on Toledo cathedral. Near eighty he carved Cardinal Archbishop Juan de Tavera's monument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-lit:
The Ambrosian liturgy and rite belong to Milan's Church, named for St. Ambrose, bishop from 374 to 397. Its origin is still disputed between leading liturgiologists, with no direct evidence of the rite's nature before about the ninth century. Early manuscripts take forms such as the Sacramentary, holding orations, prophecies, epistles, gospels, prefaces, and post-communions.

The entry surveys the liturgical year, the Divine Office with its psalter distribution, and the Mass. The Mass's present form is shown by analysis against the Roman rite, much agreeing word for word. Baptism's ceremonies differ in order from Rome's: renunciation, ephphatha, sufflation, and unction among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-white:
Andrew White, missionary, was born in London in 1579 and died near London in 1656. He entered Saint Alban's College, Valladolid, in 1595, matriculated at Douai, and was ordained about 1605. Sent on the mission, he was seized and banished in 1606. He joined the Jesuits in 1607 at Louvain. In 1609 he was back in England, labouring in the south. He taught Scripture, theology, and Hebrew at Louvain and Liege.

His labours with Lord Baltimore's colony earned him the title Apostle of Maryland. He landed on Saint Clement's Island, where Mass was celebrated. For years he laboured among settlers and natives of the Patuxent and Potomac. In 1640 he baptized Chitomachon, Emperor of Piscataway, before Governor Calvert. He wrote a grammar, dictionary, and catechism in the idiom, the first Englishman to give an Indian language grammatical form. Virginia marauders seized him and sent him in irons to London for trial as a priest in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antofogaste:
A Catholic mission district in northern Chile, the Vicariate Apostolic of Antofogaste answered to Rome through its congregation for church affairs. A treaty of 1884 moved its Bolivian portion to Chile. In 1895 the district held about forty-four thousand people, with some sixteen thousand in its main city, across nearly forty-seven thousand square miles.

Six parishes served the district, from Tocopilla and Cobija to Calama and the Atacama settlements, each named for a saint or for Mary. Appeals from its vicar went to the Archbishop of Santiago, though the vicariate itself depended on the Holy See. The entry gives a compact portrait of church order on a mining frontier whose borders had just been redrawn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appetite:
Appetite, from Latin words for seeking toward, means a tendency or direction, and modern writers give it a psychological sense. Baldwin's dictionary defines it as an organic need shown in consciousness by certain sensations, with hunger, thirst, and sex as the recognized appetites. The need of air, exercise, and sleep falls under the same definition. Appetence, a wider term, covers strivings that gain satisfaction in some positive state or result.

For the schoolmen, the medieval scholastic thinkers, appetite meant far more. In Thomas Aquinas it includes all forms of inner inclination, found in all beings, even unconscious ones. It is an inclination toward what is good and suitable, and a turning away from what harms. The entry contrasts a narrow modern psychology of bodily needs with a medieval philosophy in which every creature strives toward its good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aquileian-rit:
The Aquileian Rite is the special liturgical use of Aquileia and some of its suffragan, or subordinate, sees, known generally as the ritus patriarchinus. Aquileia fell into schism, or separation, during the Three Chapters quarrel under Bishop Macedonius, who ruled from 539 to 556, and became a schismatic patriarchate lasting until 700. Many allusions mention its special rite, but they give no clear account of what it was.

The earliest instructive document is an eighth-century capitulare, a list of readings, added by a Lombard hand to the sixth-century Codex Richdigeranus. Morin and Haase argue that it represents Aquileian use, and if so it reveals its calendar from Advent to June: five Sundays of Advent, St. Stephen's Day on 27 December as in Jerusalem-Antioch rites, no Septuagesima, and two Sundays preparing for Lent. The entry rebuilds a lost rite from a single list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archimandrite:
An archimandrite, from Greek words for command and sheepfold, is in the Greek rite the superior of one monastery or of several monasteries. The term appears to have arisen in the fourth century in the far East, in Mesopotamia and Persia, and spread to Egypt and the Asia Minor region. In the fifth and later centuries it appears often in Greek fathers and council acts. It was widely adopted in the West, where it lingered in occasional use until the ninth century.

At first the archimandrite was simply abbot of his own house, but gradually he gained authority over a number of monasteries. By the eleventh century archimandrites of great centres such as Mount Athos and Bithynia's Mount Olympus matched western abbots general. Today the Greek church knows two kinds: original monastic officers ruling their own houses, and honorary archimandrites holding the title without that rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-welt:
Benedict Welte, a German scholar of the Old Testament, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Ratzenried in Württemberg in 1825, he died in 1885 after a life split between the classroom and the writing desk. Study at Tübingen and Bonn, with a focus on the Old Testament and Eastern languages, led to ordination and a Tübingen chair in 1840.

Writing, more than teaching, was his field. He finished a predecessor's introduction to the Old Testament, translated an Armenian life of St. Mesrob, and published a study and translation of the Book of Job. With Heinrich Wetzer he then edited a twelve-volume encyclopedia of Catholic theology, writing two hundred of its articles himself before eye disease ended his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-eliza:
Blessed Elizabeth of Reute, called the good Betha, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Waldsee in Swabia on 25 November 1386, she died on her birthday in 1420. From childhood she showed rare piety under her confessor Conrad Kugelin, provost of St. Peter's at Waldsee, and at fourteen she took the Third Order habit but lived at home.

After long pleading she left home without parental support for a house of prayer, enduring leprosy and other sicknesses with heavenly patience learned from Christ's Passion, which she made her constant meditation. Marks of the thorns and scourging appeared on her body, and she foretold Martin V's election and the Western Schism's end. Clement XIII ratified her cult in 1766.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-sebas: Sebastian Newdigate, a courtier turned Carthusian monk, was executed at Tyburn in 1535 for denying Henry VIII's supremacy over the Church. Educated at Cambridge, he befriended Henry and served as privy councillor, but, widowed in 1524, entered the London Charterhouse. Arrested in May 1535, he spent fourteen days bound to a pillar in the Marshalsea. He refused the king's offers of riches and honors, and died with William Exmew and Humphrey Middlemore on 19 June.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlos-maria-:
Carlos María Bustamante was a Mexican statesman and historian born at Oaxaca in November 1774 who died in Mexico in September 1848. He took up law in 1796, joined attempts to win independence from Spain, and opposed Iturbide's bid to turn the new republic into a hereditary monarchy. Repeatedly jailed and banished, he still held important government posts through the republic's hardest years.

The war with the United States grieved him deeply. He lived only about a year past its close, leaving a frank sketch of the war as a sad record of Mexican decay. His 1833 autobiography counts as a fragment of contemporary history, and he earned distinction by publishing colonial-era works long left in manuscript and partly forgotten. Alamán praised him warmly, above all for his private character and domestic virtues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-hermi:
Charles Hermite, born at Dieuze in Lorraine in 1822 and dead at Paris in 1901, ranks among the century's great mathematicians. He studied at Nancy, then at the Paris colleges of Henri IV and Louis-le-Grand. As a boy he read Lagrange on numerical equations and Gauss on the theory of numbers. In 1842 his first original paper proved simply Abel's claim that the fifth-degree equation admits no algebraic solution.

A correspondence with Jacobi in 1843 and 1844 yielded two articles, on extending an Abel theorem on elliptic functions to Abelian functions and on transforming elliptic functions. His teaching aimed less at rigorous minuteness than at stirring admiration for the simple and beautiful, and his published lecture courses influenced widely. In 1858 elliptic functions let him solve the fifth-degree equation. In 1873 he proved e transcendent, a result Lindemann used in 1882 for pi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-ignat:
Charles Ignatius White was an editor and historian born at Baltimore in 1807 and dead at Washington in 1878. His classical studies took him to Mt. St. Mary's, Emmittsburg, and St. Mary's College, Baltimore, and his theology to St. Sulpice in Paris, where he was ordained priest in 1830. Back in Baltimore he worked in parishes there and at Pikesville until 1857, when he became rector of St. Matthew's in Washington, a charge he held until his death.

He founded the Religious Cabinet, a Baltimore monthly, in 1842, and relaunched it as the Metropolitan Magazine in 1853. He also edited the weekly Catholic Mirror. These journals, in the formative years before the Civil War, powerfully advanced the Church in America both spiritually and materially. He translated Balmes on Protestantism and Catholicity compared and compiled a life of Elizabeth Ann Seton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-lucei:
An entry on Charles Lucien Jules Laurent Bonaparte, Prince of Canino and Musignano, nephew of Napoleon and a noted ornithologist, a student of birds. Born in Paris in 1803 as the eldest son of Lucien Bonaparte, he was educated in Italy and married his cousin Zenaïde in 1822. He then spent years in the United States, where Joseph Bonaparte, his wife's father, lived, and threw himself into natural science.

Bonaparte completed Wilson's Ornithology of the United States in four volumes, describing more than a hundred new species he had found himself. Back in Europe from 1828, he settled in Rome, inherited his father's princely titles in 1840, and entered Italian politics, serving as deputy of Viterbo in the Roman Republic of 1849. Exiled after its fall, he later directed the Jardin des Plantes in Paris and kept publishing on birds until his death in 1857.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-adrien:
Claude-Adrien Nonnotte, a controversialist born at Besancon on 29 July 1711 and dead there on 3 September 1793, entered the Society of Jesus at nineteen and preached at Amiens, Versailles, and Turin. Chiefly he is known for his writings against Voltaire. When Voltaire issued his Essai sur les moeurs in 1754, Nonnotte answered anonymously with a critical examination. He revised it when the work finished in 1758 and published it at Avignon in two volumes in 1762.

He treated Voltaire's historical and doctrinal errors simply, calmly, and dispassionately, and his book reached a sixth edition in 1774 with translations into Italian, German, Polish, and Portuguese. Voltaire retorted for twenty years with sarcasm, insult, and calumny. After the Jesuits were suppressed, Nonnotte withdrew to Besancon and added a third volume in 1779. His Dictionnaire philosophique de la religion of 1772 answered Voltaire's philosophical dictionary, and Clement the Thirteenth praised him by Brief in 1768.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collegiate:
William Fanning's entry explains collegiate as an adjective for churches and institutions whose members form a college. Collegiate churches took cathedral churches as their model. Their canons hold rights and duties much like cathedral capitulars. One difference matters: they have no voice in ruling the diocese, even when the see stands vacant. Their main work is the solemn celebration of the Divine Office in choir. By Charlemagne's time many wealthy collegiate churches already stood across his empire, above all in Germany and France.

Erection of a collegiate body needs the authority of the Holy See. Collegiate churches ordinarily fall under the bishop's jurisdiction. Yet their members owe the bishop no service outside their own church. Fanning sets out their privileges, including rights of nominating and presenting candidates, which in many places were still in force when he wrote.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comtesse-de-l:
Pierre Marique's entry follows the Comtesse de La Fayette, memoirist and novelist, born at Paris in 1634, dead in 1693. She knew Latin and Italian, taught partly by Menage. Wit and talent won her Paris's lead. With the Marquise de Sévigné, she embodied Les Précieuses, who shaped Louis XIV's young court. Friends included Condé, Huet, La Rochefoucauld, Bossuet, La Fontaine.

She was confidante of Princess Henrietta, the king's sister-in-law. Her first novel, La Princesse de Montpensier, appeared unsigned in 1662. Zayde followed in 1670; her masterpiece La Princesse de Clèves in 1678 pictures Fronde society in sixteenth-century scenes. Its moral beauty recalls Corneille; it counts as the first French psychological novel. Clear and lively, its style avoids vulgar words, the one Précieuse trace. Her court memoirs for 1688, 1689 close the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curate:
This entry explains the curate, from the Latin for care, as one charged with the cure, or care, of souls. The Church of England still uses it in that broad sense, and the French cure denotes a parish priest. In English-speaking countries, however, curate has come to mean an assistant priest, sent by the bishop to help the rector or parish priest.

Technically the parish priest holds the cure, while his helpers are vicars and coadjutors, but the entry uses curate in its accepted English sense. It traces the office from the early Church, when each diocese had one church in the bishop's city, through growth that multiplied churches and priests in city and country. The standing and duties of English curates are treated with legal references.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-amelote: An entry on Denis Amelote, a French Oratorian born at Saintes in 1609 who died in Paris in 1678. Ordained in 1631 and a doctor of the Sorbonne, he gave French readers a New Testament translation in four volumes, issued between 1666 and 1670, that was prized and often reprinted. Most of his other Scripture works draw on that edition, and he also wrote in defence of papal rulings against the Jansenists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desire-raoul-:
A life of Désiré Raoul Rochette, a French archaeologist born at Saint-Amand in 1789 who died in Paris in 1854. After classical study at Bourges and the École Normale, he took a grammar chair at Louis-le-Grand in 1810 and married the sculptor Houdon's daughter. An Institute prize for a memoir on Greek colonies came in 1813, and in 1815 he succeeded Guizot in the Sorbonne chair of modern history.

Election to the Academy of Inscriptions followed in 1816, then a keepership of medals and antiques in 1818. A censor's post in 1820 turned students against him and stalled his lectures. He moved to the archaeology chair in 1824, and became perpetual secretary of the Academy of Fine Arts in 1839. Books on Greek colonies, the Cimmerian Bosphorus, Pompeii, and archaeology itself anchor his output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-francis:
Diego Francisco Aduarte was a Dominican missionary and historian born at Saragossa in 1566. He sailed for the Philippines in 1594 and landed at Manila the next year. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry singles out his work among the Chinese residents of the islands, where his preaching met with rare success.

Voyages to Siam and Cochin China in aid of native rulers brought hunger, thirst, and danger from treacherous hosts. Yet he pressed on for years by sea and land. His History of the Province of the Holy Rosary, printed at Manila in 1634, remains the entry's centerpiece, a rare chronicle of the Dominican missions of the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dionysius-the:
Dionysius the Areopagite is usually taken to be the judge of the Areopagus whom Saint Paul converted at Athens. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry untangles two great errors that grew around his name. First, a set of famous mystical writings was ascribed to him, though they came from a later hand. Second, he was popularly matched with Saint Denis, the first bishop of Paris and martyr of Gaul.

The entry sets aside the Paris legend and takes up the writer himself, his works, and their fate across the ages. It sorts the writings, weighs their contents and character, and traces how they were handed down. Readers meet a shadowy author whose books shaped medieval thought far beyond what his true name could claim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-ferna:
Domingo Fernandez Navarrete was a Dominican missionary and archbishop born about 1610 at Penafiel in Old Castile. He took the habit about 1630 and was offered chairs of Thomist theology at several Spanish universities. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he turned them down to preach to the heathen. He sailed in 1646 with twenty-seven brethren by way of Mexico to the Philippines, landing there in June 1648.

He taught theology at the Dominican University of Saint Thomas in Manila, then went to China in 1657. After learning the tongue he labored chiefly in Fo-kien until persecution broke out in 1665. Forbidden to preach, he wrote instead, leaving historical, political, and religious treatises on China and a Chinese catechism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donato-braman:
Donato Bramante, also called d'Agnolo for his father Angelo, was an Italian architect and painter born about 1444 at Monte Asdrualdo. He died at Rome on 11 March 1514. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that little is known of his youth and that Vasari erred often about his early growth. Scholars now fairly agree that Laurana, who built Urbino's ducal palace, pointed him toward the High Renaissance.

His work falls into two periods, Milan first and Rome after. Milan shows a picturesque, decorative manner, while Rome shows the purer High Renaissance style in works as perfect as their age allowed. The entry cites Geymuller on his first plans for Saint Peter's, the crown of his Roman years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durham-rite:
The Durham Rite is known first from the Ritual of the Church of Durham, also called the Ritual of King Aelfrith. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry dates the manuscript to the early ninth century and keeps it in the Durham cathedral library. It holds chapters, chants, and above all collects from Epiphany to Easter, then a proper and a common of saints, with many forms for blessings. Most of it bears an interlinear Anglo-Saxon translation.

Blank pages later gained hymns, exorcisms, and a list of contractions from canon law books, added by later scribes. The entry traces the rite's links to Durham and prints related texts from the Surtees Society. For students of old English worship, it opens a service book written when Northumbria still prayed in two tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-east-syrian-r:
The East Syrian Rite, also called Chaldean, Assyrian, or Persian, serves Nestorians and Eastern Catholic bodies across Syria, Mesopotamia, Persia, and Malabar. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the name Chaldean, which in Syriac meant magician, but in European tongues came to mean Syrian nationality and the Syriac tongue. Seventeenth-century Latin missionaries at Mosul attached the name to East Syrian Catholics, distinguishing them from West Syrians and Nestorians.

The entry traces the rite's history and its liturgy, down to the consecration of altars. There the whole altar is anointed with fresh olive oil blessed by the bishop, not oil of the holy horn. Four consecration crosses mark the sanctuary walls. It offers a full portrait of a rite that bridges East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edme-mariotte:
Edme Mariotte was a French physicist and priest, born at Dijon about 1620 and dead at Paris in 1684. Ordained to the priesthood, he was made prior of Saint-Martin-sous-Beaune near Dijon in reward for his work in science. He belonged to the Royal Society of Science from its start in 1666, and his collected works came out at Leyden in 1717.

His name lives on through the gas law of 1676. It first appeared in an essay on air. At a fixed heat, the bulk of a gas shrinks as the weight pressing on it grows. The entry also covers his tests on water pressure, the swing of weights, the flow of water, and his flask for a steady stream. It sketches a man who trusted careful trial, doubt, and plain rules of thought over guesswork.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-white:
Edward White was an Irish emigrant whose family left a mark on American Catholic life, born in County Limerick late in the eighteenth century and dead in December 1863. Early in the nineteenth century he crossed to America and settled at Binghamton in New York. There he founded and ran a school for young women, which lasted from 1830 until his wife's death in 1851.

White had nine children. Five of his daughters entered religious orders, the best known being Madame Catherine White of the Religious of the Sacred Heart, who wrote school books on mythology, classical literature, and church history. His eldest son James became a prominent lawyer in New York City. The entry is a short family record, valued chiefly for the children it names.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmanuel-sche:
Emmanuel Schelstrate was a Belgian theologian, born at Antwerp in 1649 and dead at Rome in 1692. While canon of Antwerp Cathedral he was called to Rome by Innocent IX and made assistant librarian of the Vatican Library. A fine scholar in early church history, he became the accredited defender of papal supremacy, which is why his writings have often been judged harshly.

His Antiquitas Illustrata of 1678 gathers papal decrees and church history, and in it he attacked Launoy's errors on the primacy of Rome. He planned a larger second edition but issued only two volumes, in 1692 and 1697. He disputed with Arnauld and Maimbourg over councils and popes, opposed the Gallican clergy's declaration of 1682, and wrote on the origin of the Anglican Church against Stillingfleet, Dean of Saint Paul's. He published many other works besides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eustathius-of:
Eustathius of Sebaste, born about 300 and dead about 377, was one of the chief founders of monastic life in Asia Minor and for years the close friend of Saint Basil. Son of Eulalius, Bishop of Sebaste, he studied under Arius, was ordained priest, and founded a community of monks whose strict ways drew censure. A synod at Gangra about 340 condemned his followers for forbidding marriage, shunning married priests, fasting on Sundays while skipping appointed fast days, and claiming special grace for their own meetings.

He became Bishop of Sebaste about 356, and Basil, then learning the monastic life, admired and defended him for years. But Eustathius wavered all his life between forms of Arianism, signed contradictory formulas, and at last led the Pneumatomachians, who denied that the Holy Ghost shares the same substance as the Father. Basil broke with him about 372.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fate:
Fate means an unseen power fixing the course of events in advance. Catholics prefer providence for God's rule and natural law for fixed physical order. The Greeks pictured fate as Moira, or three sisters named Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos. Romans matched them with their own Parcae, or Fata.

Thinkers sought a cause for events that seemed to follow no law. Some turned to the stars, supposing heavenly bodies shaped earthly fortunes. The Stoics made fate universal, while Epicureans denied it through the atoms' swerve. Catholic teaching holds God's decree firm, yet never predetermines the abuse of free will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-groote:
Gerard Groote, who founded the Brethren of the Common Life, turned from rich prebends to devout poverty. Born at Deventer in 1340, he studied at Aachen and the Sorbonne in medicine, theology, and canon law. He taught at Deventer's chapter school in 1362 and carried a secret mission to Urban V at Avignon. At Cologne he taught philosophy and theology on two prebends and ample means.

Meeting his Sorbonne fellow Henry of Calcar, prior of Munnikhuizen, Groote stripped himself of honors and goods. He spent three years in retreat there under Ruysbroek's influence and emerged a preacher with diaconate and licence for Utrecht. Youths flocked to him, and with his disciple Florence Radewyns he founded the Brethren at Zwolle to work, pray, and copy good books together. His fearless attacks on vice cost him his licence, though he appealed to the pope. He died of pestilence caught ministering to the sick in 1384.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-nacch:
Giacomo Nacchiante, also called Naclantus, was a Dominican theologian born at Florence, who died at Chioggia in 1569. He studied at Bologna beside Michael Ghislieri, the future Pius V, and later taught philosophy and theology in Rome. Paul III made him Bishop of Chioggia in 1544. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his career through the Council of Trent and the doubts it raised about him.

At Trent he protested the fourth session's decree that church traditions be received with the same reverence as Scripture. He then gave reverent assent once the great assembly had confirmed it. Later doubts about his orthodoxy faded, the article says, because Pius IV trusted him with grave affairs. His works, printed at Venice in 1567, include commentaries on Ephesians and Romans, a marrow of Scripture, and treatises in theology and metaphysics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gil-vicente:
Gil Vicente was a Portuguese dramatist born about 1470, who was still living in 1536. He left the study of law for literature, and his humorous lyrics appear in Garcia de Resende's Cancioneiro. A Catholic Encyclopedia article styles him, with good reason, the father of the Portuguese drama, on the strength of no fewer than forty-two plays.

Ten of his pieces are in Spanish, fourteen in Portuguese, and the rest mix the two tongues. Many were written for religious and national festivals or for events in the royal family, while others aimed only at entertainment. His first play, Visitacao, celebrated the birth of John III in 1502. Court ladies and gentlemen acted beside him in palace performances, and his seventeen religious autos, the Obras de devocao, show a genuinely devout Catholic at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hakodate:
Japan's northern diocese of Hakodate covers six provinces of northern Nippon with Yezo, the Kuriles, and southern Saghalin. It holds about nine million people, including 17,000 Ainu, the last remnant of the islands' first population. A vicariate from April 1891 and a diocese that June, it was entrusted to the Paris Foreign Missions, with twenty-four missionaries, one Japanese priest, and twenty residences by 1908.

Sixteenth-century Christianity survives only in crosses and images hidden in families and pagoda treasuries, and present Catholics are converts, mostly won before 1895, when faith still seemed the ground of civilization. Materialism and national pride have since made conversions rare, yet 345 adults were baptized in 1908. The writer expects the Japanese, lovers of truth who admire Catholic order and self-sacrifice, to come in numbers yet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-digby-b:
Henry Digby Beste, born at Lincoln in 1768, was educated at Magdalen College, Oxford, took Anglican deacon's orders in 1791, and preached at Lincoln. Doubts about the Established Church's spiritual authority, deepened by conversation with the Abbé Beaumont, led to his reception into the Catholic Church in 1798. His early writings defended Christianity against French philosophers and republicans and argued for priestly absolution in terms later Tractarians claimed.
