Katie Lundquist of Lawrence Livermore led this project on faster atmospheric simulation, summed up in a September 2026 final report. Emergency work, such as tracking a nuclear release, needs weather models that run in hours, not days. Older tools were too slow for that operational pace and for shrinking global forecasts down to city scale.

The team extended a model called ERF, built for the largest computers, with particles for cloud and debris physics, terrain and building detail, and city energy models. Runs sped up about one hundred fold. Nuclear cloud rise cases ran faster than real time and matched observations from four past atmospheric tests well. Urban flow checks against a 2003 field campaign were the most accurate yet reported.
doe-osti-17120804-2026-accomplishments-r:
Scarlett Widgeon Paisner and Los Alamos colleagues file a 2026 accomplishments report, issued 4 October 2026, on ceramic fuel forms for the SPARC criticality facility planned at Idaho National Laboratory. SPARC is a zero power split table reactor for testing fuel forms that support reactor licensing. Plate or brick shapes were favored because they pack more uranium at the assembly faces.

Work centered on high assay low enriched uranium dioxide bricks, with a target size of 3 by 2 by 1 inches. Test pellets pressed with small loads guided the powder process. Binder share, mixing method, and pressing load were varied, and sintered density was measured for each. Higher loads near 100 megapascals gave no density gain. Ball milled mixes reached the best density, about 93 percent of theoretical. A rectangular punch and die set was ordered for brick making.
doe-osti-2479474-a-simple-macaw-equation:
A deliberately simple equation of state called MACAW is built in Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-24-32805. The authors are Tariq Dennis Aslam and Jose Eduardo Lozano Sanchez, and the report was issued in March 2026. An equation of state links pressure, volume, and temperature, which simulation codes need for every material they model. The authors construct theirs from a Helmholtz free energy split into two parts.

The first part is a cold curve, the energy at zero temperature, written in a MACAW form equal to the classic Murnaghan relation. It needs three parameters, tied to the bulk modulus and its pressure derivative. The second part adds heat through a specific heat model that levels off at the Dulong-Petit limit. A constant Grüneisen parameter then fixes how the temperature scale shifts with volume. Six parameters define the model, and the paper derives its pressure from them.
doe-osti-2583146-passive-wireless-sensor:
Final technical report DE-FE0031912, from West Virginia University under Edward M. Sabolsky and covering October 2020 to May 2025, builds battery-free sensors for the inside of coal boilers. Flexible operation, ramping plants up and down with the grid, punishes boiler metal, yet wired sensors rarely survive the heat. The team developed chipless radio-frequency identification tags that work from 25 to 1,300 degrees Celsius and simply reflect a reader's signal.

The sensor is a microstrip patch antenna in peel-and-stick form, applied to metal parts without changing their shape. An interrogator antenna covers the broad frequency range the tags answer on. Accelerated high-temperature tests tied the tags' responses to corrosion and cracking as they developed. Through-wall reading was also investigated, so tags sealed inside metal housings could still report. The aim is continuous health monitoring of boiler components in service, for safety and efficiency.
doe-osti-2587509-wildfire-electric-grid-:
Brian Pierre, manager of electric power systems research at Sandia National Laboratories, presented these slides, SAND2025-10655R, on wildfire and grid security. The deck pursues two goals at once: cutting the wildfires that power lines start, and cutting the damage wildfires do to the grid and the critical systems that depend on it.

Pierre frames the stakes with recent history. Key United States wildfire events from 2014 to 2024 are charted from national climate and fire data, work he shares with Soroush Vahedi and Junbo Zhao. Utility lawsuits run to hundreds of millions of dollars, with the Thomas, Camp, Archie Creek, Zogg, and Dixie fires named as examples. The slides survey the modeling toolbox for fire risk, spread forecasting, and behavior analysis. Other laboratories' tools get a nod, including PNNL's RADR-Fire, INL's AHA, Argonne's WildfireGPT, and an EPRI tool inventory.
doe-osti-2588293-characterizing-integras:
Ved Patel of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this report, SAND2025-11068R, with Ellis Torrance sharing credit, on a machine learning attack on a genomics puzzle. Genomic islands are mobile DNA chunks that insert into host genomes. Each carries an integrase enzyme that targets a specific attachment site. Predicting that site from the enzyme's protein sequence is the goal.

Patel assembled over 491,000 curated single-integrase records, then embedded the proteins and DNA with language models, ESM-2 and DNABERT. Unsupervised clustering found real structure: 1,153 integrase clusters matching known taxonomic groups. Prediction, though, kept cheating. A regression model scored a perfect but meaningless zero error by predicting the average site. A Siamese network stayed at random chance, even with hard negatives. A multi-feature model reached low test error by learning yet another shortcut. The report's value is its honesty about failure modes in biological machine learning.
doe-osti-2588550-evs-scale-nextgen-profi:
Namrata Kogalur, Saroj Shinde, Keith Davidson, and Marco Gaxiola of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory produced this characterization report under the EVs@Scale NextGen Profiles project, dated September 2025. Richard Carlson of Idaho National Laboratory and Omer Onar of Oak Ridge National Laboratory share the work. EVSE is the supply equipment that charges electric vehicles. This volume benchmarks how units actually behave on the bench.

Both plug-in units and wireless power transfer systems were characterized. Each type has its own hardware setup and measurement parameters. Steady-state power transfer tests anchor the results. One finding tracks phase-to-phase current imbalance. In one unit, the imbalance shrank as total current rose, the system balancing itself at higher loads. A second unit showed no such trend and ran with lower imbalance throughout. Data like this feeds the profiles modelers use to predict what mass vehicle charging does to the grid.
doe-osti-2588567-glass-property-composit:
John Vienna leads a nine-author Pacific Northwest National Laboratory team in this August 2025 update of glass property-composition models. Xiaonan Lu, Pavel Ferkl, and six colleagues share the work. The models serve direct feed high-level waste flowsheet development. That is Hanford's plan to feed pretreated tank waste straight to vitrification, skipping a separate pretreatment step.

Property-composition models predict how a glass will behave from its oxide recipe alone. Viscosity, durability, and crystallization decide whether a melt can be poured and the product will pass. Direct feed changes the incoming waste compositions, so the models need refreshed fits and wider validity ranges. The report works oxide by oxide through the composition space. Component ranges are tabulated for constituents from titania to vanadia. Engineers use the models to test whether a feed blend makes acceptable glass before anyone melts anything.
doe-osti-2589380-evaluation-of-hanford-s:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2025-00235, by B. Barkai, asks whether boiling down Hanford's liquid waste can free up scarce tank space. Only about 4.1 million gallons of space remain in the site's double-shell tanks, and building more tanks is not an option. Vacuum evaporation could shrink the liquid, but concentrating it might grow solids or make it more corrosive.

The OLI Studio program simulated the surface liquid in a group of tanks, using measured ion levels to build each recipe. Each mix was evaporated at 50 degrees Celsius under a pressure of 60 Torr, then cooled back to normal conditions. Several million gallons of space were created, with only about 100,000 to 200,000 gallons of new solids. Pitting risk barely changed, and no mix turned aggressive. Results hold only for the tested heat and pressure.
doe-osti-2589600-mpact-safeguards-modeli:
The fiscal year 2025 update on safeguards modeling for the MPACT program is Sandia report SAND2025-11634. Authors Nathan Shoman, Philip Honnold, Ramon Pulido, Tania Rivas, and Anna Taconi cover software that tracks nuclear material so losses or diversion show up in the accounts. Three linked tool families are involved: facility models, a systems library, and an analysis package called MAPIT.

The year's biggest step added three new models to the systems library, with new building blocks in the facility modeler, including its first fully custom block. Both modeling tools gained support for discrete items, so countable objects and bulk material stay consistent. MAPIT gained the GEMUF test, a sequential check for material loss across accounting periods. Bug fixes from user reports round out the release.
doe-osti-2998146-assessment-and-simulati:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory status report PNNL-38392, by Katherine Muller, Amanda Lawter, Glenn Hammond, and co-authors, dated September 2025, tackles a delivery problem in Hanford's vadose zone cleanup. Nine cleanup technologies were screened for the 200-DV-1 area; five are solid amendments, particles meant to lock contaminants in place underground. Lab tests say the particles work. Getting them where they belong, without plugging the soil, is the hard part.

A particle transport model was added to the PFLOTRAN simulator to predict how far injected slurries travel and where they settle. Correlation analysis found the deposition rate tied most strongly to the ratio involving amendment particle size among the suspension traits tested. Column tests had already shown plugging and short travel distances. Field planners can now screen suspension recipes on screen before drilling.
doe-osti-2998962-development-of-the-phot:
Leonardo Favilla's Fermilab student report, FERMILAB-TM-2903-STUDENT, covers two months of work on the photon detector system for DUNE. The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment will use huge liquid argon detectors, and its Vertical Drift design reads particle tracks as drifting charge. Flashes of scintillation light give each event its start time, so light sensors line the detector walls.

Favilla helped prepare the test setup and checked its electrical and optical parts. He took repeated data sets while swapping silicon photomultiplier boards and the boards that turn their signals into light pulses for fibre readout. His analysis code cleaned noisy waveforms, subtracted baselines, and found signal peaks. From those peaks he built finger plots, charts whose bands count single photons, and fitted detector gain. Future plans include noise rejection, signal-to-noise values and photon detection efficiency.
doe-osti-3000001-modular-hydronic-room-c:
Kashif Nawaz, Lei Gao and Yeonjin Bae of Oak Ridge National Laboratory give the final report for CRADA NFE-24-10120, ORNL/TM-2025/3990, dated October 2025, on a modular hydronic room conditioning system. Hydronic systems heat and cool rooms with water carried through coils, and their heart is the fin-tube heat exchanger: water in tubes, air across fins. Better design models for that coil mean smaller, cheaper, more efficient room units.

The team built a design and optimisation framework around a detailed coil model, with heat transfer and pressure drop correlations fitted to real geometry and materials. A prototype coil was built and installed on site for testing. Model output was then benchmarked against measured heating and cooling runs, including a sensible heat rate comparison between simulation and experiment. Gaps between prediction and measurement drove refinements. The validated model supports design choices that trade thermal performance against fan and pump costs.
doe-osti-3000821-optimization-of-functio:
Kaila Bertsch of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory gives an abbreviated final report, LLNL-TR-2013016, dated November 2025, on materials that change their recipe gradually from one end to the other. Such functionally graded materials suit parts that face heat on one face and cold on the other. Joining two metals outright leaves a sharp, weak seam; grading smooths the transition away. Directed energy deposition, a printing method that feeds metal powder into a laser melt pool, can lay that gradient down.

Modelling and experiments were woven together. A path-planning tool, ESPEI, designs the composition route between metals, and print and post-process settings were tuned toward conventional quality. The team produced and tested gradients joining titanium, tantalum, niobium alloys, molybdenum alloys, stainless steel and chromium, among others. The short report summarises the approach and the combinations proven, for energy, aerospace and defence parts in extreme service.
doe-osti-3001723-landscan-mosaic-rapid-p:
Andrew Zimmer, Carson Woody, Daniel Adams and Marie Urban of Oak Ridge publish an emergency population map in November 2025: LandScan Mosaic's rapid update for Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa, version 1. Melissa, a category 5 storm, made landfall on 28 October 2025. Responders needed to know not where Jamaicans normally live, but where they were now: displaced, sheltered, or cut off in flooded districts of the island's west.

Analysts fused Microsoft's open building damage assessments, Global Flood Monitoring exposure data, reported displacement figures and shelter locations from Jamaica's disaster office onto the LandScan Mosaic base population. Of nearly 450,000 buildings in western Jamaica, the analysis graded how many were damaged, and shifted population counts accordingly. The Geospatial Science and Human Security Division produces these updates for exactly such moments: situational awareness, operational planning and consequence assessment while normal statistics lag weeks behind the storm.
doe-osti-3001923-control-oriented-models:
Hisham Mahmood, Buxin She, Gian Paramo and PNNL colleagues publish an overview in September 2025 of the controls behind tomorrow's converter dominated grid. The building blocks are direct current links: multi terminal high voltage DC networks, medium voltage DC feeders, and solid state transformers. These are power electronic devices that route electricity fast. Composing them could integrate offshore wind, move power between regions, support feeders and harden resilience.

Shareable transient and phasor models anchor the work. An MT-HVDC framework is exercised on a nine bus test system and a 240 bus mini WECC case with five offshore wind plants. Wind plant response, medium voltage DC loops on an IEEE 16 bus system, and an Olympic Peninsula corridor study each get a section. Solid state transformer gaps are flagged too. The report is a co design reference: models planners can run, with demonstrations kept neutral where vendor controls are proprietary.
doe-osti-3002276-energy-capture-avenues-:
Naushita Sharma and Paul Lemar survey energy recovery in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4030, dated October 2025. Wastewater plants spend heavily on energy, yet the sewage they treat carries energy of its own. Biogas from digestion, heat in the effluent, and flow through outfalls can all be tapped. The report maps the avenues open to a typical treatment plant.

Chapters weigh each option's readiness and fit, from combined heat and power engines burning biogas to upgraded renewable natural gas for pipelines. An appendix collects hard lessons from past projects: set performance targets early, train staff before startup, manage warranties, and involve operators from concept stage. The guide speaks to plant managers and city engineers who must sell an energy project to their boards and make it run afterward.
doe-osti-3002319-modular-hydronic-room-c:
Kashif Nawaz, Lei Gao, and Yeonjin Bae close CRADA project NFE-24-10120 in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3990, dated October 2025. The project developed a modular hydronic room conditioning system: equipment that heats and cools rooms with water loops instead of moving large volumes of air. Modular units suit retrofits and buildings that need room-by-room control.

The team built a computer model of the system's heat exchanger and checked it against experiments. The model proved useful as a design tool inside an optimization loop. Its limits are stated plainly: assumptions in the heat transfer correlations, and weaker handling of condensation and turbulent flow. The authors recommend refining those correlations and the moisture treatment next. Manufacturers gain a validated starting model rather than a blank page.
doe-osti-3008117-targeted-mobile-measure:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0021047, by Anita Rapp of Texas A&M University with team members Sarah Brooks and Christopher Nowotarski, reports mobile measurements taken during the TRACER field campaign near Houston. The campaign studied how aerosols and weather together shape deep convective storms.

The team's Rapid Onsite Atmospheric Measurement Van, ROAM-V, carried aerosol and atmospheric instruments to wherever the day's sea-breeze and bay-breeze fronts set up. Over 30 deployments sampled continental, maritime, outflow, and post-frontal air on the far side of the fronts from the fixed ARM sites. The dataset is already in use beyond the team, and campaign papers appeared in American Meteorological Society journals.
doe-osti-3014711-visolis-microbial-chemi:
Automation for screening a microbial chemical library fills this CRADA final report dated November 11, 2025, covering work by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory with Visolis Inc. and Sandia's NTESS. Visolis breeds microbe variants that make a chemical intermediate on the path to bio-based products, and the lab built high-throughput workflows to test them faster. Nathan Hillson was the Berkeley Lab contact.

Qtray plating scaled from two trays per batch to six, a gain of more than 40 percent in efficiency. New steps cover colony picking for arrayed libraries, where software marks colonies yellow when pickable and red when not, plus high-throughput batch feeding of the cultures. The report closes with no publications and no subject inventions arising from the work.
doe-osti-3014926-ceramic-membrane-solar-:
CRADA final report CRD-21-17552, dated January 2026, designs a solar desalination pilot built on ceramic membranes. The National Laboratory of the Rockies issued it, with a University of Connecticut team. The work supports the American Made Challenges Solar Prize. It covers the design stage. The system is a solar-powered vacuum membrane distillation unit. It is meant for high-salinity waters. Craig Turchi was the lab technical contact.

UConn designed multi-element modules around single-channel ceramic membranes. Fraunhofer IKTS in Germany made the membranes. Testing used the university's existing rig. The scale-up table compares pilot and full-size plants. Feed rises from 16 to 200 cubic meters a day. Permeate rises from 3 to 100. Thermal energy per volume drops from 500 to 168 kilowatt-hours per cubic meter. Membrane area grows from 3.4 to 85 square meters at the assumed flux.
doe-osti-3022723-summary-of-carbon-dioxi:
ANL report ANL-25/24 Volume 1, by Stephen Folga and four colleagues, inventories the carbon dioxide pipeline system of North America and the incident record that goes with it. Carbon capture projects plan to move far more carbon dioxide than today's network carries. This volume assembles the baseline facts: where pipelines run, who regulates them, and what has gone wrong historically.

State-by-state tables map the regulatory patchwork, showing which states certify pipeline safety programs with PHMSA under federal law and which run their own rules through public service commissions or pipeline safety bureaus. Incident data drawn from federal reporting let readers judge the historical failure record for themselves. The volume is the factual foundation of a three-volume set on carbon dioxide transport and storage.
doe-osti-3022933-bryan-mound-geomechanic:
Kyung Won Chang of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this geomechanical model update for Bryan Mound, a salt formation used for storage caverns. Report SAND2026-18013 replaces guesswork about the underground salt with a fresh computer mesh and a new round of simulations. Salt creeps slowly under pressure, and that creep can shrink caverns and strain the borehole casings that reach them.

Chang ran simulations with known pressure histories through January 29, 2025, while varying the low-stress steady-state creep coefficients. Earlier Bryan Mound models matched measured surface subsidence better than they matched cavern volume loss. The new model gives cavern volume loss higher priority, since knowing how fast caverns close matters for judging cavern integrity and casing safety over time.
doe-osti-3023590-low-cost-all-temperatur:
Evan House of WH Power, Inc. of College Park, Maryland, closes ARPA-E award DE-AR0001796, which ran September 2023 to September 2025, with partners Chunsheng Wang at the University of Maryland and Liangbing Hu at Yale. The project built a zinc-pulp battery for stationary storage, aiming at low cost and operation across extreme temperatures. Pulp-based electrodes use cheap, abundant materials instead of costly metals.

Milestone tables record a zinc baseline that cycled for more than 1,000 hours from minus 80 to plus 60 degrees, with coulombic efficiency up to about 99.8 percent. Thick manganese dioxide cathodes reached 60 milligrams per square centimeter in the optimized design and up to 250 without cracks. Pouch cells passed 100 milliamp-hours with under 10 percent spread between units, and cycle life projections at 2C pointed past 10,000 cycles.
doe-osti-3023708-crankcase-gas-rerouting:
Daniel B Olsen of Colorado State University led award DE-AR0001536, with Caterpillar Inc. on the team, and this final report, dated August 2025, covers July 2022 through June 2025. Lean-burn natural gas engines leak methane through their crankcases, and methane is a potent greenhouse gas. The project built a system that reroutes and filters crankcase gas so the methane is handled instead of vented.

Engine testing at the university demonstrated the approach, while Caterpillar pushed product development on engine lines facing higher methane penalty exposure than the test engine's platform. Filtration systems were compared across designs. The authors note the final production layout will likely differ from the first test device, with differences in company content and in details tuned for durability and cost.
doe-osti-3023819-progress-update-on-the-:
Ward Small of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory updates progress on an in situ load retention aging vessel in LLNL-TR-2011481, dated September 2025, a nine-page engineering note. The vessel ages material samples while they sit under load, so researchers can watch how holding force holds up or fades over time without opening the setup. This update covers the heating and measurement hardware being fitted.

A custom three-piece silicone heater jacket will wrap the vessel. It runs through two controllers, one for the bottom and middle pieces and one for the top, by way of a relay module tied to a laptop. Resistance temperature devices inside each piece feed back control signals. A DEWESoft IOLITE-R12 acquisition system logs the three load cells and the thermocouples that track test conditions.
doe-osti-3025230-water-vapor-resistant-s:
Olivier Sudre of RTX Corporation's Pratt and Whitney unit reports award DE-FE0032225, running March 2023 to November 2025, dated March 20, 2026. Hydrogen-burning turbines run their hot parts in steam-rich exhaust, and water vapor attacks silicon carbide composites, the ceramic materials favored for those parts. The project developed a SiC/SiC composite that resists that attack, for the National Energy Technology Laboratory.

One defense is a layered matrix that can seal its own cracks. Zirconium diboride layers were deposited alongside silicon carbide, since boron near zirconium helps form a stable sealing glass. The diboride reacts with boron trichloride more readily than with ammonia, widening the process window. An exploratory batch ran eight layers of each material, each diboride layer under unique temperature and gas flow settings, to downselect conditions.
doe-osti-3029247-icons-solid-state-compo:
Patel, Dharmesh N., of Los Alamos National Laboratory presents ICONS in report LA-UR-26-22676, issued in April 2026. ICONS stands for Integrated Composite Optical Neutron Sensor. It is a solid-state neutron detector offered as a substitute for the helium-3 gas tubes used in most systems today. The sheet lists the design at Technology Readiness Level 5, meaning prototypes have been tested in simulated settings close to real use.

Helium-3 tubes work well, but they depend on a scarce gas supply and on sealed, pressurized tubes. ICONS uses common materials instead, needs no pressurized gas, and can be built at larger sizes. It also separates neutron signals from background radiation inside one solid platform, which suits nuclear material checks.
doe-osti-3030147-additively-manufactured:
Xingbo Liu of West Virginia University led this final report under award DE-FE31819, for a project that ran from October 2019 to November 2025. Fossil power plants join unlike metals with welds that often fail early when plants cycle up and down. The team built a swap-in part by 3D printing: a graded composite transition joint whose mix shifts smoothly from one metal to the other. The target plants are advanced ultra-supercritical units, plus older plants needing repairs.

All ten stated goals were met, from design codes to a field test at Southwest Research Institute. Work covered heat treatment, welding, strength tests, and cost study, and it lifted the design to technology readiness level 7. Corrosion trials showed the P91 steel side pitted far worse than the 304 side after short salt exposure.
doe-osti-3031084-bridging-the-gap-for-po:
Luis Fernando Enriquez-Contreras, S. M. Shafiul Alam, Megan Jordan Culler, and colleagues at Idaho National Laboratory sum up a workshop in report INL/RPT-26-89901, dated February 2026. The lab 2025 Data Center Workshop, on enabling data center growth through nuclear energy, drew over 100 stakeholders. Artificial intelligence demand is growing faster than the grid can adapt, and the report lists the infrastructure gaps that follow from that mismatch.

Themes include resource adequacy, slow interconnection queues, and the jumpy load behavior of artificial intelligence training runs, which strains old planning habits. Attendees backed hybrid builds: behind-the-meter generation, microgrids, and storage beside the centers. Later pages flag water use and noise, noting some cities now treat data centers like industrial users, with sound studies and noise dashboards.
doe-osti-3098418-annual-summary-report-f:
B. Sun of INTERA wrote this fiscal year 2025 annual summary, DOE/HFO-2025-31, published in March 2026 for the Energy Department Hanford Field Office. Federal waste rules require a composite analysis for low-level waste burial on Hanford Central Plateau. The analysis, first issued for fiscal 2020, adds up dose from all disposal sources together, not site by site. Each year a summary checks whether anything changed enough to reopen the study.

The summary follows the federal disposal authorization standard and traces the long build of the analysis, from planning in fiscal 2015 through scoping in 2016 and 2017. Annex pages revisit site performance studies, such as Waste Management Area C, whose groundwater, air, and intruder pathways were modeled in three dimensions. The closed tank farm results feed the site-wide totals.
doe-osti-3362545-glass-property-composit:
Xiaonan Lu, John D. Vienna, Pavel Ferkl, and colleagues at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory update glass math in this February 2026 report, version EWG3.0. Hanford Waste Treatment Plant will melt direct-feed high-level waste into glass. Before a recipe is picked, models must predict how a given mix will behave: will it pour, crystallize, or leach too fast? The update gathers early models built for this flowsheet plus models from the open literature.

The tables span dozens of oxides, from boron and calcium down to trace curium and americium, each with fitted values. Constraints ride alongside the models so flowsheet studies can reject mixes that would fail plant rules. The work feeds design of the High-Level Waste Facility and the test programs that check glass durability before hot operations begin.
doe-osti-3362674-electron-storage-ring-p:
Z. Zapata of Brookhaven National Laboratory leads the design report for the Electron-Ion Collider electron storage ring power supplies, BNL-229720-2026-TECH, dated April 2026. D. Bruno, W. Contesini, and eight more contributors share the work. The collider, approved in January 2020, will smash electrons into ions to probe the glue that holds atomic nuclei together. Hundreds of magnets steer the electron ring, and each needs a clean, steady power feed.

One chapter details ground fault detection for store-bought supply units. A sense resistor watches for leakage current, and a precision amplifier turns it into a voltage the controller reads. The resistor value trades safety against sensitivity: too high blinds the detector, too low lets fault current run. The hardest case pairs high circuit resistance with high inductance, starving the fault signal.
doe-osti-3363315-geology-of-the-one-eart:
Carl Carman, Mansour Khosravi, Dibya Koirala, and colleagues at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign describe the geology of the One Earth Energy site (report DOE-UIUC-0031892-22, May 2026). The site is one of two in the Illinois Storage Corridor CarbonSAFE Phase III project, which aims to speed commercial carbon storage and win Class VI injection permits at each site. Principal investigator Roland Okwen leads the work at the Illinois State Geological Survey.

Crews drilled the One Earth Energy #1 test well in 2022 and ran four 2D seismic lines plus a small 3D survey. Core and log data characterize the Mt. Simon Sandstone storage interval and the Eau Claire Formation seal. Petrophysical analysis reports porosity ranges, pore sizes, and mineral content for selected zones.
doe-osti-3365795-large-load-impacts-to-d:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21384, by Thad Haines and printed in May 2026, simulates what very large new loads do to a distribution feeder's hosting capacity. Hosting capacity is how much new demand or generation a feeder can accept before voltage or thermal limits break. Data centers and industrial customers now arrive in multi-megawatt steps that old feeders were never built for.

Four feeders form the baseline. Scenarios add 2 megawatts on one feeder, which stayed acceptable, then 2 and 4 megawatts on another feeder, judged marginally and significantly unacceptable. Capacitor banks of 2 and 8 megavars were tested as mitigation, with voltage impacts detailed for each case. Thermal headroom far exceeded voltage headroom in the baseline, a pattern planners will recognize: voltage, not wire capacity, binds first.
doe-osti-3366510-partial-support-for-the:
A final report for DOE grant DE-SC0013511, covering April 2021 to May 2025, documents partial federal support for the Federal Committee for Meteorological Services and Supporting Research. The Office of the Federal Coordinator for Meteorology knits together the weather work of a dozen agencies. Its working groups cover earth system prediction, observing systems, atmospheric transport and dispersion, and tropical cyclones.

The work included a multi-agency switch to new station IDs under the WMO observing system, set out in 2020 guidelines. The atmospheric transport group pivoted when COVID canceled its annual George Mason conference, and kept coordinating online. The tropical cyclone forum reviews the national hurricane forecast program yearly with emergency managers. The report is the paper trail for coordination work that rarely produces papers.
doe-osti-3374739-esd-ethernet-signal-dif:
Idaho National Laboratory poster INL/MIS-25-88053, dated September 2025, by Laasya M. Koduru with Keith D. Mecham, presents the Ethernet Signal Differentiator, or ESD. Gigabit and automotive Ethernet send two signals down one wire pair at the same time. The merged stream is hard to read without an active tap. A tap delays the traffic, which can upset sensitive control systems. The poster asks whether learning software can split the merged signal while only listening.

The project trained a bidirectional LSTM network on merged captures. It learned to recover each side of the conversation on its own. A tool called TRUSTEE then distilled the model into a plain decision tree. The tree matched the model well, with agreement scores of 0.87 and 0.85 on two test signals. Fidelity scores reached 0.92 and 0.91, a check that the simple tree stays honest to the network.
doe-osti-3374854-a-field-and-laboratory-:
A Building America final technical report, dated June 2026, measures how often home heating and cooling systems run with faults. David Yuill leads a six-person team at the University of Nebraska. Seyed Ali Rooholghodos and Yifeng Hu are next on the author list. Faults such as low refrigerant charge or blocked airflow waste energy in silence. Owners rarely know anything is wrong. The study pairs field surveys of real homes with lab tests of faulted units.

Homes were picked to stand for most Building America climate zones. The team then mined the field data for patterns. House size, build year, thermostat type, and unit efficiency all went into the search. The goal is plain: show which faults are common, where they cluster, and what they cost. Those facts can steer installer training and code rules toward the faults that matter most.
doe-osti-3377786-evs-scale-nextgen-profi:
EVs@Scale: NextGen Profiles EVSE Characterization 2025, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5400-98814 from June 2026, records bench tests of electric vehicle charging equipment. Eight authors are printed: Keith Davidson, Darren Paschedag, Isaac Tolbert, Derek Jackson, Pranav Gadamsetty, Namrata Kogalur, Marco Gaxiola, and Saroj Shinde. The goal is repeatable profiles of how chargers behave.

The test rig pairs charging power cabinets and a dispenser kiosk with an electric vehicle emulator load, which stands in for a car battery. Single-port setups measure one session at a time; a dual setup with two liquid-cooled CCS connectors measures multi-port, multi-session charging. Using an emulator avoids the time real battery charging and discharging would take, so the team can run many conditions, including off-nominal ones.
doe-osti-3377889-west-africa-battery-ene:
Amy Rose of the National Laboratory of the Rockies discusses battery storage tariffs in an April 2026 deck for a West Africa capacity building program. Payment design is the subject: how a battery energy storage system gets paid shapes whether projects pencil out. Key topics are asset classification, the compensation mechanism, value stacking, contract design, and system efficiency and degradation.

Storage fits poorly into existing power sector boxes, since one system can act as generation, a network asset, or load, and it both charges and discharges. Charging the battery for both injections and withdrawals can block viable projects. A worked example shows the arithmetic of losses: 95 percent charging efficiency times 97 percent discharging gives 92.2 percent round-trip, so power must sell for at least 7.8 percent above the charging price.
doe-osti-3377910-barriers-and-opportunit:
Barriers and Opportunities for Energy Technology Adoption in Juneau, Alaska, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5400-100062 from June 2026, asks a plain question. What helps, and what blocks, households and organizations in Juneau from adopting new energy technology? The authors are Carolina Jaime-Anson, Lis Blanco, and Anne E. Corrigan. The evidence comes from people, not models: the research approach rests on focus groups and interviews.

An executive summary lays out the approach, the project takeaways, and the conclusion up front. The body then works through the interview and focus group findings in order. Juneau's isolation shapes the questions. The capital city cannot be reached by road, and its energy choices are local ones. The report closes with the impact the team expects the findings to have on adoption work there.
doe-osti-3390995-cooperative-support-of-:
Fermilab closes CRADA number FRA-2022-0029 with a final report dated March 23, 2026. The subject is cooperative support of the Fermilab site's natural areas and related programs. Walter Levernier is the Fermilab technical contact. The agreement's other party is Fermilab Natural Areas. The Office of Science sponsors the program. It is an unusual entry in the CRADA file: land stewardship rather than hardware.

A national laboratory is also a landscape. The Fermilab site holds prairie and other natural areas that need continuing care. The cooperative arrangement supported that work and related programs. As Article X of the agreement requires, the final report goes to the Office of Scientific and Technical Information. It goes as part of the public record of federally funded work, including its list of subject inventions.
doe-osti-3395387-implementing-induction-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4702, dated July 2026, implements induction-heated time-at-temperature testing workflows for irradiated materials. Six authors are printed: Kory Linton, Mackenzie Ridley, Anthony Guajardo, Kara Krogh, Ethan Shipulski, and M. Nedim Cinbiz. The milestone number is M2FT-26OR020202021, in the Advanced Fuels Campaign.

Time-at-temperature testing holds a specimen at heat for a set period to see how its properties drift, the slow aging a reactor imposes. Doing that to irradiated material, inside hot cells with remote handling, needs a heating method that is fast, controllable, and safe at a distance; induction heating fits. The report is the workflow volume: how the tests are set up, run, and recorded, so the campaign's post-irradiation examination line can repeat them the same way every time.
doe-osti-3396327-carbon-capture-and-util:
Global Algae Innovations' final report for award DE-FE0032104, covering September 1, 2021 to December 31, 2025, presents carbon capture and utilization for protein and fatty acids. David A. Hazlebeck was principal investigator. Partners were TSD Management Associates and Algenesis. Where the companion algae projects sold fuel and feed, this one aimed the harvest at food and chemical ingredients.

The project built an engineering-scale integrated system in four linked parts. An absorber system captures carbon dioxide and delivers it to the ponds. An open raceway cultivation system grows the algae. Oil extraction from the harvested algae and oil fractionation into usable products complete the chain. Techno-economic and life cycle analyses close the volume. They weigh the process as a business and as a carbon proposition. Invention disclosures are listed at the end.
doe-osti-3490009-quantifying-growth-of-t:
Pacific Northwest report PNNL-38762, by Grace Black and dated December 2025, measures growth of three common bacteria fed phytic acid. Media mix changes growth, so recipes were varied on purpose. Optical density readings track growth over time in small wells.

Cultures were diluted to an optical density of 0.1 before tests. Cells spun for 5 minutes at 7,000 times gravity, then moved to fresh medium. Wells held 250 microliters each, with four replicates per mix. Carbon source tests used six replicates and eight blanks. Soil and gut researchers learn which media let bacteria use this common phosphorus store.
doe-osti-3520822-pharos-promethium-high-:
ORNL/SPR-2025/4226 is a 2025 report from Oak Ridge National Laboratory that introduces PHAROS, an automated system to recover promethium-147 from fission product waste. Benjamin Roach leads the project, with Kevin Gaddis and Evan Williams in the evidence record. Promethium-147 powers nuclear batteries and lights, yet domestic supply is scarce.

A high-pressure ion chromatography column does the separation in a closed loop. Automated handling aims for loss-free recovery of high-purity material. Tests use trace-metal-grade acids inside a radiological fume hood. Samples up to 500 milliroentgens on contact can be handled there. A steady domestic source would serve defense and device makers.
doe-osti-3683713-distributed-model-based:
Sandia-linked paper SAND2026-25752R studies a shared planning method for groups of moving agents. Five authors are printed, led by Seth Golembeski, Keith L. Gibson, and Alexander Gross of Georgia Tech. Some authors also hold Sandia posts. The method, Distributed Model-Based Diffusion, plans paths for many vehicles at once. Joint planning is plagued by curved, non-smooth costs and sheer size. Late messages make it harder still.

The team proves the method pulls toward a noise floor in a finite number of steps. That proof holds even when messages lag, within a bounded delay. Tests covered three tasks: a circle-swap task for small ground robots, a shared driving task, and a mock aerial combat game. Even with lag added, the shared method cut circle-swap finish time by about a third. It also raised the aerial combat win rate by about a quarter over the central version.
doe-osti-3687294-karuk-tribe-community-s:
Karuk Tribe's final technical report, dated October 6, 2025, closes award DE-IE0000160 for community solar systems. Sara Spence is the named author, and Joshua Saxon served as project manager. Partners were SunRenu Solar and WattHub Renewables. Total project cost ran near $3.92 million, split almost evenly between the Energy Department and the Tribe. Three builds make up the project, all on tribal lands in northern California.

A ground-mounted array beside the tribal casino supplies that large load. Solar plus storage went onto thirty-nine elder homes across Yreka, Happy Camp, and Orleans. Batteries there keep medical gear, heat, and food cold through the area's frequent long outages. A small system also serves the Happy Camp Wellness Center. All work finished between May and December 2023, though four homes waited until March 2024 for a utility transformer swap. The systems are slated to save the Tribe over $200,000 a year.
doe-osti-3740808-oak-ridge-national-labo:
An Oak Ridge capability report dated September 19, 2025 lays out the lab's light water reactor test bed and fuel shipping kit. Eleven authors are printed, led by Nathan Capps, Jason Harp, and Peter Doyle. Spent fuel rods must travel safely from power plants to the lab first. Two casks handle that work: the Battelle Research Reactor cask and a legal-weight truck cask from NAC. Rods unload into hot cells for close study.

Inside, a suite of rigs probes fuel behaviour. One station replays loss-of-coolant crashes; thirteen such tests are logged, three on commercial accident-tolerant fuels. The data feed regulator and vendor bids to raise burnup limits and license new fuels. One test showed spacer grids block both cladding bulge and fuel breakup. Other kit bakes rods, checks burnup, and runs fatigue tests. A mini fuel line in the High Flux Isotope Reactor rounds out the bed.
doe-osti-3920948-contingency-base-energy:
J. C. Tucker and J. K. Goddard of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote a user guide, dated September 2026, for the Contingency Base Energy Management System. The software watches power and fuel use at deployed military camps. This volume is the one meant for the staff who run the system day to day.

Screens show the whole camp at a glance, then let the user drill into buildings, generators, fuel tanks, and weather. Generator panels show live output, and a marker turns green when a unit runs at a good, fuel-saving level. Tank views track stored fuel. Step-by-step text walks operators through the menu tree and each detail screen. With it, camp staff can spot waste, plan generator runs, and keep power steady on less fuel.
doe-osti-3920966-contingency-base-energy:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory staff J. C. Tucker and J. K. Goddard wrote the administrator's companion to the Contingency Base Energy Management System manuals in September 2026. The system tracks power generation, fuel, and buildings at deployed camps. This volume covers the setup and control tasks that ordinary operators do not touch.

Most pages can be opened with no login at all, but a few key pages ask for an administrator name and password. Chief among them is the Installation Setup page, which shapes how the system is built for a site. Chapters walk through starting the software, reading the camp status screen, and changing guarded settings in the right order. Site managers get the full path from first launch to a camp display they can trust.
doe-osti-3920988-contingency-base-energy:
Getting the Contingency Base Energy Management System running at a new camp is the job of this installation manual by J. C. Tucker and J. K. Goddard of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, dated September 2026. The system monitors generators, fuel, and buildings at deployed bases. Installers follow this volume before operators ever see a screen.

The steps begin with the files on the install media. One package holds the database link files that let the Ignition platform use Windows security. A gateway backup file loads the project itself, and a blank database backup gives the new site a clean start. Further parts cover added query tools and checks that the camp screen comes up right. Done in order, the manual takes a bare computer to a live energy display.
donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-egypt-c:
Donovan Pasha and Some People of Egypt, complete, by Gilbert Parker, gathers all four volumes of his Egyptian tales in one text. Parker explains in his introduction that the book was planned as a herald. The Weavers, his Egyptian novel, followed it in 1907. Fifteen stories stand in the contents. They run from While the Lamp Holds Out to Burn to The Light of Other Days.

Dicky Donovan moves through them all. He is the Khedive's English secretary, small and unremarkable to look at. He knows Egypt from the inside. Officers like Fielding and Wyndham succeed or blunder around him. Egyptian soldiers, sheikhs, and dancing girls get their own tales. Parker never ruled Egypt and said so. He built his Cairo from travel, reading, and soldiers' talk. The set remains his most popular short work: an occupied country rendered as a chessboard of honor, debt, and sudden violence.
dryden-s-palamon-and-arcite:
John Dryden's Palamon and Arcite, edited by George E. Eliot for school study, presents Dryden's retelling of Chaucer's Knight's Tale. Eliot, English master at the Morgan School, dedicates the volume to Henry A. Beers of Yale, who first aroused his interest in Dryden.

The preface admits the difficulty of editing a classic for schools, since colleges vary their examination demands from year to year. Eliot therefore offers a generally comprehensive outline, which teachers may fill in as they please. Students meeting Dryden for the first time will find Palamon and Arcite, the tale of two knights' rivalry in love and war, nobly told.
embers-complete:
Embers, complete, by Gilbert Parker, holds all three volumes of his collected songs and poems in one text. Parker the novelist wrote verse from the beginning of his career. The first volume opens with the title poem and Rosleen. Irish exile songs stand beside sea pieces and desert calls. Mary Callaghan and Me, Kildare, and You'll Travel Far and Wide set the early tone.

Volume 3 ends the gathering in Camden Town and at Juniper Cove. An Arab Love Song, a camel driver addressing his camel, and the Australian Stockrider widen the map. Parker's three worlds all sing here: Ireland remembered, Egypt imagined, Canada and Australia traveled. The poems are lyrics for recitation, plain in diction and strong in refrain. Read whole, Embers is the diary under the novels. The same longing for home, and the same restlessness that forbids it, drive every story Parker ever told.
ernest-maltravers-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton calls Ernest Maltravers the most mature and comprehensive of his novels in the preface to the edition of 1840, printed in this complete text. He dedicates the book to the great German people, a race of thinkers and critics. The novel follows Ernest, a young man of genius, through love, authorship, and ambition in his own time.

Maltravers grows feared as well as known, the narrator says, wielding weapons none could contemn. Lytton declines to follow him step by step, describing only the principal events of his intellectual life. The preface also owns Godolphin as his and looks back to Pelham, written when he was little more than a boy. Nine books carry Ernest from Alice Darvil to Lady Florence and fame.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-complete:
Charles Cotton's English translation gathers Michel de Montaigne's whole Essays into one large file, edited by William Carew Hazlitt. Montaigne (1533-1592), a French judge turned country landowner, built the book across twenty years of retirement. He called each short piece an essay, a trial of his judgment. His own mind serves as the main subject throughout.

All three books stand here in order, from early chapters on sorrow, idleness, and liars to late studies of vanity and experience. Friendship, cannibals, custom, cruelty, books, coaches, and repentance show the range of his curiosity. A life of Montaigne, his letters, and an editor's preface frame the essays themselves. Latin quotations crowd the pages, yet the talk stays personal and plain. Anyone who wants the complete work in one place, rather than split across separate volumes, starts with this file.
essays-on-taste:
Two Augustan voices debate taste in Essays on Taste, an Augustan Reprint Society volume from the Clark Memorial Library. The reprints take two of the twenty letters of John Gilbert Cooper's Letters Concerning Taste, third edition of 1757, the first having appeared in 1755. John Armstrong's pieces come from his two-volume Miscellanies of 1770, one first printed there and others from 1758 under the name Launcelot Temple.

Ralph Cohen introduces the pair. Armstrong's verse bullies a mumbling ape of taste who boasts ten thousand a year and yelps in the House of Commons. Cooper's letters argue taste as a rational pleasure, fit for polite readers. The bibliographical note sorts the editions and pseudonyms with care.
etiquette:
Emily Post, named on the title page as Mrs. Price Post, published Etiquette with Funk and Wagnalls in New York and London in 1922. The subtitle states its range plainly: in society, in business, in politics, and at home. A note inside records a first edition in July 1922 and a second that September. Photographs and facsimiles of social forms appear throughout, from a bride's bouquet to the place setting at a formal dinner.

Post gives direct rules for the occasions of her world: weddings at church and at home, afternoon tea, dinners with and without silver, guests, servants, and the care of a house. A closing chapter treats the growth of good taste in America. The advice is firm but often kind, aimed at sparing people embarrassment. Readers get the standard American manners manual of its era, in full period detail.
eugene-aram-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton dedicated Eugene Aram to Sir Walter Scott in a warm letter that opens the complete text. The story, given here in one file with all five books, centers on Eugene Aram, a learned and solitary man known in his village as the Student. In the quiet place called Grassdale he wins the love of Madeline Lester, and marriage is planned. Yet Aram carries a secret from his past, and men who know it begin to close in.

Old violence returns as proof: a dug-up skull with a fracture that a surgeon says no natural decay could make. The closing book brings a trial. Readers get the full arc of a story about guilt, learning, and a past that will not stay buried.
europmc-pmc7119644-REWRITE: How common is autism in American kids? The ADDM Network's 2016 watch across 11 US sites gauged autism's share among 8-year-olds nationwide. Counting cases carefully to grasp the true scope for families and schools across the country.
evan-harrington-complete:
George Meredith's Evan Harrington, complete in one volume, tells the whole story of a tailor's son in love with a lady. Melchisedec Harrington, the great Mel of Lymport, leaves his son Evan a trade, a temper, and three ambitious sisters. The eldest becomes Countess de Saldar and plots Evan's rise. Evan himself sails, travels, and shines in company.

Across forty-seven chapters Evan courts Rose Jocelyn while hiding his shop. The Jocelyns of Beckley Park stand for county pride and horror of trade. Cricket matches, picnics, letters, and duels of wit fill the middle. Evan writes himself tailor, then calls himself gentleman, as honesty slowly wins. Meredith's comedy asks whether worth lies in birth, work, or character. It remains one of his sunniest novels, dense with talk and alive with social observation.
eve-s-diary-complete:
Twain's Eve's Diary is a comic diary told in the voice of Eve in Eden. Mark Twain presents it as translated from the original. This complete text carries illustrations by Lester Ralph. Eve writes day by day from her first day of life.

She begins by noting she is almost a whole day old and feels like an experiment. She resolves to keep a careful record for future historians. Early entries praise the new world yet fault its rushed finish. Too many stars sit in some places and too few in others, she writes. Her curious, earnest tone drives the humor. The diary form lets Twain retell creation through fresh, literal eyes.
falkland-complete:
Lytton's Falkland, Complete gathers all four books of his earliest prose fiction. Edward Bulwer-Lytton wrote the tale in boyhood, before Pelham made his name. He later withdrew it from print, judging its morality harshly. This text restores it in his collected works with his son's consent.

A prefatory note explains the restoration at length. Tauchnitz's continental edition had kept the tale abroad for years. Since it could not in practice be withheld, the editors print it openly. They attach the record of the author's own verdict to the text. The novel follows Erasmus Falkland and Emily Mandeville through Books 1 to 4. Her journal and Mrs. St. John's letter carry parts of the telling.
fires-and-firemen-from-the-eclectic-maga:
The Eclectic Magazine of Foreign Literature reprinted Fires and Firemen in its May 1855 number, taking the article from the Quarterly Review. The piece reviews the annual reports of Mr. Braidwood, superintendent of London's Fire Brigade. Its stations, the article says, strike every stranger to the metropolis. A sentinel waits, and the red artillery gleams ready.

London firefighting becomes spectacle and system at once. Horses tear foaming through crowded streets, a hundred arms work the pump, and the fire-escape swings in for the shrieking figure at the window. Braidwood's reports supply the facts underneath the drama: engines, stations, and discipline. The article argues that an organized brigade, not parish engines and volunteers, saves a modern city. American readers of the Eclectic met London's model whole. It is journalism of admiration, and a founding text of professional fire service history.
frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-musician-c:
Frederick Niecks's Frederick Chopin, as a Man and Musician, complete in the third edition of 1902, joins both volumes in one file. His first preface dates from 1888, when the work was the first full Chopin biography. A proem on Poland and the Poles precedes nineteen chapters in the first volume alone. The second volume completes the life and judges the works.

Niecks states his guiding principle plainly: facts collected, conclusions drawn, both placed before the reader. He laboured, he says, to avoid diffuseness and rhapsody, the besetting sins of writers on music. Liszt's earlier life of Chopin is weighed and found exuberant. Letters, pupils' memories, and documents carry the narrative from Warsaw to Paris and the grave. This is the scholarly Chopin, the source from which the popular ones descend. Its bulk is its virtue: everything Niecks could verify is here.
fromont-and-risler-complete:
Alphonse Daudet's Paris factory novel is presented whole in Fromont and Risler, Complete, the full English text of the Fromont Jeune et Risler Aine story. Risler the elder, a Swiss engineer of tireless honesty, joins the Fromont wallpaper firm as working partner. Georges Fromont, the heir, prefers pleasure and leaves the ledgers to others. Sidonie Chebe, the pretty girl from the shop across the street, marries Risler to reach the great house.

Inside, balls, dresses, and bills pile up while cashier Sigismond keeps the true accounts in silence. Sidonie's affair with Georges, her wedding-day waltz partner, spends the firm's money and Risler's trust together. Frantz, the younger brother who loved her first, suffers at the household's edge. Daudet follows the discovery and the honest man's end with a storyteller's speed. Readers taking the novel whole get the complete design: factory, shop, and parlor bound in one tragedy of trust.
gerfaut-complete:
Charles de Bernard won the French Academy's crown with Gerfaut, his best novel, and this complete English edition holds it whole. An essay opens the file, calling Bernard a pupil of Balzac with a lighter hand. Octave de Gerfaut, a young writer fresh from conquering Paris letters, visits the castle of Baron de Bergenheim. An attachment grows between the guest and the baron's wife.

Workman Lambernier, cursing his master by the roadside, sounds the first note of revenge. Inside the chateau, dinners and hunts cover a love that deepens by glances. The Baron's humor cracks at his own table as suspicion settles on his wife. Marillac and Mademoiselle de Corandeuil supply comedy around the tragedy. Bernard drives the design to exposure and grief. Readers taking Gerfaut whole see why the Academy prized it: Balzac's province, drawn with polish and a colder heart.
godolphin-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton first let Godolphin into the world without his name on it, then owned it in a playful dedication to Count Alfred d'Orsay. He calls the book his unfilial offspring, long disowned and now keen to parade its debts to the most accomplished gentleman of the time. The novel is a tale of fashionable London life, first published in the 1830s.

Percy Godolphin moves through salons, country houses, and Rome, torn between the wild, simple Lucilla and the brilliant Constance, who weds another and shines in society. Love, pride, and the world's cold rules grind against each other. Lytton's style is ornate and full of talk about feeling and rank. This complete text lets a reader follow the whole arc, from first meetings to the last discoveries about Godolphin's heart.
govdocs-archive_org-WOIlluminatiFreemaso:
Helen Peters wrote The Union Jack to argue that Britain's national flag is no innocent emblem. In her reading, the flag's design embodies a conspiracy that mocks Christ, and the British Empire's rulership amounted to a usurpation of Christ's rightful sovereignty.

Peters decodes the flag's crosses and colors as hidden religious statements, building her case from symbolism and scripture. The book belongs to the fringe end of writing about flags, where designs are treated as coded messages from secret powers. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers curious about that tradition of interpretation.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAWatergate_CI: Government material filed under the heading CIA Watergate makes up this file, released without a fuller description. The CIA's threads into Watergate were real: the burglars included former agency men, and Howard Hunt carried an agency past into the White House plumbers. The administration pressed the CIA to help shield the break-in investigation. Those threads filled hearing rooms for two years. The file is kept as titled, a fragment of that record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClarkWilliamKem:
Dr. William Kemp Clark directed neurosurgery at Parkland Hospital and was among the doctors who attended President Kennedy in Trauma Room One. These research notes work through his Warren Commission deposition of March 21, 1964.

The notes concentrate on his time sequences and on the press conference of November 22, 1963, where Clark announced the President's death and described the wounds as he understood them. Clark's early public words about the wounds became evidence in every later argument over the shots' direction. A researcher's notes on the deposition show the case being rebuilt from its testimony, page by page.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeathCertificat:
An FBI memorandum deals with an odd side problem after President Kennedy's death: copies of his death certificate. The Texas Registrar of Vital Statistics had been issuing copies of the certificate. Both the Secret Service and the FBI made inquiries into how those copies were being given out.

Behind the inquiries sat a suspected scheme to sell numerous copies of the document. A president's death certificate had obvious value as a souvenir or worse, and officials wanted the flow stopped or explained. The memo shows the Bureau handling the paperwork fallout of the assassination, far from the shooting itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FOIAPrivacyActR: Opening pages of Washington Hunt, a book by Bert Andrews published by Random House in New York, survive in this file. Despite the catalog label attached to it, the file does not contain the FOIA Privacy Act appeal that the label describes. What a reader gets instead is the start of Andrews's book, so the entry stands as a short excerpt under a mismatched archive label.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HollywoodReport:
Jay Carr wrote for the Hollywood Reporter on August 15, 1991 about Oliver Stone on the defensive. Stone's film JFK advanced a conspiracy account of the Kennedy assassination, and critics attacked its history before it even opened. Stone answered in the piece's headline words: I have done all my homework.

A director defending a film in the trade press is show business and history at once. Stone's JFK forced a national argument about who killed Kennedy, fought out in interviews like this one. Carr's piece preserves the defense at the height of that controversy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-IntelligenceAge:
William Greider wrote an article headlined Again, Government Claims the Power to Snoop, with a second headline noting the FBI infiltrates an anti-draft group. His subject is the reach of government surveillance in America. An infiltrated draft-resistance group serves as his evidence that the power was being used at home.

Greider wrote for readers who remembered the exposure of domestic spying programs. Each new claim of authority, he argues, repeats an old pattern. The article preserves that argument in the press of the day, with the anti-draft infiltration as its case in point.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RedRosesFromTex:
Nerin E. Gun's book 'Red Roses From Texas' is preserved here in full text. It was published by Frederick Muller in London. Gun, a Turkish-born journalist, wrote one of the early books on the Kennedy assassination, drawing on the European view of Dallas and on his own reporting.

Early assassination books set the terms the debate still uses: doubts about the lone gunman, interest in Oswald's travels, suspicion of official haste. Gun's was among the first written from outside the United States. The full text lets readers test his account directly, rather than through later summaries. It also preserves the London edition of a book that reached American readers in the first wave of Warren Report criticism.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WATE_WATE: nsia-WATE WATE: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-philip-corso-william:
Philip J. Corso, a retired Army colonel, claimed he personally handled alien technology recovered from the Roswell crash site. Written with William J. Birnes, The Day After Roswell appeared in 1997, fifty years after the famous 1947 incident in New Mexico.

Corso says the Army quietly fed pieces of the wreckage to American industry under his direction. In his account, that seeding helped produce later tools and devices, while officials kept the source secret from the public. The book became a landmark of UFO literature and remains highly controversial, since its claims rest on Corso's word rather than documents readers can test.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Cub:
Journalist Lisa Howard built a back channel between Washington and Fidel Castro's Cuba in the early 1960s. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 624, published in April 2018. It appeared as the Castro era was ending and draws on records of her quiet work.

Howard's efforts aimed at rapprochement, a thaw between two hostile governments. The posting calls her method intimate diplomacy, meaning personal trust used where formal talks could not go. Her story shows how much Cold War diplomacy ran through private people. It also preserves the papers behind a channel that stayed hidden for years.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In 1960 an American intelligence report reached a firm conclusion about Israel's new nuclear site: it was for weapons. William Burr and Avner Cohen edited this briefing book, number 877, published in December 2024. The report dates from the site's earliest years, when its purpose was publicly denied.

Evidence here is limited to the editors, number, and the report's conclusion. That conclusion alone carries weight. It means Washington's analysts identified a weapons purpose at the start of a program Israel would not acknowledge for decades. The posting belongs to the long documentary trail of an open secret, told from inside the watching government.

How much nuclear force is enough to deter an enemy? William Burr edited this briefing book, number 779, published in October 2021, on the Navy's case for finite deterrence. Navy leaders worried that hair-trigger readiness and vulnerable missile silos could frighten an enemy into striking first.

Chief of Naval Operations Arleigh Burke argued that even the maddest Russian was deterred, because the Soviets had striven too hard to industrialize to risk devastation. A Navy report described the war plan's result as a smoking, radiating ruin at the end of two hours. The documents show admirals arguing that enough was enough, against services demanding more.

On October 6, 1977, President Jimmy Carter did something no president had done: he personally took part in a nuclear drill. The exercise, code-named Ivory Item, was a Missile Attack Conference. Carter and his top officials rehearsed the response to a simulated surprise nuclear strike on the United States.

A rehearsal at that level tests more than machinery. It forces a president to practice the gravest decision in the job, with the clock running, before any real crisis arrives. The posting preserves the record of that practice session. It shows the command system being exercised by the one person whose orders it exists to carry.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness: When Hungarians rose against communist rule in 1956, the United States encouraged them with broadcasts but sent no help as Soviet tanks crushed the revolt. Whether America acted wrongly, or could not have acted, is debated to this day. This briefing-book page revives that debate over American action and inaction during the revolution. The evidence here is the title alone. A companion Archive volume prints Eisenhower's private conclusion that neither military operations nor uprisings were feasible in Soviet-held Europe.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Archive_CREW: Records of a president's calls with foreign heads of state are among the most sensitive papers a White House creates, and among the first historians need. A National Security Archive briefing book page records the Archive, the watchdog group CREW, and historians jointly asking a federal judge to order those records preserved. The request belonged to the wider fight over whether the Trump White House kept the records the law requires. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, marking the legal ask and its coalition.
guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-complete:
Sir Walter Scott's Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer, complete in fifty-eight chapters, opens with a young Oxford man lost in Dumfriesshire. Guy Mannering reaches Ellangowan on the night Harry Bertram is born, and casts the child's horoscope for sport. Meg Merrilies, the gypsy, takes the prophecy in earnest. The stars, she insists, will keep their appointments.

Harry is stolen by smugglers, Ellangowan falls to the lawyer Glossin's machinations, and years pass. The heir returns from India unrecognized, as Vanbeest Brown, loving Lucy Bertram, who does not know her brother. Hatteraick the smuggler, the kidnapped child's nurse, and Meg's deathbed pursuit force the truth out. Dominie Sampson, the learned, starving tutor, supplies the comedy. Scott invented the regional novel of Scotland here as much as in Waverley: dialect, law, gypsies, and coast smuggling in one design. The astrology was a joke; the prophecy was the plot.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-compl:
Edward Bulwer Lytton dedicated Harold, the Last of the Saxon Kings to his friend C. T. D'Eyncourt, under whose roof much of it was composed, and whose library fed it. The dedicatory epistle says the idea of a historical romance on the Norman Invasion had long possessed him, and the chronicles of that time had long been familiar. He owns an old habit of lingering over a plan for years before a sentence advances. The book appeared in 1848.

Harold Godwinson rises through the last years of Saxon England: the court of Edward the Confessor, the house of Godwin, and the gathering Norman storm. His love for Edith, his oath to William, and the two invasions of 1066 drive the tale to Hastings. Lytton loads the story with learning, in notes and long descriptive chapters. This complete text is the stateliest of his novels, a national epic in prose.
hector-s-inheritance-or-the-boys-of-smit:
Hector's Inheritance, or the Boys of Smith Institute, by Horatio Alger Jr, opens inside Castle Roscoe, where wealth has made one man bold. Alger shows Mr Roscoe ringing for the mail and looking over his lawn and avenue of trees with exultation. All of it may be his, he tells himself, if he dares, and he owes something, he adds, to his son.

Chapter headings promise the counterweight: Hector learns a secret, resents an insult, fights a skirmish, and prepares to leave home. The inheritance of the title hangs on the scheme Roscoe is hatching in his library. Sent to the Smith Institute among its boys, Hector must hold his honesty and his claim against adult plotting. Alger writes his familiar pattern with a school setting: a wronged boy, a hidden paper trail, and fortune waiting on proof of character.
henry-clay-s-remarks-in-house-and-senate:
Henry Clay speaks twice in this short file of his remarks in Congress. The first speech, in the House on January 19, 1819, concerns the Seminole War and General Jackson's invasion of Florida. The second, in the Senate on January 16, 1837, opposes the expunging resolutions.

The expunging fight asked the Senate to black out its earlier censure of President Jackson from its own journal. Clay asks what patriotic purpose such an act could serve and warns against sanctioning violence against the record itself. His sentences show the Great Compromiser as a debater, formal, sarcastic, and constitutional. Both speeches capture Jacksonian-era battles over executive power that Clay fought for decades.
hesiod-homeric-hymns-homerica-evelyn-whi:
Translator Hugh Evelyn-White gathered Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and the Homerica in one volume. Hesiod was a Greek farmer-poet who sang of work and the gods' birth. The hymns praise single gods in epic style.

Works and Days gives farming lore mixed with myth and moral advice. The Theogony traces the gods from chaos to Zeus. The hymns honor Apollo, Hermes, and other powers. Loose fragments round out the set. The volume is a compact doorway into early Greek religion and song, older than most of the classics beside it.
historic-doubts-relative-to-napoleon-buo:
Richard Whately first published this sly pamphlet in 1819. The hosted copy is a new edition of 1865. Whately borrows Hume's test for miracles and turns it on Napoleon. If far, strange tales need strong proof, he asks, what proof have we that Buonaparte ever lived?

The joke has a point: men doubt old wonders yet swallow fresh news whole. Whately piles up gaps and clashes in the tale of Napoleon. Some readers missed the satire and took it as real doubt. The preface laughs at both errors. It remains a neat lesson in how belief is built from mere report.
history-of-greece-vol-5-grote:
George Grote, a Victorian banker turned historian, wrote a vast history of ancient Greece. Volume Five carries his story into the great age of Athens. His work reshaped how the English-speaking world saw Greek democracy.

Grote defends Athens and its leaders against older, harsher judges. He covers wars, laws, and the rise of Athenian power in detail. His prose is formal but clear and full of learning. The set remains a landmark of classical history. This volume suits readers who want the drama of Greece told by a master advocate.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1586-8:
John Lothrop Motley's chapters nine to twenty, complete in one file, carry his History of the United Netherlands through 1586 to 1589. The question whether Elizabeth should accept the sovereignty opens the sequence. Leicester's quarrels with the States, his finance, and his counsellors fill the first chapters. Paul Buys intrigues, is imprisoned, and illustrates the opposition's fate.

Drake's visit and the Babington plot lead toward the Armada year. Leicester departs, Barneveld rises, and the provinces govern themselves in his absence. Philip in his cabinet and the great fleet off Calais dominate the close. Alexander's siege of Bergen-op-Zoom ends the file in 1589. This is the dramatic heart of Motley's work, where the republic outlives its English governor and survives Spain's supreme effort. A drunken supper quarrel sits beside the fate of nations, in his manner.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1590-9:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands for 1590 to 1599, complete in chapters twenty-one to thirty-seven, covers the republic's heroic decade. The assassination of Henry III concentrates all forces as the file opens. The United Provinces struggle against Philip becomes a war for independence in earnest. Maurice reforms the army and its martial science.

Sieges at Steenwyk and Gertruydenberg show the new method at work. France's civil war, Farnese's death, and Henry IV's conversion fill the middle. Vervins, the transfer of the provinces, and Philip's death close the political arc. Van Linschoten's travels open the commercial future in the final chapter. Motley's pace quickens as his republic prospers. This is the sunniest stretch of his history, where survival turns into greatness and the Dutch become a world power.
hofmannsthal-gedichte:
Hugo von Hofmannsthal wrote poems of unearthly beauty before he was twenty, a boy genius of Viennese modernism. His Gedichte, given here in German, gather the lyrics on which that early fame rests. Transience, beauty, and the mystery of existence shimmer through the collection's brief forms.

Few poets anywhere have matched the finish of these youthful verses, written while he still signed himself Loris. Ballads, sonnets, and dreamlike lyrics move between splendor and quiet dread. The poems stand among the glories of German poetry in any century. Reading them in the original repays even modest German richly. They also explain why Vienna watched this teenager as if he were already a classic.
homo-sum-complete:
Homo Sum in complete form presents Georg Ebers and his desert novel whole, in Clara Bell's English translation. Ebers explains that work on a history of the Sinai peninsula drew him into old accounts of monks, martyrs, and hermits. One tale stayed with him: a cave dweller who accepted expulsion for a sin another man had committed, and stayed silent until the guilty man confessed.

From that seed grows Paulus, an anchorite, meaning a monk who lives alone, at the oasis of Pharan below Mount Sinai. Young Hermas, raised in the desert by his father Stephanus, strains against the narrow life and falls through Sirona, a Roman officer's wife. Paulus takes the blame and the punishment. Desert prayer, family grief, and a hard idea of love carry the full story to its close.
how-to-write-special-feature-articles-a-:
Willard Grosvenor Bleyer wrote this handbook for feature writers, from Madison in August 1919. Bleyer directed the journalism course at the University of Wisconsin. His readers are reporters, correspondents, and free-lance writers. Their market is the popular magazine and the newspaper's magazine section.

Part One maps the field, the preparation, and the hunt for subjects. Appeal, article types, beginnings, and style follow in order. Titles, manuscripts, and photographs close the course. A specimen interview shows a boy who wants to be a shoffer, at a 2.40 clip. Part Two gives an outline for practice. It is a complete trade school in one volume.
in-the-blue-pike-complete:
In the Blue Pike in complete form gathers the whole strolling player novel by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary T Safford. Ebers opens with Cyriax, a wandering performer punished by the Nuremberg magistrates. They cropped his tongue for blasphemy, meaning reckless speech against God. His curses now come out in sounds almost nobody can follow. His wife leads him by a chain, like a tame bear.

Lame, sick, and aging fairground folk make up the troupe. At the center stands Kuni, a rope dancer whose health and luck are failing. She nurses a sick mother and twins when their helper gives up. Then she sets out on pilgrimage, a religious journey, to Altotting and far Santiago de Compostela. The road costs her last penny. Cold nights on deck ruin her cough. Charity among the very poor carries the book.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
In the Fire of the Forge in complete form holds the whole Nuremberg romance by Georg Ebers, translated from the German by Mary J Safford. Ebers opens on the eve of St Medard's Day in 1281, with moonlight over the imperial free city. Emperor Rudolph is in residence, and the wealthy Ortlieb household sits quiet under its linden tree while soldiers are kept indoors by imperial order.
