A heavier step overtakes him, and a good-humoured voice gives the salutation of the evening.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p: Paradise, the third part of Dante Alighieri's Vision, appears in the English verse of the Rev. H. F. Cary, with art by Gustave Doré. Only the title page and a full list of cantos, from canto one through canto thirty-three, are present here. No verse text appears, so the climb through the spheres of heaven can be traced only from that list of cantos.

Purgatory, the second part of Dante Alighieri's Vision, appears in the English verse of the Rev. H. F. Cary, with art by Gustave Doré. A list of all thirty-three cantos opens the volume. Two lines of canto one follow, where the poet's bark of song lifts its sail on better waves. Little more than the title page, the canto list, and those first lines are present here.
the-dwelling-place-of-light-complete:
Winston Churchill's novel The Dwelling-Place of Light, dated 1917, opens in the mill city of Hampton, New England. Edward Bumpus, at fifty-five, keeps the gate of the vast Chippering Mill, torn from his old Yankee ledge like a stone rolled by a glacier. The smoky town, full of new tongues, seems to him a bad dream on his own soil.

His daughter Janet works in the mill office and draws the owner's eye. Labour strife, desire, and old faith clash round her. Churchill, the American novelist, maps a nation changed by mills and migrants.
the-early-life-of-mark-rutherford-w-hale:
The Early Life of Mark Rutherford, printed by Oxford University Press in 1913, prints the notes of W. Hale White, who wrote as Mark Rutherford. His son's foreword tells how the elder White, asked to set down facts for his kin, left the notes to his daughter in his will. She held back, then chose to print them for a wider circle.

White recalls a strict chapel childhood, doubt, and slow self-making. The spare, honest tone matches his famed novels of faith lost and found. Few English lives of the mind read so plain and true.
the-ebb-tide-a-trio-and-quartette:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Lloyd Osbourne wrote The Ebb-Tide together, a tale of the South Seas. Part one opens at night on the beach at Papeete, Tahiti. Round the Pacific, the authors say, white men of all ranks spread trade and disease; some thrive, some rot, and some lack bread in a land of plenty. Three such men sit under a purao tree.

Herrick, Davis, and Huish, broke and shamed, plot to steal a schooner. Stevenson's late tale is bleak where his boy books were bright. Greed and rot, not gold, wait at the end of their cruise.
the-eighteenth-brumaire-of-louis-bonapar: Karl Marx's brilliant 1852 analysis of how Louis Napoleon seized power in France. "History repeats itself, first as tragedy, then as farce": the most quoted line in all of Marx. Witty, savage, and profound, it is political writing at its highest pitch.
the-emperor-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Emperor, in Clara Bell's English rendering, tells of Roman Egypt in Hadrian's day. Ebers's preface says he planned the tale fourteen years back, out of lectures on Rome's rule in Egypt, but set it aside for science. It completes his Egypt set: Uarda for Pharaonic times, An Egyptian Princess for Persian rule, The Sisters for Greek days, and Homo Sum for the desert monks.

Hadrian's visit to Alexandria drives the plot, round the sculptor Pollux, the steward's daughters, and the youth Antinous. Ebers packs the tale with learned, lived detail of the ancient city.
the-expedition-of-the-donner-party-and-i:
Eliza P. Donner Houghton's The Expedition of the Donner Party and Its Tragic Fate tells the tale from inside the family. Contents open with the Pacific Coast in 1845, Senator Benton's speeches, and Frémont's reports, which fired her father George Donner's kin to form the first emigrant party from Illinois to California. Then come the start, the Kansas plains, and letters from her mother on the road.

Fort Laramie, a Fourth of July camp, and Hastings's open letter mark the turn toward ruin. Houghton, a child survivor, writes with care and grief. Her book is a prime first-hand source.
the-forsyte-saga-complete: John Galsworthy wrote The Forsyte Saga, and this complete copy is present here only in front matter and the start of its contents. The contents open with a preface, then The Man of Property in parts. The first heads name an at home at Old Jolyon's, a dinner at Swithin's, plans of a house, and the death of Aunt Ann. No page of the novel itself can be read in this opening portion, so the tale's scenes cannot be stated from this front matter alone.
the-golden-bowl-complete:
Henry James wrote The Golden Bowl. It is dated 1904. This record holds Volumes I and II, complete. Book First is called The Prince. Part First opens in London. The Prince walks there and thinks on the city. He has always liked London when it came to him.

The Prince is a modern Roman. He finds by the Thames a truer image of the old empire than by the Tiber. He drifts into Bond Street. He stops at shop windows full of silver, gold, and jewels. The goods lie tumbled together like loot of far-off wins. His loose gaze and rich tastes mark him at once. He is a man of old name and fine feeling. He is set in a world of costly things, marriages, and money.
the-great-conspiracy-complete:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record holds the complete work. His preface sets his aim. He will present authentic facts with historical accuracy. He will be fair in grouping them. He will be true and just in the conclusions drawn. He will not mince words. He seeks favor in no quarter.

Logan traces the conspiracy from its obscure birth. It began in the minds of a few ambitious men in the earliest days of the Republic. It ran through nullification. It reached the bitter and bloody period of armed rebellion. It reaches a still more sinister development of his own day. He worked, he says, from the voluminous records open at the seat of government. He lets the chief actors speak where he can. Conspirators and Union leaders alike get their say.
the-great-war-syndicate:
Frank R. Stockton wrote The Great War Syndicate. Stockton is named as author of The Lady or the Tiger and Rudder Grange. The tale opens in the spring of a year near the close of the nineteenth century. Relations between the United States and Great Britain are strained. The fishing schooner Eliza Drum sails from a port in Maine. She makes for the banks of Newfoundland.

A new system guards the American fishing fleet. United States cruisers stay on the grounds. They warn American craft from the three-mile limit. They watch the British naval vessels. The Eliza Drum works too well at her fishing. She hauls cod at a point two and three-quarter miles, or three and a quarter, from the Canadian coast. The answer depends on the nationality of the calculator. The British cruiser Dog Star seizes her. The American cruiser Lennehaha arrives too late.
the-grounds-of-christianity-examined-by-: George Bethune English wrote The Grounds of Christianity Examined by Comparing the New Testament with the Old. English held the degree A.M. The book was printed at Boston in 1813. Its motto is: First understand, then judge. English dedicates it to the intelligent and the candid. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the dedication, and the start of a contents list. The chapters set out the marks of the Messiah given by the Hebrew prophets. They test the character of Jesus by those marks.
the-heart-of-mid-lothian-complete:
Walter Scott wrote The Heart of Mid-Lothian. The tale belongs to Tales of My Landlord, second series. The title page credits Jedediah Cleishbotham as collector and arranger. He is named as schoolmaster and parish clerk of Gandercleugh. An editor's introduction opens the volume. It reports that Scott began the tale almost before he had finished Rob Roy.

The introduction quotes a letter of November 10, 1817. Scott wrote it to Archibald Constable after talks with another firm fell through. Scott promises the best volumes yet. He says he prides himself on the first tale. The editor also notes a planned romance on the Scotch regalia. Scott never wrote that romance. Sibling volume records carry the same front matter.
the-helpmate:
May Sinclair wrote The Helpmate, published in New York by Henry Holt and Company in 1907. She is named as the author of The Divine Fire, Superseded, and Audrey Craven. Book one, chapter one opens at four in the morning in a hotel bedroom. Mrs. Walter Majendie lies awake on the edge of the bed, her face turned toward a dim line of sea.

She has lain still since midnight while her husband sleeps beside her. On their wedding night, only days before, his childlike sleep had moved her to deep tenderness. Now a new and devastating idea must be fitted against a beloved belief, and five hours of thought end in a low sob as a church clock strikes the dawn.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-comp: Don Quixote, by Miguel de Cervantes, stands here as Part I in full, in John Ormsby's translation. An editor's note explains that the cover and pictures come from the 1880 J. W. Clark edition, with engravings by Gustave Dore, while the text is Ormsby's. The contents list Part I chapters starting with the character and pursuits of Don Quixote of La Mancha and his first sally from home. Only the editor's note and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-comp: Don Quixote, Volume II in full, comes from Miguel de Cervantes, in John Ormsby's translation. The contents list the Part II chapters in order. Chapter one treats the visit of the curate and the barber. They come to speak with Don Quixote about his malady. Chapter two treats Sancho Panza's dispute with the niece and housekeeper. Chapter three treats the talk with the Bachelor Samson Carrasco. Front matter is all that is present here. The novel itself does not appear.
the-history-of-napoleon-buonaparte:
John Gibson Lockhart wrote The History of Napoleon Buonaparte, shown in an edition first issued in February 1906, with the author dated 1794-1854. Front pages quote Lockhart's own praise of Napoleon from Blackwood's Magazine: nations yet to come, he wrote, will look back on the history as on a grand and supernatural romance.

An editorial note places Lockhart between camps. He was neither an idolater of Napoleon, as Hazlitt was, nor one of the decriers. His stance is linked to the lofty impartiality he praised in Sir Walter Scott's earlier life of Napoleon. Readers are primed for a biography that admires energy and ambition while keeping a British point of view in view.
the-house-in-good-taste: Elsie de Wolfe set out her decorating ideas in this volume. The Century Company published it in New York in 1913. Photographs in color and black and white illustrate it. Only the opening pages and contents are present here. Her room-by-room advice does not itself appear. The contents still map her approach. Suitability, simplicity, and proportion come first. Later chapters treat walls, color, and doors. Others cover windows, artificial light, and halls. Separate chapters handle drawing-rooms, bedrooms, and dining-rooms. Small apartments get a chapter of their own.
the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-complete:
René Bazin's novel Une Tache d'Encre appears here complete in English. E. Lavisse supplied a long life of the author as preface. Bazin was born at Angers in 1853. He studied for the bar there. He became a lawyer and a law professor. His college was the Catholic University of his native city. He wrote early for leading French journals. His tales of province life won wide praise only with the new century.

Lavisse praises his depth of mind and pure style. The books preach patience and home virtues without dullness. The Ink Stain itself dates from 1888. It is a romance of scholarly life. The French Academy crowned it. The Academy elected Bazin in 1903. It had given him the Prix Vitet in 1896. Lavisse jokes that his books are safe anywhere. Even cloistered readers could take them in hand.
the-inside-of-the-cup-complete: Winston Churchill's novel is presented here complete. Its contents spread across eight volumes of the first issue. The Waring Problems open the story. A rector, a lost parishioner, and a woman of the song follow. Only the contents pages are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The headings trace a clergyman's crisis in stages. They name riddles of the twentieth century. The divine discontent and a messenger in the church appear. The crucible, reconstruction, and an arraignment follow. A vestry meeting and a final retribution close the arc.
the-lamp-of-fate:
Margaret Pedler dedicated this novel to Audrey Heath. Heath was her stories' fairy godmother. Pedler had outlined its plot to her one afternoon. An epigraph from the Rubaiyat fronts the book. What lamp of destiny guides children stumbling in the dark, it asks. Chapter I, The Ninth Generation, opens in a silent house. It smells of disinfectants. Hushed, swift steps sound upstairs. Hugh Vallincourt stands at his study window. He stares with unseeing eyes at the lawns and leafless trees. He waits for news of a son and heir.

He never doubts it will be a son. Chance alone made the Vallincourt first-born a boy eight times running. The pattern reads as a hallmark of heavenly approval. Pedler builds her melodrama on that certainty. A family's pride in its unbroken line of heirs is the subject. The lamp of fate burns over a birth.
the-landlord-at-lion-s-head-complete:
William Dean Howells explains in a bibliographical note how a Vermont mountain seen from Lake Champlain gave him his title. French pioneers called the peak Le Lion Couchant, while Yankees preferred the Camel Hump name. Howells saw a sleeping lion and named his planned summer hotel novel from that shape.

He wrote the story over about a year and saw it serialized before book publication in 1896. The complete record presents the whole novel about a landlord, his hotel, and the guests whose lives cross there. Howells treats ambition and manners with close, quiet observation.
the-lane-that-had-no-turning-complete: Gilbert Parker gathered his Pontiac tales into a complete set, dedicated to Sir Wilfrid Laurier in a letter recalling work begun in 1892. Only the contents and the start of that dedication are present here, listing the title tale plus stories across four volumes, among them Parpon the Dwarf, Mathurin, and Medallion Whim. The tales themselves do not appear in this record, so readers see the full plan of the collection without its opening story.
the-last-of-the-barons-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton prefaces his historical novel with a long letter defending fiction that borrows people from real records. He argues that a tale can fill cold chronicle outlines with color, habit, and motive. Research, he says, should sober the fancy that brings an age to life.

The complete novel turns to England under Edward IV and to Earl Warwick, the great baron known as the Kingmaker. Court intrigue, rebellion, and private love cross through the story. Lytton asks readers to learn how people of that age thought and felt, not just what dates they filled.
the-life-of-napoleon-i-complete: John Holland Rose wrote his life of Napoleon the First with new material from British official records, first published in December 1901. Only the title pages and the start of the contents are present here for the complete work, in a 1910 Bell edition dedicated to Lord Acton. A note on the Republican calendar opens the contents list. Rose motto from Napoleon tells his son to read and reflect on history often. The biography itself is not included in this record.
the-log-of-the-empire-state:
Geneve L. A. Shaffer wrote The Log of the Empire State after sailing as the special representative of the San Francisco Examiner on the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce's Commercial Relationship Tour of the Orient. Her introduction explains that the Chamber asked her to cover the three months' trip in a little book. The ship's party leaves San Francisco like one great happy family, waving to crowds on the docks.

Chapter one keeps the mood light. Passengers joke that their first debate is not crossing the bar but opening the ship's bar, and the last passenger aboard is Bulah, a handsome mare bound for Yokohama. Shaffer writes a cheerful travel log of a trade mission, mixing civic pride with shipboard comedy.
the-luck-of-the-mounted-a-tale-of-the-ro: Sergeant Ralph S. Kendall, an ex-member of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, wrote The Luck of the Mounted. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York in 1920, and Kendall dedicated it to his comrades of the force. Only the title pages, an epigraph from the Ingoldsby Legends, the dedication, and the opening verse of chapter one are present, so the tale itself does not appear. That verse calls for a song of days that are gone, to be sung by the non-commissioned officers of the Mounted Police.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m:
Azel Ames, a physician and member of the Pilgrim Society, wrote The Mayflower and Her Log, covering July 15, 1620 to May 6, 1621, chiefly from original sources. His introduction addresses descendants of the Pilgrims who landed at Plymouth. Ames argues that every detail of the colonists' preparations, ships, and voyage holds supreme interest today. Too little of it, he says, has been readily accessible for reference.

Ames recalls the Separatist congregation organized under John Robinson and its flight from persecution to Holland. The congregation lived at Leyden before resolving to cross the sea for larger life and liberty. The book gathers what can be known of the Merchant Adventurers who backed the venture and of the colonists themselves. A Lowell quotation on the title page ranks the shipload beside the fugitives Moses led from Egypt. Readers get a documented reconstruction of the most famous emigrant voyage in American memory.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-complete: Anthony Hamilton wrote the Memoirs of Count Grammont, presented here in an edition with notes by Sir Walter Scott. Only the title information and contents are present here, so the memoirs themselves do not appear. The contents promise a biographical sketch of Hamilton, then follow the Chevalier Grammont to the siege of Trino and the court of Turin. Later chapters bring his banishment from the French court after a reply to Cardinal Mazarin, his arrival at the English court, and his falling in love with Miss Hamilton.
the-money-master-complete:
Gilbert Parker's novel The Money Master is given here in a record labelled Complete. Its contents arrange the story in five epochs, each named for its span of the hero's life, plus an epilogue. Jean Jacques Barbille stands at the centre from the first chapter, The Grand Tour of Jean Jacques Barbille, onward.

Parker's introduction calls the novel a place by itself among his books. Critics, he notes, welcomed it as a return to Canada, where his first fiction success came, though he qualifies the point by recalling The Right of Way, published in 1901. Later epochs bring a clerk of the court's tale, a man from outside, misfortunes, and bells of memory, as the contents trace Jean Jacques toward an offered bargain and an encampment.
the-notebooks-of-leonardo-da-vinci-compl:
Jean Paul Richter translated Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks for the 1888 edition. The record is called the complete notebooks, yet the opening pages are headed Volume 1, and the same preface opens the separate Volume 1 record as well. Richter's preface tells the sad fate of Leonardo's best known works, two left unfinished and the Last Supper hurt by decay and poor repairs.

Richter also explains why the manuscripts stayed unread for so long. Leonardo wrote backwards, with his left hand, in rough letters that take much practice to read. The notebooks hold his notes on art and science, gathered from scattered manuscripts that collectors had prized for centuries.
the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-complete: George Meredith wrote the novel The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, and this record is the complete text in a 1905 printing. Only the contents are present here. The list runs to forty-two chapters, so the story itself does not appear. Titles trace a young hero's trials from The Inmates of Raynham Abbey onward. Other titles, such as Clare's Diary and The System Encounters the Wild Oats Special Plea, hint at a father raising his son by a system. A separate Volume 1 record carries the same opening titles.
the-outdoor-girls-in-a-winter-camp-or-gl: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls in a Winter Camp, or Glorious Days on Skates and Ice Boats, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The lists show this as the fourth Outdoor Girls book, after Deepdale, Rainbow Lake, and a Motor Car, with Florida next. Hope's Bobbsey Twins volumes, from the first book to Snow Lodge, fill the lower list.
the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-linco:
Arthur Brooks Lapsley edited The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln in a Constitutional Edition, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt, an essay by Carl Schurz, and an address by Joseph Choate. The record is called the complete papers, yet the pages present are headed Volume 1. The introductory part opens with Lincoln's speech of November 10, 1864, answering a serenade after his re-election.

In that speech Lincoln asks whether a government not too strong for liberty can be strong enough to survive great emergencies. He urges his hearers to study the Civil War's events as philosophy, not as wrongs to avenge. The editor calls the speech typical of Lincoln's common sense and lofty standard.
the-parasite:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this tale of mesmerism in 1894, in the years of his Holmes fame. Its theme is the theft of a man's will by the mind of a strong foe. Doyle had read much on hypnotism, the hot theme of the late Victorian years.

A young man of science scoffs at the claim that minds can rule minds at a range. A woman with the gift then takes his will in hand and bends his life to her ends. The tale is the most grim of its age on the dread of lost self rule.
the-parisians-complete:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton wrote the novel The Parisians. A prefatory note by the author's son opens the record. He explains that The Parisians and Kenelm Chillingly began about the same time, from one central idea first expressed in The Coming Race. The three books form a special group apart from Bulwer-Lytton's other works, warning against popular social and political theories.

The son contrasts the two novels. Chillingly is a romance about one character; The Parisians is a novel about a whole community. Its real hero is Parisian society itself, drawn in a wide, crowded canvas with no single figure given pride of place. The same note opens the Volume 1 record.
the-people-for-whom-shakespeare-wrote:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The People for Whom Shakespeare Wrote. He opens with the death of Queen Elizabeth on March 24, 1603, and Sir Robert Cary's unsent ride to tell King James of Scotland, which earned Cary a barony. On his way south the king scattered knighthoods freely, making twenty-eight at Theobald's alone.

Warner sketches the age through Sir Richard Baker's Chronicle. Baker, born in 1568, wrote of James's reign, when tilting and the Yeomen of the Guard lost their luster. He praised Bacon, Camden, and John Donne among the learned men of the time. The essay rebuilds the audience and the world that Shakespeare's plays first played to.
the-perfect-tribute:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews published The Perfect Tribute in 1908. The story opens on November 18, 1863, as a special train leaves Washington for Gettysburg. Judges, cabinet members, and the general-in-chief ride with the Marine Band, and among them towers Abraham Lincoln, sad, preoccupied, and awkward, journeying to consecrate the national cemetery the next day.

Lincoln's mind is low and unhopeful. A speech is expected of him before thousands, and he doubts himself beside Edward Everett, the finished orator of the day, who rides in the same car. Andrews builds her famous tale on the President's melancholy journey and the address he fears will fail. The tribute of her title is paid the next day.
the-pirate:
Captain Frederick Marryat's The Pirate begins in the Bay of Biscay in the latter part of June, in a year in the seventeen nineties. A gale is dying down. At the centre of a vast circle of water floats one object: the hull of a vessel, dismasted and waterlogged. It rises only now and then above the waves. Marryat pauses to reflect on how many ships have been abandoned through ignorance or fear.

The ship is the Circassian, homeward from New Orleans with a cargo mostly of cotton. Her crew left her five days earlier in two boats. One boat swamped with all hands. Life still remains aboard. In the caboose, the cooking house on deck, sit three survivors: a man, a woman, and a child. The woman nurses a pale European infant at her breast while spray washes over them, too spent to speak.
the-pit-prop-syndicate: Freeman Wills Crofts's The Pit Prop Syndicate appears here through its contents alone. Only the chapter list is present, so the mystery itself does not appear. Part One, The Amateurs, opens at a sawmill on the Lesque. It follows a cruise, visits of a vessel named the Girondin, a depot at Ferriby, and a second cargo. It ends with Merriman desperate and gaining an unexpected ally. Part Two, The Professionals, begins with a chapter headed Murder! and brings in Inspector Willis, working toward the secret of the syndicate.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes is shown here through opening contents covering the first sections of the collected poems. Here only the contents list appears, so the poems themselves are absent. After a short address to readers, earlier poems of 1830 to 1836 are listed. Among them are Old Ironsides, The Last Leaf, The Cambridge Churchyard, and Poetry: A Metrical Essay. Additional poems, 1837 to 1848, name Lexington and a song for the Boston dinner given to Charles Dickens on February 1, 1842. After-dinner verses appear too.
the-pomp-of-the-lavilettes-complete:
Gilbert Parker's The Pomp of the Lavilettes is introduced by the author's own account of the book's odd history. It is the only book of his he ever sold outright. In 1896 Mr. Lamson, of the Boston publishers Lamson and Wolffe, came to Atlantic City and bought the English, American, and colonial rights. Parker says he always felt he could get the book back one day. He doubted it would ever make a phenomenal sale.

The story, set in 1837, brings a ne'er-do-well of the overseas aristocracy into a secluded French-Canadian society. That invasion gave the book its hold on him. So did the collision between French feeling and the British executive's prejudices in Quebec. Parker calls it a short advance scout for The Right of Way. He vouches for its pictures of French life in Canada as faithful and closely observed.
the-red-lily-complete:
A biographical preface introduces Anatole France before the novel begins. France was born Jacques-Anatole Thibault in Paris. His birth date was April 16, 1844. His father kept a bookshop on the Quai Malaquais. The College Stanislas educated the boy. The preface traces his early verse of 1873 and 1876. It places him among the Parnassian poets.

The preface also lists his journalism in many reviews. It names his post as librarian to the Senate. It notes his election to the French Academy in 1896. Novels named include Thais and the present work of 1894. The Academy crowned that work. Readers thus meet the author first. Separate volume records in the set carry only edition headers. This fuller record adds the critical preface instead.
the-right-of-way-complete: Gilbert Parker arranges his Canadian novel in six volumes. One combined listing covers them all here. Charley passes through a trial and a verdict first. Five years go by in the headings. A woman in heliotrope appears. Rosalie arrives, and a tailor makes a midnight foray. A stolen cross and signs from heaven follow. Women who saw and women who kept silent close the list. Only the heading is present here. The opening volumes of the combined list appear with it. Separate volume records carry the same contents in parts.
the-sea-kings-of-crete: The Rev. James Baikie, F.R.A.S., wrote The Sea-Kings of Crete. Adam and Charles Black published the second edition at London in 1913. Thirty-two full-page illustrations from photographs are promised. Baikie dedicated the book to his sisters and brothers. The portion shown gives title matter and the start of the contents only. The first chapter treats the legends, and the second the Homeric civilization. Schliemann and his work come third. Two chapters on the palace of broad Knossos follow.
the-seaboard-parish-complete:
George MacDonald, LL.D., wrote The Seaboard Parish. The record is labeled complete, yet the pages shown are headed Volume I. Its contents are expressly the contents of volume one. Chapters include Constance's birthday, a sick chamber, and two Sunday evenings. Theodora's doom and Connie's dream also appear. The list ends with the narrator's first sermon in the seaboard parish.

Chapter one, called Homiletic, opens as a letter to dear friends. The narrator admits he begins a new book like an old sermon. A lifetime of preaching shapes whatever he says or writes, he says. He thought he had bidden his readers farewell, he adds. Now he sits again at his writing-table for them. He imagines his whispered words heard aloud by multitudes he cannot see.
the-seats-of-the-mighty-complete: Gilbert Parker's The Seats of the Mighty bills itself as the memoirs of Captain Robert Moray. He served in the Virginia Regiment and afterwards in Amherst's Regiment. Parker dedicated the book to the memory of Madge Henley. The pages shown give the dedication and a full contents list only. No chapter text follows. Thirty chapters run from an escort to the citadel through a chamber of torture. Wolfe at Montmorenci and a secret of the tapestry come late. An appendix excerpt from The Scot in New France is also listed.
the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-entert:
George Meredith called The Shaving of Shagpat an Arabian entertainment. The dates 1898 and 1909 both appear on its front matter. A long contents list promises many tales within the tale. The Story of Bhanavar the Beautiful comes early. The Genie Karaz, the Well of Paravid, and the Talking Hawk follow. The Lily of the Enchanted Sea and the Palace of Aklis also appear. The flashes of the blade precede the conclusion.

Book one opens with The Thwackings. It was ordained, Meredith writes, that Shibli Bagarag should shave Shagpat. Shibli was nephew to Baba Mustapha, chief barber to the Court of Persia. Shagpat was the son of Shimpoor, of a line of clothiers. They had followed that trade for generations, Meredith adds, even to the illustrious Shagpat himself.
the-sisters-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Sisters is presented here as a complete volume, translated from the German by Clara Bell. Ebers dedicated it to Herr Eduard von Hallberger. The dedication closes twenty years of warm, unbroken friendship, he writes. Four of his works first saw the light under Hallberger's care. This fifth book was partly written in Hallberger's beautiful home at Tutzing. Sibling volume records share this same dedication and preface.

The preface explains the novel's seed. Fragments of the Royal Archives of Memphis survived by a marvellous combination of circumstances, Ebers says. They hold petitions in Greek, written for two twin sisters. The sisters served Serapis as pourers out of the libations. Such documents have great value for the history of manners, he argues. They show the monastic idea striking root in a heathen temple.
the-story-of-my-life-complete: Georg Ebers's autobiography, from childhood to manhood, appears in Mary J. Safford's translation from the German, in a complete edition also divided into separate volumes. Only the dedicatory poem To My Sons is present here. Ebers imagines the ivy on his grave. He asks his sons to look back over his struggles toward the light. They should learn from his errors. They should follow the twofold light that guided him. The narrative itself does not appear.
the-stowmarket-mystery-or-a-legacy-of-ha: Louis Tracy published this mystery, subtitled a legacy of hate, in 1904. Only the title page and contents appear in this record. The contents list twenty-seven chapters. They begin with the Stowmarket mystery itself and David Hume's story. A dream and a library window follow. A ko-katana and a black museum come next. A Mr. Okasaki appears. What the stationmaster saw, Margaret's secret, and Holden's story close the heads. The mystery itself does not appear.
the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-complete:
Ernest A. Vizetelly's preface introduces Paris, the closing novel of Émile Zola's Three Cities trilogy, in this complete edition. He explains that Abbé Pierre Froment, the doubting priest who found no faith at Lourdes and no hope at Rome, here reaches his logical conclusion. The trilogy, Vizetelly says, is essentially symbolical. Froment stands for Man, caught between the Roman Catholic Church on one side and Reason and Life on the other, with victory going to the latter.

Vizetelly defends Zola's case as applied to France, where he claims Catholicism is fast crumbling despite advertised revivals. The policy of Leo XIII, he argues, came too late for French masses who see a religion of death. Readers get the whole trilogy's meaning stated plainly before the Paris story opens.
the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-complete: Émile Zola's Rome, second novel of the Three Cities trilogy, is given here in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation as a complete edition whose opening leaves are a detailed table of contents. That table maps four parts. It begins with Froment's first impressions and his book on a rejuvenated Christianity. Then come the Boccanera family, cardinals of the Church, Romans of new Italy, the Vatican, Leo XIII, and the temporal power. No chapter text follows, so the contents serve as an itinerary of Zola's Roman inquiry without its scenes.
the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-well-k:
George Meredith's Tragic Comedians, a study in a well-known story, dated 1892, opens by defending the word 'fantastical.' Nature herself pushes forth fantastically wherever she drinks her fill of sunlight. Human nature, a wandering ship with a drunken pilot, a mutinous crew, and an angry captain, fits the word as completely as a skull-cap fits a stormy infant. Meredith bids readers accept the fantastical in us as worthy of study.

His pair of tragic comedians belong to history, and their last chapter is written in red blood. The man was a leader of a host, hope of a party, who fell in his prime through love; the woman laid her hand in the slayer's. Meredith, inventing nothing, studies the real passion of Ferdinand Lassalle and Helene von Dönniges as a problem of spirit and flesh.
the-trail-of-the-sword-complete: Gilbert Parker's Trail of the Sword is presented in this complete record as a double contents list, printed twice over, with no chapter text. The novel is built in four epochs. They run from An Envoy Extraordinary and The Kidnapping through Friends in Council and Out of the Net. A treasure house, a captive's gift, and a brother's blood crying from the ground come later. The final epoch ends with the sword sheathed. Parker's Canadian romance of Iberville and Jessica Leveret is outlined here, but no scene appears.
the-translation-of-a-savage-complete:
Gilbert Parker's introduction to The Translation of a Savage, in this complete edition, recalls writing it in the early autumn of 1893 at Hampstead Heath. Hampstead, scarcely invaded by lodging-house keepers, kept its literary and artistic character, and Parker saw more people carrying books there than anywhere else in England. Perched above London, he looked toward the Atlantic and wrote the novel in one concentrated, ceaseless effort. The Daily Chronicle's phrase for his work, a tour de force, fits this book too, he says.

The genre compelled him to finish in one continuous impulse, so his letters arrived only once a week and no friend knew where he was. The fifteen chapters that follow carry an Indigenous bride, Lali, from the Canadian North into an English country family. Parker's account of the writing frames a story made at white heat.
the-trespasser-complete:
Gilbert Parker's introduction to The Trespasser, in this complete edition, tells how the novel was commissioned while he studied French Canada in the winter of 1892. A letter from his London publisher, Arrowsmith, asked for a novel of fifty or sixty thousand words for his Annual. Hugh Conway's Called Back and Anthony Hope's Prisoner of Zenda had appeared in that Annual. Parker cabled acceptance. The summer of 1893 found him at Audierne in Brittany with artist friends.

Most of the book was written outdoors, in a walled garden on a hillside. The rest was written in a tower-like, all-windowed room used when it rained. Coffee was served at half past six. Peaches and figs grew on the walls around his outdoor workshop. The eighteen chapters that follow carry Gaston, one in search of a kingdom, between two worlds, through heritage, conquest, and an intolerable love.
the-wandering-jew-complete:
Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew is prefaced in this complete edition by a note on the author, who lived from 1804 to 1857. Sue trained as a physician and surgeon, then spent six years in the French Navy. Inheriting his father's estate in 1830 freed him to write, and his first novel succeeded beyond expectation.

The note traces his rise through sea stories and fictionised fact to national fame with The Mysteries of Paris. The Wandering Jew brought worldwide renown, but exile followed Louis Napoleon's coup, and Sue died in banishment five years later. Contents for book one list a prologue at the lands end of the world, then Morok, Dagobert, Rose and Blanche, and extracts from General Simon's diary.
the-woman-in-white:
Wilkie Collins built The Woman in White as a story told by many voices in three epochs. Drawing teacher Walter Hartright begins the account. Solicitor Vincent Gilmore and Marian Halcombe continue it. Later sections come from a housekeeper, a doctor, and even a tombstone. Count Fosco's narrative appears near the end. Hartright concludes the whole.

Hartright opens with a bold claim about women's patience and men's resolution. He argues that courts alone cannot uncover every suspicious case. Money, he hints, too often oils the machinery of the law. So witnesses must tell the story themselves. Readers get one of the great Victorian sensation novels, unfolding piece by piece.
the-works-of-john-greenleaf-whittier-com:
A publishers' advertisement introduces volume one of The Complete Works of John Greenleaf Whittier. The Standard Library Edition rearranged his poems and prose. Whittier himself revised the texts, or approved the revisions. He added head-notes explaining the subjects and occasions of poems. Dates of first publication are given throughout. Those dates, the publishers note, mark when pieces were written.

Early poems Whittier had discarded were restored by request. They stand in an appendix in order of appearance. The edition aims to be complete and retrospective. Students of the poet's career, the publishers promise, will find abundant material. Volume one gathers his narrative and legendary poems.
the-world-english-bible-web-complete:
A complete World English Bible in one record begins, as the Bible itself does, with Genesis. Creation opens the text: God creates the heavens and the earth. The earth sits formless, empty, and dark. God's Spirit hovers over the waters. Then light is spoken into being. God divides light from darkness and names them Day and Night.

Footnotes explain Hebrew details, such as a grammatical marker after the word God. Verse numbers keep every line easy to cite. Because the whole Bible sits in one record, readers can move from Genesis to Revelation without switching files. The opening chapters set the pattern of numbered verses used throughout.
the-world-for-sale-complete: Gilbert Parker's The World for Sale is shown here through a full contents list and the start of an introduction. Three books divide the novel into twenty-seven chapters. Ingolby and two rival towns anchor the early chapters. Jethro Fawe's arrival promises trouble. Later titles mention a sultan, a bridge keeper, and a sleeper. The introduction begins by calling the book a tale of the primitive and lonely West. The introduction breaks off soon after that opening line.
the-yosemite: John Muir's The Yosemite is shown here through its dedication, acknowledgments, and contents list. Muir dedicates the book to Robert Underwood Johnson, the park's originator. He thanks Professor Whitney and Dr. Bunnell for Yosemite history material. Sixteen chapters cover the valley's storms, trees, birds, and glaciers. Galen Clark and Hetch Hetchy Valley get chapters. Appendices promise park legislation and a table of distances. The chapters themselves start beyond the pages present.
the-young-lady-s-mentor-a-guide-to-the-f: The Young Lady's Mentor, published in Philadelphia in 1852, offers guidance through letters to unknown friends. Its author signs herself only as a Lady. A contents list maps the character lessons. Contentment, temper, and truthfulness come first. Envy, selfishness, and self-control follow. Economy and cultivation of the mind also appear. Amusements and women's influence on society close the list. The letters themselves do not appear in the pages present.
their-silver-wedding-journey-complete:
William Dean Howells wrote the novel that opens here in its complete form, drawn from the 1899 edition in three volumes. Editor Basil March faces pressure from his business partner Fulkerson to take a long rest. His wife, his doctor, and his overdue sabbatical year all point the same way.

Fulkerson promises the magazine will manage without him and urges him to book passage at once. March resists calling the trip a pleasure unless duty requires it. Readers get a comic, observant story about marriage, work, and travel, told through talk between colleagues who know each other well.
thomas-wingfold-curate:
George MacDonald, LL.D., published Thomas Wingfold, Curate in three volumes, and volume one opens with Helen Lingard. A swift grey November wind roars through every chimney like organ pipes. Helen has spent the day writing to her brother Leopold at Cambridge and missed her walk.

MacDonald insists her good health and sensible nature do not make her unfeeling. Weather lifts or lowers her spirits, and a new dress pleases her. She turns from the stormy garden toward her fireside. Readers should note this opening matches the separate volume-one record exactly; both present the same first chapter.
tom-swift-and-his-electric-locomotive-or: Two Miles a Minute on the Rails is the promise in the Tom Swift electric locomotive story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. A tempting offer opens the story, trouble starts, and a contract is signed by chapter six. Barbed wire entanglements, an enemy in the dark, and a missing Koku follow. Chapter one begins by quoting the offer of a locomotive able to run two miles a minute, then stops. The contents and that fragment are what is present here.
trinity-site:
The U.S. Department of Energy's Trinity Site booklet, issued through the National Atomic Museum at Albuquerque, explains the first atomic test. Its contents cover the test itself, the Jumbo vessel, and the Schmidt-McDonald ranch house. A bibliography and museum notes close the booklet.

On Monday morning, July 16, 1945, the Manhattan Engineer District tested the bomb in the New Mexico desert, under the code name Trinity. The site lay on the Alamogordo Bombing and Gunnery Range, about 230 miles south of Los Alamos. Ranchers had left the grazing land in 1942, and a remote corner was set aside for the project in September 1944. Eight candidate sites were weighed before this one won.
vandover-and-the-brute:
Frank Norris's Vandover and the Brute, issued in 1914, opens inside its hero's faulty memory. Vandover wonders that he can recall so little of his past in order. What he took for the story of his life proves, on closer look, to be a few stray scenes. Memory kept them with no regard for their weight. A great sorrow may sit beside a trifle, each as sharp as the other.

One scene always returns. He is about eight years old, on his family's move from Boston to San Francisco. At a depot in western New York, on a hot day, men lift his mother from the train with great care. She lies back on pillows in a long steamer chair, plainly an invalid. Norris starts a tale of slow decline with that tender, troubled picture. A sick mother, and a child watching: the scene holds both.
vittoria-complete: George Meredith wrote Vittoria, a novel of Italy in revolt. The pages here give its contents only, so the story itself is not shown. The list is arranged in books. Book one climbs Monte Motterone and names Signorina Vittoria. A spy, a warning, and a letter follow. Later books move to Verona, to the maestro's door, and to the opera of Camilla. A duel in a mountain pass comes later still. Book six turns to episodes of the revolt and the war, with tobacco riots.
viviette: William J. Locke wrote Viviette, published in 1916. Pages present here hold the title page, a contents list of six chapters, a list of pictures, and the first two lines of chapter one, so the story itself is barely begun. Contents name the brothers, the conspirators, Katherine, a pair of famous duelling pistols, a crisis, and Viviette taking a risk. Chapter one opens with Viviette telling Dick he ought to go about in skins like a primitive man, while Katherine Holroyd looks up from her needlework.
voices-for-the-speechless-selections-for:
Abraham Firth, secretary of the American Humane Association, chose the pieces in Voices for the Speechless in 1883. The book holds selections for schools and private reading. Lines of Longfellow and Cowper on the title page plead the cause of dumb mouths that have no speech. The pieces aim to stand between an animal and woe, and to teach pity for beasts that serve man.

A section of moral lessons opens the matter here. Firth asks readers to study the moral in brutes. The ox stands as an emblem of patient, plodding service. The horse and the dog show a loyalty no human devotion has surpassed. He tells of an Arab horse that found its bound master in the dark. It seized his girdle in its teeth, ran all night to bring him home, and then fell dead from the effort. Such tales carry the book's humane plea.
wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-conspirac:
John Richardson's Wacousta, or The Prophecy, turns on Pontiac's war against the British posts, after France ceded Canada to England. Its preface lays out the chief's plan. Pontiac bound the tribes in one federation, to wipe out nine western posts. He would invest one fort at a time and cut it off from all help. He would offer terms of surrender, and break them once the gates opened. Seven posts fell by that trust, the preface says.

Only Detroit and Michilimackinac still held out. All the chief's craft turned toward taking them. A record labeled complete carries this same preface, yet its pages head themselves volume one of three. That is the same opening as the separate first-volume record. Richardson, a soldier who knew the frontier, built his tale on that siege: a garrison, a prophecy, and an enemy whose mercy was a trap.
waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-comple:
A publishers' note fronts this copy of Sir Walter Scott's Waverley, the first of the Caledonian series. That series holds fifty books, with all of Scott's works. The publishers call an ideal edition of Scott a long-held ambition. They quote Hazlitt's judgment that his works are almost a new edition of human nature. Later generations, they trust, will prize them still more highly than his own did.

Such an edition, they argue, must join fine typography, the best text to be had, and fine pictures. The pictures must please in themselves, and add to the reader's pleasure and grasp of the book. The same note, word for word, fronts the separate volume-one record of this set. This record, though named complete, heads its pages Volume I. The tale itself follows: Edward Waverley's passage from an English barracks into the Jacobite rising of 1745, among Highland chiefs and Hanoverian officers.
what-s-mine-s-mine-complete:
George MacDonald wrote What's Mine's Mine, a Highland novel in three volumes. This record, though named as the complete set, shows the same first volume opening as the separate volume one record. Its contents list is for volume one only. Chapter one begins in a rich London dining room that the narrator finds grand yet dull.

Every chair and sideboard in the room follows class custom, not true choice. A big fire blazes in the grate. From this city start, the contents point toward hills, a lake, wolves, and a clan Christmas. MacDonald sets wealth and fashion against wild Highland life. The clash of those worlds drives the tale.
what-will-he-do-with-it-complete:
Lord Lytton, writing as Pisistratus Caxton, wrote What Will He Do With It? This record is named as the complete work, yet its opening matches the separate volume one record: volume one, book one, chapter one. The tale starts at a summer fair in a pretty Surrey village. Booths line the street with toys, ribbons, crockery, and gilded gingerbread.

On the green stand shows with a mermaid, a giant, and a calf with two heads. A stage promises a grand play of a cruel baron and a bandit's child. Music from drums, fifes, and a hand organ fills the air. Lytton opens a long tale of Lionel Haughton and Guy Darrell in this fair-day crowd.
wild-youth-complete:
Gilbert Parker wrote Wild Youth, a Canadian tale in two volumes. This record, named as the complete work, lists all eighteen chapters and opens the tale. Askatoon, Parker says, had more character than any other western town. Its people were bright by nature, and the town slept with one eye open.

The Mazarine family takes possession in chapter one, and a girl named Louise enters next. Orlando has an adventure, and the list names a warning, cross trails, and youth having its way. This record shares its opening chapter with the separate volume one record. Parker sets young love against a stern prairie town and an older man's claim.
woman-in-white: Wilkie Collins wrote this famous sensation novel, first published in 1859. Pages present here hold a contents list for a modern edition, naming a preface from 1860 and a revised preface from 1861. The list shows the story told in epochs, starting with drawing teacher Walter Hartright. His opening section runs to eleven numbered parts. No story text itself appears in these pages, so the mystery plot stays undescribed here.
works-of-john-bunyan-complete:
George Offor edited this gathering of John Bunyan's writings, with notes and a life sketch. Pages present here head the volume as Volume First, covering experimental, doctrinal, and practical works, even though the record is named as the complete works. That heading clash is stated plainly here. The memoir opens by stressing Bunyan's poor birth. He worked as a brazier, soldiered, then married a religious wife.

Offor frames Bunyan's rise as proof of grace working through lowly vessels. Bible verses open the memoir in support. Readers get sermons, treatises, and spiritual autobiography from a famed Puritan preacher. The edition aims at study as much as devotion.
yvette:
Guy de Maupassant wrote this tale of Paris night life. Chapter one opens outside the Cafe Riche near eleven at night. Jean de Servigny urges his friend Leon Saval to walk rather than take a cab. Crowds flow along the boulevard, drinking and chatting in summer ease. Cafes spill light over sidewalk tables and bottles. The two friends stroll in evening dress, flowers in their buttonholes, after dining well.

The contents promise Saval's initiation, love at Bougival, and a turn from emotion to philosophy. A young man's education in pleasure drives the tale. Readers get glittering surfaces with hard knowledge underneath, in Maupassant's manner.
zadig-or-the-book-of-fate: Voltaire wrote this oriental tale, shown here in an English rendering printed in London in 1749. Pages present here hold the title page and the start of a dedication to the Sultana Sheraa, signed by Sadi. The title page calls the work an oriental history and prints a Latin motto from Virgil about following fate. Zadig's adventures themselves do not begin in these pages. The dedication breaks off just as it starts.
zibeline-complete:
Philippe de Massa wrote this French romance, rendered into English by D. Knowlton Ranous. An introduction by Jules Claretie praised the tale, which won a French Academy crown in 1892. The opening life sketch traces Massa's cavalry career and stage successes. His heroine, Valentine de Vermont, inherits a fur fortune built on a gambling win. She heads to Paris to spend it and to repay the man her father ruined.

Envious Paris ladies nickname her Zibeline, after a rare wild animal. Her wealth, boldness, and generosity set Paris buzzing. The ruined man, a war hero, gains back his fortune and her heart. Readers get a light society romance.
zicci-a-tale-complete:
No author's name is printed in the pages present here for this tale. Book one opens in gardens at Naples on a summer evening. Young Englishman Glyndon suddenly turns pale and trembles among his friends. A grave stranger of about thirty claims to understand the shudder. He describes a cold awe that creeps over people sitting alone at night. Hair bristles, blood curdles, and something unearthly seems near, he says.

The stranger insists he knows the signs of that visitation well. Glyndon's surprise only deepens the mystery. An occult tale of fate and a commanding adept unfolds from this meeting. Readers get atmosphere first and answers later, by design.
zola-three-cities-complete:
Vizetelly translated Zola's Three Cities whole: Lourdes, Rome, and Paris. The first novel opens on a train packed with pilgrims and patients in third class. They chant the Ave maris Stella as the train leaves the Orleans terminus at dawn.

Marie, feverish on her couch of pain, cries out with joy at the city walls. Her father and Abbe Pierre Froment watch her with fond worry. The ride to Lourdes will take more than twenty-two hours, until past three next morning. Froment, a priest losing his faith, seeks truth in each city in turn, and the set forms Zola's plea for reason and justice.
